Manganese forms a variety of oxides: [MnO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese(II)_oxide "Manganese(II) oxide"), [Mn 3 O 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese(II,III)_oxide "Manganese(II,III) oxide"), [Mn 2 O 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese(III)_oxide "Manganese(III) oxide"), [MnO 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese_dioxide "Manganese dioxide"), MnO 3 and [Mn 2 O 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese_heptoxide "Manganese heptoxide"). Manganese(II) oxide is an inorganic compound that forms green crystals. Like many monoxides, MnO adopts the [rock salt structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubic_crystal_system#Rock-salt_structure "Cubic crystal system"), where cations and anions are both octahedrally coordinated. Also like many oxides, manganese(II) oxide is often [nonstoichiometric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonstoichiometric "Nonstoichiometric"): its composition can vary from MnO to MnO 1.045.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-G&W-6) Manganese(II,III) oxide is formed when any manganese oxide is heated in air above 1000°C.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-G&W-6) Considerable research has centred on producing nanocrystalline Mn 3 O 4 and various syntheses that involve oxidation of Mn II or reduction of Mn VI.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-9) Manganese(III) oxide is unlike many other transition metal oxides in that it does not adopt the [corundum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corundum "Corundum") ([Al 2 O 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium_oxide "Aluminium oxide")) structure.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-G&W-6) Two forms are generally recognized, α-Mn 2 O 3 and γ-Mn 2 O 3,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-Wells-10) although a high pressure form with the CaIrO 3 structure has been reported too.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-11) Manganese(IV) oxide is a blackish or brown solid occurs naturally as the mineral [pyrolusite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrolusite "Pyrolusite"), which is the main ore of manganese and a component of [manganese nodules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese_nodule "Manganese nodule"). The principal use for MnO 2 is for dry-cell [batteries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battery_(electricity) "Battery (electricity)"), such as the [alkaline battery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkaline_battery "Alkaline battery") and the [zinc–carbon battery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zinc%E2%80%93carbon_battery "Zinc–carbon battery").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-G&W-6) Manganese(VII) oxide is dark green in its [crystalline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystalline "Crystalline") form. The liquid is green by reflected light and red by transmitted light.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-brauer-12) It is soluble in [carbon tetrachloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_tetrachloride "Carbon tetrachloride"), and decomposes when in contact with water.

#### Technetium

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_7_element&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Technetium")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Technetium%28IV%29_oxide.png/250px-Technetium%28IV%29_oxide.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Technetium(IV)_oxide.png)

Technetium(IV) oxide

Technetium's main oxides are [technetium(IV) oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technetium(IV)_oxide "Technetium(IV) oxide") and [technetium(VII) oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technetium(VII)_oxide "Technetium(VII) oxide"). Technetium(IV) oxide was first produced in 1949 by electrolyzing a solution of [ammonium pertechnetate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammonium_pertechnetate "Ammonium pertechnetate") under [ammonium hydroxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammonium_hydroxide "Ammonium hydroxide"). It has often been used to separate technetium from [molybdenum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molybdenum "Molybdenum") and rhenium.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-tc-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-radio-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-electro-15) More efficient ways are the reduction of ammonium pertechnetate by [zinc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zinc "Zinc") metal and [hydrochloric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrochloric_acid "Hydrochloric acid"), [stannous chloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stannous_chloride "Stannous chloride"), [hydrazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrazine "Hydrazine"), [hydroxylamine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydroxylamine "Hydroxylamine"), [ascorbic acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascorbic_acid "Ascorbic acid"),[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-radio-14) by the hydrolysis of [potassium hexachlorotechnetate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potassium_hexachlorotechnetate?action=edit&redlink=1 "Potassium hexachlorotechnetate (page does not exist)")[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-magnet-16) or by the decomposition of ammonium pertechnetate at 700°C under an inert atmosphere.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-tc-13)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-img-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-at-18) It reacts with oxygen to produce technetium(VII) oxide at 450°C.

Technetium(VII) oxide can be prepared directly by the oxidation of technetium at 450-500°C.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-19) It is a rare example of a molecular binary metal oxide. Other examples are [ruthenium(VIII) oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruthenium(VIII)_oxide "Ruthenium(VIII) oxide") and [osmium(VIII) oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osmium(VIII)_oxide "Osmium(VIII) oxide"). It adopts a [centrosymmetric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centrosymmetric "Centrosymmetric") corner-shared bi-tetrahedral structure in which the terminal and bridging Tc−O bonds are 167pm and 184 pm respectively and the Tc−O−Tc angle is 180°.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-20)

#### Rhenium

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_7_element&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Rhenium")]

Rhenium's main oxides are [rhenium(IV) oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhenium(IV)_oxide "Rhenium(IV) oxide") and [rhenium(VII) oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhenium(VII)_oxide "Rhenium(VII) oxide"). Rhenium(IV) oxide is a gray to black crystalline solid that can be formed by [comproportionation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comproportionation "Comproportionation").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-21) At high temperatures it undergoes [disproportionation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disproportionation "Disproportionation"). It is a laboratory reagent that can be used as a [catalyst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalyst "Catalyst"). It adopts the [rutile structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rutile_structure "Rutile structure"). It forms [perrhenates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perrhenate "Perrhenate") with alkaline [hydrogen peroxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_peroxide "Hydrogen peroxide") and [oxidizing acids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxidizing_acid "Oxidizing acid").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-22) In molten sodium hydroxide it forms sodium rhenate:[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-23)

2 NaOH + ReO 2 → Na 2 ReO 3 + H 2 O
Rhenium(VII) oxide can be formed when rhenium or its oxides or sulfides are oxidized a 500-700°C in air.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-Schmidt-24) It dissolves in water to give [perrhenic acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perrhenic_acid "Perrhenic acid"). Heating Re 2 O 7 gives rhenium(IV) oxide, signalled by the appearance of the dark blue coloration.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-Brauer-25) In its solid form, Re 2 O 7 consists of alternating octahedral and tetrahedral Re centres. It is the raw material for all rhenium compounds, being the volatile fraction obtained upon roasting the host ore.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-26)

Rhenium, in addition to the +4 and +7 oxidation states, also forms a [trioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhenium_trioxide "Rhenium trioxide"). It can be formed by reducing rhenium(VII) oxide with [carbon monoxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_monoxide "Carbon monoxide") at 200 C or elemental rhenium at 4000 C.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-27) It can also be reduced with [dioxane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dioxane "Dioxane").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-Glemser-28) It is a red solid with a metallic lustre that resembles [copper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copper "Copper") in appearance, and is the only stable [trioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trioxide "Trioxide") of the group 7 elements.

### Halides

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_7_element&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Halides")]

#### Manganese

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_7_element&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Manganese")]

Manganese can form compounds in the +2, +3 and +4 oxidation states. The manganese(II) compounds are often light pink solids. Like some other metal difluorides, MnF 2 crystallizes in the [rutile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rutile "Rutile") structure, which features octahedral Mn centers.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-29) and it is used in the manufacture of special kinds of [glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass "Glass") and [lasers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laser "Laser").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-30) Scacchite is the natural, anhydrous form of manganese(II) chloride.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-31) The only other currently known mineral systematized as manganese chloride is kempite - a representative of the atacamite group, a group of hydroxide-chlorides.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-32) It can be used in place of [palladium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palladium "Palladium") in the [Stille reaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stille_reaction "Stille reaction"), which couples two carbon atoms using an [organotin compound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organotin_compound "Organotin compound").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-Mn(II)_halide-33) It can be used as a pink pigment or as a source of the manganese ion or iodide ion. It is often used in the lighting industry.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-Mn(II)_halide-33)

#### Technetium

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_7_element&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Technetium")]

The following binary (containing only two elements) technetium halides are known: [TcF 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TcF6 "TcF6"), TcF 5, [TcCl 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TcCl4 "TcCl4"), TcBr 4, TcBr 3, α-TcCl 3, β-TcCl 3, TcI 3, α-TcCl 2, and β-TcCl 2. The [oxidation states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxidation_state "Oxidation state") range from Tc(VI) to Tc(II). Technetium halides exhibit different structure types, such as molecular octahedral complexes, extended chains, layered sheets, and metal clusters arranged in a three-dimensional network.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-AS-35) These compounds are produced by combining the metal and halogen or by less direct reactions.

TcCl 4 is obtained by chlorination of Tc metal or Tc 2 O 7 Upon heating, TcCl 4 gives the corresponding Tc(III) and Tc(II) chlorides.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-AS-35)

TcCl 4 → α-TcCl 3 + 1/2 Cl 2 TcCl 3 → β-TcCl 2 + 1/2 Cl 2
The structure of TcCl 4 is composed of infinite zigzag chains of edge-sharing TcCl 6 octahedra. It is isomorphous to transition metal tetrachlorides of [zirconium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zirconium "Zirconium"), [hafnium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hafnium "Hafnium"), and [platinum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platinum "Platinum").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-AS-35)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/de/Chloro-containing_coordination_complexes_of_technetium_%28Tc-99%29.jpg/250px-Chloro-containing_coordination_complexes_of_technetium_%28Tc-99%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Chloro-containing_coordination_complexes_of_technetium_(Tc-99).jpg)

Chloro-containing coordination complexes of technetium (Tc-99) in various oxidation states: Tc(III), Tc(IV), Tc(V), and Tc(VI) represented.

Two polymorphs of [technetium trichloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technetium_trichloride "Technetium trichloride") exist, α- and β-TcCl 3. The α polymorph is also denoted as Tc 3 Cl 9. It adopts a confacial [bioctahedral structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octahedral_molecular_geometry#Bioctahedral_molecular_geometry "Octahedral molecular geometry").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-36) It is prepared by treating the chloro-acetate Tc 2(O 2 CCH 3)4 Cl 2 with HCl. Like [Re 3 Cl 9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trirhenium_nonachloride "Trirhenium nonachloride"), the structure of the α-polymorph consists of triangles with short M-M distances. β-TcCl 3 features octahedral Tc centers, which are organized in pairs, as seen also for [molybdenum trichloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molybdenum_trichloride "Molybdenum trichloride"). TcBr 3 does not adopt the structure of either trichloride phase. Instead it has the structure of [molybdenum tribromide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molybdenum_tribromide "Molybdenum tribromide"), consisting of chains of confacial octahedra with alternating short and long Tc—Tc contacts. TcI 3 has the same structure as the high temperature phase of [TiI 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titanium(III)_iodide "Titanium(III) iodide"), featuring chains of confacial octahedra with equal Tc—Tc contacts.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-AS-35)

Several anionic technetium halides are known. The binary tetrahalides can be converted to the hexahalides [TcX 6]2− (X = F, Cl, Br, I), which adopt [octahedral molecular geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octahedral_molecular_geometry "Octahedral molecular geometry").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-s8-37) More reduced halides form anionic clusters with Tc–Tc bonds. The situation is similar for the related elements of Mo, W, Re. These clusters have the nuclearity Tc 4, Tc 6, Tc 8, and Tc 13. The more stable Tc 6 and Tc 8 clusters have prism shapes where vertical pairs of Tc atoms are connected by triple bonds and the planar atoms by single bonds. Every technetium atom makes six bonds, and the remaining valence electrons can be saturated by one axial and two [bridging ligand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridging_ligand "Bridging ligand") halogen atoms such as [chlorine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chlorine "Chlorine") or [bromine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bromine "Bromine").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-38)

#### Rhenium

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_7_element&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Rhenium")]

The most common rhenium chlorides are [ReCl 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhenium_hexachloride "Rhenium hexachloride"), [ReCl 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhenium_pentachloride "Rhenium pentachloride"), [ReCl 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhenium_tetrachloride "Rhenium tetrachloride"), and [ReCl 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhenium_trichloride "Rhenium trichloride").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-G&W-6) The structures of these compounds often feature extensive Re-Re bonding, which is characteristic of this metal in oxidation states lower than VII. Salts of [Re 2 Cl 8]2− feature a [quadruple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadruple_bond "Quadruple bond") metal-metal bond. Although the highest rhenium chloride features Re(VI), fluorine gives the d 0 Re(VII) derivative [rhenium heptafluoride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhenium_heptafluoride "Rhenium heptafluoride"). Bromides and iodides of rhenium are also well known.

Like tungsten and molybdenum, with which it shares chemical similarities, rhenium forms a variety of [oxyhalides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxohalide "Oxohalide"). The oxychlorides are most common, and include ReOCl 4, ReOCl 3.

### Organometallic compounds

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_7_element&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Organometallic compounds")]

#### Manganese

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_7_element&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Manganese")]

Main article: [Organomanganese chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organomanganese_chemistry "Organomanganese chemistry")

Organomanganese compounds were first reported in 1937 by Gilman and Bailee who described the reaction of [phenyllithium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phenyllithium "Phenyllithium") and [manganese(II) iodide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese(II)_iodide "Manganese(II) iodide") to form phenylmanganese iodide (PhMnI) and diphenylmanganese (Ph 2 Mn).[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-Cahiez2009-39)

Following this precedent, other organomanganese halides can be obtained by alkylation of [manganese(II) chloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese(II)_chloride "Manganese(II) chloride"), [manganese(II) bromide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese(II)_bromide "Manganese(II) bromide"), and [manganese(II) iodide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese(II)_iodide "Manganese(II) iodide"). Manganese iodide is attractive because the anhydrous compound can be prepared in situ from manganese and [iodine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iodine "Iodine") in [ether](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diethyl_ether "Diethyl ether"). Typical alkylating agents are [organolithium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organolithium "Organolithium") or [organomagnesium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organomagnesium "Organomagnesium") compounds.

The chemistry of organometallic compounds of Mn(II) are unusual among the [transition metals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transition_metal "Transition metal") due to the high ionic character of the Mn(II)-C bond.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-40) The reactivity of organomanganese compounds can be compared to that of [organomagnesium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organomagnesium_chemistry "Organomagnesium chemistry") and [organozinc compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organozinc_compound "Organozinc compound"). The [electronegativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronegativity "Electronegativity") of Mn (1.55) is comparable to that of Mg (1.31) and Zn (1.65), making the carbon atom (EN = 2.55) [nucleophilic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nucleophilic "Nucleophilic"). The [reduction potential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reduction_potential "Reduction potential") of Mn is also intermediate between Mg and Zn.

#### Technetium

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_7_element&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Technetium")]

Main article: [Organotechnetium chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organotechnetium_chemistry "Organotechnetium chemistry")

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/25/Tc_CNCH2CMe2%28OMe%29_6Cation.png/250px-Tc_CNCH2CMe2%28OMe%29_6Cation.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tc_CNCH2CMe2(OMe)_6Cation.png)

[Technetium (99mTc) sestamibi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technetium_(99mTc)_sestamibi "Technetium (99mTc) sestamibi") ("Cardiolite") is widely used for imaging of the heart.

Technetium forms a variety of [coordination complexes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordination_complex "Coordination complex") with organic ligands. Many have been well-investigated because of their relevance to [nuclear medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_medicine "Nuclear medicine").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-41)

Technetium forms a variety of compounds with Tc–C bonds, i.e. organotechnetium complexes. Prominent members of this class are complexes with CO, arene, and cyclopentadienyl ligands.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-Alberto-42) The binary carbonyl Tc 2(CO)10 is a white volatile solid.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-43) In this molecule, two technetium atoms are bound to each other; each atom is surrounded by [octahedra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octahedron "Octahedron") of five carbonyl ligands. The bond length between technetium atoms, 303 pm,[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-45) is significantly larger than the distance between two atoms in metallic technetium (272 pm). Similar [carbonyls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbonyl "Carbonyl") are formed by technetium's [congeners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congener_(chemistry) "Congener (chemistry)"), manganese and rhenium.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwochau2000286,_328-46) Interest in organotechnetium compounds has also been motivated by applications in [nuclear medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_medicine "Nuclear medicine").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-Alberto-42) Unusual for other metal carbonyls, Tc forms aquo-carbonyl complexes, prominent being [Tc(CO)3(H 2 O)3]+.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-Alberto-42)

#### Rhenium

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_7_element&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Rhenium")]

Main article: [Organorhenium chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organorhenium_chemistry "Organorhenium chemistry")

[Dirhenium decacarbonyl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirhenium_decacarbonyl "Dirhenium decacarbonyl") is the most common entry to organorhenium chemistry. Its reduction with sodium [amalgam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amalgam_(chemistry) "Amalgam (chemistry)") gives Na[Re(CO)5] with rhenium in the formal oxidation state −1.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-47) Dirhenium decacarbonyl can be oxidised with [bromine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bromine "Bromine") to [bromopentacarbonylrhenium(I)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bromopentacarbonylrhenium(I) "Bromopentacarbonylrhenium(I)"):[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-48)

Re 2(CO)10 + Br 2 → 2 Re(CO)5 Br
Reduction of this pentacarbonyl with [zinc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zinc "Zinc") and [acetic acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acetic_acid "Acetic acid") gives [pentacarbonylhydridorhenium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentacarbonylhydridorhenium "Pentacarbonylhydridorhenium"):[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-Urb-49)

Re(CO)5 Br + Zn + HOAc → Re(CO)5 H + ZnBr(OAc)
[Methylrhenium trioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methylrhenium_trioxide "Methylrhenium trioxide") ("MTO"), CH 3 ReO 3 is a volatile, colourless solid has been used as a [catalyst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalyst "Catalyst") in some laboratory experiments. It can be prepared by many routes, a typical method is the reaction of Re 2 O 7 and [tetramethyltin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetramethyltin "Tetramethyltin"):

Re 2 O 7 + (CH 3)4 Sn → CH 3 ReO 3 + (CH 3)3 SnOReO 3
Analogous alkyl and aryl derivatives are known. MTO catalyses for the oxidations with [hydrogen peroxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_peroxide "Hydrogen peroxide"). Terminal [alkynes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkyne "Alkyne") yield the corresponding acid or ester, internal alkynes yield diketones, and [alkenes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkene "Alkene") give epoxides. MTO also catalyses the conversion of [aldehydes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aldehyde "Aldehyde") and [diazoalkanes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diazoalkane "Diazoalkane") into an alkene.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-50)

### Polyoxometalates

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_7_element&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Polyoxometalates")]

Main article: [Polyoxometalate §Polyoxotechnetates and rhenates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyoxometalate#Polyoxotechnetates_and_rhenates "Polyoxometalate")

The polyoxotechnetate (polyoxometalate of technetium) contains both Tc(V) and Tc(VII) in ratio 4: 16 and is obtained as the [hydronium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydronium "Hydronium") salt [H 7 O 3]4[Tc 20 O 68]·4H 2 O by concentrating an HTcO 4 solution.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-51) The first empirically isolated polyoxorhenate was the white [Re 4 O 15]2− and contained Re(VII) in both octahedral and tetrahedral coordination.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-52)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_7_element&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: History")]

### Manganese

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_7_element&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Manganese")]

Manganese dioxide, which is abundant in nature, has long been used as a pigment. The cave paintings in [Gargas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gargas,_Haute-Garonne "Gargas, Haute-Garonne") that are 30,000 to 24,000 years old are made from the mineral form of MnO 2 pigments.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-53) Manganese compounds were used by Egyptian and Roman glassmakers, either to add to, or remove, color from glass.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-54) Use as "glassmakers soap" continued through the [Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages") until modern times and is evident in 14th-century glass from [Venice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice "Venice").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-ItGlass-55)

### Technetium and rhenium

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_7_element&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Technetium and rhenium")]

Rhenium ([Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_language "Latin language"): _Rhenus_ meaning: "[Rhine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhine "Rhine")")[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-56) was the last-discovered of the elements that have a stable isotope (other new elements discovered in nature since then, such as [francium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francium "Francium"), are radioactive).[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-usgs-57) The existence of a yet-undiscovered element at this position in the [periodic table](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodic_table "Periodic table") had been first predicted by [Dmitri Mendeleev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dmitri_Mendeleev "Dmitri Mendeleev"). Other calculated information was obtained by [Henry Moseley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Moseley "Henry Moseley") in 1914.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-58) In 1908, [Japanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") chemist [Masataka Ogawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masataka_Ogawa "Masataka Ogawa") announced that he had discovered the 43rd element and named it _nipponium_ (Np) after [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") (_Nippon_ in Japanese). In fact, what he had was rhenium (element 75), not [technetium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technetium "Technetium").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-nipponium2022-60) The symbol Np was later used for the element [neptunium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neptunium "Neptunium"), and the name "nihonium", also [named after Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Names_of_Japan#Nihon_and_Nippon "Names of Japan"), along with symbol Nh, was later used for [element 113](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nihonium "Nihonium"). Element 113 was also discovered by a team of Japanese scientists and was named in respectful homage to Ogawa's work.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-61)

Rhenium was rediscovered by [Walter Noddack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Noddack "Walter Noddack"), [Ida Noddack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ida_Tacke "Ida Tacke"), and [Otto Berg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Berg_(scientist) "Otto Berg (scientist)") in [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany"). In 1925 they reported that they had detected the element in platinum ore and in the mineral [columbite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbite "Columbite"). They also found rhenium in [gadolinite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gadolinite "Gadolinite") and [molybdenite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molybdenite "Molybdenite").[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-'Ekamangane'-62) In 1928 they were able to extract 1 g of the element by processing 660 kg of molybdenite.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-1g-63) It was estimated in 1968 that 75% of the rhenium metal in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") was used for research and the development of [refractory metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refractory_metal "Refractory metal") alloys. It took several years from that point before the superalloys became widely used.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-65)

The [discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_the_chemical_elements "Discovery of the chemical elements") of element 43 was finally confirmed in a 1937 experiment at the [University of Palermo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Palermo "University of Palermo") in Sicily by [Carlo Perrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlo_Perrier "Carlo Perrier") and [Emilio Segrè](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emilio_Segr%C3%A8 "Emilio Segrè").[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-66) In mid-1936, Segrè visited the United States, first [Columbia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University") in New York and then the [Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Berkeley_National_Laboratory "Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory") in California. He persuaded [cyclotron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclotron "Cyclotron") inventor [Ernest Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Lawrence "Ernest Lawrence") to let him take back some discarded cyclotron parts that had become [radioactive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioactive "Radioactive"). Lawrence mailed him a [molybdenum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molybdenum "Molybdenum") foil that had been part of the deflector in the cyclotron.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-67)

### Bohrium

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_7_element&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Bohrium")]

Two groups claimed [discovery of the element bohrium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_chemical_element_discoveries "Timeline of chemical element discoveries"). Evidence of bohrium was first reported in 1976 by a Soviet research team led by [Yuri Oganessian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuri_Oganessian "Yuri Oganessian"), in which targets of [bismuth-209](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bismuth-209 "Bismuth-209") and [lead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead "Lead")-208 were bombarded with accelerated nuclei of [chromium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium "Chromium")-54 and [manganese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese "Manganese")-55 respectively.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-68) Two activities, one with a half-life of one to two milliseconds, and the other with an approximately five-second half-life, were seen. Since the ratio of the intensities of these two activities was constant throughout the experiment, it was proposed that the first was from the [isotope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotope "Isotope") bohrium-261 and that the second was from its daughter [dubnium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubnium "Dubnium")-257. Later, the dubnium isotope was corrected to dubnium-258, which indeed has a five-second half-life (dubnium-257 has a one-second half-life); however, the half-life observed for its parent is much shorter than the half-lives later observed in the definitive discovery of bohrium at [Darmstadt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darmstadt "Darmstadt") in 1981. The [IUPAC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Union_of_Pure_and_Applied_Chemistry "International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry")/IUPAP Transfermium Working Group (TWG) concluded that while dubnium-258 was probably seen in this experiment, the evidence for the production of its parent bohrium-262 was not convincing enough.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-93TWG-69)

In 1981, a German research team led by [Peter Armbruster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Armbruster "Peter Armbruster") and [Gottfried Münzenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gottfried_M%C3%BCnzenberg "Gottfried Münzenberg") at the [GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GSI_Helmholtz_Centre_for_Heavy_Ion_Research "GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research") (GSI Helmholtzzentrum für Schwerionenforschung) in Darmstadt bombarded a target of bismuth-209 with accelerated nuclei of chromium-54 to produce five atoms of the isotope bohrium-262:[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-262Bh-70)

[209 83 Bi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bismuth-209 "Bismuth-209") + [54 24 Cr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium-54 "Chromium-54") → [262 107 Bh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohrium-262 "Bohrium-262") + [n](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron "Neutron")
This discovery was further substantiated by their detailed measurements of the alpha decay chain of the produced bohrium atoms to previously known isotopes of [fermium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermium "Fermium") and [californium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Californium "Californium"). The [IUPAC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Union_of_Pure_and_Applied_Chemistry "International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry")/IUPAP Transfermium Working Group (TWG) recognised the GSI collaboration as official discoverers in their 1992 report.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-93TWG-69)

## Occurrence and production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_7_element&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Occurrence and production")]

### Manganese

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_7_element&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Manganese")]

Main article: [Manganese §Production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#Production "Manganese")

Manganese comprises about 1000[ppm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parts_per_million "Parts per million")(0.1%) of the [Earth's crust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_crust "Earth's crust") and is the [12th most abundant element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abundance_of_elements_in_Earth's_crust "Abundance of elements in Earth's crust").[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-Emsley2001-71) Soil contains 7–9000 ppm of manganese with an average of 440 ppm.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-Emsley2001-71) The atmosphere contains 0.01 μg/m 3.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-Emsley2001-71) Manganese occurs principally as [pyrolusite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrolusite "Pyrolusite") ([MnO 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese(IV)_oxide "Manganese(IV) oxide")), [braunite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braunite "Braunite") (Mn 2+Mn 3+6)(SiO 12),[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-72)[psilomelane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psilomelane "Psilomelane")(Ba,H 2 O)2 Mn 5 O 10, and to a lesser extent as [rhodochrosite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodochrosite "Rhodochrosite") ([MnCO 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese(II)_carbonate "Manganese(II) carbonate")).

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/World_Manganese_Production_2006.svg/500px-World_Manganese_Production_2006.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:World_Manganese_Production_2006.svg)

Percentage of manganese output in 2006 by countries[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-USGSMCS2009-73)

The most important manganese ore is pyrolusite ([MnO 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese(IV)_oxide "Manganese(IV) oxide")). Other economically important manganese ores usually show a close spatial relation to the iron ores, such as [sphalerite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphalerite "Sphalerite").[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-Holl-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-75) Land-based resources are large but irregularly distributed. About 80% of the known world manganese resources are in South Africa; other important manganese deposits are in Ukraine, Australia, India, China, [Gabon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabon "Gabon") and Brazil.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-USGSMCS2009-73) According to 1978 estimate, the [ocean floor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ocean_floor "Ocean floor") has 500 billion tons of [manganese nodules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese_nodule "Manganese nodule").[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-76) Attempts to find economically viable methods of harvesting manganese nodules were abandoned in the 1970s.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-77)

In South Africa, most identified deposits are located near [Hotazel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hotazel "Hotazel") in the [Northern Cape Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Cape_Province "Northern Cape Province"), with a 2011 estimate of 15 billion tons. In 2011 South Africa produced 3.4 million tons, topping all other nations.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-Mbendi-78)

Manganese is mainly mined in South Africa, Australia, China, Gabon, Brazil, India, Kazakhstan, Ghana, Ukraine and Malaysia.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-79)

For the production of [ferromanganese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferromanganese "Ferromanganese"), the manganese ore is mixed with iron ore and carbon, and then reduced either in a blast furnace or in an electric arc furnace.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-IndMin-80) The resulting [ferromanganese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferromanganese "Ferromanganese") has a manganese content of 30 to 80%.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-Holl-74) Pure manganese used for the production of iron-free alloys is produced by [leaching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leaching_(metallurgy) "Leaching (metallurgy)") manganese ore with [sulfuric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfuric_acid "Sulfuric acid") and a subsequent [electrowinning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrowinning "Electrowinning") process.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-hydrometI-81)

[![Image 12: Contains reactions and temperatures, as well as showing advanced processes such as the heat exchanger and milling process.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Manganese_Process_Flow_Diagram.jpg/330px-Manganese_Process_Flow_Diagram.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Manganese_Process_Flow_Diagram.jpg)

Process flow diagram for a manganese refining circuit.

A more progressive extraction process involves directly reducing (a low grade) manganese ore in a heap leach. This is done by [percolating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percolation "Percolation") natural gas through the bottom of the heap; the natural gas provides the heat (needs to be at least 850°C) and the reducing agent (carbon monoxide). This reduces all of the manganese ore to manganese oxide (MnO), which is a leachable form. The ore then travels through a [grinding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mill_(grinding) "Mill (grinding)") circuit to reduce the particle size of the ore to between 150 and 250 μm, increasing the surface area to aid leaching. The ore is then added to a leach tank of [sulfuric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfuric_acid "Sulfuric acid") and [ferrous iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron(II) "Iron(II)") (Fe 2+) in a 1.6:1 ratio. The iron reacts with the [manganese dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese_dioxide "Manganese dioxide") (MnO 2) to form [iron(III) oxide-hydroxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron(III)_oxide-hydroxide "Iron(III) oxide-hydroxide") (FeO(OH)) and elemental manganese (Mn):

This process yields approximately 92% recovery of the manganese. For further purification, the manganese can then be sent to an electrowinning facility.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-ManganeseRecovery-82)

In 1972 the [CIA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Intelligence_Agency "Central Intelligence Agency")'s [Project Azorian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Azorian "Project Azorian"), through billionaire [Howard Hughes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Hughes "Howard Hughes"), commissioned the ship _[Hughes Glomar Explorer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hughes\_Glomar\_Explorer "Hughes Glomar Explorer")_ with the cover story of harvesting manganese nodules from the sea floor.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-83) That triggered a rush of activity to collect manganese nodules, which was not actually practical. The real mission of _Hughes Glomar Explorer_ was to raise a sunken [Soviet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_of_Soviet_Socialist_Republics "Union of Soviet Socialist Republics") submarine, the [K-129](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_submarine_K-129_(1960) "Soviet submarine K-129 (1960)"), with the goal of retrieving Soviet code books.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-azorian-84)

An abundant resource of manganese in the form of [Mn nodules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese_nodule "Manganese nodule") found on the ocean floor.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-85)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-86) These nodules, which are composed of 29% manganese,[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-87) are located along the [ocean floor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seabed "Seabed") and the potential impact of mining these nodules is being researched. Physical, chemical, and biological environmental impacts can occur due to this nodule mining disturbing the seafloor and causing sediment plumes to form. This suspension includes metals and inorganic nutrients, which can lead to contamination of the near-bottom waters from dissolved toxic compounds. Mn nodules are also the grazing grounds, living space, and protection for endo- and epifaunal systems. When theses nodules are removed, these systems are directly affected. Overall, this can cause species to leave the area or completely die off.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-88) Prior to the commencement of the mining itself, research is being conducted by [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") affiliated bodies and state-sponsored companies in an attempt to fully understand [environmental impacts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_issues "Environmental issues") in the hopes of mitigating these impacts.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-89)

### Technetium

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_7_element&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Technetium")]

Main article: [Technetium §Occurrence and Production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technetium#Occurrence_and_Production "Technetium")

Technetium was created by bombarding [molybdenum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molybdenum "Molybdenum") atoms with [deuterons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deuteron "Deuteron") that had been accelerated by a device called a [cyclotron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclotron "Cyclotron"). Technetium occurs naturally in the Earth's [crust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crust_(geology) "Crust (geology)") in minute concentrations of about 0.003 parts per trillion. Technetium is so rare because the [half-lives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half-life "Half-life") of 97 Tc and 98 Tc are only 4.2 million years. More than a thousand of such periods have passed since the formation of the [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"), so the probability of survival of even one atom of [primordial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primordial_nuclide "Primordial nuclide") technetium is effectively zero. However, small amounts exist as spontaneous [fission products](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fission_product "Fission product") in [uranium ores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uranium_ore "Uranium ore"). A kilogram of uranium contains an estimated 1[nanogram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orders_of_magnitude_(mass) "Orders of magnitude (mass)") (10−9 g) equivalent to ten trillion atoms of technetium.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-blocks-90)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-91)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-92) Some [red giant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_giant "Red giant") stars with the spectral types S-, M-, and N contain a spectral absorption line indicating the presence of technetium.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHammond2004[httpsarchiveorgdetailscrchandbookofche81lidepagen905_p._4-1]-93)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-94) These red giants are known informally as [technetium stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technetium_star "Technetium star").

### Rhenium

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_7_element&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Rhenium")]

Main article: [Rhenium §Production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhenium#Production "Rhenium")

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/40/Molybdenit_1.jpg/250px-Molybdenit_1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Molybdenit_1.jpg)

Molybdenite

Rhenium is one of the rarest elements in [Earth's crust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_crust "Earth's crust") with an average concentration of 1 ppb;[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-G&W-6)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-:1-95) other sources quote the number of 0.5 ppb making it the 77th most abundant element in Earth's crust.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEmsley2001[httpsarchiveorgdetailsnaturesbuildingb0000emslpage358_358%E2%80%93360]-96) Rhenium is probably not found free in nature (its possible natural occurrence is uncertain), but occurs in amounts up to 0.2%[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-G&W-6) in the mineral [molybdenite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molybdenite "Molybdenite") (which is primarily [molybdenum disulfide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molybdenum_disulfide "Molybdenum disulfide")), the major commercial source, although single molybdenite samples with up to 1.88% have been found.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-Rousch-97)[Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chile "Chile") has the world's largest rhenium reserves, part of the copper ore deposits, and was the leading producer as of 2005.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-98) It was only recently that the first rhenium [mineral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mineral "Mineral") was found and described (in 1994), a rhenium [sulfide mineral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfide_mineral "Sulfide mineral") (ReS 2) condensing from a [fumarole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fumarole "Fumarole") on [Kudriavy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kudriavy "Kudriavy") volcano, [Iturup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iturup "Iturup") island, in the [Kuril Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuril_Islands "Kuril Islands").[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-99) Kudriavy discharges up to 20–60 kg rhenium per year mostly in the form of rhenium disulfide.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-100)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-101) Named [rheniite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rheniite "Rheniite"), this rare mineral commands high prices among collectors.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-102)

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/37/Ammonium_perrhenate.jpg/250px-Ammonium_perrhenate.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ammonium_perrhenate.jpg)

Ammonium perrhenate

Most of the rhenium extracted comes from [porphyry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porphyry_(geology) "Porphyry (geology)")[molybdenum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molybdenum "Molybdenum") deposits.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-103) These ores typically contain 0.001% to 0.2% rhenium.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-G&W-6) Roasting the ore volatilizes rhenium oxides.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-Rousch-97)[Rhenium(VII) oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhenium(VII)_oxide "Rhenium(VII) oxide") and [perrhenic acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perrhenic_acid "Perrhenic acid") readily dissolve in water; they are leached from flue dusts and gasses and extracted by precipitating with [potassium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potassium_chloride "Potassium chloride") or [ammonium chloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammonium_chloride "Ammonium chloride") as the [perrhenate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perrhenate "Perrhenate") salts, and purified by [recrystallization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recrystallization_(chemistry) "Recrystallization (chemistry)").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-G&W-6) Total world production is between 40 and 50 tons/year; the main producers are in Chile, the United States, Peru, and Poland.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-USGS_2012_summary-104) Recycling of used Pt-Re catalyst and special alloys allow the recovery of another 10 tons per year. Prices for the metal rose rapidly in early 2008, from $1000–$2000 per [kg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilogram "Kilogram") in 2003–2006 to over $10,000 in February 2008.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-minormetals-105)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-106) The metal form is prepared by reducing [ammonium perrhenate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammonium_perrhenate "Ammonium perrhenate") with [hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen "Hydrogen") at high temperatures:[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-Brauer-25)

2 NH 4 ReO 4 + 7 H 2 → 2 Re + 8 H 2 O + 2 NH 3 There are technologies for the associated extraction of rhenium from productive solutions of underground leaching of uranium ores.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-107)

### Bohrium

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_7_element&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Bohrium")]

Bohrium is a synthetic element that does not occur in nature. Very few atoms have been synthesized, and also due to its radioactivity, only limited research has been conducted. Bohrium is only produced in nuclear reactors and has never been isolated in pure form.

## Applications

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_7_element&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Applications")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b7/Fac-MbpyCO3X.png/250px-Fac-MbpyCO3X.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fac-MbpyCO3X.png)

Structure of the facial isomer of M(R-bpy)(CO)3 X where M = Mn, Re; X = Cl, Br; R-bpy = 4,4'-disubstituted-2,2'-bipyridine

The [_facial_ isomer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octahedral_molecular_geometry "Octahedral molecular geometry") of both rhenium and manganese 2,2'-bipyridyl tricarbonyl halide complexes have been extensively researched as catalysts for [electrochemical carbon dioxide reduction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrochemical_reduction_of_carbon_dioxide "Electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide") due to their high selectivity and stability. They are commonly abbreviated as M(R-bpy)(CO)3 X where M = Mn, Re; R-bpy = 4,4'-disubstituted [2,2'-bipyridine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2,2%E2%80%B2-Bipyridine "2,2′-Bipyridine"); and X = Cl, Br.

### Manganese

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_7_element&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Manganese")]

The rarity of rhenium has shifted research toward the manganese version of these catalysts as a more sustainable alternative.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-:2-108) The first reports of catalytic activity of Mn(R-bpy)(CO)3 Br towards CO 2 reduction came from Chardon-Noblat and coworkers in 2011.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-109) Compared to Re analogs, Mn(R-bpy)(CO)3 Br shows catalytic activity at lower overpotentials.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-:3-110)

The catalytic mechanism for Mn(R-bpy)(CO)3 X is complex and depends on the steric profile of the bipyridine ligand. When R is not bulky, the catalyst dimerizes to form [Mn(R-bpy)(CO)3]2 before forming the active species. When R is bulky, however, the complex forms the active species without dimerizing, reducing the overpotential of CO 2 reduction by 200-300 mV. Unlike Re(R-bpy)(CO)3 X, Mn(R-bpy)(CO)3 X only reduces CO 2 in the presence of an acid.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-:3-110)

### Technetium

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_7_element&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: Technetium")]

[![Image 16: Upper image: two drop-like features merged at their bottoms; they have a yellow centre and a red rim on a black background. Caption: Graves' Disease Tc-Uptake 16%. Lower image: red dots on black background. Caption: 250 Gy (30mCi) + Prednison.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/3f/Basedow-vor-nach-RIT.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Basedow-vor-nach-RIT.jpg)

Technetium [scintigraphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_medicine "Nuclear medicine") of a neck of [Graves' disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graves'_disease "Graves' disease") patient

[Technetium-99m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technetium-99m "Technetium-99m") ("m" indicates that this is a [metastable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_isomer#Metastable_isomers "Nuclear isomer") nuclear isomer) is used in radioactive isotope [medical tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_medicine "Nuclear medicine"). For example, Technetium-99m is a [radioactive tracer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioactive_tracer "Radioactive tracer") that medical imaging equipment tracks in the human body.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-blocks-90)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-bbc-20150530-111)[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-112) It is well suited to the role because it emits readily detectable 140[keV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronvolt "Electronvolt")[gamma rays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_ray "Gamma ray"), and its half-life is 6.01 hours (meaning that about 94% of it decays to technetium-99 in 24 hours).[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-enc-113) The chemistry of technetium allows it to be bound to a variety of biochemical compounds, each of which determines how it is metabolized and deposited in the body, and this single isotope can be used for a multitude of diagnostic tests. More than 50 common [radiopharmaceuticals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiopharmaceuticals "Radiopharmaceuticals") are based on technetium-99m for imaging and functional studies of the [brain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_brain "Human brain"), heart muscle, [thyroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thyroid "Thyroid"), [lungs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_lung "Human lung"), [liver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liver "Liver"), [gall bladder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gall_bladder "Gall bladder"), [kidneys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kidney "Kidney"), [skeleton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_skeleton "Human skeleton"), [blood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood "Blood"), and [tumors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tumor "Tumor").[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwochau2000414-114) Technetium-99m is also used in radioimaging.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-115)

The longer-lived isotope, technetium-95m with a half-life of 61 days, is used as a [radioactive tracer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioactive_tracer "Radioactive tracer") to study the movement of technetium in the environment and in plant and animal systems.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwochau200012%E2%80%9327-116)

Technetium-99 decays almost entirely by beta decay, emitting beta particles with consistent low energies and no accompanying gamma rays. Moreover, its long half-life means that this emission decreases very slowly with time. It can also be extracted to a high chemical and isotopic purity from radioactive waste. For these reasons, it is a [National Institute of Standards and Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institute_of_Standards_and_Technology "National Institute of Standards and Technology") (NIST) standard beta emitter, and is used for equipment calibration.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwochau200087-117) Technetium-99 has also been proposed for optoelectronic devices and [nanoscale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanotechnology "Nanotechnology")[nuclear batteries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_battery "Nuclear battery").[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-118)

Like [rhenium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhenium "Rhenium") and [palladium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palladium "Palladium"), technetium can serve as a [catalyst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalyst "Catalyst"). In processes such as the [dehydrogenation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dehydrogenation "Dehydrogenation") of [isopropyl alcohol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isopropyl_alcohol "Isopropyl alcohol"), it is a far more effective catalyst than either rhenium or palladium. However, its radioactivity is a major problem in safe catalytic applications.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwochau200087%E2%80%9390-119)

When steel is immersed in water, adding a small concentration (55[ppm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parts_per_notation "Parts per notation")) of potassium pertechnetate(VII) to the water protects the [steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steel "Steel") from corrosion, even if the temperature is raised to 250°C (523 K).[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEmsley2001425-120) For this reason, pertechnetate has been used as an anodic [corrosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corrosion "Corrosion") inhibitor for steel, although technetium's radioactivity poses problems that limit this application to self-contained systems.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-121) While (for example) CrO 2−

4 can also inhibit corrosion, it requires a concentration ten times as high. In one experiment, a specimen of carbon steel was kept in an aqueous solution of pertechnetate for 20 years and was still uncorroded.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEmsley2001425-120) The mechanism by which pertechnetate prevents corrosion is not well understood, but seems to involve the reversible formation of a thin surface layer ([passivation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passivation_(chemistry) "Passivation (chemistry)")). One theory holds that the pertechnetate reacts with the steel surface to form a layer of technetium [dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxide "Oxide") which prevents further corrosion; the same effect explains how iron powder can be used to remove pertechnetate from water. The effect disappears rapidly if the concentration of pertechnetate falls below the minimum concentration or if too high a concentration of other ions is added.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwochau200091-122)

As noted, the radioactive nature of technetium (3 MBq/L at the concentrations required) makes this corrosion protection impractical in almost all situations. Nevertheless, corrosion protection by pertechnetate ions was proposed (but never adopted) for use in [boiling water reactors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boiling_water_reactor "Boiling water reactor").[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwochau200091-122)

### Rhenium

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_7_element&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: Rhenium")]

The catalytic activity of Re(bpy)(CO)3 Cl for carbon dioxide reduction was first studied by Lehn et al.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-123) and Meyer et al.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-124) in 1984 and 1985, respectively. Re(R-bpy)(CO)3 X complexes exclusively produce CO from CO 2 reduction with [Faradaic efficiencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faraday_efficiency "Faraday efficiency") of close to 100% even in solutions with high concentrations of water or [Brønsted acids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Br%C3%B8nsted%E2%80%93Lowry_acid%E2%80%93base_theory "Brønsted–Lowry acid–base theory").[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-:2-108)

The catalytic mechanism of Re(R-bpy)(CO)3 X involves reduction of the complex twice and loss of the X ligand to generate a five-coordinate active species which binds CO 2. These complexes will reduce CO 2 both with and without an additional acid present; however, the presence of an acid increases catalytic activity.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-:2-108) The high selectivity of these complexes to CO 2 reduction over the competing [hydrogen evolution reaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_splitting "Water splitting") has been shown by [density functional theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Density_functional_theory "Density functional theory") studies to be related to the faster kinetics of CO 2 binding compared to H+ binding.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-:3-110)

### Bohrium

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_7_element&action=edit&section=30 "Edit section: Bohrium")]

Bohrium is a synthetic element and is too radioactive to be used in anything.

## Toxicity and precautions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_7_element&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: Toxicity and precautions")]

Manganese compounds are less toxic than those of other widespread metals, such as [nickel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nickel "Nickel") and [copper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copper "Copper").[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-125) However, exposure to manganese dusts and fumes should not exceed the ceiling value of 5 mg/m 3 even for short periods because of its toxicity level.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-126) Manganese poisoning has been linked to impaired motor skills and cognitive disorders.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-127)

Technetium has low chemical toxicity. For example, no significant change in blood formula, body and organ weights, and food consumption could be detected for rats which ingested up to 15 μg of technetium-99 per gram of food for several weeks.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-128) In the body, technetium quickly gets converted to the stable TcO−

4 ion, which is highly water-soluble and quickly excreted. The radiological toxicity of technetium (per unit of mass) is a function of compound, type of radiation for the isotope in question, and the isotope's half-life.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwochau2000371%E2%80%93381-129) However, it is radioactive, so all isotopes must be handled carefully. The primary hazard when working with technetium is inhalation of dust; such [radioactive contamination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioactive_contamination "Radioactive contamination") in the lungs can pose a significant cancer risk. For most work, careful handling in a [fume hood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fume_hood "Fume hood") is sufficient, and a [glove box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glove_box "Glove box") is not needed.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwochau200040-130)

Very little is known about the toxicity of rhenium and its compounds because they are used in very small amounts. Soluble salts, such as the rhenium halides or perrhenates, could be hazardous due to elements other than rhenium or due to rhenium itself.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEmsley2001358%E2%80%93361-131) Only a few compounds of rhenium have been tested for their acute toxicity; two examples are potassium perrhenate and rhenium trichloride, which were injected as a solution into rats. The perrhenate had an [LD 50](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Median_lethal_dose "Median lethal dose") value of 2800 mg/kg after seven days (this is very low toxicity, similar to that of table salt) and the rhenium trichloride showed LD 50 of 280 mg/kg.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-132)

## Biological role

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_7_element&action=edit&section=32 "Edit section: Biological role")]

Main article: [Manganese in biology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese_in_biology "Manganese in biology")

Of the group 7 elements, only manganese has a role in the human body. It is an essential trace nutrient, with the body containing approximately 10 [milligrams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milligram "Milligram") at any given time. It is present as a [coenzyme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coenzyme "Coenzyme") in biological processes that include macronutrient metabolism, bone formation, and [free radical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_radical "Free radical") defense systems. It is a critical component in dozens of proteins and enzymes.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-:4-133) The manganese in the human body is mainly concentrated in the bones, and the soft tissue remainder is concentrated in the liver and kidneys.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEmsley2001[httpsarchiveorgdetailsnaturesbuildingb0000emslpage249_249%E2%80%93253]-134) In the human brain, the manganese is bound to manganese [metalloproteins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metalloprotein "Metalloprotein"), most notably [glutamine synthetase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glutamine_synthetase "Glutamine synthetase") in [astrocytes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astrocyte "Astrocyte").[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_element#cite_note-135) Technetium, rhenium, and bohrium have no known biological roles. Technetium is, however, used in radioimaging.

The discoveries of the 118 [chemical elements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_element "Chemical element") known to exist as of 2026 are presented here in chronological order. The elements are listed generally in the order in which each was first defined as the pure element, as the exact date of discovery of most elements cannot be accurately determined. There are plans to synthesize more elements, and it is not known how many elements are possible.

Each element's [name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_elements_by_name "List of elements by name"), [atomic number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_number "Atomic number"), year of first report, name of the discoverer, and notes related to the discovery are listed.

## Modern discoveries

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Timeline_of_chemical_element_discoveries&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Modern discoveries")]

For 18th-century discoveries, around the time that [Antoine Lavoisier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoine_Lavoisier "Antoine Lavoisier") first questioned the [phlogiston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phlogiston "Phlogiston") theory, the recognition of a new "[earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth_(historical_chemistry) "Earth (historical chemistry)")" has been regarded as being equivalent to the discovery of a new element (as was the general practice then). For some elements (e.g. Be, B, Na, Mg, Al, Si, K, Ca, Mn, Co, Ni, Zr, Mo),[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_chemical_elements#cite_note-51) this presents further difficulties as their [compounded forms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_compound "Chemical compound") were widely known since medieval or even ancient times, even though the elements as "elemental" constituents of those compounds were not. Since the true nature of those compounds was sometimes only gradually discovered, it is sometimes very difficult to name one specific discoverer.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_chemical_elements#cite_note-Miskowiec-3)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_chemical_elements#cite_note-Miskowiec2-52) In such cases the first publication on their chemistry is noted, and a longer explanation given in the notes.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_chemical_elements#cite_note-Miskowiec-3)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_chemical_elements#cite_note-Miskowiec2-52)

**Group 5** is a [group of elements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(periodic_table) "Group (periodic table)") in the [periodic table](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodic_table "Periodic table"). Group 5 contains [vanadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadium "Vanadium") (V), [niobium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niobium "Niobium") (Nb), [tantalum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tantalum "Tantalum") (Ta) and [dubnium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubnium "Dubnium") (Db).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-1) This group lies in the [d-block](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D-block "D-block") of the periodic table. This group is sometimes called the **vanadium group** or **vanadium family** after its lightest member; however, the group itself has not acquired a [trivial name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trivial_name "Trivial name") because it belongs to the broader grouping of the [transition metals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transition_metal "Transition metal").

As is typical for early transition metals, niobium and tantalum have only the group [oxidation state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxidation_state "Oxidation state") of +5 as a major one, and are quite electropositive (it is easy to donate electrons) and have a less rich coordination chemistry (the chemistry of metallic ions bound with molecules). Due to the effects of the [lanthanide contraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lanthanide_contraction "Lanthanide contraction"), the decrease in ionic radii in the [lanthanides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lanthanide "Lanthanide"), they are very similar in properties. Vanadium is somewhat distinct due to its smaller size: it has well-defined +2, +3 and +4 states as well (although +5 is more stable).

The lighter three Group 5 elements occur naturally and share similar properties; all three are hard [refractory metals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refractory_metals "Refractory metals") under standard conditions. The fourth element, [dubnium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubnium "Dubnium"), has been synthesized in laboratories, but it has not been found occurring in nature, with half-life of the most stable isotope, dubnium-268, being only 16 hours, and other isotopes even more [radioactive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioactive "Radioactive").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_5_element&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]
