Andrés Manuel del Río, the discoverer of vanadium

_Group 5_ is the new IUPAC name for this group; the old style name was _group VB_ in the old US system (CAS) or _group VA_ in the European system (old IUPAC). Group 5 must not be confused with the group with the old-style group crossed names of either _VA_ (US system, CAS) or _VB_ (European system, old IUPAC); that group is now called the [pnictogens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pnictogen "Pnictogen") or group 15.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Fluck_1988-2)

### Vanadium

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_5_element&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Vanadium")]

Vanadium was [discovered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_the_chemical_elements "Discovery of the chemical elements") in 1801 by the Spanish mineralogist [Andrés Manuel del Río](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9s_Manuel_del_R%C3%ADo "Andrés Manuel del Río"). Del Río extracted the element from a sample of Mexican "brown lead" ore, later named [vanadinite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadinite "Vanadinite"). He found that its salts exhibit a wide variety of colors, and as a result he named the element _panchromium_ (Greek: παγχρώμιο "all colors"). Later, Del Río renamed the element _erythronium_ (Greek: ερυθρός "red") because most of the salts turned red upon heating. In 1805, French chemist [Hippolyte Victor Collet-Descotils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippolyte_Victor_Collet-Descotils "Hippolyte Victor Collet-Descotils"), backed by del Río's friend Baron [Alexander von Humboldt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_von_Humboldt "Alexander von Humboldt"), incorrectly declared that del Río's new element was an impure sample of [chromium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium "Chromium"). Del Río accepted Collet-Descotils' statement and retracted his claim.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Cintas-3)

In 1831 Swedish chemist [Nils Gabriel Sefström](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nils_Gabriel_Sefstr%C3%B6m "Nils Gabriel Sefström") rediscovered the element in a new oxide he found while working with [iron ores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_ore "Iron ore"). Later that year, [Friedrich Wöhler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_W%C3%B6hler "Friedrich Wöhler") confirmed del Río's earlier work.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-sefs-4) Sefström chose a name beginning with V, which had not yet been assigned to any element. He called the element _vanadium_ after [Old Norse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Norse "Old Norse")_[Vanadís](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List\_of\_names\_of\_Freyja "List of names of Freyja")_ (another name for the [Norse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norse_mythology "Norse mythology")[Vanir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanir "Vanir") goddess [Freyja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freyja "Freyja"), whose attributes include beauty and fertility), because of the many beautifully colored [chemical compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_compound "Chemical compound") it produces.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-sefs-4) In 1831, the geologist [George William Featherstonhaugh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_William_Featherstonhaugh "George William Featherstonhaugh") suggested that vanadium should be renamed _rionium_ after del Río, but this suggestion was not followed.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-5)

### Niobium and tantalum

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_5_element&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Niobium and tantalum")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/Charles_Hatchett._Soft-ground_etching_by_F._C._Lewis_after_T_Wellcome_V0002614_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Charles_Hatchett._Soft-ground_etching_by_F._C._Lewis_after_T_Wellcome_V0002614_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Charles_Hatchett._Soft-ground_etching_by_F._C._Lewis_after_T_Wellcome_V0002614_(cropped).jpg)

Charles Hatchett, the discover of niobium

Niobium was [identified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_the_chemical_elements "Discovery of the chemical elements") by English chemist [Charles Hatchett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Hatchett "Charles Hatchett") in 1801.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Hatchett_1802a-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Hatchett_1802b-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Hatchett_1802c-8) He found a new element in a mineral sample that had been sent to England from [Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connecticut "Connecticut"), United States in 1734 by John Winthrop F.R.S. (grandson of [John Winthrop the Younger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Winthrop_the_Younger "John Winthrop the Younger")) and named the mineral _columbite_ and the new element _columbium_ after _[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia\_(name) "Columbia (name)")_,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-9) the poetic name for the United States.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Noyes-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-1853_Mining_Journal-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-12) However, after the 15th Conference of the Union of Chemistry in Amsterdam in 1949, the name niobium was chosen for element 41.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Contro-13) The _columbium_ discovered by Hatchett was probably a mixture of the new element with tantalum, which was first discovered in 1802 by [Anders Gustav Ekeberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anders_Gustav_Ekeberg "Anders Gustav Ekeberg").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Noyes-10)

[![Image 10](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c2/Anders_Gustaf_Ekeberg.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Anders_Gustaf_Ekeberg.jpg)

Anders Gustav Ekeberg, the discoverer of tantalum

Subsequently, there was considerable confusion[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Wolla-14) over the difference between niobium (columbium) and the closely related tantalum. In 1809, English chemist [William Hyde Wollaston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hyde_Wollaston "William Hyde Wollaston") compared the oxides derived from both niobium - [columbite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbite "Columbite"), with a density 5.918 g/cm 3, and tantalum - [tantalite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tantalite "Tantalite"), with a density over 8 g/cm 3, and concluded that the two oxides, despite the significant difference in density, were identical; thus he kept the name tantalum.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Wolla-14) This conclusion was disputed in 1846 by German chemist [Heinrich Rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich_Rose "Heinrich Rose"), who argued that there were two different elements in the tantalite sample, and named them after children of [Tantalus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tantalus "Tantalus"): _niobium_ (from [Niobe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niobe "Niobe")) and _[pelopium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelopium "Pelopium")_ (from [Pelops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelops "Pelops")).[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Pelop-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-16) This confusion arose from the minimal observed differences between tantalum and niobium. The claimed new elements _pelopium_, _[ilmenium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilmenium "Ilmenium")_, and _dianium_[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Dianium-17) were in fact identical to niobium or mixtures of niobium and tantalum.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Ilmen-18) Pure tantalum was not produced until 1903.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Emsley-19)

### Dubnium

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_5_element&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Dubnium")]

The last element of the group, [dubnium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubnium "Dubnium"), does not occur naturally and so must be synthesized in a laboratory. The first reported detection was by a team at the [Joint Institute for Nuclear Research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Institute_for_Nuclear_Research "Joint Institute for Nuclear Research") (JINR), which in 1968 had produced the new element by bombarding an [americium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americium "Americium")-243 target with a beam of [neon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neon "Neon")-22 ions, and reported 9.4 MeV (with a half-life of 0.1–3 seconds) and 9.7 MeV (_t_ 1/2>0.05 s) [alpha activities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_decay "Alpha decay") followed by alpha activities similar to those of either 256 103 or 257 103. Based on prior theoretical predictions, the two activity lines were assigned to 261 105 and 260 105, respectively.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-1993_report-20)

After observing the alpha decays of element 105, the researchers aimed to observe the [spontaneous fission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spontaneous_fission "Spontaneous fission") (SF) of the element and study the resulting fission fragments. They published a paper in February 1970, reporting multiple examples of two such activities, with half-lives of 14 ms and 2.2±0.5 s. They assigned the former activity to 242mf Am[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-21) and ascribed the latter activity to an isotope of element 105. They suggested that it was unlikely that this activity could come from a transfer reaction instead of element 105, because the yield ratio for this reaction was significantly lower than that of the 242mf Am-producing transfer reaction, in accordance with theoretical predictions. To establish that this activity was not from a (22 Ne,_x_ n) reaction, the researchers bombarded a 243 Am target with 18 O ions; reactions producing 256 103 and 257 103 showed very little SF activity (matching the established data), and the reaction producing heavier 258 103 and 259 103 produced no SF activity at all, in line with theoretical data. The researchers concluded that the activities observed came from SF of element 105.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-1993_report-20)

JINR then attempted an experiment to create element 105, published in a report in May 1970. They claimed that they had synthesized more nuclei of element 105 and that the experiment confirmed their previous work. According to the paper, the isotope produced by JINR was probably 261 105, or possibly 260 105.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-1993_report-20) This report included an initial chemical examination: the thermal gradient version of the gas-chromatography method was applied to demonstrate that the chloride of what had formed from the SF activity nearly matched that of [niobium pentachloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niobium(V)_chloride "Niobium(V) chloride"), rather than [hafnium tetrachloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hafnium_tetrachloride "Hafnium tetrachloride"). The team identified a 2.2-second SF activity in a volatile chloride portraying eka-tantalum properties, and inferred that the source of the SF activity must have been element 105.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-1993_report-20)

In June 1970, JINR made improvements on their first experiment, using a purer target and reducing the intensity of transfer reactions by installing a [collimator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collimator "Collimator") before the catcher. This time, they were able to find 9.1 MeV alpha activities with daughter isotopes identifiable as either 256 103 or 257 103, implying that the original isotope was either 260 105 or 261 105.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-1993_report-20)

[![Image 11: Photo of Niels Bohr](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/Niels_Bohr.jpg/250px-Niels_Bohr.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Niels_Bohr.jpg)

[![Image 12: Photo of Otto Hahn](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/Otto_Hahn_%28Nobel%29.jpg/250px-Otto_Hahn_%28Nobel%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Otto_Hahn_(Nobel).jpg)

Danish nuclear physicist [Niels Bohr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niels_Bohr "Niels Bohr") and German nuclear chemist [Otto Hahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Hahn "Otto Hahn"), both proposed as possible namesakes for element 105

A [controversy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transfermium_Wars "Transfermium Wars") erupted on who had discovered the element, which each group suggesting its own name: the Dubna group named the element _nielsbohrium_ after [Niels Bohr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niels_Bohr "Niels Bohr"), while the Berkeley group named it _hahnium_ after [Otto Hahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Hahn "Otto Hahn").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-transuranium-22) Eventually a joint working party of [IUPAC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUPAC "IUPAC") and [IUPAP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUPAP "IUPAP"), the Transfermium Working Group, decided that credit for the discovery should be shared. After various compromises were attempted, where element 105 was called _kurchatovium_, _joliotium_ and _hahnium_, in 1997 IUPAC officially named the element dubnium after Dubna,[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-97IUPAC-23)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Emsley-19) and _nielsbohrium_ was eventually simplified to _bohrium_ and used for [element 107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohrium "Bohrium").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-24)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-IUPAC97-25)

## Chemical properties

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_5_element&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Chemical properties")]

Like other groups, the members of this family show patterns in its [electron configuration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron_configuration "Electron configuration"), especially the outermost shells. (The expected 4d 3 5s 2 configuration for niobium is a very low-lying excited state at about 0.14 eV.)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-26)

| [Electron configurations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron_configuration "Electron configuration") of group 5 elements |
| --- |
| [_Z_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_number "Atomic number") | [Element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_element "Chemical element") | Electrons per [shell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron_shell "Electron shell") | [Electron configuration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron_configuration "Electron configuration") |
| 23 | V, vanadium | 2, 8, 11, 2 | [Ar] 3d 3 4s 2 |
| 41 | Nb, niobium | 2, 8, 18, 12, 1 | [Kr] 4d 4 5s 1 |
| 73 | Ta, tantalum | 2, 8, 18, 32, 11, 2 | [Xe] 4f 14 5d 3 6s 2 |
| 105 | Db, dubnium | 2, 8, 18, 32, 32, 11, 2 | [Rn] 5f 14 6d 3 7s 2 |

Most of the chemistry has been observed only for the first three members of the group (the chemistry of dubnium is not very established, but what is known appears to match expectations for a heavier congener of tantalum). All the elements of the group are reactive metals with a high melting points (1910°C, 2477°C, 3017°C). The reactivity is not always obvious due to the rapid formation of a stable oxide layer, which prevents further reactions, similarly to trends in group 3 or group 4. The metals form different oxides: vanadium forms [vanadium(II) oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadium(II)_oxide "Vanadium(II) oxide"), [vanadium(III) oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadium(III)_oxide "Vanadium(III) oxide"), [vanadium(IV) oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadium(IV)_oxide "Vanadium(IV) oxide") and [vanadium(V) oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadium(V)_oxide "Vanadium(V) oxide"), niobium forms [niobium(II) oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niobium(II)_oxide "Niobium(II) oxide"), [niobium(IV) oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niobium(IV)_oxide "Niobium(IV) oxide") and [niobium(V) oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niobium(V)_oxide "Niobium(V) oxide"), but out of tantalum oxides only [tantalum(V) oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tantalum(V)_oxide "Tantalum(V) oxide") is characterized. Metal(V) oxides are generally nonreactive and act like acids rather than bases, but the lower oxides are less stable. They, however, have some unusual properties for oxides, such as high electric conductivity.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-HollemanAF-27)

All three elements form various [inorganic compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inorganic_chemistry "Inorganic chemistry"), generally in the oxidation state of +5. Lower oxidation states are also known, but in all elements other than vanadium,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-HollemanAF2-28) they are less stable, decreasing in stability with atomic mass increase.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Greenwood956-29)

### Compounds

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_5_element&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Compounds")]

#### Oxides

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_5_element&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Oxides")]

Vanadium forms oxides in the +2, +3, +4 and +5 [oxidation states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxidation_state "Oxidation state"), forming [vanadium(II) oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadium(II)_oxide "Vanadium(II) oxide") (VO), [vanadium(III) oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadium(III)_oxide "Vanadium(III) oxide") (V 2 O 3), [vanadium(IV) oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadium(IV)_oxide "Vanadium(IV) oxide") (VO 2) and [vanadium(V) oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadium(V)_oxide "Vanadium(V) oxide") (V 2 O 5). Vanadium(V) oxide or vanadium pentoxide is the most common, being precursor to most alloys and compounds of vanadium, and is also a widely used [industrial catalyst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_catalyst "Industrial catalyst").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Ullmann-30)

Niobium forms oxides in the oxidation states +5 ([Nb 2 O 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niobium_pentoxide "Niobium pentoxide")),[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-31) +4 ([NbO 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niobium_dioxide "Niobium dioxide")), and the rarer oxidation state, +2 ([NbO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niobium_monoxide "Niobium monoxide")).[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Greenwood&Earnshaw2nd-32) Most common is the pentoxide, also being precursor to almost all niobium compounds and alloys.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-HollemanAF-27)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Cardarelli-33)

[Tantalum pentoxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tantalum_pentoxide "Tantalum pentoxide") (Ta 2 O 5) is the most important compound from the perspective of applications. Oxides of tantalum in lower oxidation states are numerous, including many [defect structures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defect_structure "Defect structure"), and are lightly studied or poorly characterized.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Greenwood&Earnshaw2nd-32)

#### Oxyanions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_5_element&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Oxyanions")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/ff/Decavanadate_polyhedra.png/250px-Decavanadate_polyhedra.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Decavanadate_polyhedra.png)

The [decavanadate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decavanadate "Decavanadate") structure

In aqueous solution, vanadium(V) forms an extensive family of [oxyanions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxyanion "Oxyanion") as established by [51 V NMR spectroscopy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadium-51_nuclear_magnetic_resonance "Vanadium-51 nuclear magnetic resonance").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Rehder-34) The interrelationships in this family are described by the [predominance diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Predominance_diagram "Predominance diagram"), which shows at least 11 species, depending on pH and concentration.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-35) The tetrahedral orthovanadate ion, VO 3−

4, is the principal species present at pH 12–14. Similar in size and charge to phosphorus(V), vanadium(V) also parallels its chemistry and crystallography. [Orthovanadate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_orthovanadate "Sodium orthovanadate") V O 3−

4 is used in [protein crystallography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protein_crystallography "Protein crystallography")[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-36) to study the [biochemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biochemistry "Biochemistry") of phosphate.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-37) Beside that, this anion also has been shown to interact with activity of some specific enzymes.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-38)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-39) The tetrathiovanadate [VS 4]3− is analogous to the orthovanadate ion.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-40)

At lower pH values, the monomer [HVO 4]2− and dimer [V 2 O 7]4− are formed, with the monomer predominant at vanadium concentration of less than c. 10−2 M (pV > 2, where pV is equal to the minus value of the logarithm of the total vanadium concentration/M). The formation of the divanadate ion is analogous to the formation of the [dichromate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dichromate "Dichromate") ion. As the pH is reduced, further protonation and condensation to [polyvanadates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadate "Vanadate") occur: at pH 4–6 [H 2 VO 4]− is predominant at pV greater than ca. 4, while at higher concentrations trimers and tetramers are formed. Between pH 2–4 [decavanadate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decavanadate "Decavanadate") predominates, though its formation from orthovanadate is optimized at pH 4–7, represented by this reaction:[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-one-41)

10 Na 3[VO 4] + 24 HOAc → Na 6[V 10 O 28] + 12 H 2 O + 24 NaOAc
In decavanadate, each V(V) center is surrounded by six oxide [ligands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ligand "Ligand").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-HollemanAF-27) Vanadic acid, H 3 VO 4 exists only at very low concentrations because protonation of the tetrahedral species [H 2 VO 4]− results in the preferential formation of the octahedral [VO 2(H 2 O)4]+ species. In strongly acidic solutions, pH<2, [VO 2(H 2 O)4]+ is the predominant species, while the oxide V 2 O 5 precipitates from solution at high concentrations.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-42) The oxide is formally the [acid anhydride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acidic_oxide "Acidic oxide") of vanadic acid. The structures of many [vanadate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadate "Vanadate") compounds have been determined by X-ray crystallography.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-43)

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9d/VinwaterPourbaixdiagram2.svg/250px-VinwaterPourbaixdiagram2.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:VinwaterPourbaixdiagram2.svg)

The [Pourbaix diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pourbaix_diagram "Pourbaix diagram") for vanadium in water, which shows the [redox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redox "Redox") potentials between various vanadium species in different oxidation states.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-44)

Vanadium(V) forms various peroxo complexes, most notably in the active site of the vanadium-containing [bromoperoxidase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bromoperoxidase "Bromoperoxidase") enzymes. The species VO(O)2(H 2 O)4+ is stable in acidic solutions. In alkaline solutions, species with 2, 3 and 4 peroxide groups are known; the last forms violet salts with the formula M 3 V(O 2)4 nH 2 O (M= Li, Na, etc.), in which the vanadium has an 8-coordinate dodecahedral structure.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-45)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-46)

Niobates are generated by dissolving the pentoxide in [basic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Base_(chemistry) "Base (chemistry)")[hydroxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydroxide "Hydroxide") solutions or by melting it in alkali metal oxides. Examples are [lithium niobate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithium_niobate "Lithium niobate") (LiNbO 3) and lanthanum niobate (LaNbO 4). In the lithium niobate is a trigonally distorted [perovskite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perovskite_(structure) "Perovskite (structure)")-like structure, whereas the lanthanum niobate contains lone NbO 3−

4 ions.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-HollemanAF-27)

Tantalates, compounds containing [TaO 4]3− or [TaO 3]− are numerous. [Lithium tantalate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithium_tantalate "Lithium tantalate") (LiTaO 3) adopts a perovskite structure. [Lanthanum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lanthanum "Lanthanum") tantalate (LaTaO 4) contains isolated TaO 3−

4 tetrahedra.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-HollemanAF-27)

#### Halides and their derivatives

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_5_element&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Halides and their derivatives")]

Twelve binary [halides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halides "Halides"), compounds with the formula VX n (n=2...5), are known. VI 4, VCl 5, VBr 5, and VI 5 do not exist or are extremely unstable; the only known pure V 5+ halide compound is [VF 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadium_pentafluoride "Vanadium pentafluoride").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-47) In combination with other reagents, [VCl 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadium(IV)_chloride "Vanadium(IV) chloride") is used as a catalyst for polymerization of [dienes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diene "Diene"). Like all binary halides, those of vanadium are [Lewis acidic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_acid "Lewis acid"), especially those of V(IV) and V(V). Many of the halides form octahedral complexes with the formula VX _n_ L 6−_n_ (X= halide; L= other ligand).[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-48)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-49)

Many vanadium [oxyhalides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxyhalide "Oxyhalide") (formula VO m X n) are known.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-50) The oxytrichloride and oxytrifluoride ([VOCl 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadium_oxytrichloride "Vanadium oxytrichloride") and [VOF 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadium(V)_oxytrifluoride "Vanadium(V) oxytrifluoride")) are the most widely studied. Akin to POCl 3, they are volatile, adopt tetrahedral structures in the gas phase, and are Lewis acidic.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-:0-51)

Niobium pentafluoride (NbF 5) is a white solid with a melting point of 79.0°C and [niobium pentachloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niobium_pentachloride "Niobium pentachloride") (NbCl 5) is yellow (see image at left) with a melting point of 203.4°C. The pentachloride is a versatile reagent used to generate the [organometallic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organometallic "Organometallic") compounds, such as [niobocene dichloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niobocene_dichloride "Niobocene dichloride") ((C

5 H

5)

2 NbCl

2).[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-53) The tetrahalides (NbX

4) are dark-coloured polymers with Nb-Nb bonds; for example, the black [hygroscopic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hygroscopic "Hygroscopic") niobium tetrafluoride (NbF 4)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-54) and dark violet niobium tetrachloride (NbCl 4).[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Macintyre-55)

Anionic halide compounds of niobium are well known, owing in part to the [Lewis acidity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_acid "Lewis acid") of the pentahalides. The most important is [NbF 7]2−, an intermediate in the separation of Nb and Ta from the ores.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-ICE-56) This heptafluoride tends to form the oxopentafluoride more readily than does the tantalum compound. Other halide complexes include octahedral [NbCl 6]−:

Nb 2 Cl 10 + 2 Cl− → 2 [NbCl 6]−
As with other metals with low atomic numbers, a variety of reduced halide cluster ions is known, the prime example being [Nb 6 Cl 18]4−.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Greenwood&Earnshaw2nd-32)

Tantalum halides span the oxidation states of +5, +4, and +3. It hydrolyzes readily to an [oxychloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxychloride "Oxychloride"). The lower halides TaX

4 and TaX

3, feature Ta-Ta bonds.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-HollemanAF-27)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Aguly-52)

## Physical properties

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_5_element&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Physical properties")]

The trends in group 5 follow those of the other early d-block groups and reflect the addition of a filled f-shell into the core in passing from the fifth to the sixth period. All the stable members of the group are silvery-blue [refractory metals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refractory_metal "Refractory metal"), though impurities of [carbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon "Carbon"), [nitrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen "Nitrogen"), and oxygen make them brittle.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Greenwood956-29) They all crystallize in the [body-centered cubic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubic_crystal_system "Cubic crystal system") structure at room temperature,[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Greenwood946-57) and dubnium is expected to do the same.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-bcc-58)

### Vanadium

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_5_element&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Vanadium")]

Vanadium is an average-hard, [ductile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ductility "Ductility"), steel-blue metal. It is electrically [conductive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conductive "Conductive") and thermally [insulating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermal_insulation "Thermal insulation"). Some sources describe vanadium as "soft", perhaps because it is ductile, [malleable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malleable "Malleable"), and not [brittle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brittle "Brittle").[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-62)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-63) Vanadium is harder than most metals and steels (see [Hardnesses of the elements (data page)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardnesses_of_the_elements_(data_page) "Hardnesses of the elements (data page)") and [iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron#Mechanical_properties "Iron")). It has good resistance to [corrosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corrosion "Corrosion") and it is stable against [alkalis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkali "Alkali") and [sulfuric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfuric_acid "Sulfuric acid") and [hydrochloric acids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrochloric_acid "Hydrochloric acid").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-HollemanAF-27) It is [oxidized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxidation "Oxidation") in air at about 933[K](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelvin "Kelvin") (660°C, 1220°F), although an oxide [passivation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passivation_(chemistry) "Passivation (chemistry)") layer forms even at room temperature.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-64)

### Niobium

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_5_element&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Niobium")]

Niobium is a [lustrous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lustre_(mineralogy) "Lustre (mineralogy)"), grey, [ductile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ductility "Ductility"), [paramagnetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramagnetism "Paramagnetism")[metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metal "Metal") in group 5 of the [periodic table](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodic_table "Periodic table") (see table), with an electron configuration in the outermost [shells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron_shell "Electron shell") atypical for group 5. Similarly atypical configurations occur in the neighborhood of [ruthenium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruthenium "Ruthenium") (44) and [rhodium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodium "Rhodium") (45).[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-65)

Although it is thought to have a [body-centered cubic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Body-centered_cubic "Body-centered cubic") crystal structure from absolute zero to its melting point, high-resolution measurements of the thermal expansion along the three crystallographic axes reveal anisotropies which are inconsistent with a cubic structure.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-66)

Niobium becomes a [superconductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superconductor "Superconductor") at [cryogenic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryogenics "Cryogenics") temperatures. At atmospheric pressure, it has the highest critical temperature of the elemental superconductors at 9.2[K](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelvin "Kelvin").[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Pein-67) Niobium has the greatest [magnetic penetration depth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superconductor#Meissner_effect "Superconductor") of any element.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Pein-67) In addition, it is one of the three elemental [Type II superconductors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_II_superconductor "Type II superconductor"), along with [vanadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadium "Vanadium") and [technetium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technetium "Technetium"). The superconductive properties are strongly dependent on the purity of the niobium metal.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Moura-68)

When very pure, it is comparatively soft and ductile, but impurities make it harder.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Nowak-69)

The metal has a low [capture cross-section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_capture#Capture_cross_section "Neutron capture") for thermal [neutrons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron "Neutron");[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-70) thus it is used in the nuclear industries where neutron transparent structures are desired.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-71)

### Tantalum

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_5_element&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Tantalum")]

Tantalum is dark (blue-gray),[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-72) dense, ductile, very hard, easily fabricated, and highly conductive of heat and electricity. The metal is renowned for its resistance to [corrosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corrosion "Corrosion") by [acids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acid "Acid"); in fact, at temperatures below 150°[C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celsius "Celsius") tantalum is almost completely immune to attack by the normally aggressive [aqua regia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aqua_regia "Aqua regia"). It can be dissolved with [hydrofluoric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrofluoric_acid "Hydrofluoric acid") or acidic solutions containing the [fluoride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluoride "Fluoride") ion and [sulfur trioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfur_trioxide "Sulfur trioxide"), as well as with a solution of [potassium hydroxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potassium_hydroxide "Potassium hydroxide"). Tantalum's high melting point of 3017°C (boiling point 5458°C) is exceeded among the elements only by [tungsten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tungsten "Tungsten"),[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-desu-73)[rhenium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhenium "Rhenium")[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Zhang2011-74)[osmium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osmium "Osmium"),[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-75) and [carbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon "Carbon").[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-triple-76)

Tantalum exists in two crystalline phases, alpha and beta. The alpha phase is relatively [ductile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ductility "Ductility") and soft; it has [body-centered cubic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Body-centered_cubic "Body-centered cubic") structure ([space group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_group "Space group")_Im3m_, lattice constant _a_ = 0.33058 nm), [Knoop hardness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knoop_hardness_test "Knoop hardness test") 200–400 HN and electrical resistivity 15–60 μΩ⋅cm. The beta phase is hard and brittle; its crystal symmetry is [tetragonal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetragonal "Tetragonal") (space group _P42/mnm_, _a_ = 1.0194 nm, _c_ = 0.5313 nm), Knoop hardness is 1000–1300 HN and electrical resistivity is relatively high at 170–210 μΩ⋅cm. The beta phase is metastable and converts to the alpha phase upon heating to 750–775°C. Bulk tantalum is almost entirely alpha phase, and the beta phase usually exists as thin films[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-77) obtained by magnetron [sputtering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sputtering "Sputtering"), [chemical vapor deposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_vapor_deposition "Chemical vapor deposition") or [electrochemical deposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrochemistry "Electrochemistry") from a [eutectic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eutectic_system "Eutectic system") molten salt solution.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-78)

### Dubnium

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_5_element&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Dubnium")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/7s_electrons_dubnium_relativistic_vs_nonrelativistic.svg/250px-7s_electrons_dubnium_relativistic_vs_nonrelativistic.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:7s_electrons_dubnium_relativistic_vs_nonrelativistic.svg)

Relativistic (solid line) and nonrelativistic (dashed line) radial distribution of the 7s valence electrons in dubnium.

A direct relativistic effect is that as the atomic numbers of elements increase, the innermost electrons begin to revolve faster around the nucleus as a result of an increase of [electromagnetic attraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnetic_attraction "Electromagnetic attraction") between an electron and a nucleus. Similar effects have been found for the outermost s [orbitals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_orbital "Atomic orbital") (and p 1/2 ones, though in dubnium they are not occupied): for example, the 7s orbital contracts by 25% in size and is stabilized by 2.6[eV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronvolt "Electronvolt").[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Haire-59)

A more indirect effect is that the contracted s and p 1/2 orbitals [shield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shielding_effect "Shielding effect") the charge of the nucleus more effectively, leaving less for the outer d and f electrons, which therefore move in larger orbitals. Dubnium is greatly affected by this: unlike the previous group 5 members, its 7s electrons are slightly more difficult to extract than its 6d electrons.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Haire-59)

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/Atomic_orbitals_dubnium.svg/250px-Atomic_orbitals_dubnium.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Atomic_orbitals_dubnium.svg)

Relativistic stabilization of the _n_ s orbitals, the destabilization of the (_n_-1)d orbitals and their spin–orbit splitting for the group 5 elements.

Another effect is the [spin–orbit interaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin%E2%80%93orbit_interaction "Spin–orbit interaction"), particularly spin–orbit splitting, which splits the 6d subshell—the [azimuthal quantum number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azimuthal_quantum_number "Azimuthal quantum number") ℓ of a d shell is 2—into two subshells, with four of the ten orbitals having their ℓ lowered to 3/2 and six raised to 5/2. All ten energy levels are raised; four of them are lower than the other six. (The three 6d electrons normally occupy the lowest energy levels, 6d 3/2.)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Haire-59)

A single ionized atom of dubnium (Db+) should lose a 6d electron compared to a neutral atom; the doubly (Db 2+) or triply (Db 3+) ionized atoms of dubnium should eliminate 7s electrons, unlike its lighter homologs. Despite the changes, dubnium is still expected to have five valence electrons; 7p energy levels have not been shown to influence dubnium and its properties. As the 6d orbitals of dubnium are more destabilized than the 5d ones of tantalum, and Db 3+ is expected to have two 6d, rather than 7s, electrons remaining, the resulting +3 oxidation state is expected to be unstable and even rarer than that of tantalum. The ionization potential of dubnium in its maximum +5 oxidation state should be slightly lower than that of tantalum and the ionic radius of dubnium should increase compared to tantalum; this has a significant effect on dubnium's chemistry.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Haire-59)

Atoms of dubnium in the solid state should arrange themselves in a [body-centered cubic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Body-centered_cubic "Body-centered cubic") configuration, like the previous group 5 elements.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-bcc-58) The predicted density of dubnium is 21.6 g/cm 3.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-density-60)

## Occurrence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_5_element&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Occurrence")]

There are 160 parts per million of vanadium in the Earth's crust, making it the [19th most abundant element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abundance_of_elements_in_Earth's_crust "Abundance of elements in Earth's crust"). [Soil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soil "Soil") contains on average 100 parts per million of vanadium, and [seawater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seawater "Seawater") contains 1.5 parts per billion of vanadium. A typical human contains 285 parts per billion of vanadium. Over 60 vanadium ores are known, including [vanadinite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadinite "Vanadinite"), [patronite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patronite "Patronite"), and [carnotite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnotite "Carnotite").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Emsley-19) There are 20 parts per million of niobium in the Earth's crust, making it the 33rd most abundant element there. Soil contains on average 24 parts per million of niobium, and seawater contains 900 parts per [quadrillion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orders_of_magnitude_(numbers)#1015 "Orders of magnitude (numbers)") of niobium. A typical human contains 21 parts per billion of niobium. Niobium is in the minerals [columbite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbite "Columbite") and [pyrochlore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrochlore "Pyrochlore").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Emsley-19) There are 2 parts per million of tantalum in the Earth's crust, making it the 51st most abundant element there. Soil contains on average 1 to 2 parts per billion of tantalum, and seawater contains 2 parts per trillion of tantalum. A typical human contains 2.9 parts per billion of tantalum. Tantalum is found in the minerals [tantalite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tantalite "Tantalite") and pyrochlore.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Emsley-19) Dubnium does not occur naturally in the Earth's crust, as it has no stable [isotopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotope "Isotope").[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-79)

## Production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_5_element&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Production")]

### Vanadium

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_5_element&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Vanadium")]

Vanadium metal is obtained by a multistep process that begins with roasting crushed ore with [NaCl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_chloride "Sodium chloride") or [Na 2 CO 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_carbonate "Sodium carbonate") at about 850°C to give [sodium metavanadate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_metavanadate "Sodium metavanadate") (NaVO 3). An aqueous extract of this solid is acidified to produce "red cake", a polyvanadate salt, which is reduced with [calcium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calcium "Calcium") metal. As an alternative for small-scale production, vanadium pentoxide is reduced with [hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen "Hydrogen") or [magnesium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnesium "Magnesium"). Many other methods are also used, in all of which vanadium is produced as a [byproduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byproduct "Byproduct") of other processes.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Moskalyk-80) Purification of vanadium is possible by the [crystal bar process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal_bar_process "Crystal bar process") developed by [Anton Eduard van Arkel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anton_Eduard_van_Arkel "Anton Eduard van Arkel") and [Jan Hendrik de Boer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Hendrik_de_Boer "Jan Hendrik de Boer") in 1925. It involves the formation of the metal iodide, in this example [vanadium(III) iodide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadium(III)_iodide "Vanadium(III) iodide"), and the subsequent decomposition to yield pure metal:[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-81)

2 V + 3 I 2⇌ 2 VI 3[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/FerroVanadium.jpg/250px-FerroVanadium.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:FerroVanadium.jpg)

Ferrovanadium chunks

Most vanadium is used as a component of a [steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steel "Steel") alloy called [ferrovanadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrovanadium "Ferrovanadium"). Ferrovanadium is produced directly by reducing a mixture of vanadium oxide, iron oxides and iron in an electric furnace. The vanadium ends up in [pig iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pig_iron "Pig iron") produced from vanadium-bearing magnetite. Depending on the ore used, the slag contains up to 25% of vanadium.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Moskalyk-80)

Approximately 70000 [tonnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonnes "Tonnes") of vanadium ore are produced yearly, with 25000 t of vanadium ore being produced in Russia, 24000 in [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa"), 19000 in China, and 1000 in [Kazakhstan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazakhstan "Kazakhstan"). 7000 t of vanadium metal are produced each year. It is impossible to obtain vanadium by heating its ore with carbon. Instead, vanadium is produced by heating [vanadium oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadium_oxide "Vanadium oxide") with calcium in a [pressure vessel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pressure_vessel "Pressure vessel"). Very high-purity vanadium is produced from a reaction of [vanadium trichloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadium_trichloride "Vanadium trichloride") with magnesium.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Emsley-19)

After the separation from the other minerals, the [mixed oxides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed_oxide "Mixed oxide") of tantalum [Ta 2 O 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tantalum_pentoxide "Tantalum pentoxide") and niobium [Nb 2 O 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niobium_pentoxide "Niobium pentoxide") are obtained. To produce niobium, the first step in the processing is the reaction of the oxides with [hydrofluoric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrofluoric_acid "Hydrofluoric acid"):[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-ICE-56)

Ta 2 O 5 + 14 HF → 2 H 2[TaF 7] + 5 H 2 O Nb 2 O 5 + 10 HF → 2 H 2[NbOF 5] + 3 H 2 O
The first industrial scale separation, developed by [Swiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland "Switzerland")[chemist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemist "Chemist")[de Marignac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Charles_Galissard_de_Marignac "Jean Charles Galissard de Marignac"), exploits the differing [solubilities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solubility "Solubility") of the complex niobium and tantalum [fluorides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluoride "Fluoride"), dipotassium oxypentafluoroniobate monohydrate (K 2[NbOF 5]·H 2 O) and dipotassium heptafluorotantalate (K 2[TaF 7]) in water. Newer processes use the liquid extraction of the fluorides from [aqueous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aqueous "Aqueous") solution by [organic solvents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organic_solvents "Organic solvents") like [cyclohexanone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclohexanone "Cyclohexanone").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-ICE-56) The complex niobium and tantalum fluorides are extracted separately from the [organic solvent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organic_solvent "Organic solvent") with water and either precipitated by the addition of [potassium fluoride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potassium_fluoride "Potassium fluoride") to produce a potassium fluoride complex, or precipitated with [ammonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammonia "Ammonia") as the pentoxide:[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-HollemanAF-27)

H 2[NbOF 5] + 2 KF → K 2[NbOF 5]↓ + 2 HF
Followed by:

2 H 2[NbOF 5] + 10 NH 4 OH → Nb 2 O 5↓ + 10 NH 4 F + 7 H 2 O
Several methods are used for the [reduction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reduction_(chemistry) "Reduction (chemistry)") to metallic niobium. The [electrolysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrolysis "Electrolysis") of a [molten mixture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molten_salt "Molten salt") of K 2[NbOF 5] and [sodium chloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_chloride "Sodium chloride") is one; the other is the reduction of the fluoride with [sodium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium "Sodium"). With this method, a relatively high purity niobium can be obtained. In large scale production, Nb 2 O 5 is reduced with hydrogen or carbon.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-HollemanAF-27) In the [aluminothermic reaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminothermic_reaction "Aluminothermic reaction"), a mixture of [iron oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_oxide "Iron oxide") and niobium oxide is reacted with [aluminium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium "Aluminium"):

3 Nb 2 O 5 + Fe 2 O 3 + 12 Al → 6 Nb + 2 Fe + 6 Al 2 O 3
Small amounts of oxidizers like [sodium nitrate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_nitrate "Sodium nitrate") are added to enhance the reaction. The result is [aluminium oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium_oxide "Aluminium oxide") and [ferroniobium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferroniobium "Ferroniobium"), an alloy of iron and niobium used in steel production.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-84)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-85) Ferroniobium contains between 60 and 70% niobium.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-tesla-86) Without iron oxide, the aluminothermic process is used to produce niobium. Further purification is necessary to reach the grade for [superconductive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superconductive "Superconductive") alloys. [Electron beam melting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron_beam_melting "Electron beam melting") under vacuum is the method used by the two major distributors of niobium.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Aguly-52)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Chou-87)

As of 2013[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_5_element&action=edit), [CBMM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Companhia_Brasileira_de_Metalurgia_e_Minera%C3%A7%C3%A3o "Companhia Brasileira de Metalurgia e Mineração") from Brazil controlled 85 percent of the world's niobium production.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-lucchesi2013-88) The [United States Geological Survey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Geological_Survey "United States Geological Survey") estimates that the production increased from 38,700 tonnes in 2005 to 44,500 tonnes in 2006.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-USGSCS2006-89)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-USGSCS2007-90) Worldwide resources are estimated to be 4.4 million tonnes.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-USGSCS2007-90) During the ten-year period between 1995 and 2005, the production more than doubled, starting from 17,800 tonnes in 1995.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-USGSCS1997-91) Between 2009 and 2011, production was stable at 63,000 tonnes per year,[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-92) with a slight decrease in 2012 to only 50,000 tonnes per year.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-93)

70,000 tonnes of tantalum ore are produced yearly. Brazil produces 90% of tantalum ore, with Canada, Australia, China, and [Rwanda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwanda "Rwanda") also producing the element. The demand for tantalum is around 1,200 tonnes per year.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Emsley-19)

### Dubnium and beyond

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_5_element&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Dubnium and beyond")]

Dubnium is produced synthetically by bombarding [actinides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Actinides "Actinides") with lighter elements.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Emsley-19) To date, no experiments in a [supercollider](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particle_accelerator "Particle accelerator") have been conducted to [synthesize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthetic_element "Synthetic element") the next member of the group, either unpentseptium (Ups) or unpentennium (Upe). As unpentseptium and unpentennium are both late [period 8 elements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Period_8_element "Period 8 element"), it is unlikely that these elements will be synthesized in the near future; current attempts have only been made on elements up to atomic number 127.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-emsley-94)

## Applications

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_5_element&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Applications")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/79/Sink_and_taps_in_the_men%27s_locker_room_3_BW.jpg/250px-Sink_and_taps_in_the_men%27s_locker_room_3_BW.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sink_and_taps_in_the_men's_locker_room_3_BW.jpg)

Niobium is often a minor component in stainless steel.

Vanadium's main application is in alloys, such as [vanadium steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadium_steel "Vanadium steel"). Vanadium alloys are used in [springs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spring_(device) "Spring (device)"), [tools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tools "Tools"), [jet engines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet_engines "Jet engines"), [armor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armor "Armor") plating, and [nuclear reactors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_reactors "Nuclear reactors"). [Vanadium oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadium_oxide "Vanadium oxide") gives ceramics a golden color, and other vanadium compounds are used as [catalysts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalysts "Catalysts") to produce [polymers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polymers "Polymers").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Emsley-19)

Small amounts of niobium are added to [stainless steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stainless_steel "Stainless steel") to improve its quality. Niobium alloys are also used in rocket nozzles because of niobium's high [corrosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corrosion "Corrosion") resistance.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Emsley-19)

Tantalum has four main types of applications. Tantalum is added into objects exposed to high temperatures, in [electronic devices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_devices "Electronic devices"), in [surgical implants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surgical_implant "Surgical implant"), and for handling corrosive substances.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Emsley-19)

Dubnium has no applications due to the difficulty of its synthesis and the very short half-lives of even its longest-lived isotopes.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Karpov_graph-95)

## Biological occurrences

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_5_element&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Biological occurrences")]

Main article: [Vanadium §Biological role](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadium#Biological_role "Vanadium")

Out of the group 5 elements, only vanadium has been identified as playing a role in the biological chemistry of living systems, but even it plays a very limited role in [biology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biology "Biology"), and is more important in ocean environments than on land.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-:0-51)

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/Bluebell_tunicates_Nick_Hobgood.jpg/250px-Bluebell_tunicates_Nick_Hobgood.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bluebell_tunicates_Nick_Hobgood.jpg)

[Tunicates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunicate "Tunicate") such as this bluebell tunicate contain vanadium as [vanabins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanabins "Vanabins").

Vanadium, essential to [ascidians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascidiacea "Ascidiacea") and [tunicates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunicate "Tunicate") as [vanabins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanabins "Vanabins"), has been known in the [blood cells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood_cell "Blood cell") of [Ascidiacea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascidiacea "Ascidiacea") (sea squirts) since 1911,[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-henze1911-96)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-michibata2002-97) in concentrations of vanadium in their blood more than 100 times higher than the concentration of vanadium in the seawater around them. Several species of macrofungi accumulate vanadium (up to 500 mg/kg in dry weight).[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-98) Vanadium-dependent [bromoperoxidase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bromoperoxidase "Bromoperoxidase") generates organobromine compounds in a number of species of marine [algae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algae "Algae").[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-99)

[Rats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rat "Rat") and [chickens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicken "Chicken") are also known to require vanadium in very small amounts and deficiencies result in reduced growth and impaired [reproduction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reproduction "Reproduction").[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-100) Vanadium is a relatively controversial [dietary supplement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dietary_supplement "Dietary supplement"), primarily for increasing [insulin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insulin "Insulin") sensitivity[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-101) and [body-building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Body-building "Body-building"). [Vanadyl sulfate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadyl_sulfate "Vanadyl sulfate") may improve glucose control in people with [type 2 diabetes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_2_diabetes "Type 2 diabetes").[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Badmaev-102) In addition, decavanadate and oxovanadates are species that potentially have many biological activities and that have been successfully used as tools in the comprehension of several biochemical processes.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-103)

## Toxicity and precautions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Group_5_element&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Toxicity and precautions")]

Pure vanadium is not known to be toxic. However, [vanadium pentoxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadium_pentoxide "Vanadium pentoxide") causes severe irritation of the eyes, nose, and throat.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Emsley-19) Tetravalent [VOSO 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadyl_sulfate "Vanadyl sulfate") has been reported to be at least 5 times more toxic than trivalent V 2 O 3.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-104) The [Occupational Safety and Health Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occupational_Safety_and_Health_Administration "Occupational Safety and Health Administration") has set an exposure limit of 0.05 mg/m 3 for vanadium pentoxide dust and 0.1 mg/m 3 for vanadium pentoxide fumes in workplace air for an 8-hour workday, 40-hour work week.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-OSHA-105) The [National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institute_for_Occupational_Safety_and_Health "National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health") has recommended that 35 mg/m 3 of vanadium be considered immediately dangerous to life and health, that is, likely to cause permanent health problems or death.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-OSHA-105) Vanadium compounds are poorly absorbed through the gastrointestinal system. Inhalation of vanadium and vanadium compounds results primarily in adverse effects on the respiratory system.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-106)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-ress-107)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-108) Quantitative data are, however, insufficient to derive a subchronic or chronic inhalation reference dose. Other effects have been reported after oral or inhalation exposures on blood parameters,[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-109)[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-110) liver,[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-111) neurological development,[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-112) and other organs[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-113) in rats.

There is little evidence that vanadium or vanadium compounds are reproductive toxins or [teratogens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teratogen "Teratogen"). Vanadium pentoxide was reported to be carcinogenic in male rats and in male and female mice by inhalation in an NTP study,[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-ress-107) although the interpretation of the results has recently been disputed.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-114) The carcinogenicity of vanadium has not been determined by the [United States Environmental Protection Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Environmental_Protection_Agency "United States Environmental Protection Agency").[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-115) Vanadium traces in [diesel fuels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diesel_fuel "Diesel fuel") are the main fuel component in [high temperature corrosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_temperature_corrosion "High temperature corrosion"). During combustion, vanadium oxidizes and reacts with sodium and sulfur, yielding [vanadate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadate "Vanadate") compounds with melting points as low as 530°C, which attack the [passivation layer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passivation_(chemistry) "Passivation (chemistry)") on steel and render it susceptible to corrosion. The solid vanadium compounds also abrade engine components.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-116)[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-117)

Niobium has no known biological role. While niobium dust is an eye and skin irritant[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Emsley-19) and a potential fire hazard, elemental niobium on a larger scale is physiologically inert (and thus hypoallergenic) and harmless. It is often used in jewelry and has been tested for use in some medical implants.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-118)[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-119) Niobium and its compounds thought to be slightly toxic. Short- and long-term exposure to niobates and niobium chloride, two water-soluble chemicals, have been tested in rats. Rats treated with a single injection of niobium pentachloride or niobates show a [median lethal dose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Median_lethal_dose "Median lethal dose") (LD 50) between 10 and 100 mg/kg.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Haley-120)[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-121)[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-122) For oral administration the toxicity is lower; a study with rats yielded a LD 50 after seven days of 940 mg/kg.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Haley-120)

Compounds containing tantalum are rarely encountered in the laboratory, and it and its compounds rarely cause injury, and when they do, the injuries are normally rashes.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Emsley-19) The metal is highly [biocompatible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biocompatible "Biocompatible")[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-Gerald_L._Burke_1940-123) and is used for body [implants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Implant_(medicine) "Implant (medicine)") and [coatings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coating "Coating"), therefore attention may be focused on other elements or the physical nature of the [chemical compound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_compound "Chemical compound").[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-124) People can be exposed to tantalum in the workplace by breathing it in, skin contact, or eye contact. The [Occupational Safety and Health Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occupational_Safety_and_Health_Administration "Occupational Safety and Health Administration") (OSHA) has set the legal limit ([permissible exposure limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permissible_exposure_limit "Permissible exposure limit")) for tantalum exposure in the workplace as 5 mg/m 3 over an 8-hour workday. The [National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institute_for_Occupational_Safety_and_Health "National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health") (NIOSH) has set a [recommended exposure limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recommended_exposure_limit "Recommended exposure limit") of 5 mg/m 3 over an 8-hour workday and a short-term limit of 10 mg/m 3. At levels of 2500 mg/m 3, tantalum is [immediately dangerous to life and health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IDLH "IDLH").[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_element#cite_note-125)

# Chem 13 News Magazine Online Archives

![Image 1: Chem 13 News magazine covers over the years](https://uwaterloo.ca/centre-advanced-science-education/sites/default/files/styles/large/public/uploads/images/chem13mag-banner2_copy14-1000x625.jpg?itok=4HjwAln-)

From 1968 to 2022 - more than 50 years! - the Department of Chemistry at the University of Waterloo published an informal magazine for teachers of introductory chemistry courses at the high school and year one college levels.

Our archives present the top 100 most accessed articles since 2012.

# Berzelius' World (1815-1844)

![Image 1: Highlight of elements discovered during the 1815 to 1844 time period](https://uwaterloo.ca/chemistry/sites/default/files/styles/large/public/uploads/images/berzelius_revised.jpg?itok=K9micYBk)

[](https://uwaterloo.ca/chemistry/community-outreach/timeline-of-elements/berzelius-world-1815-1844)The next step in preparing the way for the Periodic Table was the development of exact analytical methods to give precise atomic weights. Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius (1779-1848) is widely credited with establishing several of these standard methods, while raising the sophistication of laboratory chemistry to new heights during the first half of the nineteenth century.

Berzelius’ laboratory skill and imagination were legendary: In 1818, he determined precise atomic weights for 45 of the known 49 elements, and by the end of his career he had characterized several new chemical elements, including thorium, silicon, cerium and zirconium. He also instituted the modern method of chemical symbols, using simple alphabet letters to represent chemical elements. "There is no living chemist to whom analytical chemistry lies under greater obligation than to Berzelius, whether we consider the number or the exactness of the analyses which he has made." – Scottish biographer Thomas Thomson (1773-1852).

Explore the elements by decade:

*   [1815-1824](https://uwaterloo.ca/chemistry/community-outreach/timeline-of-elements/berzelius-world-1815-1844#1815): Selenium, Cadmium, Silicon
*   [1825-1834](https://uwaterloo.ca/chemistry/community-outreach/timeline-of-elements/berzelius-world-1815-1844#1825): Aluminum, Bromine, Thorium
*   [1835-1844](https://uwaterloo.ca/chemistry/community-outreach/timeline-of-elements/berzelius-world-1815-1844#1835): Lanthanum, Terbium, Erbium, Ruthenium

Read more about the ["Berzelius' World"](https://uwaterloo.ca/chem13-news-magazine/september-2019/feature/berzelius-world) in the _Chem 13 News_ article by James Marshall.

**Marsden State High School**

 Waterford West, Queensland, Australia

 Teacher: Daniel Bischa

 Artist: Jaceb Blake

The following aspects of selenium are represented:

*   Moon: Selenium was named after the Greek word for moon.
*   Red: One allotrope of selenium is red (the other grey) and it is used in glass to give a red colour or balance the colour from other impurities.
*   Jöns Jacob Berzelius: Discovered selenium in 1817.
*   Selenium rectifier: A common early use for selenium.
*   Paint.net was used to blend the images that had licences that allowed re-use with modification.

![Image 3: Cadmium element tile design by Woodland Christian High School](https://uwaterloo.ca/chemistry/sites/default/files/uploads/images/cadmium-48-woodland-christian-high-school-3000x2319.jpg)

### [](https://uwaterloo.ca/chemistry/community-outreach/timeline-of-elements/berzelius-world-1815-1844)Cadmium, 48

**Woodland Christian High School**

 Breslau, Ontario, Canada

 Teacher: Marianne Bruinsma

 Artist: Olivia Lise

Friedrich Stromeyer, a German chemist discovered cadmium in 1817. Cadmium is used commonly for rechargeable batteries. Cadmium is a metal. In 1912, a Japanese mining company released cadmium into the Jinzū River killing fish and causing Itai-itai disease. Now know for its toxicity, Van Gogh's "Starry Night" and "Sunflower" painting likely used cadmium as a pigment for reds, oranges and yellows. My artwork was made digitally using Paint Tool Sai and my digital art tablet. I did traditional concept sketches, but ended up doing it digitally based on the sketches.

![Image 4: Silicon element tile design by St. John's Kilmarnock School](https://uwaterloo.ca/chemistry/sites/default/files/uploads/images/silicon-14-st-johns-kilmarnock-school-3000x2319.jpg)

**St. John's Kilmarnock School**

 Breslau, Ontario, Canada

 Teacher: Sarah Regli

 Artist: Max Dai

Silicon is a semiconducting material that serves as the basis for many electronic devices. The inspiration for the artwork was a circuit board, seemingly so simple, yet so powerful and life-changing in a technological world. The colour scheme used is to represent the first preparation and characterization of silicon by Swedish chemist Jöns Jakob Berzelius in 1823.

**Tannum Sands State High School**

 Tannum Sands, Queensland, Australia

 Teacher: Lisa Mazzer

 Artists: Hannah Brooke, Lhea Hermosa, Sarah Leu

Aluminium is extracted from its ore bauxite. The use of aluminium exceeds that of any other metal except iron as its properties make it suitable for many design and fabrication purposes. It is soft and lightweight with a dull silvery appearance, non-toxic, non-magnetic and non-sparking. Aluminium atoms have 13 electrons which is why it is element 13. In artwork design, the discoverer of aluminium, Hans Christian Østerd, who first successfully extracted from bauxite in 1825, was made prominent. The background is an old village from the 1820s and the atomic number and symbol are included.

 Belo Horizonte, MG, Brasil

 Teacher: Alfredo Luis Mateus

 Artists: Fernanda Narciso Dias, Larissa Venâncio de Faria, Maria Eduarda Alves Viana

We discussed in class about the periodic table and the element timeline. We brainstormed ideas about bromine. The main aspects selected were: its use on photographic film, on medicines and pesticides, the discovery, its occurrence in sea water and algae, and the bad smell that gave bromine its name. The students made drawings that were scanned and colorized on the computer. This was a very collaborative work, with the help of our art teacher.

 Teacher: Maria Elisabeth Sletvold

 Artist: Leksvik Kjemi 1

Norwegian priest Morten Thrane Esmark found some black mineral samples on Løvøya, which he couldn't identify. His father, a professor of mineralogy, sent the samples to Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius. Berzelius was credited for discovering the element thorium in these mineral samples. Thorium is named after Thor, the Norse god of Thunder, also depicted in the artwork.

**Boston Latin Academy**

 Boston, Massachusetts, USA

 Teacher: Katherine Fogarty

 Artist: Labonno Ranga

While researching about the discovery of lanthanum, I came across an experiment that Carl G. Mosander conducted looking for impurities within samples of cerium. I discovered that he slowly poured dilute nitric acid onto cerium nitrate in order to expose the possible impurities existing in the samples of cerium. He found a new substance in the test tube which he later named lanthanum. I thought what better way to portray the history of the finding of lanthanum than to illustrate the experiment that had unintentionally found the element.

![Image 9: Terbium element tile design by Ankeny Centennial High School](https://uwaterloo.ca/chemistry/sites/default/files/uploads/images/terbium-65-ankeny-centennial-high-school-3000x2319.jpg)

**Ankeny Centennial High School**

 Ankeny, Iowa, USA

 Teacher: Mark Hey

 Artist: Jordan Su

Terbium was discovered in 1843 by Carl Gustav, and has 26 isotopes. Terbium is a rare earth metal, but it's still found in a lot of items that are used every day. Terbium is found in speakers, earbuds, laser pointers, x-rays, low energy light bulbs and medical x-rays. Because of its many uses, I tried to put as many of its uses into my terbium piece. In addition, an alloy of terbium, dysprosium, and iron forms the basis of "flat" speakers, and its ability to manipulate magnetic fields is what gives terbium this ability; also portrayed in my art.

 Wigan, Greater Manchester, United Kingdom

In our research we found that erbium, a rare earth metal, was discovered in Ytterby, a small town located in Sweden, by Carl Gustav Mosander. Yttrium, ytterbium and terbium were also discovered here. The artwork shows a sign post, Mosander, and a laser as it has found use in lasers and fiber optics due to its unique optical properties. The colour scheme of grey and pink reflect the pale silver colouration of the element and its naturally occurring form of erbium oxide which is a pink powder used to pigment glass or glazes.

Discovered by Karl Klaus in 1844, ruthenium is a precious metal used in alloys and only found in the Ural Mountains (represented by the background mountain scene). In 2018 researchers at University of Minnesota identified that it is the fourth element that displays ferromagnetic properties (represented by the horseshoe magnet) at room temperature. The Sun represents one of its current uses in solar panels.
