In 1871, the existence of gallium was first predicted by Russian chemist [Dmitri Mendeleev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dmitri_Mendeleev "Dmitri Mendeleev"), who named it "[eka-aluminium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mendeleev's_predicted_elements "Mendeleev's predicted elements")" from its position in his [periodic table](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodic_table "Periodic table"). He also predicted several properties of eka-aluminium that correspond closely to the real properties of gallium, such as its [density](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Density "Density"), [melting point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melting_point "Melting point"), oxide character, and bonding in chloride.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-48)

Comparison between Mendeleev's 1871 predictions and the known properties of gallium[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-GreenwoodEarnshaw2nd-17):217| Property | Mendeleev's predictions | Actual properties |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Atomic weight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_weight "Atomic weight") | ~68 | 69.723 |
| Density | 5.9 g/cm 3 | 5.904 g/cm 3 |
| Melting point | Low | 29.767°C |
| Formula of oxide | M 2 O 3 | Ga 2 O 3 |
| Density of oxide | 5.5 g/cm 3 | 5.88 g/cm 3 |
| Nature of hydroxide | amphoteric | amphoteric |

Mendeleev further predicted that eka-aluminium would be discovered by means of the [spectroscope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectroscope "Spectroscope"), and that metallic eka-aluminium would dissolve slowly in both acids and alkalis and would not react with air. He also predicted that M 2 O 3 would dissolve in acids to give MX 3 salts, that eka-[aluminium salts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium_salt "Aluminium salt") would form basic salts, that eka-aluminium sulfate should form [alums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alum "Alum"), and that anhydrous MCl 3 should have a greater volatility than ZnCl 2. All of these predictions were later proven accurate.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-GreenwoodEarnshaw2nd-17):217

Gallium was discovered using [spectroscopy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectroscopy "Spectroscopy") by French chemist [Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul-%C3%89mile_Lecoq_de_Boisbaudran "Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran") in 1875 from its characteristic spectrum (two [violet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violet_(color) "Violet (color)") lines) in a sample of [sphalerite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphalerite "Sphalerite").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Bois-49)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-50) Later that year, Lecoq obtained the free metal by [electrolysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrolysis "Electrolysis") of the [hydroxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium(III)_hydroxide "Gallium(III) hydroxide") in [potassium hydroxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potassium_hydroxide "Potassium hydroxide") solution.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Weeks-51)

He named the element "gallia", from [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin "Latin")_Gallia_ meaning '[Gaul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaul "Gaul")', a name for his native land of France. It was later claimed that, in a multilingual [pun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pun "Pun") of a kind favoured by men of science in the 19th century, he had also named gallium after himself: _Le coq_ is French for 'the rooster', and the Latin word for 'rooster' is _gallus_. In an 1877 article, Lecoq denied this conjecture.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Weeks-51)

Originally, de Boisbaudran determined the density of gallium as 4.7 g/cm 3, the only property that failed to match Mendeleev's predictions; Mendeleev then wrote to him and suggested that he should remeasure the density, and de Boisbaudran then obtained the correct value of 5.9 g/cm 3, that Mendeleev had predicted exactly.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-GreenwoodEarnshaw2nd-17):217

From its discovery in 1875 until the era of semiconductors, the primary uses of gallium were high-temperature thermometrics and metal alloys with unusual properties of stability or ease of melting (some such being liquid at room temperature).

The development of [gallium arsenide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium_arsenide "Gallium arsenide") as a [direct bandgap semiconductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_and_indirect_band_gaps "Direct and indirect band gaps") in the 1960s ushered in the most important stage in the applications of gallium.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-GreenwoodEarnshaw2nd-17):221 In the late 1960s, the [electronics industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronics_industry "Electronics industry") started using gallium on a commercial scale to fabricate light emitting diodes, [photovoltaics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photovoltaics "Photovoltaics") and semiconductors, while the metals industry used it[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-petkof78-52) to reduce the melting point of [alloys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alloys "Alloys").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-azomga-53)

First blue [gallium nitride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium_nitride "Gallium nitride") LED were developed in 1971–1973, but they were feeble.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-54) Only in the early 1990s [Shuji Nakamura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuji_Nakamura "Shuji Nakamura") managed to combine GaN with [indium gallium nitride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indium_gallium_nitride "Indium gallium nitride") and develop the modern blue LED, now making the basis of ubiquitous white LEDs, which [Nichia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nichia "Nichia") commercialized in 1993. He and two other Japanese scientists received a [Nobel in Physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physics "Nobel Prize in Physics") in 2014 for this work.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-55)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-56)

Global gallium production slowly grew from several tens of t/year in the 1970s til ca. 2010, when it passed 100 t/yr and rapidly accelerated,[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-57) by 2024 reaching about 450 t/yr.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-58)

## Occurrence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gallium&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Occurrence")]

Gallium does not exist as a free element in the Earth's crust, and the few high-content minerals, such as gallite (CuGaS 2), are too rare to serve as a primary source.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Frenzel-2016b-59) The abundance [in the Earth's crust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth#Chemical_composition "Earth") is approximately 16.9[ppm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parts_per_million "Parts per million"). It is the 34th most abundant element in the crust.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Burton-60) This is comparable to the crustal abundances of [lead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead "Lead"), [cobalt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobalt "Cobalt"), and [niobium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niobium "Niobium"). Yet unlike these elements, gallium does not form its own ore deposits with concentrations of > 0.1 wt.% in ore. Rather it occurs at trace concentrations similar to the crustal value in zinc ores,[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Frenzel-2016b-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-FrenzelMeta-2016-61) and at somewhat higher values (~ 50 ppm) in aluminium ores, from both of which it is extracted as a by-product. This lack of independent deposits is due to gallium's geochemical behaviour, showing no strong enrichment in the processes relevant to the formation of most ore deposits.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Frenzel-2016b-59)

The [United States Geological Survey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Geological_Survey "United States Geological Survey") (USGS) estimates that more than 1 million tons of gallium is contained in known reserves of bauxite and zinc ores.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-USGSCS2008-62)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-USGSCS2006-63) Some coal [flue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flue "Flue")[dusts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dust "Dust") contain small quantities of gallium, typically less than 1% by weight.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-64)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-65)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-66)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-67) However, these amounts are not extractable without mining of the host materials (see below). Thus, the availability of gallium is fundamentally determined by the rate at which bauxite, zinc ores, and coal are extracted.

## Production and availability

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gallium&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Production and availability")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c0/6N_Gallium_sealed_in_vacuum_ampoule.jpg/250px-6N_Gallium_sealed_in_vacuum_ampoule.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:6N_Gallium_sealed_in_vacuum_ampoule.jpg)

99.9999% (6N) gallium sealed in vacuum ampoule

Gallium is produced exclusively as a [by-product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/By-product "By-product") during the processing of the ores of other metals. Its main source material is [bauxite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bauxite#Source_of_gallium "Bauxite"), the chief ore of [aluminium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium "Aluminium"), but minor amounts are also extracted from sulfidic zinc ores ([sphalerite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphalerite "Sphalerite") being the main host mineral).[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Frenzel-2016a-68)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-FrenzelMeta-2016-61) In the past, certain coals were an important source.

During the processing of [bauxite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bauxite "Bauxite") to [alumina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium_oxide "Aluminium oxide") in the [Bayer process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayer_process "Bayer process"), gallium accumulates in the [sodium hydroxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_hydroxide "Sodium hydroxide") liquor. From this it can be extracted by a variety of methods. The most recent is the use of [ion-exchange resin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ion-exchange_resin "Ion-exchange resin").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Frenzel-2016a-68) Achievable extraction efficiencies critically depend on the original concentration in the feed bauxite. At a typical feed concentration of 50 ppm, about 15% of the contained gallium is extractable.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Frenzel-2016a-68) The remainder reports to the [red mud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_mud "Red mud") and [aluminium hydroxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium_hydroxide "Aluminium hydroxide") streams. Gallium is removed from the ion-exchange resin in solution. Electrolysis then gives gallium metal. For [semiconductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor "Semiconductor") use, it is further purified with [zone melting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zone_melting "Zone melting") or single-crystal extraction from a melt ([Czochralski process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czochralski_process "Czochralski process")). Purities of 99.9999% are routinely achieved and commercially available.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Moskalyk-69)

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/Bauxite_Jamaica_1984.jpg/250px-Bauxite_Jamaica_1984.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bauxite_Jamaica_1984.jpg)

Bauxite mine in [Jamaica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamaica "Jamaica") (1984)

Its by-product status means that gallium production is constrained by the amount of bauxite, sulfidic zinc ores (and coal) extracted per year. Therefore, its availability needs to be discussed in terms of supply potential. The supply potential of a by-product is defined as that amount which is economically extractable from its host materials _per year_ under current market conditions (i.e. technology and price).[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-70) Reserves and resources are not relevant for by-products, since they _cannot_ be extracted independently from the main-products.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-71) Recent estimates put the supply potential of gallium at a minimum of 2,100 t/yr from bauxite, 85 t/yr from sulfidic zinc ores, and potentially 590 t/yr from coal.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Frenzel-2016a-68) These figures are significantly greater than current production (375 t in 2016).[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-72) Thus, major future increases in the by-product production of gallium will be possible without significant increases in production costs or price. The average price for low-grade gallium was $120 per kilogram in 2016 and $135–140 per kilogram in 2017.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-usgs2018-73)

In 2017, the world's production of low-grade gallium was c.315 tons—a decrease of 15% from 2016. China, Japan, South Korea, Russia, and Ukraine were the leading producers, while Germany ceased primary production of gallium in 2016. The yield of high-purity gallium was ca. 180 tons, mostly originating from China, Japan, Slovakia, UK and U.S. The 2017 world annual production capacity was estimated at 730 tons for low-grade and 320 tons for refined gallium.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-usgs2018-73)

China produced c.250 tons of low-grade gallium in 2016 and c.300 tons in 2017. It also accounted for more than half of global [LED](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light-emitting_diode "Light-emitting diode") production.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-usgs2018-73)As of July 2023,[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gallium&action=edit) China accounted for between 80%[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-74) and 95% of its production.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-75)As of August 2023,[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gallium&action=edit) China produced 80% of the world's gallium, according to the Critical Raw Materials Alliance. China started restricting exports of both materials. They are key to the semiconductor industry and there is a 'chip war' between China and the US.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-76) In 2025, [Rio Tinto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_Tinto_(corporation) "Rio Tinto (corporation)") and [Indium Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indium_Corporation "Indium Corporation") partnered to mine the first primary gallium in North America.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-77) In July 2025, the US think tank [Center for Strategic and International Studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_for_Strategic_and_International_Studies "Center for Strategic and International Studies") wrote: "China is increasingly weaponizing its chokehold over critical minerals amid intensifying economic and technological competition with the United States. The critical mineral gallium, which is crucial to defense industry supply chains and new energy technologies, has been at the front line of China's strategy."[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-csis-78) In 2024, China produced 98 percent of the world's low-purity gallium (source: [United States Geological Survey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Geological_Survey "United States Geological Survey") (USGS)).[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-csis-78)

## Applications

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gallium&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Applications")]

Semiconductor applications dominate the commercial demand for gallium, accounting for 98% of the total. The next major application is for [gadolinium gallium garnets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gadolinium_gallium_garnet "Gadolinium gallium garnet").[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Ullmann-79) As of 2022, 44% of world use went to light fixtures and 36% to integrated circuits, with smaller shares equal to ~7% going to photovoltaics and magnets each.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-80)

### Semiconductors

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gallium&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Semiconductors")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/31/Blue_LED_and_Reflection.jpg/250px-Blue_LED_and_Reflection.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Blue_LED_and_Reflection.jpg)

Gallium-based blue LEDs

Extremely high-purity (>99.9999%) gallium is commercially available to serve the [semiconductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor "Semiconductor") industry. [Gallium arsenide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium_arsenide "Gallium arsenide") (GaAs) and [gallium nitride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium_nitride "Gallium nitride") (GaN) used in electronic components represented about 98% of the gallium consumption in the United States in 2007. About 66% of semiconductor gallium is used in the U.S. in integrated circuits (mostly gallium arsenide), such as the manufacture of ultra-high-speed logic chips and [MESFETs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MESFET "MESFET") for low-noise microwave preamplifiers in cell phones. About 20% of this gallium is used in [optoelectronics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optoelectronic "Optoelectronic").[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-USGSCS2008-62)

Worldwide, gallium arsenide makes up 95% of the annual global gallium consumption.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Moskalyk-69) It amounted to $7.5 billion in 2016, with 53% originating from cell phones, 27% from wireless communications, and the rest from automotive, consumer, fiber-optic, and military applications. The recent increase in GaAs consumption is mostly related to the emergence of [3G](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3G "3G") and [4G](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4G "4G")[smartphones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smartphone "Smartphone"), which employ up to 10 times the amount of GaAs in older models.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-usgs2018-73)

Gallium arsenide and gallium nitride can also be found in a variety of optoelectronic devices which had a market share of $15.3 billion in 2015 and $18.5 billion in 2016.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-usgs2018-73)[Aluminium gallium arsenide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium_gallium_arsenide "Aluminium gallium arsenide") (AlGaAs) is used in high-power infrared laser diodes. The semiconductors gallium nitride and [indium gallium nitride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indium_gallium_nitride "Indium gallium nitride") are used in blue and violet optoelectronic devices, mostly [laser diodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laser_diode "Laser diode") and [light-emitting diodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light-emitting_diode "Light-emitting diode"). For example, gallium nitride 405 nm diode lasers are used as a violet light source for higher-density [Blu-ray Disc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blu-ray_Disc "Blu-ray Disc") compact data disc drives.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-81)

Other major applications of gallium nitride are cable television transmission, commercial wireless infrastructure, power electronics, and satellites. The GaN radio frequency device market alone was estimated at $370 million in 2016 and $420 million in 2016.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-usgs2018-73)

[Multijunction photovoltaic cells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multijunction_photovoltaic_cell "Multijunction photovoltaic cell"), developed for [satellite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite "Satellite") power applications, are made by [molecular-beam epitaxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molecular-beam_epitaxy "Molecular-beam epitaxy") or [metalorganic vapour-phase epitaxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metalorganic_vapour-phase_epitaxy "Metalorganic vapour-phase epitaxy") of [thin films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thin_film "Thin film") of gallium arsenide, [indium gallium phosphide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indium_gallium_phosphide "Indium gallium phosphide"), or [indium gallium arsenide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indium_gallium_arsenide "Indium gallium arsenide"). The [Mars Exploration Rovers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_Exploration_Rover "Mars Exploration Rover") and several satellites use triple-junction gallium arsenide on germanium cells.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-82) Gallium is also a component in [photovoltaic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photovoltaic "Photovoltaic") compounds (such as copper indium gallium selenium sulfide Cu(In,Ga)(Se,S)2) used in solar panels as a cost-efficient alternative to [crystalline silicon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystalline_silicon "Crystalline silicon").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-83)

### Galinstan and other alloys

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gallium&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Galinstan and other alloys")]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/Galinstan_on_glass.jpg/250px-Galinstan_on_glass.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Galinstan_on_glass.jpg)

Galinstan easily wetting a piece of ordinary glass

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/Gallium_alloy_3D_prints_%2826519727708%29.jpg/250px-Gallium_alloy_3D_prints_%2826519727708%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gallium_alloy_3D_prints_(26519727708).jpg)

Owing to their low melting points, gallium and its alloys can be shaped into various 3D forms using [3D printing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3D_printing "3D printing") and [additive manufacturing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Additive_manufacturing "Additive manufacturing").

Gallium readily [alloys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alloy "Alloy") with most metals, and is used as an ingredient in [low-melting alloys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low-melting_alloy "Low-melting alloy"). The nearly [eutectic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eutectic "Eutectic") alloy of gallium, [indium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indium "Indium"), and [tin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tin "Tin") is a room temperature liquid used in medical thermometers. This alloy, with the trade-name _[Galinstan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galinstan "Galinstan")_ (with the "-stan" referring to the tin, _stannum_ in Latin), has a low melting point of −19°C (−2.2°F).[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-84) this family of alloys can also be used to cool computer chips in place of water, and as a replacement for [thermal paste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermal_grease "Thermal grease") in high-performance computing.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-85)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-86) Gallium alloys have been evaluated as substitutes for mercury [dental amalgams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dental_amalgam "Dental amalgam"), but these materials have yet to see wide acceptance. Liquid alloys containing mostly gallium and indium have been found to precipitate gaseous CO 2 into solid carbon and are being researched as potential methodologies for [carbon capture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_capture_and_storage "Carbon capture and storage") and possibly [carbon removal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_dioxide_removal "Carbon dioxide removal").[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-87)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-88)

Because gallium [wets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wetting "Wetting") glass or [porcelain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porcelain "Porcelain"), gallium can be used to create brilliant [mirrors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirror "Mirror"). When the wetting action of gallium-alloys is not desired (as in Galinstan glass thermometers), the glass must be protected with a transparent layer of [gallium(III) oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium(III)_oxide "Gallium(III) oxide").[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-89)

Due to their high [surface tension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_tension "Surface tension") and [deformability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluid_mechanics "Fluid mechanics"),[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-90) gallium-based liquid metals can be used to create [actuators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Actuator "Actuator") by controlling the surface tension.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-91)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-92)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-93) Researchers have demonstrated the potentials of using liquid metal actuators as [artificial muscle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_muscles "Artificial muscles") in robotic actuation.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-94)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-95)

The [plutonium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plutonium "Plutonium") used in [nuclear weapon pits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plutonium_pit "Plutonium pit") is stabilized in the [δ phase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allotropes_of_plutonium "Allotropes of plutonium") and made machinable by [alloying with gallium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plutonium%E2%80%93gallium_alloy "Plutonium–gallium alloy").[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-96)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-97)

### Biomedical applications

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gallium&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Biomedical applications")]

Although gallium has no natural function in biology, gallium ions interact with processes in the body in a manner similar to [iron(III)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferric#Ferric_iron_and_life "Ferric"). Because these processes include [inflammation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inflammation "Inflammation"), a marker for many disease states, several gallium salts are used (or are in development) as [pharmaceuticals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharmaceutical_drug "Pharmaceutical drug") and [radiopharmaceuticals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiopharmacology "Radiopharmacology") in medicine. Interest in the anticancer properties of gallium emerged when it was discovered that 67 Ga(III) citrate injected in tumor-bearing animals localized to sites of tumor. Clinical trials have shown gallium nitrate to have antineoplastic activity against non-Hodgkin's lymphoma and urothelial cancers. A new generation of gallium-ligand complexes such as tris(8-quinolinolato)gallium(III) (KP46) and gallium maltolate has emerged.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-98)[Gallium nitrate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium_nitrate "Gallium nitrate") (brand name Ganite) has been used as an intravenous pharmaceutical to treat [hypercalcemia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypercalcemia "Hypercalcemia") associated with tumor [metastasis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metastasis "Metastasis") to bones. Gallium is thought to interfere with [osteoclast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osteoclast "Osteoclast") function, and the therapy may be effective when other treatments have failed.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-99)[Gallium maltolate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium_maltolate "Gallium maltolate"), an oral, highly absorbable form of gallium(III) ion, is an anti-proliferative to pathologically proliferating cells, particularly cancer cells and some bacteria that accept it in place of ferric iron (Fe 3+). Researchers are conducting clinical and preclinical trials on this compound as a potential treatment for a number of cancers, infectious diseases, and inflammatory diseases.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-100)

When gallium ions are mistakenly taken up in place of iron(III) by bacteria such as _[Pseudomonas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudomonas "Pseudomonas")_, the ions interfere with respiration, and the bacteria die. This happens because iron is redox-active, allowing the transfer of electrons during respiration, while gallium is redox-inactive.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-101)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-102)

A complex [amine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amine "Amine")-[phenol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phenol "Phenol") Ga(III) compound MR045 is selectively toxic to parasites resistant to [chloroquine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chloroquine "Chloroquine"), a common drug against [malaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaria "Malaria"). Both the Ga(III) complex and chloroquine act by inhibiting crystallization of [hemozoin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hemozoin "Hemozoin"), a disposal product formed from the digestion of blood by the parasites.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-103)[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-104)

#### Radiogallium salts

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gallium&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Radiogallium salts")]

[Gallium-67](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium-67 "Gallium-67")[salts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_(chemistry) "Salt (chemistry)") such as gallium [citrate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citrate "Citrate") and gallium [nitrate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrate "Nitrate") are used as [radiopharmaceutical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiopharmaceutical "Radiopharmaceutical") agents in the [nuclear medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_medicine "Nuclear medicine") imaging known as [gallium scan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium_scan "Gallium scan"). The [radioactive isotope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radionuclide "Radionuclide")67 Ga is used, and the compound or salt of gallium is unimportant. The body handles Ga 3+ in many ways as though it were Fe 3+, and the ion is bound (and concentrates) in areas of inflammation, such as infection, and in areas of rapid cell division. This allows such sites to be imaged by nuclear scan techniques.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Nordberg-105)

[Gallium-68](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium-68 "Gallium-68"), a positron emitter with a half-life of 68 min, is now used as a diagnostic radionuclide in PET-CT when linked to pharmaceutical preparations such as [DOTATOC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DOTATOC "DOTATOC"), a [somatostatin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somatostatin "Somatostatin") analogue used for [neuroendocrine tumors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuroendocrine_tumors "Neuroendocrine tumors") investigation, and [DOTA-TATE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DOTA-TATE "DOTA-TATE"), a newer one, used for neuroendocrine [metastasis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metastasis "Metastasis") and lung neuroendocrine cancer, such as certain types of _[microcytoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microcytoma?action=edit&redlink=1 "Microcytoma (page does not exist)")_. Gallium-68's preparation as a pharmaceutical is chemical, and the radionuclide is extracted by [elution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elution "Elution") from germanium-68, a [synthetic radioisotope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthetic_radioisotope "Synthetic radioisotope") of [germanium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germanium "Germanium"), in [gallium-68 generators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium-68_generator "Gallium-68 generator").[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-106)

### Other uses

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gallium&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Other uses")]

**Neutrino detection**: Gallium is used for [neutrino detection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutrino_detection "Neutrino detection"). Possibly the largest amount of pure gallium ever collected in a single location is the Gallium-Germanium Neutrino Telescope used by the [SAGE experiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SAGE_(Soviet-American_Gallium_Experiment) "SAGE (Soviet-American Gallium Experiment)") at the [Baksan Neutrino Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baksan_Neutrino_Observatory "Baksan Neutrino Observatory") in Russia. This detector contains 55–57 tonnes (~9 cubic metres) of liquid gallium.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-107) Another experiment was the [GALLEX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GALLEX "GALLEX") neutrino detector operated in the early 1990s in an Italian mountain tunnel. The detector contained 12.2 tons of watered gallium-71. [Solar neutrinos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_neutrino "Solar neutrino") caused a few atoms of 71 Ga to become radioactive 71[Ge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germanium "Germanium"), which were detected. This experiment showed that the solar neutrino flux is 40% less than theory predicted. This deficit ([solar neutrino problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_neutrino_problem "Solar neutrino problem")) was not explained until better solar neutrino detectors and theories were constructed (see [SNO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudbury_Neutrino_Observatory "Sudbury Neutrino Observatory")).[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-108)

**Ion source**: Gallium is also used as a [liquid metal ion source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_metal_ion_source "Liquid metal ion source") for a [focused ion beam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Focused_ion_beam "Focused ion beam"). For example, a focused gallium-ion beam was used to create the world's smallest book, _[Teeny Ted from Turnip Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teeny\_Ted\_from\_Turnip\_Town "Teeny Ted from Turnip Town")_.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-pr-109)

**Lubricants**: Gallium serves as an additive in [glide wax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glide_wax "Glide wax") for skis and other low-friction surface materials.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-110)

**Flexible electronics**: Materials scientists speculate that the properties of gallium could make it suitable for the development of flexible and wearable devices.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Kleiner-111)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Tang-112)

**Hydrogen generation**: Gallium disrupts the [protective oxide layer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passivation_(chemistry) "Passivation (chemistry)") on aluminium, allowing water to react with the aluminium in [AlGa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AlGa "AlGa") to produce hydrogen gas.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Amberchan_2022-113)

**Humor**: A well-known [practical joke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Practical_joke "Practical joke") among chemists is to fashion gallium spoons and use them to serve tea to unsuspecting guests, since gallium has a similar appearance to its lighter homolog aluminium. The spoons then melt in the hot tea.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Sam_Kean2010-114)

## Gallium in the ocean

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gallium&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Gallium in the ocean")]

Advances in trace element testing have allowed scientists to discover traces of dissolved gallium in the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Dissolved_Gallium_in_the_Open_Ocean-115) In recent years, dissolved gallium concentrations have presented in the [Beaufort Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaufort_Sea "Beaufort Sea").[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Dissolved_Gallium_in_the_Open_Ocean-115)[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Dissolved_Gallium_in_the_Beaufort_S-116) These reports reflect the possible profiles of the Pacific and Atlantic Ocean waters.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Dissolved_Gallium_in_the_Beaufort_S-116) For the Pacific Oceans, typical dissolved gallium concentrations are between 4 and 6 pmol/kg at depths <~150 m. In comparison, for Atlantic waters 25–28 pmol/kg at depths >~350 m.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Dissolved_Gallium_in_the_Beaufort_S-116)

Gallium has entered oceans mainly through aeolian input, but having gallium in our oceans can be used to resolve aluminium distribution in the oceans.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Shiller_87%E2%80%9399-117) The reason for this is that gallium is geochemically similar to aluminium, just less reactive. Gallium also has a slightly larger surface water residence time than aluminium.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Shiller_87%E2%80%9399-117) Gallium has a dissolved profile similar to that of aluminium, due to this gallium can be used as a tracer for aluminium.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Shiller_87%E2%80%9399-117) Gallium can also be used as a tracer of aeolian inputs of iron.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Dissolved_Gallium_in_the_northwest-118) Gallium is used as a tracer for iron in the northwest Pacific, south and central Atlantic Oceans.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Dissolved_Gallium_in_the_northwest-118) For example, in the northwest Pacific, low gallium surface waters, in the subpolar region suggest that there is low dust input, which can subsequently explain the following [high-nutrient, low-chlorophyll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-nutrient,_low-chlorophyll "High-nutrient, low-chlorophyll") environmental behavior.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Dissolved_Gallium_in_the_northwest-118)

Chemical compound

Metallic gallium is not toxic. However, several gallium compounds are toxic.

Gallium halide complexes can be toxic.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-121) The Ga 3+ ion of soluble gallium salts tends to form the insoluble hydroxide when injected in large doses; precipitation of this hydroxide resulted in [nephrotoxicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nephrotoxicity "Nephrotoxicity") in animals. In lower doses, soluble gallium is tolerated well and does not accumulate as a poison, instead being excreted mostly through urine. Excretion of gallium occurs in two phases: the first phase has a [biological half-life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_half-life "Biological half-life") of 1 hour, while the second has a biological half-life of 25 hours.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-Nordberg-105)

Inhaled Ga 2 O 3 particles are probably toxic.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium#cite_note-122)

**Manganese** is a [chemical element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_element "Chemical element"); it has the [symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symbol_(chemistry) "Symbol (chemistry)")**Mn** and [atomic number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_number "Atomic number") 25. It is a hard, brittle, silvery metal, often found in [minerals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mineral "Mineral") in combination with [iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron "Iron"). First isolated in the 1770s, manganese is a [transition metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transition_metal "Transition metal") with many industrial [alloy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alloy "Alloy") uses, particularly in [stainless steels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stainless_steel "Stainless steel") in which it improves strength, workability, and resistance to wear. Various [manganese oxides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese_oxide "Manganese oxide") are used as oxidising agents, as rubber additives, and in glass making, fertilizers, and ceramics. [Manganese sulfate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese_sulfate "Manganese sulfate") can be used as a fungicide.

Manganese is also an essential human [dietary element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dietary_element "Dietary element"), important in [macronutrient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macronutrient "Macronutrient") metabolism, bone formation, and [free radical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_radical "Free radical") defense systems. It is a critical component in dozens of [proteins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protein "Protein") and [enzymes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enzyme "Enzyme").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Erikson-2019-8) It is found mostly in the bones, but also the liver, kidneys, and brain.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Emsley2001-9) In the human brain, manganese is bound to manganese [metalloproteins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metalloprotein "Metalloprotein"), most notably [glutamine synthetase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glutamine_synthetase "Glutamine synthetase") in [astrocytes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astrocyte "Astrocyte").

Manganese in the form of the deep violet salt [potassium permanganate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potassium_permanganate "Potassium permanganate") is commonly used in laboratories as an [oxidizer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxidizing_agent "Oxidizing agent"). Potassium permanganate is also used as a [biocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biocide "Biocide") in [water treatment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_treatment "Water treatment").

It occurs at the [active sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Active_site "Active site") in some [enzymes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enzymes "Enzymes").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-10) Of particular interest is the use of a Mn–O [cluster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atom_cluster "Atom cluster"), the [oxygen-evolving complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen-evolving_complex "Oxygen-evolving complex"), in the production of oxygen by plants.

## Characteristics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Characteristics")]

### Physical properties

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Physical properties")]

Manganese is a silvery-gray [metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metal "Metal") that resembles [iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron "Iron"). It is hard and very brittle, difficult to melt, but oxidizes easily.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Holl-11) Manganese and its common ions are [paramagnetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramagnetic "Paramagnetic").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-magnet-12) Manganese tarnishes slowly in air and [oxidizes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxidation "Oxidation") ("rusts") like iron in water containing dissolved oxygen.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-13)

### Isotopes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Isotopes")]

Main article: [Isotopes of manganese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotopes_of_manganese "Isotopes of manganese")

Naturally occurring manganese is composed of one stable [isotope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotope "Isotope"), 55 Mn. Several [radioisotopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioisotope "Radioisotope") have been isolated and described, ranging from 46 Mn to 72 Mn; the most stable ones are 53 with a [half-life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half-life "Half-life") of 3.7 million years, 54 Mn with a half-life of 312.08 days, and 52 Mn with a half-life of 5.591 days. All of the remaining [radioactive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioactive "Radioactive") isotopes have half-lives of less than three hours, and the majority of less than one minute. The primary [decay mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decay_mode "Decay mode") in isotopes lighter than the most abundant stable isotope, 55 Mn, is [electron capture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron_capture "Electron capture"), and the primary mode in heavier isotopes is [beta decay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_decay "Beta decay"). Manganese also has three [meta states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meta_state "Meta state").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Audi-14)

Manganese is part of the [iron group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_group "Iron group") of elements, which are thought to be synthesized in [massive stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massive_star "Massive star") shortly before the [supernova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supernova "Supernova") explosion.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-15)53 Mn decays to 53 Cr with a half-life of 3.7 million years. Because of its short half-life, 53 Mn is relatively rare; it is produced by the impact of [cosmic rays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_rays "Cosmic rays") on [iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron "Iron").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-16)

Chromium and manganese are found together sufficiently for measurement of both to find application in [isotope geology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotope_geology "Isotope geology"), and the Mn/Cr ratios here for [dating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiometric_dating "Radiometric dating") the early Solar System. Mn–Cr isotopic ratios reinforce the evidence from [26 Al](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium-26 "Aluminium-26") and [107 Pd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palladium-107 "Palladium-107") for the early history of the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System"). Variations in 53 Cr/52 Cr and Mn/Cr ratios from several [meteorites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meteorite "Meteorite") suggest a non-zero initial 53 Mn/55 Mn ratio, which indicate that Cr isotopic composition variations must result from _in situ_ decay of 53 Mn in differentiated planetary bodies. Hence, 53 Mn provides additional evidence for [nucleosynthetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nucleosynthesis "Nucleosynthesis") processes immediately before the coalescence of the Solar System.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-17)

### Allotropes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Allotropes")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/64/Alpha-Mn.png/250px-Alpha-Mn.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alpha-Mn.png)

Unit cell of an α-Mn crystal[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f8/Beta-Mn.png/250px-Beta-Mn.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Beta-Mn.png)

Unit cell of a β-Mn crystal

Four [allotropes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allotropy "Allotropy") (structural forms) of solid manganese are known, labeled α, β, γ and δ, and occur at successively higher temperatures. All are metallic, stable at standard pressure, and have a cubic crystal lattice, but they vary widely in their atomic structures.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Young_1975-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Dhananjayan_1969-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Kemmitt_1973-20)

**Alpha manganese** (α-Mn) is the equilibrium phase at room temperature. It has a [body-centered cubic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Body-centered_cubic "Body-centered cubic") lattice and is unusual among elemental metals in that it has a very complex [unit cell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_cell "Unit cell"), with 58 atoms per cell (29 atoms per [primitive unit cell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_cell#Primitive_cell "Unit cell")) with manganese atoms in four different types of surroundings (sites).[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Bradley_1927-21)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Young_1975-18) It is [paramagnetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramagnetic "Paramagnetic") at room temperature and [antiferromagnetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiferromagnetic "Antiferromagnetic") at temperatures below 95 K (−178°C).[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Lawson_1994-22)

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/Phase_diagram_of_manganese_%281975%29.png/250px-Phase_diagram_of_manganese_%281975%29.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Phase_diagram_of_manganese_(1975).png)

Phase diagram of manganese[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Young_1975-18)

**Beta manganese** (β-Mn) forms when heated above the transition temperature of 973 K (700°C; 1,290°F). It has a primitive cubic structure with 20 atoms per unit cell at two types of sites, which is as complex as that of any other elemental metal.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Prior_2004-23) It is easily obtained as a [metastable phase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metastability "Metastability") at room temperature by rapid quenching of manganese at 850°C (1,120 K; 1,560°F) in ice water. It does not show [magnetic ordering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetism "Magnetism"), remaining paramagnetic down to the lowest temperature measured (1.1 K).[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Prior_2004-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Funahashi_1984-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Duschanek_1989-25)

**Gamma manganese** (γ-Mn) forms when heated above 1,370 K (1,100°C; 2,010°F). It has a simple face-centered cubic structure (four atoms per unit cell). When quenched to room temperature it converts to β-Mn, but it can be stabilized at room temperature by alloying it with at least 5 percent of other elements (such as C, Fe, Ni, Cu, Pd or Au). These solute-stabilized alloys distort into a face-centered [tetragonal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetragonal_crystal_system "Tetragonal crystal system") structure.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Bacon_1970-26)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Duschanek_1989-25)

**Delta manganese** (δ-Mn) forms when heated above 1,406 K (1,130°C; 2,070°F) and is stable up to the manganese melting point of 1,519 K (1,250°C; 2,270°F). It has a [body-centered cubic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Body-centered_cubic "Body-centered cubic") structure (two atoms per cubic unit cell).[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Dhananjayan_1969-19)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Duschanek_1989-25)

## Chemical compounds

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Chemical compounds")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Chlorid_manganat%C3%BD.JPG/250px-Chlorid_manganat%C3%BD.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Chlorid_manganat%C3%BD.JPG)

[Manganese(II) chloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese(II)_chloride "Manganese(II) chloride") crystals – the pale pink color of Mn(II) salts is due to a [spin-forbidden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin-forbidden_reactions "Spin-forbidden reactions") 3d transition.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-27)

Common [oxidation states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxidation_state "Oxidation state") of manganese are +2, +4, and +7, although all oxidation states from −3 to +7 have been observed. Manganese in oxidation state +7 is represented by salts of the intensely purple permanganate anion MnO 4−.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGreenwoodEarnshaw19971042%E2%80%931046-28)[Potassium permanganate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potassium_permanganate "Potassium permanganate") is a commonly used laboratory [reagent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reagent "Reagent") because of its oxidizing properties; it is used as a topical medicine (for example, in the treatment of fish diseases). Solutions of potassium permanganate were among the first stains and fixatives to be used in the preparation of biological cells and tissues for electron microscopy.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-29)

Aside from various permanganate salts, Mn(VII) is represented by the unstable, volatile derivative Mn 2 O 7. [Oxyhalides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxyhalide "Oxyhalide") (MnO 3 F and MnO 3 Cl) are powerful [oxidizing agents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxidation "Oxidation").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Holl-11) The most prominent example of Mn in the +6 oxidation state is the green anion [manganate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganate "Manganate"), MnO 4 2−. Manganate salts are intermediates in the extraction of manganese from its ores. Compounds with oxidation states +5 are somewhat elusive, and often found associated to an oxide (O 2−) or [nitride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitride "Nitride") (N 3−) ligand.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-30) One example is the blue anion [hypomanganate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypomanganate "Hypomanganate")MnO 4 3−.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGreenwoodEarnshaw19971049%E2%80%931051-31)

Mn(IV) is somewhat enigmatic because it is common in nature but far rarer in synthetic chemistry. The most common Mn ore, [pyrolusite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrolusite "Pyrolusite"), is MnO 2. It is the dark brown pigment of many [cave drawings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cave_drawing "Cave drawing")[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-32) and is also a common ingredient in [dry cell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dry_cell "Dry cell") batteries.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGreenwoodEarnshaw19971048-33) Complexes of Mn(IV), such as in [K 2 MnF 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese(IV)_fluoride#Fluoromanganate(IV)_complexes "Manganese(IV) fluoride"), are known but are rarer than those of manganese in the lower oxidation states. Mn(IV)-OH complexes are an intermediate in some [enzymes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enzyme "Enzyme"), including the oxygen-evolving center (OEC) in plants.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGreenwoodEarnshaw19971056-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-35)

Simple derivatives of Mn 3+ are rarely encountered but can be stabilized by suitably [alkaline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkaline "Alkaline") ligands. [Manganese(III) acetate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese(III)_acetate "Manganese(III) acetate") is an oxidant useful in [organic synthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organic_synthesis "Organic synthesis"). Solid compounds of manganese(III) are characterized by a strong purple-red color and a preference for distorted [octahedral coordination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octahedral_coordination "Octahedral coordination") resulting from the [Jahn-Teller effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jahn-Teller_effect "Jahn-Teller effect").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-36)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/KMnO4_in_H2O.jpg/250px-KMnO4_in_H2O.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:KMnO4_in_H2O.jpg)

Aqueous solution of KMnO 4 illustrating the deep purple of Mn(VII) as it occurs in permanganate

A particularly common oxidation state for manganese in aqueous solution is +2, which has a pale pink color. Many manganese(II) compounds are known, such as the [aquo complexes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquo_complex "Aquo complex") derived from [manganese(II) sulfate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese(II)_sulfate "Manganese(II) sulfate") (MnSO 4) and [manganese(II) chloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese(II)_chloride "Manganese(II) chloride") (MnCl 2). This oxidation state is also seen in the mineral [rhodochrosite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodochrosite "Rhodochrosite") ([manganese(II) carbonate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese(II)_carbonate "Manganese(II) carbonate")). Manganese(II) commonly exists with a [high-spin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin_states_(d_electrons) "Spin states (d electrons)") ground state, with 5 unpaired electrons, because of its high pairing energy. There are no spin-allowed d–d transitions in manganese(II), which explain its faint color.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-37)

### Organomanganese compounds

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Organomanganese compounds")]

Main article: [Organomanganese chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organomanganese_chemistry "Organomanganese chemistry")

Manganese forms a large variety of organometallic derivatives, i.e., compounds with Mn-C bonds. The organometallic derivatives include numerous examples of Mn in its lower oxidation states, i.e. Mn(−III) up through Mn(I). This area of organometallic chemistry is attractive because Mn is inexpensive and of relatively low toxicity.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-39)

Of greatest commercial interest is [methylcyclopentadienyl manganese tricarbonyl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methylcyclopentadienyl_manganese_tricarbonyl "Methylcyclopentadienyl manganese tricarbonyl") (MMT), which is used as an [anti-knock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-knock "Anti-knock") compound added to [gasoline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gasoline "Gasoline") in some countries, featuring Mn(I).[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-ullmann-40) Consistent with other aspects of Mn(II) chemistry, [manganocene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganocene "Manganocene") (Mn(C 5 H 5)2) is high-spin. In contrast, its neighboring metal, iron, forms an air-stable, low-spin derivative in the form of [ferrocene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrocene "Ferrocene") (Fe(C 5 H 5)2). When conducted under an atmosphere of [carbon monoxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_monoxide "Carbon monoxide"), reduction of Mn(II) salts gives [dimanganese decacarbonyl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimanganese_decacarbonyl "Dimanganese decacarbonyl")Mn 2(CO)10, an orange and volatile solid. The air-stability of this Mn(0) compound (and its many derivatives) reflects the powerful electron-acceptor properties of carbon monoxide. Many [alkene complexes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkene_complex "Alkene complex") and [alkyne complexes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkyne_complex "Alkyne complex") are derived from Mn 2(CO)10.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGreenwoodEarnshaw19971062%E2%80%931069-41)

In Mn(CH 3)2(dmpe)2 ([dmpe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dmpe "Dmpe") = (CH 3)2 PCH 2 CH 2 P(CH 3)2), Mn(II) is low spin, which contrasts with the high spin character of its precursor, MnBr 2(dmpe)2 .[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-42) Poly[alkyl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkyl_group "Alkyl group") and poly[aryl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aryl_group "Aryl group") derivatives of manganese often exist in higher oxidation states, reflecting the electron-releasing properties of alkyl and aryl ligands. One example is [Mn(CH 3)6]2−.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-43)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: History")]

The origin of the name manganese is complex. In ancient times, two black minerals were identified from the regions of the [Magnetes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetes "Magnetes") (either [Magnesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Magnesia "Ancient Magnesia"), located within modern Greece, or [Magnesia ad Sipylum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnesia_ad_Sipylum "Magnesia ad Sipylum"), located within modern Turkey).[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-LanguageHAt-44) They were both called _magnes_ from their place of origin, but were considered to differ in sex. The male _magnes_ attracted iron, and was the iron ore now known as [lodestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lodestone "Lodestone") or [magnetite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetite "Magnetite"), and which probably gave us the term [magnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnet "Magnet"). The female _magnes_ ore did not attract iron, but was used to decolorize glass. This female _magnes_ was later called _magnesia_, known now in modern times as [pyrolusite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrolusite "Pyrolusite") or [manganese dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese_dioxide "Manganese dioxide").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-45) Neither this mineral nor elemental manganese is magnetic. In the 16th century, manganese dioxide was called _manganesum_ (note the two Ns instead of one) by glassmakers, possibly as a corruption and concatenation of two words, since [alchemists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alchemy "Alchemy") and glassmakers eventually had to differentiate a _magnesia nigra_ (the black ore) from _[magnesia alba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnesia\_alba "Magnesia alba")_ (a white ore, also from Magnesia, also useful in glassmaking). Italian physician [Michele Mercati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michele_Mercati "Michele Mercati") called magnesia nigra _manganesa_, and finally the metal isolated from it became known as _manganese_ ([German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language "German language"): _Mangan_). The name _magnesia_ was eventually used to refer only to the white magnesia alba (magnesium oxide), which provided the name [magnesium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnesium "Magnesium") for the free element when it was isolated much later.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-46)

[![Image 14: A drawing of a left-facing bull, in black, on a cave wall](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/Lascaux_painting.jpg/250px-Lascaux_painting.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lascaux_painting.jpg)

Some of the cave paintings in [Lascaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lascaux "Lascaux"), [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"), use manganese-based pigments.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Lascaux-47)

Manganese dioxide, which is abundant in nature, has long been used as a pigment. The cave paintings in [Gargas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gargas,_Haute-Garonne "Gargas, Haute-Garonne") that are 30,000 to 24,000 years old are made from the mineral form of MnO 2 pigments.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-48)

Manganese compounds were used by Egyptian and Roman glassmakers, either to add to, or remove, color from glass.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-49) Use as "glassmakers soap" continued through the [Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages") until modern times and is evident in 14th-century glass from [Venice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice "Venice").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-ItGlass-50)

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f6/Gahn_Johan_Gottlieb.jpg/250px-Gahn_Johan_Gottlieb.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gahn_Johan_Gottlieb.jpg)

Credit for first isolating manganese is usually given to [Johan Gottlieb Gahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johan_Gottlieb_Gahn "Johan Gottlieb Gahn").

Because it was used in glassmaking, manganese dioxide was available for experiments by alchemists, the first chemists. [Ignatius Gottfried Kaim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ignatius_Gottfried_Kaim "Ignatius Gottfried Kaim") (1770) and [Johann Glauber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Glauber "Johann Glauber") (17th century) discovered that manganese dioxide could be converted to [permanganate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permanganate "Permanganate"), a useful laboratory reagent.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-51) By the mid-18th century, the Swedish chemist [Carl Wilhelm Scheele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Wilhelm_Scheele "Carl Wilhelm Scheele") used manganese dioxide to produce [chlorine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chlorine "Chlorine"). First, [hydrochloric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrochloric_acid "Hydrochloric acid"), or a mixture of dilute [sulfuric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfuric_acid "Sulfuric acid") and [sodium chloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_chloride "Sodium chloride") was made to react with manganese dioxide, and later hydrochloric acid from the [Leblanc process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leblanc_process "Leblanc process") was used and the manganese dioxide was recycled by the [Weldon process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weldon_process "Weldon process").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-52)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-ullmann-40)

Scheele and others were aware that pyrolusite (mineral form of manganese dioxide) contained a new element. [Johan Gottlieb Gahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johan_Gottlieb_Gahn "Johan Gottlieb Gahn") isolated an impure sample of manganese metal in 1774, which he did by [reducing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reduction-oxidation "Reduction-oxidation") the dioxide with [carbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon "Carbon").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-journal1927-53) Ignatius Gottfried Kaim also may have reduced manganese dioxide to isolate the metal, but that is uncertain.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Miskowiec-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-55)

The manganese content of some iron ores used in Greece led to speculations that steel produced from that ore contains additional manganese, making the [Spartan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sparta "Sparta") steel exceptionally hard.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-56) Around the beginning of the 19th century, manganese was used in steelmaking and several patents were granted. In 1816, it was documented that iron alloyed with manganese was harder but not more brittle. In 1837, British academic [James Couper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Couper_(academic)?action=edit&redlink=1 "James Couper (academic) (page does not exist)") noted an association between miners' heavy exposure to manganese and a form of [Parkinson's disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parkinson's_disease "Parkinson's disease").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Couper_1837_41%E2%80%9342-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-58) In 1912, United States patents were granted for protecting firearms against rust and corrosion with manganese phosphate electrochemical conversion coatings, and the process has seen widespread use ever since.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-59)

The invention of the [Leclanché cell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leclanch%C3%A9_cell "Leclanché cell") in 1866 and the subsequent improvement of batteries containing manganese dioxide as cathodic [depolarizer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depolarizer "Depolarizer") increased the demand for manganese dioxide. Until the development of batteries with [nickel–cadmium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nickel%E2%80%93cadmium_battery "Nickel–cadmium battery") and lithium, most batteries contained manganese. The [zinc–carbon battery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zinc%E2%80%93carbon_battery "Zinc–carbon battery") and the [alkaline battery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkaline_battery "Alkaline battery") normally use industrially produced manganese dioxide because naturally occurring manganese dioxide contains impurities. In the 20th century, manganese dioxide was widely used as the cathode for commercial disposable dry batteries of both the standard (zinc–carbon) and alkaline types.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-ChiuZMnO2-60)

Manganese is essential to iron and [steel production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steelmaking "Steelmaking") by virtue of its [sulfur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfur "Sulfur")-fixing, [deoxidizing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deoxidized_steel "Deoxidized steel"), and [alloying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alloying "Alloying") properties.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-USGSMCS2009-61) This application was first recognized by the British metallurgist [Robert Forester Mushet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Forester_Mushet "Robert Forester Mushet") (1811–1891), who introduced the element to the steel manufacture process in 1856 in the form of [spiegeleisen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiegeleisen "Spiegeleisen").[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-62)

## Occurrence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Occurrence")]

See also: [Category:Manganese minerals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Manganese_minerals "Category:Manganese minerals")

Manganese comprises about 1000[ppm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parts_per_million "Parts per million") (0.1%) of the [Earth's crust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_crust "Earth's crust") and is the [12th most abundant element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abundance_of_elements_in_Earth's_crust "Abundance of elements in Earth's crust").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Emsley2001-9) Soil contains 7–9000 ppm of manganese with an average of 440 ppm.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Emsley2001-9) The atmosphere contains 0.01 μg/m 3.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Emsley2001-9) Manganese occurs principally as [pyrolusite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrolusite "Pyrolusite") ([MnO 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese(IV)_oxide "Manganese(IV) oxide")), [braunite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braunite "Braunite") ((Mn 2+,Mn 3+)6 SiO 12),[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-63)[psilomelane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psilomelane "Psilomelane")(Ba,H 2 O)2 Mn 5 O 10, and to a lesser extent as [rhodochrosite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodochrosite "Rhodochrosite") ([MnCO 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese(II)_carbonate "Manganese(II) carbonate")).

Scale is in mm Mineral [rhodochrosite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodochrosite "Rhodochrosite") ([manganese(II) carbonate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese(II)_carbonate "Manganese(II) carbonate"))
