Percentage of manganese output in 2006 by countries[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-USGSMCS2009-61)

The most important manganese ore is pyrolusite ([MnO 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese(IV)_oxide "Manganese(IV) oxide")). Other economically important manganese ores usually show a close spatial relation to the iron ores, such as [sphalerite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphalerite "Sphalerite").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Holl-11)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-64) Land-based resources are large but irregularly distributed. About 80% of the known world manganese resources are in South Africa; other important manganese deposits are in Ukraine, Australia, India, China, [Gabon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabon "Gabon") and Brazil.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-USGSMCS2009-61)

Manganese is mainly mined in South Africa, Australia, China, Gabon, Brazil, India, Kazakhstan, Ghana, Ukraine and Malaysia.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-65) In South Africa, most identified deposits are located near [Hotazel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hotazel "Hotazel") in the [Northern Cape Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Cape_Province "Northern Cape Province"), ([Kalahari manganese fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalahari_manganese_fields?action=edit&redlink=1 "Kalahari manganese fields (page does not exist)")), with a 2011 estimate of 15 billion tons. In 2011 South Africa produced 3.4 million tons, topping all other nations.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Mbendi-66)

### Oceanic environment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Oceanic environment")]

Main article: [Manganese nodule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese_nodule "Manganese nodule")

An abundant resource of manganese is in the form of manganese nodules found on the [ocean floor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ocean_floor "Ocean floor").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-67) These nodules, which are composed of 29% manganese,[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-68) are located along the ocean floor. The [environmental impacts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_issues "Environmental issues") of nodule collection are of interest.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-69)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-70) According to 1978 estimate, the ocean floor has 500 billion tons of [manganese nodules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese_nodule "Manganese nodule").[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-71)As of April 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit), attempts to find economically viable methods of harvesting manganese nodules are still ongoing, however, none has been commercialized.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-72)

In 1972, the [CIA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Intelligence_Agency "Central Intelligence Agency")'s [Project Azorian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Azorian "Project Azorian"), through billionaire [Howard Hughes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Hughes "Howard Hughes"), commissioned the ship _[Hughes Glomar Explorer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hughes\_Glomar\_Explorer "Hughes Glomar Explorer")_ with the cover story of harvesting [manganese nodules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese_nodules "Manganese nodules") from the sea floor.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-73) This cover story triggered a rush of activity to collect manganese nodules. The real mission of _Hughes Glomar Explorer_ was to raise a sunken [Soviet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_of_Soviet_Socialist_Republics "Union of Soviet Socialist Republics") submarine, the [K-129](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_submarine_K-129_(1960) "Soviet submarine K-129 (1960)"), with the goal of retrieving Soviet code books.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-azorian-74)

Manganese also occurs in the oceanic environment, as dissolved manganese (dMn), which is found throughout the world's oceans, 90% of which originates from hydrothermal vents.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Hernroth-2020-75) Particulate Mn develops in buoyant plumes over an active vent source, while the dMn behaves conservatively.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Ray-2017-76) Mn concentrations vary between the water columns of the ocean. At the surface, dMn is elevated due to input from external sources such as rivers, dust, and shelf sediments. Coastal sediments normally have lower Mn concentrations, but can increase due to anthropogenic discharges from industries such as mining and steel manufacturing, which enter the ocean from river inputs. Surface dMn concentrations can also be elevated biologically through photosynthesis and physically from coastal upwelling and wind-driven surface currents. Internal cycling such as photo-reduction from UV radiation can also elevate levels by speeding up the dissolution of Mn-oxides and oxidative scavenging, preventing Mn from sinking to deeper waters.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Sim-2019-77) Elevated levels at mid-depths can occur near mid-ocean ridges and hydrothermal vents. The hydrothermal vents release dMn enriched fluid into the water. The dMn can then travel up to 4,000 km due to the microbial capsules present, preventing exchange with particles, lowing the sinking rates. Dissolved Mn concentrations are even higher when oxygen levels are low. Overall, dMn concentrations are normally higher in coastal regions and decrease when moving offshore.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Sim-2019-77)

### Soils

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Soils")]

Manganese occurs in soils in three oxidation states: the divalent cation, Mn 2+ and as brownish-black oxides and hydroxides containing Mn (III,IV), such as MnOOH and MnO 2. Soil pH and oxidation-reduction conditions affect which of these three forms of Mn is dominant in a given soil. At pH values less than 6 or under anaerobic conditions, Mn(II) dominates, while under more alkaline and aerobic conditions, Mn(III,IV) oxides and hydroxides predominate. These effects of soil acidity and aeration state on the form of Mn can be modified or controlled by microbial activity. Microbial respiration can cause both the oxidation of Mn 2+ to the oxides, and it can cause reduction of the oxides to the divalent cation.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-78)

The Mn(III,IV) oxides exist as brownish-black stains and small nodules on sand, silt, and clay particles. These surface coatings on other soil particles have high surface area and carry negative charge. The charged sites can adsorb and retain various cations, especially heavy metals (e.g., Cr 3+, Cu 2+, Zn 2+, and Pb 2+). In addition, the oxides can adsorb organic acids and other compounds. The adsorption of the metals and organic compounds can then cause them to be oxidized while the Mn(III,IV) oxides are reduced to Mn 2+ (e.g., Cr 3+ to Cr(VI) and colorless [hydroquinone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydroquinone "Hydroquinone") to tea-colored [quinone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quinone "Quinone") polymers).[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-79)

## Production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Production")]

See also: [Manganese production by country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese_production_by_country "Manganese production by country")

A significant proportion of the manganese ore mined, around 85% in the United States, is used in iron and [steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steel "Steel") production, such as in the production of [ferromanganese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferromanganese "Ferromanganese").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-80) For the production of ferromanganese, the manganese ore is mixed with iron ore and carbon, and then reduced either in a blast furnace or in an [electric arc furnace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_arc_furnace "Electric arc furnace").[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-IndMin-81) The resulting ferromanganese has a manganese content of 30–80%.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Holl-11) Pure manganese used for the production of iron-free alloys is produced by [leaching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leaching_(metallurgy) "Leaching (metallurgy)") manganese ore with [sulfuric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfuric_acid "Sulfuric acid") and a subsequent [electrowinning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrowinning "Electrowinning") process.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-hydrometI-82)

[![Image 22: Contains reactions and temperatures, as well as showing advanced processes such as the heat exchanger and milling process.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Manganese_Process_Flow_Diagram.jpg/500px-Manganese_Process_Flow_Diagram.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Manganese_Process_Flow_Diagram.jpg)

Process flow diagram for a manganese refining circuit

A more progressive extraction process involves directly reducing (a low grade) manganese ore by [heap leaching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heap_leaching "Heap leaching"). This is done by [percolating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percolation "Percolation") natural gas through the bottom of the heap; the natural gas provides the heat (needs to be at least 850°C) and the reducing agent (carbon monoxide). This reduces all of the manganese ore to [Manganese(II) oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese(II)_oxide "Manganese(II) oxide") (MnO), which is a leachable form. The ore then travels through a [grinding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mill_(grinding) "Mill (grinding)") circuit to reduce the particle size of the ore to between 150 and 250 μm, increasing the surface area to aid leaching. The ore is then added to a leach tank of sulfuric acid and [ferrous iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron(II) "Iron(II)") (Fe 2+) in a 1.6:1 ratio. The iron reacts with the [manganese dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese_dioxide "Manganese dioxide") (MnO 2) to form [iron hydroxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_hydroxide "Iron hydroxide") (FeO(OH)) and elemental manganese (Mn).[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-ManganeseRecovery-83)

This process yields greater than 90% recovery of the manganese. For further purification, the manganese can then be sent to an [electrowinning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrowinning "Electrowinning") facility.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-ManganeseRecovery-83)

## Applications

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Applications")]

### Steel

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Steel")]

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/M1917helmet.jpg/250px-M1917helmet.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:M1917helmet.jpg)

U.S. M1917 [combat helmet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combat_helmet "Combat helmet"), a variant of [Brodie helmet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brodie_helmet "Brodie helmet"), made from [Hadfield steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadfield_steel "Hadfield steel") manganese alloy

Manganese is essential to iron and [steel production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steelmaking "Steelmaking") by virtue of its [sulfur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfur "Sulfur")-fixing, [deoxidizing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deoxidized_steel "Deoxidized steel"), and [alloying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alloying "Alloying") properties. Manganese has no satisfactory substitute in these applications in metallurgy.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-USGSMCS2009-61) Steelmaking,[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-84) including its ironmaking component, has accounted for most manganese demand, presently in the range of 85% to 90% of the total demand.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-hydrometI-82) Manganese is a key component of low-cost [stainless steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stainless_steel "Stainless steel").[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-85)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-86) Often ferromanganese (usually about 80% manganese) is the intermediate in modern processes.

Small amounts of manganese improve the workability of steel at high temperatures by forming a high-melting sulfide and preventing the formation of a liquid [iron sulfide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_sulfide "Iron sulfide") at the grain boundaries. If the manganese content reaches 4%, the embrittlement of the steel becomes a dominant feature. The embrittlement decreases at higher manganese concentrations and reaches an acceptable level at 8%. Steel containing 8 to 15% of manganese has a high [tensile strength](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensile_strength "Tensile strength") of up to 863 MPa.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-87)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-88) Steel with 12% manganese was discovered in 1882 by [Robert Hadfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Hadfield "Robert Hadfield") and is still known as [Hadfield steel (mangalloy)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mangalloy "Mangalloy"). It was used for British military [steel helmets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brodie_helmet "Brodie helmet") and later by the U.S. military.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-89)

### Aluminium alloys

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Aluminium alloys")]

Main article: [Aluminium alloy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium_alloy "Aluminium alloy")

Manganese is used in production of alloys with aluminium. Aluminium with roughly 1.5% manganese has increased resistance to corrosion through grains that absorb impurities which would lead to [galvanic corrosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galvanic_corrosion "Galvanic corrosion").[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-90) The corrosion-resistant [aluminium alloys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium_alloy "Aluminium alloy") 3004 and 3104 (0.8 to 1.5% manganese) are used for most [beverage cans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverage_can "Beverage can").[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Al3004-91) Before 2000, more than 1.6 million [tonnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonne "Tonne") of those alloys were used; at 1% manganese, this consumed 16,000 tonnes of manganese.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Al3004-91)

### Batteries

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Batteries")]

[Manganese(IV) oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese(IV)_oxide "Manganese(IV) oxide") was used in the original type of dry cell [battery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battery_(electricity) "Battery (electricity)") as an electron acceptor from zinc, and is the blackish material in carbon–zinc type flashlight cells. The manganese dioxide is reduced to the manganese oxide-hydroxide MnO(OH) during discharging, preventing the formation of hydrogen at the anode of the battery.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-BattHist-92)

MnO 2 + H 2 O + e− → MnO(OH) + OH−
The same material also functions in newer [alkaline batteries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkaline_battery "Alkaline battery") (usually battery cells), which use the same basic reaction, but a different electrolyte mixture. In 2002, more than 230,000 tons of manganese dioxide was used for this purpose.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-ChiuZMnO2-60)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-BattHist-92)

### Resistors

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Resistors")]

Copper alloys of manganese, such as [Manganin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganin "Manganin"), are commonly found in metal element [shunt resistors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shunt_resistor "Shunt resistor") used for measuring relatively large amounts of current. These alloys have very low [temperature coefficient of resistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temperature_coefficient_of_resistance "Temperature coefficient of resistance") and are resistant to sulfur. This makes the alloys particularly useful in harsh automotive and industrial environments.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-93)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-ShuntDatasheet-94)

### Fertilizers and feed additive

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Fertilizers and feed additive")]

[Manganese oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese(II)_oxide "Manganese(II) oxide") and [sulfate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese_sulfate "Manganese sulfate") are components of fertilizers. In the year 2000, an estimated 20,000 tons of these compounds were used in fertilizers in the US alone. A comparable amount of Mn compounds was also used in animal feeds.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-ullmann-40)

### Niche

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Niche")]

[Methylcyclopentadienyl manganese tricarbonyl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methylcyclopentadienyl_manganese_tricarbonyl "Methylcyclopentadienyl manganese tricarbonyl") is an additive in some [unleaded gasoline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unleaded_gasoline "Unleaded gasoline") to boost [octane rating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octane_rating "Octane rating") and reduce [engine knocking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engine_knocking "Engine knocking").[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-95)

Manganese(IV) oxide (manganese dioxide, MnO 2) is used as a reagent in [organic chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organic_chemistry "Organic chemistry") for the [oxidation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxidation "Oxidation") of benzylic [alcohols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcohol_(chemistry) "Alcohol (chemistry)") (where the [hydroxyl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydroxyl "Hydroxyl") group is adjacent to an [aromatic ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aromatic_ring "Aromatic ring")).[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-96) Manganese dioxide has been used since antiquity to oxidize and neutralize the greenish tinge in glass from trace amounts of iron contamination.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-ItGlass-50)MnO 2 is also used in the manufacture of oxygen and chlorine and in drying black paints. In some preparations, it is a brown [pigment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pigment "Pigment") for [paint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paint "Paint") and is a constituent of natural [umber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umber "Umber").[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-straightouttathetheumberwikiarticle-97)

[Tetravalent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetravalence "Tetravalence") manganese is used as an [activator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Activator_(phosphor) "Activator (phosphor)") in red-emitting [phosphors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphor "Phosphor"). While many compounds are known which show [luminescence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luminescence "Luminescence"),[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-98) the majority are not used in commercial application due to low efficiency or deep red emission.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-99)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-100) However, several Mn 4+ activated fluorides were reported as potential red-emitting phosphors for warm-white LEDs.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-101)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-102) But to this day, only K 2 SiF 6:Mn 4+ is commercially available for use in warm-white [LEDs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LED "LED").[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-103)

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8c/1945-P-Jefferson-War-Nickel-Reverse.JPG/250px-1945-P-Jefferson-War-Nickel-Reverse.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1945-P-Jefferson-War-Nickel-Reverse.JPG)

World-War-II-era 5-cent coin (1942-5 identified by mint mark P, D or S above dome) made from a 56% copper-35% silver-9% manganese alloy

The metal is occasionally used in coins; until 2000, the only United States coin to use manganese was the ["wartime" nickel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_nickel#1938%E2%80%931945:_Early_minting;_World_War_II_changes "Jefferson nickel") from 1942 to 1945.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-104) An alloy of 75% copper and 25% nickel was traditionally used for the production of nickel coins. However, because of shortage of nickel metal during the war, it was substituted by more available silver and manganese, thus resulting in an alloy of 56% copper, 35% silver and 9% manganese. Since 2000, [dollar coins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dollar_(United_States_coin) "Dollar (United States coin)"), for example the [Sacagawea dollar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacagawea_dollar "Sacagawea dollar") and the [Presidential $1 coins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_$1_Coin_Program "Presidential $1 Coin Program"), are made from a brass containing 7% of manganese with a pure copper core.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-105)

Manganese compounds have been used as pigments and for the coloring of ceramics and glass. The brown color of ceramic is sometimes the result of manganese compounds.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-106) In the glass industry, manganese compounds are used for two effects. [Manganese(III)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese(III)_oxide "Manganese(III) oxide") reacts with [iron(II)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron(II)_oxide "Iron(II) oxide") to reduce strong green color in glass by forming less-colored iron(III) and slightly pink manganese(II), compensating for the residual color of the iron(III).[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-ItGlass-50) Larger quantities of manganese are used to produce pink colored glass. In 2009, [Mas Subramanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mas_Subramanian "Mas Subramanian") and associates at [Oregon State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon_State_University "Oregon State University") discovered that manganese can be combined with [yttrium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yttrium "Yttrium") and [indium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indium "Indium") to form an intensely [blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue "Blue"), non-toxic, inert, fade-resistant [pigment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pigment "Pigment"), [YInMn Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YInMn_Blue "YInMn Blue"),[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-107) the first new blue pigment discovered in 200 years.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-108)

## Biochemistry

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Biochemistry")]

Main article: [Manganese in biology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese_in_biology "Manganese in biology")

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/Arginase.jpeg/330px-Arginase.jpeg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Arginase.jpeg)

Reactive center of arginase with boronic acid [inhibitor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enzyme_inhibitor "Enzyme inhibitor") – the manganese atoms are shown in yellow.

Many classes of [enzymes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enzyme "Enzyme") contain manganese [cofactors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cofactor_(biochemistry) "Cofactor (biochemistry)") including [oxidoreductases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxidoreductase "Oxidoreductase"), [transferases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transferase "Transferase"), [hydrolases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrolase "Hydrolase"), [lyases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyase "Lyase"), [isomerases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isomerase "Isomerase") and [ligases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ligase "Ligase"). Other enzymes containing manganese are [arginase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arginase "Arginase") and a Mn-containing [superoxide dismutase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superoxide_dismutase "Superoxide dismutase") ([Mn-SOD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mn-SOD "Mn-SOD")). Some [reverse transcriptases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reverse_transcriptase "Reverse transcriptase") of many [retroviruses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retrovirus "Retrovirus") (although not [lentiviruses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lentivirus "Lentivirus") such as [HIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV "HIV")) contain manganese. Manganese-containing [polypeptides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polypeptides "Polypeptides") are the [diphtheria toxin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diphtheria_toxin "Diphtheria toxin"), [lectins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lectin "Lectin"), and [integrins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrin "Integrin").[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Mnzym-109)

The [oxygen-evolving complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen-evolving_complex "Oxygen-evolving complex") (OEC), containing four atoms of manganese, is a part of photosystem II contained in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts. The OEC is responsible for the terminal [photooxidation of water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_evolution "Oxygen evolution") during the [light reactions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_reactions "Light reactions") of [photosynthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis "Photosynthesis"), i.e., it is the catalyst that makes the O 2 produced by plants.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-110)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-111)

## Human health and nutrition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Human health and nutrition")]

Manganese is an essential human [dietary element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mineral_(nutrient) "Mineral (nutrient)") and is present as a [coenzyme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coenzyme "Coenzyme") in several biological processes, which include macronutrient metabolism, bone formation, and [free radical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_radical "Free radical") defense systems. Manganese is a critical component in dozens of proteins and enzymes.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Erikson-2019-8) The human body contains about 12 mg of manganese, mostly in the bones. The soft tissue remainder is concentrated in the liver and kidneys.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Emsley2001-9) In the human brain, the manganese is bound to manganese [metalloproteins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metalloprotein "Metalloprotein"), most notably [glutamine synthetase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glutamine_synthetase "Glutamine synthetase") in [astrocytes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astrocyte "Astrocyte").[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-112)

### Regulation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Regulation")]

The [U.S. Institute of Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Institute_of_Medicine "U.S. Institute of Medicine") (IOM) updated Estimated Average Requirements (EARs) and Recommended Dietary Allowances (RDAs) for minerals in 2001. For manganese, there was not sufficient information to set EARs and RDAs, so needs are described as estimates for [Adequate Intakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adequate_Intake "Adequate Intake") (AIs). As for safety, the IOM sets [Tolerable upper intake levels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tolerable_upper_intake_level "Tolerable upper intake level") (ULs) for vitamins and minerals when evidence is sufficient. In the case of manganese, the adult UL is set at 11 mg/day. Collectively the EARs, RDAs, AIs and ULs are referred to as [Dietary Reference Intakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dietary_Reference_Intake "Dietary Reference Intake") (DRIs).[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-MnDRI-113) Manganese deficiency is rare.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-114)

The [European Food Safety Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Food_Safety_Authority "European Food Safety Authority") (EFSA) refers to the collective set of information as Dietary Reference Values, with Population Reference Intake (PRI) instead of RDA, and Average Requirement instead of EAR. AI and UL are defined the same as in the United States. For people ages 15 and older, the AI is set at 3.0 mg/day. AIs for pregnancy and lactation are 3.0 mg/day. For children ages 1–14 years, the AIs increase with age from 0.5 to 2.0 mg/day. The adult AIs are higher than the U.S. RDAs.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-115) The EFSA reviewed the same safety question and decided that there was insufficient information to set a UL.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-116)

For U.S. food and dietary supplement labeling purposes, the amount in a serving is expressed as a percent of Daily Value (%DV). For manganese labeling purposes, 100% of the Daily Value was 2.0 mg, but as of 27 May 2016 it was revised to 2.3 mg to bring it into agreement with the RDA.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-FedReg-117)[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-118) A table of the old and new adult daily values is provided at [Reference Daily Intake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reference_Daily_Intake "Reference Daily Intake").

Excessive exposure or intake may lead to a condition known as [manganism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganism "Manganism"), a [neurodegenerative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neurodegeneration "Neurodegeneration") disorder that causes [dopaminergic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dopamine "Dopamine") neuronal death and symptoms similar to [Parkinson's disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parkinson's_disease "Parkinson's disease").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Emsley2001-9)[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-119)

### Deficiency

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Deficiency")]

Main article: [Manganese deficiency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese_deficiency_(medicine) "Manganese deficiency (medicine)")

Manganese deficiency in humans, which is rare, results in a number of medical problems.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-MnDRI-113) A deficiency of manganese causes skeletal deformation in animals and inhibits the production of collagen in wound healing.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-120)

## Exposure

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Exposure")]

### In water

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: In water")]

Waterborne manganese has a greater [bioavailability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bioavailability_(medicine) "Bioavailability (medicine)") than dietary manganese. According to results from a 2010 study,[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Bouchard_138%E2%80%93143-121) higher levels of exposure to manganese in [drinking water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drinking_water "Drinking water") are associated with increased [intellectual impairment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intellectual_impairment "Intellectual impairment") and reduced [intelligence quotients](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelligence_quotient "Intelligence quotient") in school-age children. It is hypothesized that long-term exposure due to inhaling the naturally occurring manganese in shower water puts up to 8.7 million Americans at risk.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-122) However, data indicates that the human body can recover from certain adverse effects of overexposure to manganese if the exposure is stopped and the body can clear the excess.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-123)

Mn levels can increase in seawater when hypoxic periods occur.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-124) Since 1990 there have been reports of Mn accumulation in marine organisms including fish, crustaceans, mollusks, and echinoderms. Specific tissues are targets in different species, including the gills, brain, blood, kidney, and liver/[hepatopancreas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hepatopancreas "Hepatopancreas"). Physiological effects have been reported in these species. Mn can affect the renewal of [immunocytes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immunocyte "Immunocyte") and their functionality, such as [phagocytosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phagocytosis "Phagocytosis") and activation of [pro-phenoloxidase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophenoloxidase "Prophenoloxidase"), suppressing the organisms' immune systems. This causes the organisms to be more susceptible to infections. As climate change occurs, pathogen distributions increase, and in order for organisms to survive and defend themselves against these pathogens, they need a healthy, strong immune system. If their systems are compromised from high Mn levels, they will not be able to fight off these pathogens and die.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Hernroth-2020-75)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Gasoline")]

Molecular model of [methylcyclopentadienyl manganese tricarbonyl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methylcyclopentadienyl_manganese_tricarbonyl "Methylcyclopentadienyl manganese tricarbonyl") (MMT)

[Methylcyclopentadienyl manganese tricarbonyl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methylcyclopentadienyl_manganese_tricarbonyl "Methylcyclopentadienyl manganese tricarbonyl") (MMT) is an additive developed to replace lead compounds for gasolines to improve the [octane rating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octane_rating "Octane rating"). MMT is used only in a few countries. When exposed to the environment, fuels containing methylcyclopentadienyl manganese tricarbonyl degrade, releasing manganese into water and soils.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-125)

### Air

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Air")]

Manganese levels in the air decreased between 1953 and 1982, with higher levels in 1953. In general, breathing air with more than 5 micrograms of manganese per cubic meter can cause symptoms of manganese exposure. In lab-grown human kidney cells, higher levels of a protein called [ferroportin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferroportin "Ferroportin") are linked to lower manganese levels inside the cells and reduced [cell damage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cytotoxicity "Cytotoxicity"), shown by better glutamate uptake and less leakage of a damage marker known as [lactate dehydrogenase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lactate_dehydrogenase "Lactate dehydrogenase").[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-126)[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-127)

### Regulation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Regulation")]

Manganese exposure in [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") is regulated by the [Occupational Safety and Health Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occupational_Safety_and_Health_Administration "Occupational Safety and Health Administration") (OSHA).[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-osha.gov-128) People can be exposed to manganese in the workplace by breathing it in or swallowing it. OSHA has set the legal limit ([permissible exposure limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permissible_exposure_limit "Permissible exposure limit")) for manganese exposure in the workplace as 5 mg/m 3 over an 8-hour workday. The [National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institute_for_Occupational_Safety_and_Health "National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health") (NIOSH) has set a [recommended exposure limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recommended_exposure_limit "Recommended exposure limit") (REL) of 1 mg/m 3 over an 8-hour workday and a short term limit of 3 mg/m 3. At levels of 500 mg/m 3, manganese is [immediately dangerous to life and health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IDLH "IDLH").[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-129) In other countries, such as [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany"), a general ceiling value for airborne manganese has been set to 0.5 mg/m 3 ([Maximale Arbeitsplatz-Konzentration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximale_Arbeitsplatz-Konzentration?action=edit&redlink=1 "Maximale Arbeitsplatz-Konzentration (page does not exist)")[[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximale%20Arbeitsplatz-Konzentration "de:Maximale Arbeitsplatz-Konzentration")]) and the maximum level of manganese in the body has been set to 20 mg/L.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-ullmann-40)

### Manganism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: Manganism")]

Manganese overexposure is most frequently associated with [manganism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganism "Manganism"), a rare neurological disorder associated with excessive manganese ingestion or inhalation. Historically, persons employed in the production or processing of manganese alloys[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-132)[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-133)[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-134) have been at risk for developing manganism; however, health and safety regulations protect workers in developed nations.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-osha.gov-128) The disorder was first described in 1837 by British academic John Couper, who studied two patients who were manganese grinders.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Couper_1837_41%E2%80%9342-57)

Manganism is a biphasic disorder. In its early stages, an intoxicated person may experience depression, mood swings, compulsive behaviors, and psychosis. Early neurological symptoms give way to late-stage manganism, which resembles [Parkinson's disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parkinson's_disease "Parkinson's disease"). Symptoms include weakness, monotone and slowed speech, an expressionless face, tremor, forward-leaning gait, inability to walk backwards without falling, rigidity, and general problems with dexterity, gait and balance.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Couper_1837_41%E2%80%9342-57)[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Cersosimo_2007_340%E2%80%93346-135) Unlike Parkinson's disease, manganism is not associated with loss of the sense of smell and patients are typically unresponsive to treatment with [L-DOPA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L-DOPA "L-DOPA").[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-136) Symptoms of late-stage manganism become more severe over time even if the source of exposure is removed and brain manganese levels return to normal.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Cersosimo_2007_340%E2%80%93346-135)

Chronic manganese exposure has been shown to produce a parkinsonism-like illness characterized by movement abnormalities.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Guilarte2015-137) This condition is not responsive to [typical therapies used in the treatment of PD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Management_of_Parkinson's_disease "Management of Parkinson's disease"), suggesting an alternative pathway to the typical [dopaminergic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dopamine "Dopamine") loss within the [substantia nigra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Substantia_nigra "Substantia nigra").[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Guilarte2015-137) Manganese may accumulate in the [basal ganglia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basal_ganglia "Basal ganglia"), leading to the abnormal movements.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Kwakye2015-138) A mutation of the SLC30A10 gene, a manganese efflux transporter necessary for decreasing intracellular Mn, has been linked with the development of this Parkinsonism-like disease.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Peres2016-139) The [Lewy bodies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewy_body "Lewy body") typical to PD are not seen in Mn-induced parkinsonism.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-Kwakye2015-138)

Animal experiments have given the opportunity to examine the consequences of manganese overexposure under controlled conditions. In (non-aggressive) rats, manganese induces mouse-killing behavior.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-140)

### Toxicity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit&section=30 "Edit section: Toxicity")]

Manganese compounds are less toxic than those of other widespread metals, such as [nickel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nickel "Nickel") and [copper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copper "Copper").[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-141) However, exposure to manganese dusts and fumes should not exceed the ceiling value of 5 mg/m 3 even for short periods because of its toxicity level.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-142)[Manganese poisoning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese_poisoning "Manganese poisoning") has been linked to [impaired motor skills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impaired_motor_skills "Impaired motor skills") and [cognitive disorders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cognitive_disorder "Cognitive disorder").[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-143)

### Neurodegenerative diseases

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manganese&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: Neurodegenerative diseases")]

A protein called [DMT1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DMT1 "DMT1") is the major transporter in manganese absorption from the intestine and may be the major transporter of manganese across the [blood–brain barrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood%E2%80%93brain_barrier "Blood–brain barrier"). DMT1 also transports inhaled manganese across the nasal [epithelium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epithelium "Epithelium"). The proposed mechanism for manganese toxicity is that dysregulation leads to [oxidative stress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxidative_stress "Oxidative stress"), [mitochondrial dysfunction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitochondrial_dysfunction "Mitochondrial dysfunction"), glutamate-mediated [excitotoxicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excitotoxicity "Excitotoxicity"), and aggregation of proteins.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese#cite_note-144)

**Chromium** is a [chemical element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_element "Chemical element"); it has [symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symbol_(chemistry) "Symbol (chemistry)")**Cr** and [atomic number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_number "Atomic number") 24. It is the first element in [group 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_6_element "Group 6 element"). It is a steely-grey, [lustrous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luster_(mineralogy) "Luster (mineralogy)"), hard, and brittle [transition metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transition_metal "Transition metal").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-10)

Chromium is valued for its high [corrosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corrosion "Corrosion") resistance and [hardness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardness "Hardness"). A major development in steel production was the discovery that steel could be made highly resistant to corrosion and discoloration by adding metallic chromium to form [stainless steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stainless_steel "Stainless steel"). Stainless steel and [chrome plating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrome_plating "Chrome plating") ([electroplating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electroplating "Electroplating") with chromium) together comprise 85% of the commercial use. Chromium is also greatly valued as a [metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metal "Metal") that is able to be highly [polished](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polishing "Polishing") while resisting [tarnishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarnish "Tarnish"). Polished chromium reflects almost 70% of the [visible spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visible_spectrum "Visible spectrum"), and almost 90% of [infrared light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrared "Infrared").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-NIST_specular_reflection-11) The name of the element is derived from the [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek "Ancient Greek") word χρῶμα, _chrōma_, meaning [color](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color "Color"),[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-12) because many chromium compounds are intensely colored.

Industrial production of chromium proceeds from [chromite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromite "Chromite") ore (mostly FeCr 2 O 4) to produce [ferrochromium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrochromium "Ferrochromium"), an iron-chromium alloy, by means of [aluminothermic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminothermic_reaction "Aluminothermic reaction") or [silicothermic reactions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicothermic_reaction "Silicothermic reaction"). [Ferrochromium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrochrome "Ferrochrome") is then used to produce alloys such as stainless steel. Pure chromium metal is produced by a different process: [roasting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roasting_(metallurgy) "Roasting (metallurgy)") and [leaching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leaching_(metallurgy) "Leaching (metallurgy)") of chromite to separate it from iron, followed by reduction with [carbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon "Carbon") and then [aluminium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium "Aluminium").

[Trivalent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trivalent "Trivalent") chromium (Cr(III)) occurs naturally in many foods and is sold as a [dietary supplement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dietary_supplement "Dietary supplement"), although there is insufficient evidence that dietary chromium provides nutritional benefit to people.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-ods-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-lpi-14) In 2014, the [European Food Safety Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Food_Safety_Authority "European Food Safety Authority") concluded that research on dietary chromium did not justify it to be recognized as an essential [nutrient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nutrient "Nutrient").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-efsa-15)

While chromium metal and Cr(III) ions are considered non-toxic, chromate and its derivatives, often called "[hexavalent chromium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hexavalent_chromium "Hexavalent chromium")", is toxic and [carcinogenic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carcinogenic "Carcinogenic"). According to the [European Chemicals Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Chemicals_Agency "European Chemicals Agency") (ECHA), [chromium trioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium_trioxide "Chromium trioxide") that is used in industrial electroplating processes is a "substance of very high concern" (SVHC).[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-16)

## Physical properties

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chromium&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Physical properties")]

### Atomic

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chromium&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Atomic")]

Gaseous chromium has a ground-state [electron configuration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron_configuration "Electron configuration") of [[Ar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argon "Argon")] 3d 5 4s 1. It is the first element in the periodic table whose configuration violates the [Aufbau principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aufbau_principle "Aufbau principle"). Exceptions to the principle also occur later in the periodic table for elements such as [copper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copper "Copper"), [niobium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niobium "Niobium") and [molybdenum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molybdenum "Molybdenum").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-CasaXPS-17)

Chromium is the first element in the 3d series where the 3d electrons start to sink into the core; they thus contribute less to [metallic bonding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallic_bonding "Metallic bonding"), and hence the melting and boiling points and the [enthalpy of atomisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enthalpy_of_atomisation "Enthalpy of atomisation") of chromium are lower than those of the preceding element [vanadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadium "Vanadium"). Chromium(VI) is a strong [oxidising agent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxidising_agent "Oxidising agent") in contrast to the [molybdenum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molybdenum "Molybdenum")(VI) and [tungsten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tungsten "Tungsten")(VI) oxides.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Greenwood1004-18)

### Bulk

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chromium&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Bulk")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a1/Chromium.jpg/250px-Chromium.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Chromium.jpg)

Sample of chromium metal

Chromium is the third hardest element after [carbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon "Carbon") ([diamond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diamond "Diamond")) and [boron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron "Boron"). Its [Mohs hardness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohs_scale_of_mineral_hardness "Mohs scale of mineral hardness") is 8.5, which means that it can scratch samples of [quartz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartz "Quartz") and [topaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topaz "Topaz"), but can be scratched by [corundum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corundum "Corundum"). Chromium is highly resistant to [tarnishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarnish "Tarnish"), which makes it useful as a metal that preserves its outermost layer from [corroding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corrosion "Corrosion"), unlike other metals such as [copper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copper "Copper"), [magnesium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnesium "Magnesium"), and [aluminium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium "Aluminium").

Chromium has a [melting point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melting_point "Melting point") of 1907°C (3465°F), which is relatively low compared to the majority of transition metals. However, it still has the second highest melting point out of all the [period 4 elements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Period_4_element "Period 4 element"), being topped by [vanadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadium "Vanadium") by 3°C (5°F) at 1910°C (3470°F). The [boiling point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boiling_point "Boiling point") of 2671°C (4840°F), however, is comparatively lower, having the fourth lowest boiling point out of the [Period 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Period_4 "Period 4")[transition metals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transition_metal "Transition metal") alone behind [copper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copper "Copper"), [manganese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese "Manganese") and [zinc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zinc "Zinc").[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-19) The [electrical resistivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_resistivity_and_conductivity "Electrical resistivity and conductivity") of chromium at 20°C is 125 [nanoohm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohm "Ohm")-[meters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meter "Meter").

Chromium has a high [specular reflection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Specular_reflection "Specular reflection") in comparison to other transition metals. In [infrared](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrared "Infrared"), at 425[μm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micrometre "Micrometre"), chromium has a maximum reflectance of about 72%, decreasing to a minimum of 62% at 750 μm before increasing again to 90% at 4000 μm.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-NIST_specular_reflection-11) When chromium is used in [stainless steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stainless_steel "Stainless steel") alloys and [polished](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polishing "Polishing"), the specular reflection decreases with the inclusion of additional metals, yet is still high in comparison with other alloys. Between 40% and 60% of the visible spectrum is reflected from polished stainless steel.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-NIST_specular_reflection-11) Chromium's high reflectivity, especially the 90% in infrared, can be attributed to chromium's magnetic properties.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-ISU_infrared-20) Chromium has unique magnetic properties; it is the only elemental solid that shows [antiferromagnetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiferromagnetic "Antiferromagnetic") ordering at room temperature and below. Above 38°C, its magnetic ordering becomes [paramagnetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramagnetic "Paramagnetic").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-fawcett-7) The antiferromagnetic properties, which cause the chromium atoms to temporarily [ionize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionization "Ionization") and bond with themselves, are present because the body-centric cubic's magnetic properties are disproportionate to the [lattice periodicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal_structure "Crystal structure"). This is due to the magnetic moments at the cube's corners and the unequal, but antiparallel, cube centers.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-ISU_infrared-20) The frequency-dependent [relative permittivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relative_permittivity "Relative permittivity") of chromium, deriving from [Maxwell's equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxwell's_equations "Maxwell's equations") and chromium's [antiferromagnetism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiferromagnetism "Antiferromagnetism"), results in increased reflectance at infrared and visible wavelengths.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-ISU_optical-21)

#### Passivation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chromium&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Passivation")]

Chromium metal in air is [passivated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passivation_(chemistry) "Passivation (chemistry)"): it forms a thin, protective surface layer of chromium oxide with the [corundum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corundum_(structure) "Corundum (structure)") structure. Passivation can be enhanced by short contact with [oxidizing acids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxidizing_acid "Oxidizing acid") like [nitric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitric_acid "Nitric acid"). Passivated chromium is stable against acids. Passivation can be removed with a strong [reducing agent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reducing_agent "Reducing agent") that destroys the protective oxide layer on the metal. Chromium metal treated in this way readily dissolves in weak acids.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-HollemanAF-22)

The surface [chromia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium(III)_oxide "Chromium(III) oxide")Cr 2 O 3 scale is adherent to the metal. In contrast, iron forms a more porous oxide which is weak and flakes easily and exposes fresh metal to the air, causing continued [rusting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rust "Rust"). At room temperature, the chromia scale is a few atomic layers thick, growing in thickness by outward [diffusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_diffusion "Atomic diffusion") of metal ions across the scale. Above 950°C volatile [chromium trioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium_trioxide "Chromium trioxide")CrO 3 forms from the chromia scale, limiting the scale thickness and oxidation protection.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-23)

Chromium, unlike iron and nickel, does not suffer from [hydrogen embrittlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_embrittlement "Hydrogen embrittlement"). However, it does suffer from nitrogen [embrittlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embrittlement "Embrittlement"), reacting with nitrogen from air and forming brittle nitrides at the high temperatures necessary to work the metal parts.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-24)

### Isotopes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chromium&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Isotopes")]

Main article: [Isotopes of chromium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotopes_of_chromium "Isotopes of chromium")

Naturally occurring chromium is composed of four stable [isotopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotope "Isotope"); 50 Cr, 52 Cr, 53 Cr and 54 Cr, with 52 Cr being the most abundant (83.789% [natural abundance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_abundance "Natural abundance")). Twenty-five [radioisotopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioisotope "Radioisotope") have been characterized, ranging from 42 Cr to 70 Cr; the most stable radioisotope is 51 Cr with a half-life of 27.70 days. All of the remaining [radioactive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioactive "Radioactive") isotopes have half-lives that are less than a day and the majority less than a minute. Chromium also has two [metastable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metastable "Metastable")[nuclear isomers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_isomer "Nuclear isomer").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-NUBASE2020-9)

The primary [decay mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decay_mode "Decay mode") before the most abundant stable isotope, 52 Cr, is [electron capture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron_capture "Electron capture") and the primary mode after is [beta decay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_decay "Beta decay").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-NUBASE2020-9)

53 Cr is the [radiogenic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiogenic "Radiogenic") decay product of [53 Mn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese-53 "Manganese-53") (half-life 3.7 million years). Chromium and manganese are found together sufficiently for measurement of both to find application in [isotope geology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotope_geology "Isotope geology"). Manganese-chromium isotope ratios reinforce the evidence from [26 Al](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium-26 "Aluminium-26") and 107[Pd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palladium "Palladium") concerning the early history of the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System"). Variations in 53 Cr/52 Cr and Mn/Cr ratios from several meteorites indicate a non-zero initial 53 Mn/55 Mn ratio that suggests Cr isotopic composition variations must result from in-situ decay of 53>Mn in differentiated planetary bodies. Hence 53 Cr provides additional evidence for [nucleosynthetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nucleosynthesis "Nucleosynthesis") processes immediately before coalescence of the Solar System.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-53Mn53Cr-25)

The ratio 53 Cr/52 Cr has also been posited as a proxy for atmospheric oxygen concentration.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-26)

## Chemistry and compounds

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chromium&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Chemistry and compounds")]

### Chromium(III)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chromium&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Chromium(III)")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3b/Chromium%28III%29-chloride-purple-anhydrous-sunlight.jpg/250px-Chromium%28III%29-chloride-purple-anhydrous-sunlight.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Chromium(III)-chloride-purple-anhydrous-sunlight.jpg)

Anhydrous chromium(III) chloride (CrCl 3

A large number of chromium(III) compounds are known, such as [chromium(III) nitrate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium_nitrate "Chromium nitrate"), [chromium(III) acetate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium(III)_acetate "Chromium(III) acetate"), and [chromium(III) oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium(III)_oxide "Chromium(III) oxide").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-33) Chromium(III) can be obtained by dissolving elemental chromium in acids like [hydrochloric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrochloric_acid "Hydrochloric acid") or [sulfuric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfuric_acid "Sulfuric acid"), but it can also be formed through the reduction of chromium(VI) by [cytochrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cytochrome "Cytochrome")[c7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cytochrome_c "Cytochrome c").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-34) The Cr 3+ ion has a similar radius (63[pm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picometer "Picometer")) to Al 3+ (radius 50 pm), and they can replace each other in some compounds, such as in [chrome alum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrome_alum "Chrome alum") and [alum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alum "Alum").

Chromium(III) tends to form [octahedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octahedral_molecular_geometry "Octahedral molecular geometry") complexes. Commercially available [chromium(III) chloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium(III)_chloride "Chromium(III) chloride") hydrate is the dark green complex [CrCl 2(H 2 O)4]Cl. Closely related compounds are the pale green [CrCl(H 2 O)5]Cl 2 and violet [Cr(H 2 O)6]Cl 3. If anhydrous violet[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-35) chromium(III) chloride is dissolved in water, the violet solution turns green after some time as the chloride in the inner [coordination sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordination_sphere "Coordination sphere") is replaced by water. This kind of reaction is also observed with solutions of [chrome alum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrome_alum "Chrome alum") and other water-soluble chromium(III) salts. A [tetrahedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrahedral_molecular_geometry "Tetrahedral molecular geometry") coordination of [chromium(III)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium(III) "Chromium(III)") has been reported for the Cr-centered [Keggin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keggin_structure "Keggin structure") anion [α−CrW 12 O 40]5−.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-36)

[Chromium(III) hydroxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium(III)_hydroxide "Chromium(III) hydroxide") (Cr(OH)3) is [amphoteric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amphoterism "Amphoterism"), dissolving in acidic solutions to form [Cr(H 2 O)6]3+, and in basic solutions to form [Cr(OH)4(H 2 O)2]−.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-37) It is dehydrated by heating to form the green chromium(III) oxide (Cr 2 O 3), a stable oxide with a crystal structure identical to that of [corundum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corundum "Corundum").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-HollemanAF-22)

### Chromium(VI)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chromium&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Chromium(VI)")]

Main article: [Hexavalent chromium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hexavalent_chromium "Hexavalent chromium")

[Chromium(VI) compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hexavalent_chromium "Hexavalent chromium") are oxidants at low or neutral pH. [Chromate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromate_and_dichromate "Chromate and dichromate") anions (CrO 4 2−) and dichromate (Cr 2 O 7 2−) anions are the principal ions at this oxidation state. They exist at an equilibrium, determined by pH:

2 CrO 4 2− + 2 H+ ⇌ Cr 2 O 7 2− + H 2 O
Chromium(VI) oxyhalides are known also and include [chromyl fluoride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromyl_fluoride "Chromyl fluoride") (CrO 2 F 2) and [chromyl chloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromyl_chloride "Chromyl chloride") (CrO 2 Cl 2).[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-HollemanAF-22) However, despite several erroneous claims, [chromium hexafluoride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium_hexafluoride "Chromium hexafluoride") (as well as all higher hexahalides) remains unknown, as of 2020.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-38)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/Chrom%28VI%29-oxid.jpg/250px-Chrom%28VI%29-oxid.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Chrom(VI)-oxid.jpg)

Chromium(VI) oxide

[Sodium chromate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_chromate "Sodium chromate") is produced industrially by the oxidative roasting of [chromite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromite "Chromite") ore with [sodium carbonate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_carbonate "Sodium carbonate"). The change in equilibrium is visible by a change from yellow (chromate) to orange (dichromate), such as when an acid is added to a neutral solution of [potassium chromate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potassium_chromate "Potassium chromate"). At yet lower pH values, further condensation to more complex [oxyanions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxyanion "Oxyanion") of chromium is possible.

Both the [chromate and dichromate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromate_and_dichromate "Chromate and dichromate") anions are strong oxidizing reagents at low pH:[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-HollemanAF-22)

Cr 2 O 7 2− + 14 H 3 O+ + 6 e− → 2 Cr 3+ + 21 H 2 O (_E_ θ = 1.33 V)
They are, however, only moderately oxidizing at high pH:[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-HollemanAF-22)

CrO 4 2− + 4 H 2 O + 3 e− → Cr(OH)3 + 5 OH− (_E_ θ = −0.13 V)[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Chroman_sodn%C3%BD.JPG/250px-Chroman_sodn%C3%BD.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Chroman_sodn%C3%BD.JPG)

[Sodium chromate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_chromate "Sodium chromate") (Na 2 CrO 4)

Chromium(VI) compounds in solution can be detected by adding an acidic [hydrogen peroxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_peroxide "Hydrogen peroxide") solution. The unstable dark blue [chromium(VI) peroxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium(VI)_peroxide "Chromium(VI) peroxide") (CrO(O 2)2) is formed, which can be stabilized as an ether adduct CrO(O 2)2·OR 2.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-HollemanAF-22)

[Chromic acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromic_acid "Chromic acid") has the hypothetical formula H 2 CrO 4. It is a vaguely described chemical, despite many well-defined chromates and dichromates being known. The dark red [chromium(VI) oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium(VI)_oxide "Chromium(VI) oxide")CrO 3, the acid [anhydride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anhydride "Anhydride") of chromic acid, is sold industrially as "chromic acid".[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-HollemanAF-22) It can be produced by mixing sulfuric acid with dichromate and is a strong oxidizing agent.

### Other oxidation states

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chromium&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Other oxidation states")]

See also: [Organochromium chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organochromium_chemistry "Organochromium chemistry")

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/eb/Chromium_carbide_Cr3C2.JPG/250px-Chromium_carbide_Cr3C2.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Chromium_carbide_Cr3C2.JPG)

[Chromium(II) carbide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium(II)_carbide "Chromium(II) carbide") (Cr 3 C 2)

Chromium(II) compounds are uncommon, in part because they readily oxidize to chromium(III) derivatives in air. Water-stable [chromium(II) chloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium(II)_chloride "Chromium(II) chloride")CrCl 2 can be made by reducing chromium(III) chloride with [zinc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zinc "Zinc"). The resulting bright blue solution created from dissolving chromium(II) chloride is stable at neutral [pH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PH "PH").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-HollemanAF-22) Some other notable chromium(II) compounds include [chromium(II) oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium(II)_oxide "Chromium(II) oxide") CrO, and [chromium(II) sulfate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium(II)_sulfate "Chromium(II) sulfate")CrSO 4. Many chromium(II) carboxylates are known. The red [chromium(II) acetate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium(II)_acetate "Chromium(II) acetate") (Cr 2(CH 3 COO)4) is somewhat famous. It features a Cr-Cr [quadruple bond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadruple_bond "Quadruple bond").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-39)

Compounds of chromium(V) are rather rare; the oxidation state +5 is only realized in few compounds but are intermediates in many reactions involving oxidations by chromate. The only binary compound is the volatile [chromium(V) fluoride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium(V)_fluoride "Chromium(V) fluoride") (CrF 5). This red solid has a melting point of 30°C and a boiling point of 117°C. It can be prepared by treating chromium metal with fluorine at 400°C and 200 bar pressure. The peroxochromate(V) is another example of the +5 oxidation state. [Potassium peroxochromate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potassium_tetraperoxochromate(V) "Potassium tetraperoxochromate(V)") (K 3 Cr(O 2)4) is made by reacting potassium chromate with hydrogen peroxide at low temperatures. This red brown compound is stable at room temperature but decomposes spontaneously at 150–170°C.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-40)

Compounds of chromium(IV) are slightly more common than those of chromium(V). The tetrahalides, [CrF 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium(IV)_fluoride "Chromium(IV) fluoride"), [CrCl 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium(IV)_chloride "Chromium(IV) chloride"), and CrBr 4, can be produced by treating the trihalides (CrX 3) with the corresponding halogen at elevated temperatures. Such compounds are susceptible to disproportionation reactions and are not stable in water. Organic compounds containing Cr(IV) state such as chromium tetra _t_-butoxide are also known.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-41)

Many Cr(0) complexes are known. [Bis(benzene)chromium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bis(benzene)chromium "Bis(benzene)chromium") and [chromium hexacarbonyl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium_hexacarbonyl "Chromium hexacarbonyl") are highlights in [organochromium chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organochromium_chemistry "Organochromium chemistry").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Most chromium(I) compounds are obtained solely by oxidation of electron-rich, [octahedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octahedral_molecular_geometry "Octahedral molecular geometry") chromium(0) complexes. Other chromium(I) complexes contain [cyclopentadienyl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclopentadienyl "Cyclopentadienyl") ligands. As verified by [X-ray diffraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-ray_diffraction "X-ray diffraction"), a Cr-Cr [quintuple bond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quintuple_bond "Quintuple bond") (length 183.51(4) pm) has also been described.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-42) Extremely bulky monodentate ligands stabilize this compound by shielding the quintuple bond from further reactions.

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/00/Chromit_1.jpg/250px-Chromit_1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Chromit_1.jpg)
