Chromium is the 21st most [abundant element in Earth's crust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abundance_of_elements_in_Earth's_crust "Abundance of elements in Earth's crust")[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Emsley-43) with an average concentration of 100 ppm. Chromium compounds are found in the environment from the [erosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erosion "Erosion") of chromium-containing rocks, and can be redistributed by volcanic eruptions. Typical background concentrations of chromium in environmental media are: atmosphere <10 ng/m 3; soil <500 mg/kg; vegetation <0.5 mg/kg; freshwater <10 μg/L; seawater <1 μg/L; sediment <80 mg/kg.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Rieuwerts-44) Chromium is mined as chromite (FeCr 2 O 4) ore.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-NRC-45)

About two-fifths of the chromite ores and concentrates in the world are produced in South Africa, about a third in Kazakhstan,[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Trump-SoHo-Bayrock-46) while India, Russia, and Turkey are also substantial producers. Untapped chromite deposits are plentiful, but geographically concentrated in Kazakhstan and southern Africa.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-USGS2015Yb-47) Although rare, deposits of [native](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_metal "Native metal") chromium exist.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-48)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-49) The [Udachnaya Pipe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Udachnaya_Pipe "Udachnaya Pipe") in Russia produces samples of the native metal. This mine is a [kimberlite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kimberlite "Kimberlite") pipe, rich in [diamonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diamond "Diamond"), and the [reducing environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redox "Redox") helped produce both elemental chromium and diamonds.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-50)

The relation between Cr(III) and Cr(VI) strongly depends on [pH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PH "PH") and [oxidative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxidative "Oxidative") properties of the location. In most cases, Cr(III) is the dominating species,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Crspeci-27) but in some areas, the ground water can contain up to 39 μg/L of total chromium, of which 30 μg/L is Cr(VI).[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-51)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chromium&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: History")]

### Early applications

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chromium&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Early applications")]

Chromium was not used anywhere until the experiments of French pharmacist and chemist [Nicolas Louis Vauquelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_Louis_Vauquelin "Nicolas Louis Vauquelin") (1763–1829) in the late 1790s.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-52)

From the 1970s, until 2019, it was widely believed that the technique of chromium plating to prevent metal [corrosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corrosion "Corrosion") had been invented in [ancient China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_China "History of China"). This technique was thought to have been used, for example, to protect bronze artifacts such as arrowheads and sword blades buried as grave goods in the [mausoleum of the First Emperor of Qin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mausoleum_of_the_First_Qin_Emperor "Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor"). However, a detailed scientific investigation in 2019 revealed that the chromium found on these artifacts originated naturally from the [lacquer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lacquer "Lacquer") applied to them. Scientists now believe that the excellent preservation of the artifacts was not due to intentional chromium plating, but rather to the burial environment: the soil was fine-grained and [alkaline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkaline "Alkaline"), which limited aeration and the growth of organic matter, thereby creating optimal conditions for metal preservation.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-53)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-54)

Chromium minerals as pigments came to the attention of the west in the eighteenth century. On 26 July 1761, [Johann Gottlob Lehmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Gottlob_Lehmann_(scientist) "Johann Gottlob Lehmann (scientist)") found an orange-red mineral in the [Beryozovskoye mines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryozovskoye_deposit "Beryozovskoye deposit") in the [Ural Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ural_Mountains "Ural Mountains") which he named _Siberian red lead_.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Meyer_1962_p.-55)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-56) Though misidentified as a [lead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead "Lead") compound with [selenium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selenium "Selenium") and [iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron "Iron") components, the mineral was in fact [crocoite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crocoite "Crocoite") with a formula of PbCrO 4.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-ChromiumVI-57) In 1770, [Peter Simon Pallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Simon_Pallas "Peter Simon Pallas") visited the same site as Lehmann and found a red lead mineral that was discovered to possess useful properties as a [pigment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pigment "Pigment") in [paints](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paint "Paint"). After Pallas, the use of Siberian red lead as a paint pigment began to develop rapidly throughout the region.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Weeks1932-58) Crocoite would be the principal source of chromium in pigments until the discovery of [chromite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromite "Chromite") many years later.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-59)

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c4/Cut_Ruby.jpg/250px-Cut_Ruby.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cut_Ruby.jpg)

The red color of rubies is due to trace amounts of chromium within the [corundum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corundum "Corundum").

In 1794, [Louis Nicolas Vauquelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Nicolas_Vauquelin "Louis Nicolas Vauquelin") received samples of crocoite [ore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ore "Ore"). He produced [chromium trioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium(VI)_oxide "Chromium(VI) oxide") (CrO 3) by mixing crocoite with [hydrochloric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrochloric_acid "Hydrochloric acid").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-ChromiumVI-57) In 1797, Vauquelin discovered that he could isolate metallic chromium by heating the oxide in a charcoal oven, for which he is credited as the one who truly discovered the element.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-60)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-61) Vauquelin was also able to detect traces of chromium in precious [gemstones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gemstone "Gemstone"), such as [ruby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruby "Ruby") and [emerald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerald "Emerald").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-ChromiumVI-57)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-62)

During the nineteenth century, chromium was primarily used not only as a component of paints, but in [tanning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanning_(leather) "Tanning (leather)") salts as well. For quite some time, the crocoite found in Russia was the main source for such tanning materials. In 1827, a larger chromite deposit was discovered near [Baltimore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore "Baltimore"), United States, which quickly met the demand for tanning salts much more adequately than the crocoite that had been used previously.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-63) This made the United States the largest producer of chromium products until the year 1848, when larger deposits of chromite were uncovered near the city of [Bursa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bursa "Bursa"), Turkey.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-NRC-45) With the development of metallurgy and chemical industries in the Western world, the need for chromium increased.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-64)

Chromium is also famous for its reflective, metallic luster when polished. It is used as a protective and decorative coating on car parts, plumbing fixtures, furniture parts and many other items, usually applied by [electroplating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electroplating "Electroplating"). Chromium was used for electroplating as early as 1848, but this use only became widespread with the development of an improved process in 1924.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Crplating-65)

## Production

Approximately 28.8 million metric tons (Mt) of marketable chromite ore was produced in 2013, and converted into 7.5 Mt of ferrochromium.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-USGS2015Yb-47) According to John F. Papp, writing for the USGS, "Ferrochromium is the leading end use of chromite ore, [and] stainless steel is the leading end use of ferrochromium."[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-USGS2015Yb-47)

The largest producers of chromium ore in 2013 have been South Africa (48%), Kazakhstan (13%), Turkey (11%), and India (10%), with several other countries producing the rest of about 18% of the world production.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-USGS2015Yb-47)

The two main products of chromium ore refining are [ferrochromium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrochromium "Ferrochromium") and metallic chromium. For those products the ore smelter process differs considerably. For the production of ferrochromium, the chromite ore (FeCr 2 O 4) is reduced in large scale in [electric arc furnace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_arc_furnace "Electric arc furnace") or in smaller smelters with either [aluminium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium "Aluminium") or [silicon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon "Silicon") in an [aluminothermic reaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminothermic_reaction "Aluminothermic reaction").[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-IndMin-66) For the production of pure chromium, the iron must be separated from the chromium in a two step roasting and leaching process. The chromite ore is heated with a mixture of [calcium carbonate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calcium_carbonate "Calcium carbonate") and [sodium carbonate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_carbonate "Sodium carbonate") in the presence of air. The chromium is oxidized to the hexavalent form, while the iron forms the stable Fe 2 O 3. The subsequent leaching at higher elevated temperatures dissolves the [chromates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromates "Chromates") and leaves the insoluble iron oxide. The chromate is converted by [sulfuric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfuric_acid "Sulfuric acid") into the dichromate.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-IndMin-66)

4 FeCr 2 O 4 + 8 Na 2 CO 3 + 7 O 2 → 8 Na 2 CrO 4 + 2 Fe 2 O 3 + 8 CO 2 2 Na 2 CrO 4 + H 2 SO 4 → Na 2 Cr 2 O 7 + Na 2 SO 4 + H 2 O
The dichromate is converted to the chromium(III) oxide by reduction with carbon and then reduced in an aluminothermic reaction to chromium.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-IndMin-66)

Na 2 Cr 2 O 7 + 2 C → Cr 2 O 3 + Na 2 CO 3 + CO Cr 2 O 3 + 2 Al → Al 2 O 3 + 2 Cr[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/World_Chromium_Production_2002.svg/250px-World_Chromium_Production_2002.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:World_Chromium_Production_2002.svg)

## Applications

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chromium&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Applications")]

The creation of metal alloys account for 85% of the available chromium's usage. The remainder of chromium is used in the [chemical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_industry "Chemical industry"), [refractory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refractory "Refractory"), and [foundry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foundry "Foundry") industries.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-69)

### Metallurgy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chromium&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Metallurgy")]

[![Image 32](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/Besteck_WMF_Stockholm_ca_1960er.jpg/250px-Besteck_WMF_Stockholm_ca_1960er.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Besteck_WMF_Stockholm_ca_1960er.jpg)

Stainless steel cutlery made from Cromargan 18/10, containing 18% chromium

Main articles: [Chrome plating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrome_plating "Chrome plating") and [Stainless steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stainless_steel "Stainless steel")

The strengthening effect of forming stable metal carbides at grain boundaries, and the strong increase in corrosion resistance made chromium an important alloying material for steel. [High-speed tool steels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-speed_steel "High-speed steel") contain 3–5% chromium. [Stainless steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stainless_steel "Stainless steel"), the primary corrosion-resistant metal alloy, is formed when chromium is introduced to [iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron "Iron") in concentrations above 11%.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Davis_2000_p.-70) For stainless steel's formation, ferrochromium is added to the molten iron. Also, nickel-based alloys have increased strength due to the formation of discrete, stable, metal, carbide particles at the grain boundaries. For example, [Inconel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inconel "Inconel") 718 contains 18.6% chromium. Because of the excellent high-temperature properties of these nickel [superalloys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superalloy "Superalloy"), they are used in [jet engines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet_engine "Jet engine") and [gas turbines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gas_turbine "Gas turbine") in lieu of common structural materials.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-superal-71)[ASTM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ASTM "ASTM") B163 relies on chromium for condenser and heat-exchanger tubes, while [castings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castings "Castings") with high strength at elevated temperatures that contain chromium are standardised with ASTM A567.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-iarc49-72)[AISI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Iron_and_Steel_Institute "American Iron and Steel Institute") type 332 is used where high temperature would normally cause [carburization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carburization "Carburization"), [oxidation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxidation "Oxidation") or [corrosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corrosion "Corrosion").[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-azom332-73)[Incoloy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incoloy "Incoloy") 800 "is capable of remaining stable and maintaining its [austenitic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austenitic "Austenitic") structure even after long time exposures to high temperatures".[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-azom800-74)[Nichrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nichrome "Nichrome") is used as resistance wire for heating elements in things like [toasters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toasters "Toasters") and space heaters. These uses make chromium a [strategic material](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_material "Strategic material"). Consequently, during World War II, U.S. road engineers were instructed to avoid chromium in yellow road paint, as it "may become a critical material during the emergency".[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-75) The United States likewise considered chromium "essential for the German war industry" and made intense diplomatic efforts to keep it out of the hands of [Nazi Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany").[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-76)

The high hardness and corrosion resistance of unalloyed chromium makes it a reliable metal for surface coating; it is still the most popular metal for sheet coating, with its above-average durability, compared to other coating metals.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-77) A layer of chromium is deposited on pretreated metallic surfaces by [electroplating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electroplating "Electroplating") techniques. There are two deposition methods: thin, and thick. Thin deposition involves a layer of chromium below 1 μm thickness deposited by [chrome plating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrome_plating "Chrome plating"), and is used for decorative surfaces. Thicker chromium layers are deposited if wear-resistant surfaces are needed. Both methods use acidic chromate or [dichromate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dichromate "Dichromate") solutions. To prevent the energy-consuming change in oxidation state, the use of chromium(III) sulfate is under development; for most applications of chromium, the previously established process is used.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Crplating-65)

In the [chromate conversion coating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromate_conversion_coating "Chromate conversion coating") process, the strong oxidative properties of chromates are used to deposit a protective oxide layer on metals like aluminium, zinc, and cadmium. This [passivation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passivation_(chemistry) "Passivation (chemistry)") and the self-healing properties of the chromate stored in the chromate conversion coating, which is able to migrate to local defects, are the benefits of this coating method.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Edwards-78) Because of environmental and health regulations on chromates, alternative coating methods are under development.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-79)

Chromic acid [anodizing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anodizing "Anodizing") (or Type I anodizing) of aluminium is another electrochemical process that does not lead to the deposition of chromium, but uses [chromic acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromic_acid "Chromic acid") as an electrolyte in the solution. During anodization, an oxide layer is formed on the aluminium. The use of chromic acid, instead of the normally used sulfuric acid, leads to a slight difference of these oxide layers.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-surface-80) The high toxicity of Cr(VI) compounds, used in the established chromium electroplating process, and the strengthening of safety and environmental regulations demand a search for substitutes for chromium, or at least a change to less toxic chromium(III) compounds.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Crplating-65)

### Pigment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chromium&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Pigment")]

The mineral [crocoite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crocoite "Crocoite") (which is also [lead chromate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead_chromate "Lead chromate")PbCrO 4) was used as a yellow pigment shortly after its discovery. After a synthesis method became available starting from the more abundant chromite, [chrome yellow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrome_yellow "Chrome yellow") was, together with [cadmium yellow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadmium_yellow "Cadmium yellow"), one of the most used yellow pigments. The pigment does not photodegrade, but it tends to darken due to the formation of chromium(III) oxide. It has a strong color, and was used for school buses in the United States and for the postal services (for example, the [Deutsche Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deutsche_Post "Deutsche Post")) in Europe. The use of chrome yellow has since declined due to environmental and safety concerns and was replaced by organic pigments or other alternatives that are free from lead and chromium. Other pigments that are based around chromium are, for example, the deep shade of red pigment [chrome red](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrome_red "Chrome red"), which is simply lead chromate with [lead(II) hydroxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead(II)_hydroxide "Lead(II) hydroxide") (PbCrO 4·Pb(OH)2). A very important chromate pigment, which was used widely in metal primer formulations, was zinc chromate, now replaced by zinc phosphate. A wash primer was formulated to replace the dangerous practice of pre-treating aluminium aircraft bodies with a phosphoric acid solution. This used zinc tetroxychromate dispersed in a solution of [polyvinyl butyral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyvinyl_butyral "Polyvinyl butyral"). An 8% solution of phosphoric acid in solvent was added just before application. It was found that an easily oxidized alcohol was an essential ingredient. A thin layer of about 10–15 μm was applied, which turned from yellow to dark green when it was cured. There is still a question as to the correct mechanism. Chrome green is a mixture of [Prussian blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prussian_blue "Prussian blue") and chrome yellow, while the chrome oxide green is [chromium(III) oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium(III)_oxide "Chromium(III) oxide").[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Cryel-81)

Chromium oxides are also used as a green pigment in the field of glassmaking and also as a glaze for ceramics.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-82) Green chromium oxide is extremely [lightfast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightfastness "Lightfastness") and as such is used in cladding coatings. It is also the main ingredient in [infrared](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrared "Infrared") reflecting paints, used by the armed forces to paint vehicles and to give them the same infrared reflectance as green leaves.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-83)

### Other uses

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chromium&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Other uses")]

[![Image 33: Components of original ruby laser.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7d/5_Maiman_Laser_Components.jpg/250px-5_Maiman_Laser_Components.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:5_Maiman_Laser_Components.jpg)

Red crystal of a ruby laser

Chromium(III) ions present in [corundum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corundum "Corundum") crystals (aluminium oxide) cause them to be colored red; when corundum appears as such, it is known as a [ruby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruby "Ruby"). If the corundum is lacking in chromium(III) ions, it is known as a [sapphire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sapphire "Sapphire").[[note 3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-84) A red-colored artificial ruby may also be achieved by doping chromium(III) into artificial corundum crystals, thus making chromium a requirement for making synthetic rubies.[[note 4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-85)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-86) Such a synthetic ruby crystal was the basis for the first [laser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laser "Laser"), produced in 1960, which relied on [stimulated emission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stimulated_emission "Stimulated emission") of light from the chromium atoms in such a crystal. Ruby has a laser transition at 694.3 nanometers, in a deep red color.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-WebbJones2004-87)

Chromium(VI) salts are used for the preservation of wood. For example, [chromated copper arsenate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromated_copper_arsenate "Chromated copper arsenate") (CCA) is used in [timber treatment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timber_treatment "Timber treatment") to protect wood from decay fungi, wood-attacking insects, including [termites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Termites "Termites"), and marine borers.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Hings-88) The formulations contain chromium based on the oxide CrO 3 between 35.3% and 65.5%. In the United States, 65,300 metric tons of CCA solution were used in 1996.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Hings-88)

Chromium(III) salts, especially [chrome alum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrome_alum "Chrome alum") and [chromium(III) sulfate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium(III)_sulfate "Chromium(III) sulfate"), are used in the tanning of [leather](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leather "Leather"). The chromium(III) stabilizes the leather by cross linking the [collagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collagen "Collagen") fibers.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-89) Chromium tanned leather can contain 4–5% of chromium, which is tightly bound to the proteins.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-NRC-45) Although the form of chromium used for tanning is not the toxic hexavalent variety, there remains interest in management of chromium in the tanning industry. Recovery and reuse, direct/indirect recycling,[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-90) and "chrome-less" or "chrome-free" tanning are practiced to better manage chromium usage.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-91)

The high heat resistivity and high melting point makes [chromite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromite "Chromite") and chromium(III) oxide a material for high temperature refractory applications, like [blast furnaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blast_furnace "Blast furnace"), cement [kilns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiln "Kiln"), molds for the firing of [bricks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brick "Brick") and as foundry sands for the [casting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casting_(metalworking) "Casting (metalworking)") of metals. In these applications, the refractory materials are made from mixtures of chromite and magnesite. The use is declining because of the environmental regulations due to the possibility of the formation of chromium(VI).[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-IndMin-66)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Barnhart1997-92)

Several chromium compounds are used as [catalysts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalyst "Catalyst") for processing hydrocarbons. For example, the [Phillips catalyst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phillips_catalyst "Phillips catalyst"), prepared from chromium oxides, is used for the production of about half the world's [polyethylene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyethylene "Polyethylene").[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-93) Fe-Cr mixed oxides are employed as high-temperature catalysts for the [water gas shift reaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_gas_shift_reaction "Water gas shift reaction").[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-94)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-95)[Copper chromite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copper_chromite "Copper chromite") is a useful [hydrogenation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogenation "Hydrogenation") catalyst.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-96)

### Uses of compounds

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chromium&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Uses of compounds")]

*   [Chromium(IV) oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium(IV)_oxide "Chromium(IV) oxide") (CrO 2) is a [magnetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetism "Magnetism") compound. Its ideal shape [anisotropy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anisotropy "Anisotropy"), which imparts high [coercivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coercivity "Coercivity") and remnant magnetization, made it a compound superior to γ−Fe 2 O 3. Chromium(IV) oxide is used to manufacture [magnetic tape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_tape "Magnetic tape") used in high-performance audio tape and standard [audio cassettes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_audio_cassette "Compact audio cassette").[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-97)
*   [Chromium(III) oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium(III)_oxide "Chromium(III) oxide") (Cr 2 O 3) is a metal polish known as green rouge.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-DoiMarinescu2011-98)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-99)
*   [Chromic acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromic_acid "Chromic acid") is a powerful oxidizing agent and is a useful compound for cleaning laboratory glassware of any trace of organic compounds.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-100) It is prepared by dissolving [potassium dichromate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potassium_dichromate "Potassium dichromate") in concentrated sulfuric acid, which is then used to wash the apparatus. [Sodium dichromate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_dichromate "Sodium dichromate") is sometimes used because of its higher solubility (50 g/L versus 200 g/L respectively). The use of dichromate cleaning solutions is now phased out due to the high toxicity and environmental concerns. Modern cleaning solutions are highly effective and chromium free.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Roth1994-101)
*   [Potassium dichromate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potassium_dichromate "Potassium dichromate") is a chemical [reagent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reagent "Reagent"), used as a titrating agent.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-102)
*   [Chromates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromate_and_dichromate "Chromate and dichromate") are added to drilling muds to prevent corrosion of steel under wet conditions.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-103)
*   [Chrome alum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrome_alum "Chrome alum") is [Chromium(III) potassium sulfate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium(III)_potassium_sulfate "Chromium(III) potassium sulfate") and is used as a [mordant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mordant "Mordant") (i.e., a fixing agent) for dyes in fabric and in [tanning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanning_(leather) "Tanning (leather)").[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Ul-Islam2017-104)
*   [Zinc chromate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zinc_chromate "Zinc chromate") is used as an anticorrosive agent for [aluminium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium "Aluminium"), especially in the aerospace industry.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-105)

## Biological role

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chromium&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Biological role")]

The possible nutritional value of chromium(III) is unproven.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-106)[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-107) Although chromium is regarded as a trace element and [dietary mineral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mineral_(nutrient) "Mineral (nutrient)"), its suspected roles in the action of [insulin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insulin "Insulin")– a hormone that mediates the metabolism and storage of carbohydrate, fat, and protein – have not been adequately established.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-ods-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-lpi-14) The [mechanism of its actions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanism_of_action "Mechanism of action") in the body is undefined, leaving in doubt whether chromium has a biological role in healthy people.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-ods-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-lpi-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-efsa-15)

In contrast, [hexavalent chromium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hexavalent_chromium "Hexavalent chromium") (Cr(VI) or Cr 6+) is highly toxic and [mutagenic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutagen "Mutagen").[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-108) Ingestion of chromium(VI) in water has been linked to stomach tumors, and it may also cause allergic [contact dermatitis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contact_dermatitis "Contact dermatitis").[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-109)

"[Chromium deficiency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium_deficiency "Chromium deficiency")", involving a lack of Cr(III) in the body, or perhaps some complex of it, such as [glucose tolerance factor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glucose_tolerance_factor "Glucose tolerance factor"), is not accepted as a medical condition, as it has no symptoms and healthy people do not require chromium supplementation.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-ods-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-lpi-14) Some studies suggest that the biologically active form of chromium(III) is transported in the body via an oligopeptide called [low-molecular-weight chromium-binding substance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low-molecular-weight_chromium-binding_substance "Low-molecular-weight chromium-binding substance") (chromodulin), which might play a role in the insulin signaling pathway.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-ods-13)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-pharmacological1-110)

The chromium content of common foods is generally low (1–13 micrograms per serving).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-ods-13)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-database-111) The chromium content of food varies widely, due to differences in soil mineral content, growing season, plant [cultivar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultivar "Cultivar"), and contamination during processing.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-lpi-14)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-database-111) Chromium (and [nickel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nickel "Nickel")) leach into food cooked in stainless steel, with the effect being largest when the cookware is new. Acidic foods that are cooked for many hours also exacerbate this effect.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-112)[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-113)

### Dietary recommendations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chromium&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Dietary recommendations")]

See also: [Chromium deficiency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium_deficiency "Chromium deficiency")

There is disagreement on chromium's status as an essential nutrient. Governmental departments from Australia, New Zealand, India, and Japan consider chromium as essential,[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-AustraliaNZ-114)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-India-115)[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Japan-116) while the United States and [European Food Safety Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Food_Safety_Authority "European Food Safety Authority") of the European Union do not.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-ods-13)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-efsa-15)

The U.S. [National Academy of Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Academy_of_Medicine "National Academy of Medicine") (NAM) updated the [Estimated Average Requirements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dietary_Reference_Intake#Parameters "Dietary Reference Intake") (EARs) and the Recommended Dietary Allowances (RDAs) for chromium in 2001. For chromium, there was insufficient information to set EARs and RDAs, so its needs are described as estimates for Adequate Intake (AI). From a 2001 assessment, AI of chromium for women ages 14 through 50 is 25 μg/day, and the AI for women ages 50 and above is 20 μg/day. The AIs for women who are pregnant are 30 μg/day, and for women who are lactating, the set AI is 45 μg/day. The AI for men ages 14 through 50 is 35 μg/day, and the AI for men ages 50 and above is 30 μg/day. For children ages 1 through 13, the AI increases with age from 0.2 μg/day up to 25 μg/day.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-ods-13) As for safety, the NAM sets Tolerable Upper Intake Levels (ULs) for vitamins and minerals when the evidence is sufficient. In the case of chromium, there is not yet enough information, hence no UL has been established. Collectively, the EARs, RDAs, AIs, and ULs are the parameters for the nutrition recommendation system known as [Dietary Reference Intake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dietary_Reference_Intake "Dietary Reference Intake") (DRI).[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-IOM-Chromium-117)

Australia and New Zealand consider chromium to be an essential nutrient, with an AI of 35 μg/day for men, 25 μg/day for women, 30 μg/day for women who are pregnant, and 45 μg/day for women who are lactating. A UL has not been set due to the lack of sufficient data.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-AustraliaNZ-114) India considers chromium to be an essential nutrient, with an adult recommended intake of 33 μg/day.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-India-115) Japan also considers chromium to be an essential nutrient, with an AI of 10 μg/day for adults, including women who are pregnant or lactating. A UL has not been set.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Japan-116)

The EFSA does not consider chromium to be an essential nutrient.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-efsa-15)[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-EFSA17-118)[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-119)

#### Labeling

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chromium&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Labeling")]

For U.S. food and dietary supplement labeling purposes, the amount of the substance in a serving is expressed as a percent of the [Daily Value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reference_Daily_Intake "Reference Daily Intake") (%DV). For chromium labeling purposes, 100% of the Daily Value was 120 μg. As of 27 May 2016, the percentage of daily value was revised to 35 μg to bring the chromium intake into a consensus with the official [Recommended Dietary Allowance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dietary_Reference_Intake "Dietary Reference Intake").[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-FedReg-120)[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-121) A table of the old and new adult daily values in the United States is provided at Reference Daily Intake.

After evaluation of research on the potential nutritional value of chromium, the European Food Safety Authority concluded that there was no evidence of benefit by dietary chromium in healthy people, thereby declining to establish recommendations in Europe for dietary intake of chromium.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-efsa-15)

### Food sources

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chromium&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Food sources")]

Food composition databases such as those maintained by the U.S. Department of Agriculture do not contain information on the chromium content of foods.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-USDA-Database-122) A wide variety of animal and vegetable foods contain chromium.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-ods-13)[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-IOM-Chromium-117) Content per serving is influenced by the chromium content of the soil in which the plants are grown, by foodstuffs fed to animals, and by processing methods, as chromium is leached into foods if processed or cooked in stainless steel equipment.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-123) One diet analysis study conducted in Mexico reported an average daily chromium intake of 30 micrograms.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-124) An estimated 31% of adults in the United States consume multi-vitamin/mineral dietary supplements,[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Kantor2016-125) which often contain 25 to 60 micrograms of chromium.

### Supplementation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chromium&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Supplementation")]

Chromium is an ingredient in [total parenteral nutrition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_parenteral_nutrition "Total parenteral nutrition") (TPN), because deficiency can occur after months of intravenous feeding with chromium-free TPN.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Stehle2016-126) It is also added to nutritional products for [preterm infants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preterm_infant "Preterm infant").[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-127) Although the mechanism of action in biological roles for chromium is unclear, in the United States chromium-containing products are sold as non-prescription dietary supplements in amounts ranging from 50 to 1,000 μg. Lower amounts of chromium are also often incorporated into multi-vitamin/mineral supplements consumed by an estimated 31% of adults in the United States.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Kantor2016-125) Chemical compounds used in dietary supplements include chromium chloride, chromium citrate, [chromium(III) picolinate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium(III)_picolinate "Chromium(III) picolinate"), [chromium(III) polynicotinate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium_polynicotinate "Chromium polynicotinate"), and other chemical compositions.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-ods-13) The benefit of supplements has not been proven.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-ods-13)[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Vincent2010-128)

#### Initiation of research on glucose

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chromium&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Initiation of research on glucose")]

The notion of chromium as a potential regulator of glucose metabolism began in the 1950s when scientists performed a series of experiments controlling the diet of rats.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-schwarz-129) The experimenters subjected the rats to a chromium deficient diet, and witnessed an inability to respond effectively to increased levels of blood glucose. A chromium-rich [Brewer's yeast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yeast "Yeast") was provided in the diet, enabling the rats to effectively metabolize glucose, and so giving evidence that chromium may have a role in glucose management.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-schwarz-129)

### Approved and disapproved health claims

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chromium&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Approved and disapproved health claims")]

In 2005, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration had approved a qualified health claim for chromium picolinate with a requirement for specific label wording:

_"One small study suggests that chromium picolinate may reduce the risk of insulin resistance, and therefore possibly may reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes. FDA concludes, however, that the existence of such a relationship between chromium picolinate and either insulin resistance or type 2 diabetes is highly uncertain."_
In other parts of the petition, the FDA rejected claims for chromium picolinate and cardiovascular disease, retinopathy or kidney disease caused by abnormally high blood sugar levels.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-130) As of March 2024, this ruling on chromium remains in effect.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-fda-enforce-131)

In 2010, chromium(III) picolinate was approved by Health Canada to be used in dietary supplements. Approved labeling statements include: a factor in the maintenance of good health, provides support for healthy glucose metabolism, helps the body to metabolize carbohydrates and helps the body to metabolize fats.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-132) The European Food Safety Authority approved claims in 2010 that chromium contributed to normal macronutrient metabolism and maintenance of normal blood glucose concentration, but rejected claims for maintenance or achievement of a normal body weight, or reduction of tiredness or fatigue.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-EFSA2010-133)

However, in a 2014 reassessment of studies to determine whether a Dietary Reference Intake value could be established for chromium, EFSA stated:[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-efsa-15)

_"The Panel concludes that no Average Requirement and no Population Reference Intake for chromium for the performance of physiological functions can be defined."_ and _"The Panel considered that there is no evidence of beneficial effects associated with chromium intake in healthy subjects. The Panel concludes that the setting of an Adequate Intake for chromium is also not appropriate."_

#### Diabetes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chromium&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Diabetes")]

Given the evidence for chromium deficiency causing problems with glucose management in the context of intravenous nutrition products formulated without chromium,[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Stehle2016-126) research interest turned to whether chromium supplementation would benefit people who have type 2 diabetes but are not chromium deficient. Looking at the results from four meta-analyses, one reported a statistically significant decrease in fasting [plasma glucose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plasma_glucose "Plasma glucose") levels and a non-significant trend in lower [hemoglobin A1C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glycated_hemoglobin "Glycated hemoglobin").[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Mauro-134) A second reported the same,[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Abdoll2013-135) a third reported significant decreases for both measures,[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Suk2014-136) while a fourth reported no benefit for either.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-137) A review published in 2016 listed 53 [randomized clinical trials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randomized_clinical_trial "Randomized clinical trial") that were included in one or more of six [meta-analyses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meta-analysis "Meta-analysis"). It concluded that whereas there may be modest decreases in fasting blood glucose and/or HbA1C that achieve statistical significance in some of these meta-analyses, few of the trials achieved decreases large enough to be expected to be relevant to clinical outcome.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Costello2016-138)

#### Body weight

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chromium&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: Body weight")]

Two [systematic reviews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systematic_review "Systematic review") looked at chromium supplements as a mean of managing body weight in overweight and obese people. One, limited to [chromium picolinate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium_picolinate "Chromium picolinate"), a common supplement ingredient, reported a statistically significant −1.1 kg (2.4 lb) weight loss in trials longer than 12 weeks.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Tian2013-139) The other included all chromium compounds and reported a statistically significant −0.50 kg (1.1 lb) weight change.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Onakpoya2013-140) Change in percent body fat did not reach statistical significance. Authors of both reviews considered the clinical relevance of this modest weight loss as uncertain/unreliable.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Tian2013-139)[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Onakpoya2013-140) The European Food Safety Authority reviewed the literature and concluded that there was insufficient evidence to support a claim.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-efsa-15)

#### Sports

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chromium&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: Sports")]

Chromium is promoted as a sports performance dietary supplement, based on the theory that it potentiates insulin activity, with anticipated results of increased muscle mass, and faster recovery of glycogen storage during post-exercise recovery.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Vincent2010-128)[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-141)[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Vinvent2003-142) A review of clinical trials reported that chromium supplementation did not improve exercise performance or increase muscle strength.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-143) The International Olympic Committee reviewed dietary supplements for high-performance athletes in 2018 and concluded there was no need to increase chromium intake for athletes, nor support for claims of losing body fat.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-144)

### Fresh-water fish

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chromium&action=edit&section=30 "Edit section: Fresh-water fish")]

Irrigation water standards for chromium are 0.1 mg/L, but some rivers in [Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh") are more than five times that amount. The standard for fish for human consumption is less than 1 mg/kg, but many tested samples were more than five times that amount.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Islam2018-145) Chromium, especially hexavalent chromium, is highly toxic to fish because it is easily absorbed across the gills, readily enters blood circulation, crosses cell membranes and bioconcentrates up the food chain. In contrast, the toxicity of trivalent chromium is very low, attributed to poor membrane permeability and little biomagnification.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Bakshi2018-146)

Acute and chronic exposure to chromium(VI) affects fish behavior, physiology, reproduction and survival. Hyperactivity and erratic swimming have been reported in contaminated environments. Egg hatching and fingerling survival are affected. In adult fish there are reports of histopathological damage to liver, kidney, muscle, intestines, and gills. Mechanisms include mutagenic gene damage and disruptions of enzyme functions.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Bakshi2018-146)

There is evidence that fish may not require chromium, but benefit from a measured amount in diet. In one study, juvenile fish gained weight on a zero chromium diet, but the addition of 500 μg of chromium in the form of chromium chloride or other supplement types, per kilogram of food (dry weight), increased weight gain. At 2,000 μg/kg the weight gain was no better than with the zero chromium diet, and there were increased DNA strand breaks.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-147)

## Precautions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chromium&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: Precautions")]

Main article: [Chromium toxicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium_toxicity "Chromium toxicity")

Water-insoluble chromium(III) compounds and chromium metal are not considered a health hazard, while the toxicity and carcinogenic properties of chromium(VI) have been known for a long time.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Barceloux-148) Because of the specific [transport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transport_protein "Transport protein") mechanisms, only limited amounts of chromium(III) enter the cells. Acute oral toxicity ranges between 50 and 150 mg/kg.[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Katz-149) A 2008 review suggested that moderate uptake of chromium(III) through dietary supplements poses no genetic-toxic risk.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Eastmond-150) In the US, the [Occupational Safety and Health Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occupational_Safety_and_Health_Administration "Occupational Safety and Health Administration") (OSHA) has designated an air [permissible exposure limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permissible_exposure_limit "Permissible exposure limit") (PEL) in the workplace as a time-weighted average (TWA) of 1 mg/m 3. The [National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institute_for_Occupational_Safety_and_Health "National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health") (NIOSH) has set a [recommended exposure limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recommended_exposure_limit "Recommended exposure limit") (REL) of 0.5 mg/m 3, time-weighted average. The [IDLH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IDLH "IDLH") (immediately dangerous to life and health) value is 250 mg/m 3.[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-151)

### Chromium(VI) toxicity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chromium&action=edit&section=32 "Edit section: Chromium(VI) toxicity")]

The acute [oral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mouth "Mouth")[toxicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toxicity "Toxicity") for [chromium(VI)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hexavalent_chromium "Hexavalent chromium") ranges between 1.5 and 3.3 mg/kg.[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Katz-149) In the body, chromium(VI) is reduced by several mechanisms to chromium(III) already in the blood before it enters the cells. The chromium(III) is excreted from the body, whereas the chromate ion is transferred into the cell by a transport mechanism, by which also [sulfate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfate "Sulfate") and [phosphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphate "Phosphate") ions enter the cell. The acute toxicity of chromium(VI) is due to its strong [oxidant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redox "Redox") properties. After it reaches the blood stream, it damages the kidneys, the liver and blood cells through oxidation reactions. [Hemolysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hemolysis "Hemolysis"), [renal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renal "Renal"), and liver failure result. Aggressive dialysis can be therapeutic.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Dayan-152)

The [carcinogenity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carcinogenity "Carcinogenity") of chromate dust has been known for a long time, and in 1890 the first publication described the elevated cancer risk of workers in a chromate dye company.[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-153)[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Langard-154) Three mechanisms have been proposed to describe the [genotoxicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genotoxicity "Genotoxicity") of chromium(VI). The first mechanism includes highly reactive [hydroxyl radicals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydroxyl_radical "Hydroxyl radical") and other reactive radicals which are by products of the reduction of chromium(VI) to chromium(III). The second process includes the direct binding of chromium(V), produced by reduction in the cell, and chromium(IV) compounds to the [DNA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA "DNA"). The last mechanism attributed the genotoxicity to the binding to the DNA of the end product of the chromium(III) reduction.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-Cohen-155)[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-156)

Chromium salts (chromates) are also the cause of [allergic reactions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allergic_reaction "Allergic reaction") in some people. Chromates are often used to manufacture, amongst other things, leather products, paints, cement, mortar and anti-corrosives. Contact with products containing chromates can lead to allergic [contact dermatitis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contact_dermatitis "Contact dermatitis") and irritant dermatitis, resulting in ulceration of the skin, sometimes referred to as "chrome ulcers". This condition is often found in workers that have been exposed to strong chromate solutions in electroplating, tanning and chrome-producing manufacturers.[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-157)[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-158)

### Environmental issues

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chromium&action=edit&section=33 "Edit section: Environmental issues")]

Because chromium compounds were used in [dyes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dye "Dye"), [paints](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paint "Paint"), and [leather](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leather "Leather")[tanning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanning_(leather) "Tanning (leather)") compounds, these compounds are often found in soil and [groundwater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groundwater "Groundwater") at active and abandoned industrial sites, needing [environmental cleanup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_cleanup "Environmental cleanup") and [remediation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_remediation "Environmental remediation"). [Primer paint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primer_(paint) "Primer (paint)") containing hexavalent chromium is still widely used for [aerospace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerospace "Aerospace") and [automobile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automobile "Automobile") refinishing applications.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-159)

In 2010, the [Environmental Working Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_Working_Group "Environmental Working Group") studied the drinking water in 35 American cities in the first nationwide study. The study found measurable hexavalent chromium in the tap water of 31 of the cities sampled, with [Norman, Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman,_Oklahoma "Norman, Oklahoma"), at the top of list; 25 cities had levels that exceeded California's proposed limit.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-160)

The more toxic hexavalent chromium form can be reduced to the less soluble trivalent oxidation state in soils by organic matter, ferrous iron, sulfides, and other reducing agents, with the rates of such reduction being faster under more acidic conditions than under more alkaline ones. In contrast, trivalent chromium can be oxidized to hexavalent chromium in soils by manganese oxides, such as Mn(III) and Mn(IV) compounds. Since the solubility and toxicity of chromium(VI) are greater than those of chromium(III), the oxidation-reduction conversions between the two oxidation states have implications for movement and bioavailability of chromium in soils, groundwater, and plants.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_note-161)

[↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium#cite_ref-85)When Cr 3+ replaces Al 3+ in [corundum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corundum "Corundum") (aluminium oxide, Al 2 O 3), [pink sapphire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pink_sapphire "Pink sapphire") or [ruby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruby "Ruby") is formed, depending on the amount of chromium.

Aluminium (the Commonwealth and preferred IUPAC name) or aluminum (North American English) is a chemical element; it has symbol Al and atomic number 13. It has a density lower than other common metals, about one-third that of steel. Aluminium has a great affinity toward oxygen, forming a protective layer of oxide on the surface when exposed to air. It visually resembles silver, both in its color and in its great ability to reflect light. It is soft, nonmagnetic, and ductile. It has one stable isotope, 27Al, which is highly abundant, making aluminium the 12th-most abundant element in the universe. The radioactivity of 26Al leads to it being used in radiometric dating.

Chemically, aluminium is a post-transition metal in the boron group; as is common for the group, aluminium forms compounds primarily in the +3 oxidation state. The aluminium cation Al3+ is small and highly charged; as such, it has more polarizing power, and bonds formed by aluminium have a more covalent character. The strong affinity of aluminium for oxygen leads to the common occurrence of its oxides in nature. Aluminium is found on Earth primarily in rocks in the crust, where it is the third-most abundant element after oxygen and silicon, rather than in the mantle, and virtually never as the free metal. It is obtained industrially by mining bauxite, a sedimentary rock rich in aluminium minerals.

The discovery of aluminium was announced in 1825 by Danish physicist Hans Christian Ørsted. The first industrial production of aluminium was initiated by French chemist Henri Étienne Sainte-Claire Deville in 1856. Aluminium became much more available to the public with the Hall–Héroult process developed independently by French engineer Paul Héroult and American engineer Charles Martin Hall in 1886, and the mass production of aluminium led to its extensive use in industry and everyday life. In 1954, aluminium became the most produced non-ferrous metal, surpassing copper. In the 21st century, most aluminium was consumed in transportation, engineering, construction, and packaging in the United States, Western Europe, and Japan. The standard atomic weight of aluminium is low in comparison with many other metals,[b] giving it the low density responsible for many of its uses.

Despite its prevalence in the environment, no living thing is known to metabolize aluminium salts, but aluminium is well tolerated by plants and animals. Because of the abundance of these salts, the potential for a biological role for them is of interest, and studies are ongoing.

Physical characteristicsedit
Bulkedit
Aluminium ingot
Three 1.0 pound (0.454 kg) bullion ingots of triple nine aluminium, iron, and copper etched with their scientific details.

Aluminium metal has an appearance ranging from silvery white to dull gray depending on its surface roughness.[c] Aluminium mirrors provides high reflectivity for light in the ultraviolet, visible (on par with silver),[16] and far infrared regions.[17] Aluminium is also good at reflecting solar radiation, although prolonged exposure to sunlight in air can deteriorate the reflectivity of the metal;[16] this may be prevented if aluminium is anodized, which adds a protective layer of oxide on the surface.[18]

The density of aluminium is 2.70 g/cm3, about one-third that of steel, much lower than other commonly encountered metals, making aluminium parts easily identifiable through their lightness.[19] Aluminium's low density compared to most other metals arises from the fact that its unit cell size is relatively large in proportion to the number of nucleons. The only lighter metals are the metals of groups 1 and 2, which, apart from beryllium and magnesium, are too reactive for structural use (and beryllium is very toxic).[20] Aluminium is not as strong or stiff as steel, but the low density makes up for this in the aerospace industry and for many other applications where light weight and relatively high strength are crucial.[21]

Pure aluminium is quite soft and lacking in strength. In most applications, various aluminium alloys are used instead because of their higher strength and hardness.[22] The yield strength of pure aluminium is 7–11 MPa, while aluminium alloys have yield strengths ranging from 200 MPa to 600 MPa.[23] Aluminium is ductile, with a percent elongation of 50–70%,[24] and malleable allowing it to be easily drawn and extruded;[25] it is also easily machined and cast.[25]

Aluminium is an excellent thermal and electrical conductor, and the amount of aluminium required to match the same amperage in copper weighs only half as much.[26] Aluminium is capable of superconductivity, with a superconducting critical temperature of 1.2 kelvin and a critical magnetic field of about 100 gauss (10 milliteslas).[27] It is paramagnetic and thus essentially unaffected by static magnetic fields.[28] However, the high electrical conductivity means that it is strongly affected by alternating magnetic fields through the induction of eddy currents.[29]

Electron shelledit

An aluminium atom has 13 electrons with an electron configuration of [Ne] 3s2 3p1,[30] with three electrons beyond a stable noble gas configuration. Accordingly, the combined first three ionization energies of aluminium are far lower than the fourth ionization energy alone.[31] Such an electron configuration is shared with the other well-characterized members of its group, boron, gallium, indium, and thallium; it is also expected for nihonium. Aluminium can surrender its three outermost electrons in many chemical reactions (see below). The electronegativity of aluminium is 1.61 on the Pauling scale.[32]

High-resolution STEM-HAADF micrograph of Al atoms viewed along the [001] zone axis.

A free aluminium atom has an atomic radius of 143 pm.[33] With the three outermost electrons removed, the radius shrinks to 39 pm for a 4-coordinated atom or 53.5 pm for a 6-coordinated atom.[33] At standard temperature and pressure, aluminium atoms (when not affected by atoms of other elements) form a face-centered cubic crystal system bound by metallic bonding provided by atoms' outermost electrons; hence, aluminium (at these conditions) is a metal.[34] This crystal system is shared by many other metals, such as lead and copper; the size of a unit cell of aluminium is comparable to that of those other metals.[34] This system, however, is not shared by the other members of its group: boron has ionization energies too high to allow metallization, thallium has a hexagonal close-packed structure, and gallium and indium have unusual structures that are not close-packed like those of aluminium and thallium. The few electrons that are available for metallic bonding in aluminium are a probable cause for it being soft with a low melting point and low electrical resistivity.[35]

Isotopesedit
Main article: Isotopes of aluminium

Aluminium has one stable isotope, 27Al, which comprises virtually all of the naturally-occurring element. This is common for elements with an odd atomic number.[d] It is therefore a mononuclidic element for standard atomic weight, which is determined completely by that isotope. Aluminium is useful in nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), as its single stable isotope (though quadrupolar) has a high NMR sensitivity.[37]

All other isotopes of aluminium are radioactive. The most stable of these is 26Al, with a half-life of 717,000 years. While it was present along with stable 27Al in the interstellar medium from which the Solar System formed (believed to have been produced by stellar nucleosynthesis also), no detectable amount could have survived the time since the formation of the planet. However, minute traces of 26Al are still produced from decay of argon in the atmosphere induced by ionizing radiation of cosmic rays. The ratio of 26Al to 10Be has been used for the radiodating of geological processes over 105 to 106 year time scales, in particular transport, deposition, sediment storage, burial times, and erosion.[38] Most meteorite scientists believe that the energy released by the decay of 26Al was responsible for the melting and differentiation of some asteroids after their formation 4.55 billion years ago.[39]

The other known isotopes of aluminium, with mass numbers ranging from 20 to 43, all have half-lives less than 7 minutes, as do the four detected metastable states.[40]

Chemistryedit
Main article: Compounds of aluminium

Aluminium combines characteristics of pre- and post-transition metals. Since it has few available electrons for metallic bonding, like the heavier group 13 elements, it has the characteristic physical properties of a post-transition metal, with longer-than-expected interatomic distances.[35] Furthermore, as Al3+ is a small and highly charged cation, it is strongly polarizing, and bonding in aluminium compounds tends towards covalency;[41] this behavior is similar to that of beryllium (Be2+), displaying an example of a diagonal relationship.[42]

The underlying core of electrons under aluminium's valence shell is that of the preceding noble gas, whereas those of the heavier group 13 elements gallium, indium, thallium, and nihonium also include a filled d-subshell and in some cases a filled f-subshell. Hence, the inner electrons of aluminium shield the valence electrons almost completely, unlike those of the heavier group 13 elements. As such, aluminium is the most electropositive metal in its group, and its hydroxide is in fact more basic than that of gallium.[41][e] Aluminium also bears minor similarities to boron (a metalloid), which is in the same group: AlX3 compounds are valence isoelectronic to BX3 compounds (they have the same valence electronic structure), and both behave as Lewis acids and readily form adducts.[43] Additionally, one of the main motifs of boron chemistry is regular icosahedral structures, and aluminium forms an important part of many icosahedral quasicrystal alloys, including the Al–Zn–Mg class.[44]

Aluminium has a high chemical affinity to oxygen, which renders it suitable for use as a reducing agent in the thermite reaction. A fine powder of aluminium reacts explosively on contact with liquid oxygen; under normal conditions, however, aluminium forms a thin oxide layer (~5 nm at room temperature)[45] that protects the metal from further corrosion by oxygen, water, or dilute acid, a process termed passivation.[41][46] Aluminium is not attacked by oxidizing acids because of its passivation. This allows aluminium to be used to store reagents such as nitric acid, concentrated sulfuric acid, and some organic acids.[47]

In hot, concentrated hydrochloric acid, aluminium reacts with water through evolution of hydrogen, and it reacts in aqueous sodium or potassium hydroxide at room temperature to form aluminates; protective passivation under these conditions is negligible.[48] Aqua regia also dissolves aluminium.[47] Aluminium is also corroded by dissolved chlorides,[49] such as common sodium chloride. The oxide layer on aluminium is also destroyed by contact with mercury due to amalgamation or by contact with salts of some electropositive metals.[41] As such, the strongest aluminium alloys are less corrosion-resistant due to galvanic reactions with alloyed copper,[50] and aluminium's corrosion resistance is greatly reduced by aqueous salts, particularly in the presence of dissimilar metals.[35]

Aluminium reacts with most nonmetals upon heating, forming compounds such as aluminium nitride (AlN), aluminium sulfide (Al2S3), and the aluminium halides (AlX3). It also forms a wide range of intermetallic compounds involving metals from every group on the periodic table.[41]

Inorganic compoundsedit

The vast majority of aluminium compounds, including all aluminium-containing minerals and all commercially significant aluminium compounds, feature aluminium in the oxidation state 3+. The coordination number of such compounds varies, but generally Al3+ is either six- or four-coordinate. Almost all compounds of aluminium(III) are colorless.[41]

Aluminium hydrolysis as a function of pH. Coordinated water molecules are omitted.[51]

In aqueous solution, Al3+ exists as the hexa-aqua cation [Al(H2O)6]3+, which has an approximate Ka of 10−5.[37] Such solutions are acidic because this cation can act as a proton donor and progressively hydrolyze until a precipitate of aluminium hydroxide, Al(OH)3, forms. This is useful for clarification of water, since the precipitate nucleates on suspended particles in the water, hence removing them. Increasing the pH even further leads to the hydroxide dissolving again as aluminate, [Al(H2O)2(OH)4]−, is formed.

Aluminium hydroxide forms both salts and aluminates and dissolves in acid and alkali, as well as on fusion with acidic and basic oxides.[41] This behavior of Al(OH)3 is termed amphoterism and is characteristic of weakly basic cations that form insoluble hydroxides and whose hydrated species can also donate their protons. One effect of this is that aluminium salts with weak acids are hydrolyzed in water to the aquated hydroxide and the corresponding nonmetal hydride: for example, aluminium sulfide yields hydrogen sulfide. However, some salts like aluminium carbonate exist in aqueous solution but are unstable as such. Only incomplete hydrolysis takes place for salts with strong acids, such as the halides, nitrate, and sulfate. For similar reasons, anhydrous aluminium salts cannot be made by heating their "hydrates": hydrated aluminium chloride is in fact not AlCl3·6H2O but [Al(H2O)6]Cl3, and the Al–O bonds are so strong that heating is not sufficient to break them and form Al–Cl bonds. This reaction is observed instead:[41]

2[Al(H2O)6]Cl3
