**Silicon** ([/ˈ s ɪ l.ɪ.k ə n/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"), [_SILL-ih-kən_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"))[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-14) is a [chemical element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_element "Chemical element"); it has [symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symbol_(chemistry) "Symbol (chemistry)")**Si** and [atomic number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_number "Atomic number") 14. It is a hard, brittle crystalline solid with a blue-grey metallic lustre, and is a [tetravalent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetravalence "Tetravalence")[non-metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-metal "Non-metal") (sometimes considered as a [metalloid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metalloid "Metalloid")) and [semiconductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor "Semiconductor"). It is a member of [group 14](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_group "Carbon group") in the periodic table: [carbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon "Carbon") is above it; and [germanium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germanium "Germanium"), [tin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tin "Tin"), [lead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead "Lead"), and [flerovium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flerovium "Flerovium") are below it. It is relatively unreactive. Silicon is a significant element that is essential for several physiological and metabolic processes in plants. Silicon is widely used as a semiconductor material in various electrical devices such as [transistors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transistor "Transistor"), [solar cells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_cell "Solar cell"), and [integrated circuits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit"). It dominates semiconductor applications due to its low cost, excellent electronic properties, and adaptable physical characteristics.

Because of its high chemical affinity for oxygen, it was not until 1823 that [Jöns Jakob Berzelius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%B6ns_Jakob_Berzelius "Jöns Jakob Berzelius") was first able to prepare it and characterize it in pure form. Its [oxides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxide "Oxide") form a family of [anions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anion "Anion") known as [silicates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicate "Silicate"). Its melting and boiling points of 1414°C and 3265°C, respectively, are the second highest among all the metalloids and nonmetals, being surpassed only by [boron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron "Boron").

Silicon is the eighth [most common element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abundance_of_the_chemical_elements "Abundance of the chemical elements") in the universe by mass, but very rarely occurs in its pure form in the Earth's crust. It is widely distributed throughout space in cosmic [dusts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dust "Dust"), [planetoids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minor_planet "Minor planet"), and [planets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planet "Planet") as various forms of [silicon dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_dioxide "Silicon dioxide") (silica) or [silicates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicate "Silicate"). More than 90% of the Earth's crust is composed of [silicate minerals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicate_minerals "Silicate minerals"), making silicon the [second most abundant element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abundance_of_elements_in_Earth's_crust "Abundance of elements in Earth's crust") in the Earth's crust (about 28% by mass), after [oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen "Oxygen").

Most silicon is used commercially without being separated, often with very little processing of the natural minerals. Such use includes industrial construction with [clays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clay "Clay"), [silica sand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silica_sand "Silica sand"), and [stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone "Stone"). Silicates are used in [Portland cement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_cement "Portland cement") for [mortar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortar_(masonry) "Mortar (masonry)") and [stucco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stucco "Stucco"), and mixed with silica sand and [gravel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravel "Gravel") to make [concrete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concrete "Concrete") for walkways, foundations, and roads. They are also used in whiteware [ceramics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceramic "Ceramic") such as [porcelain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porcelain "Porcelain"), and in traditional [silicate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicate "Silicate")-based [soda–lime glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soda%E2%80%93lime_glass "Soda–lime glass") and many other specialty [glasses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass "Glass"). Silicon compounds such as [silicon carbide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_carbide "Silicon carbide") are used as abrasives and components of high-strength ceramics. Silicon is the basis of the widely used synthetic polymers called [silicones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicone "Silicone").

The late 20th century to early 21st century has been described as the Silicon Age (also known as the [Digital Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_Age "Digital Age") or [Information Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_Age "Information Age")) because of the large impact that elemental silicon has on the modern world economy. The small portion of very highly purified elemental silicon used in [semiconductor electronics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_electronics "Semiconductor electronics") (<15%) is essential to the [transistors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transistors "Transistors") and [integrated circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") chips used in most modern technology such as [smartphones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smartphone "Smartphone") and other [computers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer "Computer"). In 2019, 32.4% of the semiconductor market segment was for networks and communications devices, and the semiconductors industry is projected to reach $726.73 billion by 2027.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Kamal-2022-15)

Silicon is an essential element in biology. Only traces are required by most animals, but some [sea sponges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_sponges "Sea sponges") and microorganisms, such as [diatoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diatoms "Diatoms") and [radiolaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiolaria "Radiolaria"), secrete skeletal structures made of silica. Silica is deposited in many plant tissues.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Cutter-16)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Silicon&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Owing to the abundance of silicon in the [Earth's crust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_crust "Earth's crust"), natural silicon-based materials have been used for thousands of years. Silicon [rock crystals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_crystal "Rock crystal") were familiar to various [ancient civilizations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_civilizations "Ancient civilizations"), such as the [predynastic Egyptians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Predynastic_Egypt "Predynastic Egypt") who used them for [beads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beads "Beads") and small [vases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vases "Vases"), as well as the [ancient Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_China "Ancient China"). [Glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass "Glass") containing [silica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silica "Silica") was manufactured by the [Egyptians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egyptians "Egyptians") since at least 1500 BC, as well as by the ancient [Phoenicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenicians "Phoenicians"). Natural [silicate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicate "Silicate") compounds were also used in various types of [mortar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortar_(masonry) "Mortar (masonry)") for construction of early human [dwellings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwellings "Dwellings").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Britannica-17)

### Discovery

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Silicon&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Discovery")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/J%C3%B6ns_Jacob_Berzelius.jpg/250px-J%C3%B6ns_Jacob_Berzelius.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:J%C3%B6ns_Jacob_Berzelius.jpg)

[Jöns Jacob Berzelius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%B6ns_Jacob_Berzelius "Jöns Jacob Berzelius") discovered silicon in 1823.

In 1787, [Antoine Lavoisier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoine_Lavoisier "Antoine Lavoisier") suspected that [silica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silica "Silica") might be an oxide of a fundamental [chemical element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_element "Chemical element"),[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-18) but the [chemical affinity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_affinity "Chemical affinity") of silicon for oxygen is high enough that he had no means to reduce the oxide and isolate the element.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-greenwood_general-19):328 After an attempt to isolate silicon in 1808, [Sir Humphry Davy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Humphry_Davy "Sir Humphry Davy") proposed the name "**silicium**" for silicon, from the Latin _silex_,_silicis_ for flint, and adding the "-ium" ending because he believed it to be a metal.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-20) Most other languages use transliterated forms of Davy's name, sometimes adapted to local phonology (e.g. [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language "German language")_Silizium_, [Turkish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_language "Turkish language")_\_silisyum\__, [Catalan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalan_language "Catalan language")_\_silici\__, [Armenian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenian_language "Armenian language")Սիլիցիում or _Silitzioum_). A few others instead use a [calque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calque "Calque") of the Latin root (e.g. [Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_language "Russian language")кремний, from кремень "flint"; [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_language "Greek language")_πυρίτιο_ from πυρ "fire"; [Finnish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_language "Finnish language")_pii_ from _piikivi_ "flint", [Czech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czech_language "Czech language")_křemík_ from _křemen_ "quartz", "flint").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-21)

[Gay-Lussac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gay-Lussac "Gay-Lussac") and [Thénard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Jacques_Th%C3%A9nard "Louis Jacques Thénard") are thought to have prepared impure [amorphous silicon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amorphous_silicon "Amorphous silicon") in 1811, through the heating of recently isolated [potassium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potassium "Potassium") metal with [silicon tetrafluoride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_tetrafluoride "Silicon tetrafluoride"), but they did not purify and characterize the product, nor identify it as a new element.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-22) Silicon was given its present name in 1817 by Scottish chemist [Thomas Thomson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Thomson_(chemist) "Thomas Thomson (chemist)"). He retained part of Davy's name but added "-on" because he believed that silicon was a [nonmetal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonmetal_(chemistry) "Nonmetal (chemistry)") similar to [boron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron "Boron") and [carbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon "Carbon").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-23) In 1824, [Jöns Jacob Berzelius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%B6ns_Jacob_Berzelius "Jöns Jacob Berzelius") prepared amorphous silicon using approximately the same method as Gay-Lussac (reducing [potassium fluorosilicate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potassium_fluorosilicate "Potassium fluorosilicate") with molten potassium metal), but purifying the product to a brown powder by repeatedly washing it.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-24) As a result, he is usually given credit for the element's discovery.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Weeks-1932-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Voronkov-2007-12) The same year, Berzelius became the first to prepare [silicon tetrachloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_tetrachloride "Silicon tetrachloride") (SiCl 4); silicon tetrafluoride had already been prepared long before in 1771 by [Carl Wilhelm Scheele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Wilhelm_Scheele "Carl Wilhelm Scheele") by dissolving silica in [hydrofluoric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrofluoric_acid "Hydrofluoric acid").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-greenwood_general-19):328[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Kipping-1937-25) In 1846, J. Von Ebelman synthesized [tetraethyl orthosilicate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetraethyl_orthosilicate "Tetraethyl orthosilicate") (Si(OC 2 H 5)4).[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Muller1965-26)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Kipping-1937-25)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e2/Silicon_single_crystal.jpg/250px-Silicon_single_crystal.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Silicon_single_crystal.jpg)

Single crystal of silicon grown by the [Czochralski process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czochralski_process "Czochralski process") used to make integrated circuits

Silicon in its more common crystalline form was not prepared until 31 years later, by [Deville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Etienne_Sainte-Claire_Deville "Henri Etienne Sainte-Claire Deville").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-27) Passing silicon chloride vapors over pure aluminum produced pure, hard octahedral crystals.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-28)[Friedrich Wöhler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_W%C3%B6hler "Friedrich Wöhler") discovered the first volatile hydrides of silicon, synthesising [trichlorosilane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichlorosilane "Trichlorosilane") in 1857 and [silane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silane "Silane") itself in 1858, but a detailed investigation of the [silanes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silanes "Silanes") was only carried out in the early 20th century by [Alfred Stock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Stock "Alfred Stock"), despite early speculation on the matter dating as far back as the beginnings of synthetic organic chemistry in the 1830s.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-greenwood_general-19):330 Similarly, the first [organosilicon compound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organosilicon_compound "Organosilicon compound"), tetraethylsilane, was synthesised by [Charles Friedel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Friedel "Charles Friedel") and [James Crafts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Crafts "James Crafts") in 1863, but detailed characterisation of organosilicon chemistry was only done in the early 20th century by [Frederic Kipping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederic_Kipping "Frederic Kipping").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-greenwood_general-19):328

Starting in the 1920s, the work of [William Lawrence Bragg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Lawrence_Bragg "William Lawrence Bragg") on [X-ray crystallography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-ray_crystallography "X-ray crystallography") elucidated the compositions of the silicates, which had previously been known from [analytical chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytical_chemistry "Analytical chemistry") but had not yet been understood, together with [Linus Pauling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linus_Pauling "Linus Pauling")'s development of [crystal chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal_chemistry "Crystal chemistry") and [Victor Goldschmidt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Goldschmidt "Victor Goldschmidt")'s development of [geochemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geochemistry "Geochemistry"). The middle of the 20th century saw the development of the chemistry and industrial use of [siloxanes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siloxane "Siloxane") and the growing use of [silicone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicone "Silicone")[polymers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polymer "Polymer"), [elastomers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elastomer "Elastomer"), and [resins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resin "Resin"). In the late 20th century, the complexity of the crystal chemistry of [silicides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicide "Silicide") was mapped, along with the [solid-state physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid-state_physics "Solid-state physics") of [doped](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doping_(semiconductor) "Doping (semiconductor)")[semiconductors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor "Semiconductor").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-greenwood_general-19):328

### Silicon semiconductors

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Silicon&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Silicon semiconductors")]

The first [semiconductor devices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_devices "Semiconductor devices") did not use silicon, but used [galena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galena "Galena"), including German [physicist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physicist "Physicist")[Ferdinand Braun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Braun "Ferdinand Braun")'s [crystal detector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal_detector "Crystal detector") in 1874 and Indian physicist [Jagadish Chandra Bose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jagadish_Chandra_Bose "Jagadish Chandra Bose")'s [radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio "Radio") crystal detector in 1901.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-computerhistory-timeline-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-computerhistory-1901-30) The first silicon semiconductor device was a silicon radio crystal detector, developed by American engineer [Greenleaf Whittier Pickard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenleaf_Whittier_Pickard "Greenleaf Whittier Pickard") in 1906.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-computerhistory-1901-30)

In 1940, [Russell Ohl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Ohl "Russell Ohl") discovered the [p–n junction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%E2%80%93n_junction "P–n junction") and [photovoltaic effects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photovoltaic_effect "Photovoltaic effect") in silicon. In 1941, techniques for producing high-purity [germanium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germanium "Germanium") and [silicon crystals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_crystal "Silicon crystal") were developed for [radar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radar "Radar")[microwave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microwave "Microwave") detector crystals during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-computerhistory-timeline-29) In 1947, physicist [William Shockley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shockley "William Shockley") theorized a [field-effect amplifier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field-effect_transistor "Field-effect transistor") made from germanium and silicon, but he failed to build a working device, before eventually working with germanium instead. The first working transistor was a [point-contact transistor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point-contact_transistor "Point-contact transistor") built by [John Bardeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bardeen "John Bardeen") and [Walter Brattain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Brattain "Walter Brattain") later that year while working under Shockley.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-31) In 1954, [physical chemist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_chemist "Physical chemist")[Morris Tanenbaum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Tanenbaum "Morris Tanenbaum") fabricated the first silicon [junction transistor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junction_transistor "Junction transistor") at [Bell Labs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell_Labs "Bell Labs").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-32) In 1955, [Carl Frosch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Frosch "Carl Frosch") and Lincoln Derick at Bell Labs accidentally discovered that [silicon dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_dioxide "Silicon dioxide") (SiO

2) could be grown on silicon.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Bassett22-34) By 1957 Frosch and Derick published their work on the first manufactured SiO

2 semiconductor oxide transistor: the first planar transistors, in which drain and source were adjacent at the same surface.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Frosch-1957-35) In 1959, [Robert Noyce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Noyce "Robert Noyce") developed the first silicon-based integrated circuit at Fairchild Semiconductor, building on prior work by [Jack Kilby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Kilby "Jack Kilby") that relied on germanium as the semiconductor.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-36)

### Silicon Age

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Silicon&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Silicon Age")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/MOSFET_Structure.png/250px-MOSFET_Structure.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MOSFET_Structure.png)

The [MOSFET](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MOSFET "MOSFET"), also known as the MOS transistor, is the key component of the Silicon Age. The first silicon semiconductor oxide planar transistor was made by Frosch and Derick in 1957.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Frosch-1957-35)

The "Silicon Age" refers to the late 20th century to early 21st century.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Feldman-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Dabrowski-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Siffert-39) This is due to silicon being the dominant material used in electronics and information technology (also known as the [Digital Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_Age "Digital Age") or [Information Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_Age "Information Age")), similar to how the [Stone Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone_Age "Stone Age"), [Bronze Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_Age "Bronze Age") and [Iron Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Age "Iron Age") were defined by the dominant materials during their respective [ages of civilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-age_system "Three-age system").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Feldman-37)

Because silicon is an important element in high-technology semiconductor devices, many places in the world bear its name. For example, the [Santa Clara Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Clara_Valley "Santa Clara Valley") in California acquired the nickname [Silicon Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_Valley "Silicon Valley"), as the element is the base material in the [semiconductor industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_industry "Semiconductor industry") there. Since then, many other places have been similarly dubbed, including [Silicon Wadi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_Wadi "Silicon Wadi") in Israel; [Silicon Forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_Forest "Silicon Forest") in Oregon; [Silicon Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_Hills "Silicon Hills") in Austin, Texas; [Silicon Slopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_Slopes "Silicon Slopes") in Salt Lake City, Utah; [Silicon Saxony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_Saxony "Silicon Saxony") in Germany; [Silicon Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangalore#Economy "Bangalore") in India; [Silicon Border](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexicali#Silicon_Border "Mexicali") in Mexicali, Mexico; [Silicon Fen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_Fen "Silicon Fen") in Cambridge, England; [Silicon Roundabout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Street_Roundabout#Silicon_Roundabout "Old Street Roundabout") in London; [Silicon Glen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_Glen "Silicon Glen") in Scotland; [Silicon Gorge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_Gorge "Silicon Gorge") in Bristol, England; [Silicon Alley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_Alley "Silicon Alley") in New York City; [Silicon Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_Beach "Silicon Beach") in Los Angeles;[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-40) and [Dubai Silicon Oasis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubai_Silicon_Oasis "Dubai Silicon Oasis") in Dubai.

## Characteristics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Silicon&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Characteristics")]

### Physical and atomic

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Silicon&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Physical and atomic")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f1/Silicon-unit-cell-3D-balls.png/250px-Silicon-unit-cell-3D-balls.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Silicon-unit-cell-3D-balls.png)

Silicon crystallizes in a [diamond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diamond "Diamond")[cubic crystal structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubic_crystal_system "Cubic crystal system") by forming [sp 3 hybrid orbitals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_hybridization "Orbital hybridization").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-41)

A silicon atom has fourteen [electrons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrons "Electrons"). In the ground state, they are arranged in the electron configuration [Ne]3s 2 3p 2. Of these, four are [valence electrons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valence_electron "Valence electron"), occupying the 3s orbital and two of the 3p orbitals. Like the other members of its group, the lighter [carbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon "Carbon") and the heavier [germanium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germanium "Germanium"), [tin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tin "Tin"), and [lead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead "Lead"), it has the same number of valence electrons as valence orbitals: hence, it can complete its [octet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octet_rule "Octet rule") and obtain the stable [noble gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noble_gas "Noble gas") configuration of [argon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argon "Argon") by forming [sp 3 hybrid orbitals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_hybridization "Orbital hybridization"), forming tetrahedral SiX

4 derivatives where the central silicon atom shares an electron pair with each of the four atoms it is bonded to.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-King-1995-42):xiii–xviii The first four [ionisation energies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionisation_energy "Ionisation energy") of silicon are 786.3, 1576.5, 3228.3, and 4354.4 kJ/mol respectively; these figures are high enough to preclude the possibility of simple cationic chemistry for the element. Following [periodic trends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodic_trend "Periodic trend"), its single-bond covalent radius of 117.6 pm is intermediate between those of carbon (77.2 pm) and germanium (122.3 pm). The hexacoordinate ionic radius of silicon may be considered to be 40 pm, although this must be taken as a purely notional figure given the lack of a simple Si 4+

 cation in reality.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-greenwood_general-19):372

#### Electrical

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Silicon&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Electrical")]

At standard temperature and pressure, silicon is a shiny [semiconductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor "Semiconductor") with a bluish-grey metallic lustre; as typical for semiconductors, its resistivity drops as temperature rises. This arises because silicon has a small energy gap ([band gap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Band_gap "Band gap")) between its highest occupied energy levels (the valence band) and the lowest unoccupied ones (the conduction band). The [Fermi level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermi_level "Fermi level") is about halfway between the [valence and conduction bands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valence_and_conduction_bands "Valence and conduction bands") and is the energy at which a state is as likely to be occupied by an electron as not. Hence pure silicon is effectively an insulator at room temperature. However, [doping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doping_(semiconductor) "Doping (semiconductor)") silicon with a [pnictogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pnictogen "Pnictogen") such as [phosphorus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphorus "Phosphorus"), [arsenic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsenic "Arsenic"), or [antimony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antimony "Antimony") introduces one extra electron per dopant and these may then be excited into the conduction band either thermally or photolytically, creating an [n-type semiconductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extrinsic_semiconductor#N-type_semiconductors "Extrinsic semiconductor"). Similarly, doping silicon with a [group 13 element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron_group "Boron group") such as [boron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron "Boron"), [aluminium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium "Aluminium"), or [gallium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium "Gallium") results in the introduction of acceptor levels that trap electrons that may be excited from the filled valence band, creating a [p-type semiconductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extrinsic_semiconductor#P-type_semiconductors "Extrinsic semiconductor").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-greenwood_general-19):332 Joining n-type silicon to p-type silicon creates a [p–n junction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%E2%80%93n_junction "P–n junction") with a common Fermi level; electrons flow from n to p, while holes flow from p to n, creating a voltage drop. This p–n junction thus acts as a [diode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diode "Diode") that can rectify alternating current that allows current to pass more easily one way than the other. A [transistor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transistor "Transistor") is an n–p–n junction, with a thin layer of weakly p-type silicon between two n-type regions. Biasing the emitter through a small forward voltage and the collector through a large reverse voltage allows the transistor to act as a [triode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triode "Triode") amplifier.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-greenwood_general-19):332

#### Crystal structure

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Silicon&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Crystal structure")]

Main article: [Allotropes of silicon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allotropes_of_silicon "Allotropes of silicon")

Silicon crystallises in a giant covalent structure at standard conditions, specifically in a [diamond cubic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diamond_cubic "Diamond cubic") crystal lattice ([space group 227](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Crystals_in_space_group_227 "Category:Crystals in space group 227")). It thus has a high melting point of 1414°C, as a lot of energy is required to break the strong covalent bonds and melt the solid. Upon melting, silicon contracts, as the long-range tetrahedral network of bonds breaks up and the voids in that network are filled in, similar to [water ice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice "Ice") when hydrogen bonds are broken upon melting. It does not have any thermodynamically stable allotropes at standard pressure, but several other crystal structures are known at higher pressures. The general trend is one of increasing [coordination number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordination_number "Coordination number") with pressure, culminating in a [hexagonal close-packed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hexagonal_close-packed "Hexagonal close-packed") allotrope at about 40[gigapascals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gigapascal "Gigapascal") known as Si–VII (the standard modification being Si–I). An allotrope called BC8 (or bc8), having a [body-centred cubic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Body-centred_cubic "Body-centred cubic") lattice with eight atoms per primitive unit cell ([space group 206](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Crystals_in_space_group_206 "Category:Crystals in space group 206")), can be created at high pressure and remains metastable at low pressure. Its properties have been studied in detail.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-43)

Silicon boils at 3265°C: this, while high, is still lower than the temperature at which its lighter congener [carbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon "Carbon") sublimes (3642°C) and silicon similarly has a lower [heat of vaporisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_of_vaporisation "Heat of vaporisation") than carbon, consistent with the fact that the Si–Si bond is weaker than the C–C bond.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-greenwood_general-19):331

It is also possible to construct [silicene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicene "Silicene") layers analogous to [graphene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphene "Graphene").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Aufray2010-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Lalmi2010-45)

### Isotopes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Silicon&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Isotopes")]

Main article: [Isotopes of silicon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotopes_of_silicon "Isotopes of silicon")

Naturally occurring silicon is composed of three stable [isotopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotope "Isotope"), 28 Si (92.24%), 29 Si (4.67%), and 30 Si (3.07%).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-NUBASE2020-13) Out of these, only the odd 29 Si is of use in [NMR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NMR "NMR") and [EPR spectroscopy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EPR_spectroscopy "EPR spectroscopy"),[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-46) and it has nuclear spin (_I_ =⁠1/2⁠).[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-greenwood_general-19):330 All three are produced in [Type Ia supernovae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_Ia_supernovae "Type Ia supernovae")[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-48) through the [oxygen-burning process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen-burning_process "Oxygen-burning process"), with 28 Si being made as part of the [alpha process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_process "Alpha process") and hence the most abundant. The fusion of 28 Si with alpha particles by [photodisintegration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photodisintegration "Photodisintegration") rearrangement in stars is known as the [silicon-burning process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon-burning_process "Silicon-burning process"); it is the last stage of [stellar nucleosynthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stellar_nucleosynthesis "Stellar nucleosynthesis") before the rapid collapse and violent explosion of the star in question in a [type II supernova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_II_supernova "Type II supernova").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Cameron-49)

Twenty-two [radioisotopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioisotopes "Radioisotopes") have been characterized, the two stablest being 32 Si with a [half-life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half-life "Half-life") of about 157 years, and 31 Si with a half-life of 2.62 hours. All the remaining [radioactive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioactive_decay "Radioactive decay") isotopes have half-lives that are less than seven seconds, and the majority of these have half-lives that are less than one-tenth of a second.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-NUBASE2020-13)32 Si undergoes low-energy [beta decay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_decay "Beta decay") to [32 P](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphorus-32 "Phosphorus-32") and then stable 32[S](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfur "Sulfur"). 31 Si may be produced by the [neutron activation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_activation "Neutron activation") of natural silicon and is thus useful for quantitative analysis; it can be easily detected by its characteristic beta decay to stable 31[P](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphorus "Phosphorus"), in which the emitted electron carries up to 1.48[MeV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronvolt "Electronvolt") of energy.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-greenwood_general-19):330

The known isotopes of silicon range in [mass number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_number "Mass number") from 22 to 45. The most common [decay mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decay_mode "Decay mode") of the isotopes with mass numbers lower than the three stable isotopes is [β+ decay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Positron_emission "Positron emission") to [aluminium isotopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium_isotopes "Aluminium isotopes"), and the most common decay mode for the heavier unstable isotopes is beta decay to [phosphorus isotopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphorus_isotopes "Phosphorus isotopes") as decay products.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-NUBASE2020-13)46 Si was reported in collisions of 70 Zn with Be in experiments at the [Radioactive Isotope Beam Factory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioactive_Isotope_Beam_Factory "Radioactive Isotope Beam Factory").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-45Si,46Si-50)

Silicon can enter the oceans through groundwater and [riverine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riverine "Riverine") transport. Large fluxes of groundwater input have an isotopic composition which is distinct from riverine silicon inputs. Isotopic variations in groundwater and riverine transports contribute to variations in oceanic 30 Si values. Currently, there are substantial differences in the isotopic values of deep water in the world's [ocean basins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanic_basin "Oceanic basin"). Between the Atlantic and Pacific oceans, there is a deep water 30 Si gradient of greater than 0.3 parts per thousand. 30 Si is most commonly associated with productivity in the oceans.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-51)

## Chemistry and compounds

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Silicon&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Chemistry and compounds")]

Main article: [Silicon compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_compounds "Silicon compounds")

Crystalline bulk silicon is rather inert, but becomes more reactive at high temperatures. Like its neighbour aluminium, silicon forms a thin, continuous surface layer of [silicon dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_dioxide "Silicon dioxide") (SiO

2) that protects the material beneath from oxidation. Because of this, silicon does not measurably react with the air below 900°C. Between 950°C and 1160°C, the formation rate of the [vitreous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitreous_lustre "Vitreous lustre") dioxide rapidly increases, and when 1400°C is reached, atmospheric [nitrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen "Nitrogen") also reacts to give the nitrides SiN and [Si 3 N 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_nitride "Silicon nitride"). Silicon reacts with gaseous [sulfur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfur "Sulfur") at 600°C and gaseous [phosphorus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphorus "Phosphorus") at 1000°C. This oxide layer nevertheless does not prevent reaction with the [halogens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halogen "Halogen"); [fluorine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluorine "Fluorine") attacks silicon vigorously at room temperature, [chlorine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chlorine "Chlorine") does so at about 300°C, and [bromine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bromine "Bromine") and [iodine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iodine "Iodine") at about 500°C. Silicon does not react with most aqueous acids, but is oxidised and complexed by [hydrofluoric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrofluoric_acid "Hydrofluoric acid") mixtures containing either chlorine or [nitric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitric_acid "Nitric acid") to form [hexafluorosilicates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hexafluorosilicic_acid "Hexafluorosilicic acid"). It readily dissolves in hot aqueous alkali to form [silicates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicate "Silicate").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-52) At high temperatures, silicon also reacts with [alkyl halides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkyl_halide "Alkyl halide"); this reaction may be catalysed by [copper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copper "Copper") to directly synthesise [organosilicon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organosilicon "Organosilicon") chlorides as precursors to [silicone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicone "Silicone") polymers. Upon melting, silicon becomes extremely reactive, alloying with most metals to form [silicides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicide "Silicide"), and reducing most metal oxides because the [heat of formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_of_formation "Heat of formation") of silicon dioxide is so large. In fact, molten silicon reacts virtually with every known kind of crucible material (except its own oxide, SiO

2).[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Grabmaier-1982-53):13 This happens due to silicon's high binding forces for the light elements and to its high dissolving power for most elements.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Grabmaier-1982-53):13 As a result, containers for liquid silicon must be made of [refractory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refractory "Refractory"), unreactive materials such as [zirconium dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zirconium_dioxide "Zirconium dioxide") or group 4, 5, and 6 borides.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-greenwood_general-19):331

Tetrahedral coordination is a major structural motif in silicon chemistry just as it is for carbon chemistry. However, the 3p subshell is rather more diffuse than the 2p subshell and does not hybridise so well with the 3s subshell. As a result, the chemistry of silicon and its heavier congeners shows significant differences from that of carbon,[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Kaupp-54) and thus octahedral coordination is also significant.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-greenwood_general-19):335 For example, the [electronegativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronegativity "Electronegativity") of silicon (1.90) is much less than that of carbon (2.55), because the valence electrons of silicon are further from the nucleus than those of carbon and hence experience smaller electrostatic forces of attraction from the nucleus. The poor overlap of 3p orbitals also results in a much lower tendency toward [catenation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catenation "Catenation") (formation of Si–Si bonds) for silicon than for carbon, due to the concomitant weakening of the Si–Si bond compared to the C–C bond:[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-King-1995-42):43 the average Si–Si bond energy is approximately 226 kJ/mol, compared to a value of 356 kJ/mol for the C–C bond.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-greenwood_general-19):374 This results in multiply bonded silicon compounds generally being much less stable than their carbon counterparts, an example of the [double bond rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_bond_rule "Double bond rule"). On the other hand, the presence of radial nodes in the 3p orbitals of silicon suggests the possibility of [hypervalence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypervalence "Hypervalence"), as seen in five and six-coordinate derivatives of silicon such as SiX−

5 and SiF 2−

6.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-55)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-King-1995-42) Lastly, because of the increasing energy gap between the valence s and p orbitals as the group is descended, the divalent state grows in importance from carbon to lead, so that a few unstable divalent compounds are known for silicon; this lowering of the main oxidation state, in tandem with increasing atomic radii, results in an increase of metallic character down the group. Silicon already shows some incipient metallic behavior, particularly in the behavior of its oxide compounds and its reaction with acids as well as bases (though this takes some effort), and is hence often referred to as a [metalloid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metalloid "Metalloid") rather than a nonmetal.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-King-1995-42) Germanium shows more, and tin is generally considered a metal.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-greenwood_general-19):328

Silicon shows clear differences from carbon. For example, [organic chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organic_chemistry "Organic chemistry") has very few analogies with silicon chemistry, while [silicate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicate "Silicate") minerals have a structural complexity unseen in [oxocarbons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxocarbon "Oxocarbon").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-greenwood_general-19):327–328 Silicon tends to resemble germanium far more than it does carbon, and this resemblance is enhanced by the [d-block contraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D-block_contraction "D-block contraction"), resulting in the size of the germanium atom being much closer to that of the silicon atom than periodic trends would predict.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-greenwood_general-19):359–361 Nevertheless, there are still some differences because of the growing importance of the divalent state in germanium compared to silicon. Additionally, the lower Ge–O bond strength compared to the [Si–O bond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon%E2%80%93oxygen_bond "Silicon–oxygen bond") strength results in the absence of "germanone" polymers that would be analogous to silicone polymers.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-greenwood_general-19):374

## Occurrence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Silicon&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Occurrence")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/Olivine-gem7-10a.jpg/250px-Olivine-gem7-10a.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Olivine-gem7-10a.jpg)

Olivine

Silicon is the eighth [most abundant element in the universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abundance_of_the_chemical_elements#Universe "Abundance of the chemical elements"), coming after [hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen "Hydrogen"), [helium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helium "Helium"), [oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen "Oxygen"), [carbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon "Carbon"), [neon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neon "Neon"), [iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron "Iron"), and [nitrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen "Nitrogen"). This differs from [abundance of elements in Earth's crust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abundance_of_elements_in_Earth's_crust "Abundance of elements in Earth's crust") due to substantial separation of the elements taking place during the formation of the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System"). Silicon makes up 27.2% of the Earth's crust by weight, second only to oxygen at 45.5%, with which it always is associated in nature. Further fractionation took place in the formation of the Earth by [planetary differentiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_differentiation "Planetary differentiation"): [Earth's core](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_core "Earth's core"), which makes up 31.5% of the mass of the Earth, has approximate composition Fe

25 Ni

2 Co

0.1 S

3; the [mantle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mantle_(geology) "Mantle (geology)") makes up 68.1% of the Earth's mass and is composed mostly of denser oxides and silicates, an example being [olivine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olivine "Olivine"), (Mg,Fe)

2 SiO

4; while the lighter siliceous minerals such as [aluminosilicates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminosilicate "Aluminosilicate") rise to the surface and form the crust, making up 0.4% of the Earth's mass.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-greenwood_general-19):329

The crystallisation of [igneous rocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igneous_rock "Igneous rock") from magma depends on a number of factors; among them are the chemical composition of the magma, the cooling rate, and some properties of the individual minerals to be formed, such as [lattice energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lattice_energy "Lattice energy"), melting point, and complexity of their crystal structure. As magma is cooled, [olivine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olivine "Olivine") appears first, followed by [pyroxene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyroxene "Pyroxene"), [amphibole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amphibole "Amphibole"), [biotite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biotite "Biotite") mica, [orthoclase feldspar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthoclase_feldspar "Orthoclase feldspar"), [muscovite mica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscovite_mica "Muscovite mica"), [quartz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartz "Quartz"), [zeolites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeolite "Zeolite"), and finally, hydrothermal minerals. This sequence shows a trend toward increasingly complex silicate units with cooling, and the introduction of [hydroxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydroxide "Hydroxide") and [fluoride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluoride "Fluoride") anions in addition to oxides. Many metals may substitute for silicon. After these igneous rocks undergo [weathering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weathering "Weathering"), transport, and deposition, [sedimentary rocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sedimentary_rock "Sedimentary rock") like clay, shale, and sandstone are formed. [Metamorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metamorphism "Metamorphism") also may occur at high temperatures and pressures, creating an even vaster variety of minerals.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-greenwood_general-19):329

There are four sources for silicon fluxes into the ocean: chemical weathering of continental rocks, river transport, dissolution of continental terrigenous silicates, and the reaction between submarine basalts and hydrothermal fluid which release dissolved silicon. All four of these fluxes are interconnected in the ocean's biogeochemical cycle as they all were initially formed from the weathering of Earth's crust.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-The_World_Ocean_Silica_Cycle-56)

Approximately 300–900 megatonnes of [aeolian dust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dust#Atmospheric "Dust") is deposited into the world's oceans each year. Of that value, 80–240 megatonnes are in the form of particulate silicon. The total amount of particulate silicon deposition into the ocean is still less than the amount of silicon influx into the ocean via riverine transportation.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Atmospheric_transport_of_silicon-57) Aeolian inputs of particulate lithogenic silicon into the North Atlantic and Western North Pacific oceans are the result of dust settling on the oceans from the Sahara and Gobi Desert, respectively.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-The_World_Ocean_Silica_Cycle-56) Riverine transports are the major source of silicon influx into the ocean in coastal regions, while silicon deposition in the open ocean is greatly influenced by the settling of aeolian dust.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Atmospheric_transport_of_silicon-57)

Ferrosilicon alloy

This reaction, known as carbothermal reduction of silicon dioxide, is usually conducted in the presence of scrap iron with low amounts of [phosphorus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphorus "Phosphorus") and [sulfur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfur "Sulfur"), producing [ferrosilicon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrosilicon "Ferrosilicon").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-greenwood_general-19):330 Ferrosilicon, an iron-silicon alloy that contains varying ratios of elemental silicon and iron, accounts for about 80% of the world's production of elemental silicon, with China, the leading supplier of elemental silicon, providing 4.6 million [tonnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonne "Tonne") (or two-thirds of world output) of silicon, most of it in the form of ferrosilicon. It is followed by Russia (610,000 t), Norway (330,000 t), Brazil (240,000 t), and the United States (170,000 t).[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-58) Ferrosilicon is primarily used by the iron and steel industry (see [below](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#Alloys)) with primary use as alloying addition in iron or steel and for de-oxidation of steel in integrated steel plants.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-greenwood_general-19):330 Most elemental silicon produced remains as a ferrosilicon alloy, and only approximately 20% is refined to metallurgical grade purity (a total of 1.3–1.5 million metric tons/year). An estimated 15% of the world production of metallurgical grade silicon is further refined to semiconductor purity.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-USGS-59)
