Leaching powdered 96–97% pure silicon with water results in ~98.5% pure silicon, which is used in the chemical industry. However, even greater purity is needed for semiconductor applications, and this is produced from the reduction of [tetrachlorosilane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrachlorosilane "Tetrachlorosilane") (silicon tetrachloride) or [trichlorosilane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichlorosilane "Trichlorosilane"). The former is made by chlorinating scrap silicon and the latter is a byproduct of [silicone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicone "Silicone") production. These compounds are volatile and hence can be purified by repeated [fractional distillation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractional_distillation "Fractional distillation"), followed by reduction to elemental silicon with very pure [zinc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zinc "Zinc") metal as the reducing agent. The spongy pieces of silicon thus produced are melted and then grown to form cylindrical single crystals, before being purified by [zone refining](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zone_refining "Zone refining"). Other routes use the thermal decomposition of [silane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silane "Silane") or [tetraiodosilane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetraiodosilane "Tetraiodosilane") (SiI

4). Another process used is the reduction of [sodium hexafluorosilicate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_hexafluorosilicate "Sodium hexafluorosilicate"), a common waste product of the phosphate fertilizer industry, by metallic [sodium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium "Sodium"): this is highly exothermic and hence requires no outside energy source. Hyperfine silicon is made at a higher purity than almost any other material: [transistor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transistor "Transistor") production requires impurity levels in silicon crystals less than 1 part per 10 10, and in special cases impurity levels below 1 part per 10 12 are needed and attained.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-greenwood_general-19):330

Silicon nanostructures can directly be produced from silica sand using conventional metalothermic processes, or the combustion synthesis approach. Such nanostructured silicon materials can be used in various functional applications including the anode of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), other ion batteries, future computing devices like memristors or photocatalytic applications.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-61)

## Applications

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Silicon&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Applications")]

### Compounds

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Silicon&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Compounds")]

Most silicon is used industrially without being purified, often with comparatively little processing from its natural form. More than 90% of the Earth's crust is composed of [silicate minerals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicate_minerals "Silicate minerals"), which are compounds of silicon and oxygen, often with metallic ions when negatively charged silicate anions require cations to balance the charge. Many of these have direct commercial uses, such as clays, [silica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silica "Silica") sand, and most kinds of building stone. Thus, the vast majority of uses for silicon are as structural compounds, either as the silicate minerals or silica (crude silicon dioxide). Silicates are used in making [Portland cement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_cement "Portland cement") (made mostly of calcium silicates) which is used in [building mortar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortar_(masonry) "Mortar (masonry)") and modern [stucco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stucco "Stucco"), but more importantly, combined with silica sand, and gravel (usually containing silicate minerals such as granite), to make the [concrete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concrete "Concrete") that is the basis of most of the very largest industrial building projects of the modern world.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-greenwood_general-19):356

Silica is used to make [fire brick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire_brick "Fire brick"), a type of ceramic. Silicate minerals are also in whiteware [ceramics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceramic "Ceramic"), an important class of products usually containing various types of fired [clay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clay "Clay") minerals (natural aluminium phyllosilicates). An example is [porcelain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porcelain "Porcelain"), which is based on the silicate mineral [kaolinite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaolinite "Kaolinite"). Traditional [glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass "Glass") (silica-based [soda–lime glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soda%E2%80%93lime_glass "Soda–lime glass")) also functions in many of the same ways, and also is used for windows and containers. In addition, specialty silica based [glass fibers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass_fiber "Glass fiber") are used for [optical fiber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optical_fiber "Optical fiber"), as well as to produce [fiberglass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiberglass "Fiberglass") for structural support and [glass wool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass_wool "Glass wool") for [thermal insulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermal_insulation "Thermal insulation").[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-62)

Silicones often are used in [waterproofing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waterproofing "Waterproofing") treatments, [molding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molding_(process) "Molding (process)") compounds, mold-[release agents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Release_agent "Release agent"), mechanical seals, high temperature [greases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lubricant "Lubricant") and waxes, and [caulking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caulking "Caulking") compounds. Silicone is also sometimes used in [breast implants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breast_implant "Breast implant"), contact lenses, [explosives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explosive "Explosive") and [pyrotechnics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrotechnics "Pyrotechnics").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-63)[Silly Putty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silly_Putty "Silly Putty") was originally made by adding [boric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boric_acid "Boric acid") to [silicone oil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicone_oil "Silicone oil").[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-64) Other silicon compounds function as high-technology abrasives and new high-strength ceramics based upon [silicon carbide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_carbide "Silicon carbide"). Silicon is a component of some [superalloys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superalloy "Superalloy").

### Alloys

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Silicon&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Alloys")]

Elemental silicon is added to molten iron as [ferrosilicon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrosilicon "Ferrosilicon") alloys to improve performance in casting thin sections and to prevent the formation of [cementite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cementite "Cementite") where exposed to outside air. The presence of elemental silicon in molten iron acts as a sink for oxygen, so that the steel carbon content, which must be kept within narrow limits for each type of steel, can be more closely controlled.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-65) Around 75% of ferrosilicon produced is used in the steel industry.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Zulehner-60):598 Silicon is an important constituent of [transformer steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transformer_steel "Transformer steel"), modifying its [resistivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resistivity "Resistivity") and [ferromagnetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferromagnetic "Ferromagnetic") properties.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Zulehner-60):598

The properties of silicon may be used to modify alloys with metals other than iron. "Metallurgical grade" silicon is silicon of 95–99% purity. About 55% of the world consumption of metallurgical purity silicon goes for production of aluminium-silicon alloys ([silumin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silumin "Silumin") alloys) for aluminium part [casts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casting "Casting"), mainly for use in the [automotive industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automotive_industry "Automotive industry"). Silicon's importance in aluminium casting is that a significantly high amount (12%) of silicon in aluminium forms a [eutectic mixture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eutectic_mixture "Eutectic mixture") which solidifies with very little thermal contraction. This greatly reduces tearing and cracks formed from stress as casting alloys cool to solidity. Silicon also significantly improves the hardness and thus wear-resistance of aluminium.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-diecasting-66)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-USGS-59) Metallurgical grade silicon is made by melting quartz or quartzite in a large arc furnace, in a carbothermal reduction process with carbon-containing material such as coal, coke or charcoal and woodchips for gas circulation. This production technique without iron is often used for [polysilicon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polysilicon "Polysilicon") production for photovoltaics and also semiconductors.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-67)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-69)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-70)

### Electronics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Silicon&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Electronics")]

Main article: [Semiconductor device fabrication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_device_fabrication "Semiconductor device fabrication")

Further information: [Semiconductor industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_industry "Semiconductor industry")

Silicon semiconductor devices enable modern information technology. The electronic applications are broad, including microelectronics, computing, optoelectronics, and nanotechnology.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Heywang-2004-71):25 Among the many advantages of silicon for electronics are: low cost, formation of large pure single crystals, not brittle, conducts heat generated by electrical activity adequately, can be micro-structured and modified in layers, and its oxide is an excellent insulator.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Heywang-2004-71):40

An estimated 15% of the world production of metallurgical grade silicon is refined to semiconductor purity.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-USGS-59) This is typically the "nine-9" or 99.9999999% purity,[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-72) nearly defect-free single [crystalline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystalline "Crystalline") material.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-73)

[Monocrystalline silicon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monocrystalline_silicon "Monocrystalline silicon") of such purity is usually produced by the [Czochralski process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czochralski_process "Czochralski process"), and is used to produce [silicon wafers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wafer_(electronics) "Wafer (electronics)") used in the [semiconductor industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_industry "Semiconductor industry"), in electronics, and in some high-cost and high-efficiency [photovoltaic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photovoltaic "Photovoltaic") applications.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Zulehner-60):580 Pure silicon is an [intrinsic semiconductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intrinsic_semiconductor "Intrinsic semiconductor"), which means that unlike metals, it conducts [electron holes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron_hole "Electron hole") and electrons released from atoms by heat. Intrinsic silicon's [electrical conductivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_conductivity "Electrical conductivity") increases with temperature due to the broadening of the [Fermi-Dirac distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermi-Dirac_distribution "Fermi-Dirac distribution"). Pure silicon has too low a conductivity (i.e., too high a [resistivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resistivity "Resistivity")) to be used as a circuit element in electronics. In practice, pure silicon is [doped](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doping_(semiconductors) "Doping (semiconductors)") with small concentrations of elements with differing valence electron count (typically boron and phosphorus), which greatly increase its conductivity and adjust its electrical response by controlling the number and type (positive or [negative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron "Electron")) of activated charge carriers. Such control is necessary for [transistors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transistor "Transistor"), [solar cells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_cell "Solar cell"), [semiconductor detectors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_detector "Semiconductor detector"), and other [semiconductor devices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_device "Semiconductor device") used in the computer industry and other technical applications.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Zulehner-60):573 In [silicon photonics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_photonics "Silicon photonics"), silicon may be used as a continuous wave [Raman laser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raman_laser "Raman laser") medium to produce coherent light.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-dekker_2008-74)

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/OxidizedSiliconWafer.jpg/250px-OxidizedSiliconWafer.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:OxidizedSiliconWafer.jpg)

Silicon wafer which has been thermally oxidized using water vapor at 1100º C for ~30 nm of silicon dioxide. The clear regions have been etched bare for subsequent doping.

In common [integrated circuits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit"), a wafer of mono-crystalline silicon (Si) serves as a mechanical support for the circuits. Circuit elements ([transistors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transistor "Transistor")) are created by doping and passivated by thin layers of [silicon oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_dioxide "Silicon dioxide"), an insulator that is easily produced on Si surfaces by processes of [thermal oxidation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermal_oxidation "Thermal oxidation") or [chemical vapor deposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_vapor_deposition "Chemical vapor deposition") (CVD) (among other methods). Thermal oxidation is most common and involves exposing Si to oxygen under the specific conditions. The resulting oxide thickness can be predicted by the [Deal–Grove model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deal%E2%80%93Grove_model "Deal–Grove model"). Silicon is the most popular material for integrated circuits due to the high stability and ease of forming its native oxide (SiO 2). The insulating oxide of silicon is not soluble in water, which gives it an advantage over [germanium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germanium "Germanium").[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-75)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable\_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_] Germanium (Ge) was used for the first version of the transistor and has similar electronic properties to silicon such as carrier [mobility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron_mobility "Electron mobility") and [band gap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Band_gap "Band gap"). However Ge based technologies ultimately failed due to the instability of the GeO 2. Germanium is still used in modern semiconductor electronics as a [dopant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dopant "Dopant") to enhance the mobility of [holes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron_hole "Electron hole") in the source and drain of [PMOS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PMOS_logic "PMOS logic").

Monocrystalline silicon is expensive to produce, and is usually justified only in production of integrated circuits, where tiny crystal imperfections can interfere with tiny circuit paths.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-76)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable\_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_] For other uses, other types of pure silicon may be employed. These include [hydrogenated amorphous silicon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogenated_amorphous_silicon "Hydrogenated amorphous silicon") and upgraded metallurgical-grade silicon (UMG-Si) used in the production of low-cost, [large-area electronics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large-area_electronics "Large-area electronics") in applications such as [liquid-crystal displays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid-crystal_display "Liquid-crystal display") and of large-area, low-cost, thin-film [solar cells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_cells "Solar cells"). Such semiconductor grades of silicon are either slightly less pure or polycrystalline rather than monocrystalline, and are produced in comparable quantities as the monocrystalline silicon: 75,000 to 150,000 metric tons per year. The market for the lesser grade is growing more quickly than for monocrystalline silicon. By 2013, polycrystalline silicon production, used mostly in solar cells, was projected to reach 200,000 metric tons per year, while monocrystalline semiconductor grade silicon was expected to remain less than 50,000 tons per year.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-USGS-59)

### Quantum dots

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Silicon&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Quantum dots")]

[Silicon quantum dots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_quantum_dots "Silicon quantum dots") are created through the thermal processing of hydrogen [silsesquioxane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silsesquioxane "Silsesquioxane") into nanocrystals ranging from a few nanometers to a few microns, displaying size dependent [luminescent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luminescence "Luminescence") properties.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-77)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-78) The nanocrystals display large [Stokes shifts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stokes_shift "Stokes shift") converting photons in the ultraviolet range to photons in the visible or infrared, depending on the particle size, allowing for applications in [quantum dot displays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_dot_display "Quantum dot display") and [luminescent solar concentrators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luminescent_solar_concentrator "Luminescent solar concentrator") due to their limited self absorption. A benefit of using silicon based [quantum dots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_dot "Quantum dot") over [cadmium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadmium "Cadmium") or [indium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indium "Indium") is the non-toxic, metal-free nature of silicon.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-79)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-80) Another application of silicon quantum dots is for sensing of hazardous materials. The sensors take advantage of the luminescent properties of the quantum dots through [quenching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quenching_(fluorescence) "Quenching (fluorescence)") of the [photoluminescence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photoluminescence "Photoluminescence") in the presence of the hazardous substance.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-81) There are many methods used for hazardous chemical sensing with a few being electron transfer, [fluorescence resonance energy transfer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F%C3%B6rster_resonance_energy_transfer "Förster resonance energy transfer"), and photocurrent generation.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-82) Electron transfer quenching occurs when the [lowest unoccupied molecular orbital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowest_unoccupied_molecular_orbital "Lowest unoccupied molecular orbital") (LUMO) is slightly lower in energy than the conduction band of the quantum dot, allowing for the transfer of electrons between the two, preventing recombination of the holes and electrons within the nanocrystals. The effect can also be achieved in reverse with a donor molecule having its [highest occupied molecular orbital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highest_occupied_molecular_orbital "Highest occupied molecular orbital") (HOMO) slightly higher than a valence band edge of the quantum dot, allowing electrons to transfer between them, filling the holes and preventing recombination. Fluorescence resonance energy transfer occurs when a complex forms between the quantum dot and a quencher molecule. The complex will continue to absorb light but when the energy is converted to the ground state it does not release a photon, quenching the material. The third method uses different approach by measuring the [photocurrent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photocurrent "Photocurrent") emitted by the quantum dots instead of monitoring the photoluminescent display. If the concentration of the desired chemical increases then the photocurrent given off by the nanocrystals will change in response.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-83)

### Thermal energy storage

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Silicon&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Thermal energy storage")]

This section is an excerpt from [Thermal energy storage § Silicon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermal_energy_storage#Silicon "Thermal energy storage").[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Thermal_energy_storage&action=edit)]

Solid or molten silicon offers much higher storage temperatures than salts with consequent greater capacity and efficiency. It is being researched as a possible more energy efficient storage technology. Silicon is able to store more than 1 MWh of energy per cubic meter at 1400°C. An additional advantage is the relative abundance of silicon when compared to the salts used for the same purpose.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-84)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-85)

Hot silicon thermal energy storing technology would be able to store significant thermal energy at extremely high temperatures (around 1400-2000°C). This would be utilized by using the white hot molten silicon to store excess electricity generated from surrounding renewable sources like solar energy and wind power. This system would enable efficient, lower costing, and a longer duration of energy storage compared to other sensible heat storage options.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Thermal_energy_storage_:2-86)

## Biological role

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Silicon&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Biological role")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/20110123_185042_Diatom.jpg/250px-20110123_185042_Diatom.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:20110123_185042_Diatom.jpg)

A diatom, enclosed in a silica cell wall

Although silicon is readily available in the form of [silicates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicate "Silicate"), very few organisms use it directly. [Diatoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diatom "Diatom"), [radiolaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiolaria "Radiolaria"), and [siliceous sponges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siliceous_sponge "Siliceous sponge") use [biogenic silica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biogenic_silica "Biogenic silica") as a structural material for their skeletons. Some plants accumulate silica in their tissues and require silicon for their growth, for example [rice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rice "Rice"). Silicon may be taken up by plants as [orthosilicic acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthosilicic_acid "Orthosilicic acid") (also known as monosilicic acid) and transported through the [xylem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xylem "Xylem"), where it forms amorphous complexes with components of the cell wall. This has been shown to improve cell wall strength and structural integrity in some plants, thereby reducing insect herbivory and pathogenic infections. In certain plants, silicon may also upregulate the production of volatile organic compounds and phytohormones which play a significant role in plant defense mechanisms.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Kim2002-87)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-plants-88)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Leroy2019-89) In more advanced plants, silica ([opal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opal "Opal")) [phytoliths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phytolith "Phytolith") provide structural support.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-90)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-abd-91)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-plants-88)

Several [horticultural crops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horticultural_crop "Horticultural crop") are known to protect themselves against [fungal plant pathogens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fungal_plant_pathogen "Fungal plant pathogen") with silica, to such a degree that [fungicide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fungicide "Fungicide") application may fail unless accompanied by sufficient silicon nutrition. Silicaceous plant defense molecules activate some [phytoalexins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phytoalexin "Phytoalexin"), meaning some of them are signalling substances producing [acquired immunity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acquired_immunity "Acquired immunity"). When deprived, some plants will substitute with increased production of other defensive substances.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-plants-88)

Life on Earth is largely composed of [carbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon "Carbon"), but [astrobiology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astrobiology "Astrobiology") considers that [extraterrestrial life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extraterrestrial_life "Extraterrestrial life") may have other [hypothetical types of biochemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypothetical_types_of_biochemistry "Hypothetical types of biochemistry"). Silicon is considered an alternative to carbon, as it can create complex and stable molecules with four covalent bonds, required for a [DNA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA "DNA")-analog, and it is available in large quantities.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-92)

### Marine microbial influences

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Silicon&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Marine microbial influences")]

Diatoms use silicon in the [biogenic silica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biogenic_silica "Biogenic silica") (bSi) form,[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-93) which is taken up by the silicon transport protein (SIT) to be predominantly used in the cell wall structure as frustules.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-94) Silicon enters the ocean in a dissolved form such as silicic acid or silicate.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Dugdale-2001-95) Since diatoms are one of the main users of these forms of silicon, they contribute greatly to the concentration of silicon throughout the ocean. Silicon forms a nutrient-like profile in the ocean due to the diatom productivity in shallow depths.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Dugdale-2001-95) Therefore, concentration of silicon is lower in the shallow ocean and higher in the deep ocean.

Diatom productivity in the upper ocean contributes to the amount of silicon exported to the lower ocean.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-96) When diatom cells are [lysed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lysis "Lysis") in the upper ocean, their nutrients such as iron, zinc, and silicon, are brought to the lower ocean through a process called [marine snow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_snow "Marine snow"). Marine snow involves the downward transfer of particulate organic matter by vertical mixing of dissolved organic matter.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-97) It has been suggested that silicon is considered crucial to diatom productivity and as long as there is silicic acid available for diatoms to use, the diatoms can contribute to other important nutrient concentrations in the deep ocean as well.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-98)

In coastal zones, diatoms serve as the major phytoplanktonic organisms and greatly contribute to biogenic silica production. In the open ocean, however, diatoms have a reduced role in global annual silica production. Diatoms in North Atlantic and North Pacific subtropical gyres only contribute about 5–7% of global annual marine silica production. The [Southern Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Ocean "Southern Ocean") produces about one-third of global marine biogenic silica.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-The_World_Ocean_Silica_Cycle-56) The Southern Ocean is referred to as having a "biogeochemical divide"[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-99) since only minuscule amounts of silicon are transported out of this region.

### Human nutrition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Silicon&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Human nutrition")]

There is some evidence that silicon is important to human health for their nail, hair, bone, and skin tissues,[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-100) for example, in studies that demonstrate that premenopausal women with higher dietary silicon intake have higher [bone density](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bone_density "Bone density"), and that silicon supplementation can increase bone volume and density in patients with [osteoporosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osteoporosis "Osteoporosis").[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-jugdaohsingh2007silicon-101) Silicon is needed for synthesis of [elastin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elastin "Elastin") and [collagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collagen "Collagen"), of which the [aorta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aorta "Aorta") contains the greatest quantity in the human body,[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-LoeperLoeper1978-102) and has been considered an [essential element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mineral_(nutrient) "Mineral (nutrient)");[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-Niels-103) nevertheless, it is difficult to prove its essentiality, because silicon is very common, and hence, deficiency symptoms are difficult to reproduce.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-lipp-104)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-105)

Silicon was recognized as a "nutritive element" by the International Plant Nutrition Institute (IPNI) and a "beneficial substance" by the Association of American Plant Food Control Officials.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-106)

## Safety

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Silicon&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Safety")]

People may be exposed to elemental silicon in the workplace by breathing it in, swallowing it, or having contact with the skin or eye. In the latter two cases, silicon poses a slight hazard as an irritant. It is hazardous if inhaled.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-msds-107) The [Occupational Safety and Health Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occupational_Safety_and_Health_Administration "Occupational Safety and Health Administration") (OSHA) has set the [legal limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permissible_exposure_limit "Permissible exposure limit") for silicon exposure in the workplace as 15 mg/m 3 total exposure and 5 mg/m 3 respiratory exposure over an eight-hour workday. The [National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institute_for_Occupational_Safety_and_Health "National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health") (NIOSH) has set a [recommended exposure limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recommended_exposure_limit "Recommended exposure limit") (REL) of 10 mg/m 3 total exposure and 5 mg/m 3 respiratory exposure over an eight-hour workday.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-108) Inhalation of [crystalline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystalline "Crystalline") silica dust may lead to [silicosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicosis "Silicosis"), an [occupational lung disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occupational_lung_disease "Occupational lung disease") marked by [inflammation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inflammation "Inflammation") and scarring in the form of [nodular lesions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nodule_(medicine) "Nodule (medicine)") in the upper lobes of the [lungs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lungs "Lungs").[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon#cite_note-PlantVoulvoulis2012-109)

**Boron** is a [chemical element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_element "Chemical element"); it has [symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_symbol "Chemical symbol")**B** and [atomic number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_number "Atomic number")5. In its crystalline form it is a brittle, dark, lustrous [metalloid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metalloid "Metalloid"); in its [amorphous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amorphous_solid "Amorphous solid") form it is a brown powder. As the lightest element of the [boron group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron_group "Boron group") it has three [valence electrons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valence_electron "Valence electron") for forming [covalent bonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covalent_bond "Covalent bond"), resulting in many compounds such as [boric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boric_acid "Boric acid"), the mineral [sodium borate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borax "Borax"), and the ultra-hard crystals of [boron carbide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron_carbide "Boron carbide") and [boron nitride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron_nitride "Boron nitride").

Boron is synthesized entirely by [cosmic ray spallation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_ray_spallation "Cosmic ray spallation") and [supernovas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supernova "Supernova") and not by [stellar nucleosynthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stellar_nucleosynthesis "Stellar nucleosynthesis"), so it is a low-abundance element in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") and in the [Earth's crust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crust_(geology) "Crust (geology)").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-14) It constitutes about 0.001 percent by weight of Earth's crust.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-15) It is concentrated on Earth by the water-solubility of its more common naturally occurring compounds, the [borate minerals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borate_mineral "Borate mineral"). These are mined industrially as [evaporites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evaporite "Evaporite"), such as [borax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borax "Borax") and [kernite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kernite "Kernite"). The largest known deposits are in [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey"), the largest producer of boron minerals.

Elemental boron is found in small amounts in [meteoroids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meteoroid "Meteoroid"), but chemically uncombined boron is not otherwise found naturally on Earth.

Several [allotropes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allotropes_of_boron "Allotropes of boron") exist: [amorphous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amorphous_solid "Amorphous solid") boron is a brown powder; crystalline boron is silvery to black, extremely hard (9.3 on the [Mohs scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohs_scale_of_mineral_hardness "Mohs scale of mineral hardness")), and a poor [electrical conductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_conductor "Electrical conductor") at room temperature (1.5 × 10−6 Ω−1 cm−1 room temperature electrical conductivity).[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-16) The primary use of the element itself is as [boron filaments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron_fiber "Boron fiber") with applications similar to [carbon fibers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_fibers "Carbon fibers") in some high-strength materials.

Boron is primarily used in chemical compounds. About half of all production consumed globally is an additive in [fiberglass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiberglass "Fiberglass") for insulation and structural materials. The next leading use is in [polymers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polymer "Polymer") and [ceramics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceramic "Ceramic") in high-strength, lightweight structural and [heat-resistant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refractory "Refractory") materials. [Borosilicate glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borosilicate_glass "Borosilicate glass") is desired for its greater strength and thermal shock resistance than ordinary soda lime glass. As [sodium perborate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_perborate "Sodium perborate"), it is used as a [bleach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bleach "Bleach"). A small amount is used as a [dopant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dopant "Dopant") in [semiconductors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor "Semiconductor") and [reagent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reagent "Reagent") intermediates in the [synthesis of organic fine chemicals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organic_synthesis "Organic synthesis"). A few boron-containing organic pharmaceuticals are used or are in study. Natural boron is composed of two stable isotopes, one of which ([boron-10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#Enriched_boron_(boron-10))) has a number of uses as a neutron-capturing agent.

[Borates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borate "Borate") have low toxicity in mammals (similar to [table salt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt "Salt")) but are more toxic to [arthropods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthropod "Arthropod") and are occasionally used as [insecticides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insecticide "Insecticide"). Boron-containing organic antibiotics are known. Although only traces are required, boron is an essential [plant nutrient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plant_nutrition "Plant nutrition").

## History

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/Brown-boron.jpg/250px-Brown-boron.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Brown-boron.jpg)

Amorphous boron powder

The word _boron_ was coined from _[borax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borax "Borax")_, the mineral from which it was isolated, by analogy with _carbon_, which boron resembles chemically.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-Greenwood&Earnshaw2nd-17):139

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/Sassolite.jpg/250px-Sassolite.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sassolite.jpg)

[Sassolite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sassolite "Sassolite")

Borax in its mineral form (then known as tincal) first saw use as a glaze, beginning in [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") circa 300 AD. Some crude borax traveled westward, and was apparently mentioned by the alchemist [Jabir ibn Hayyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jabir_ibn_Hayyan "Jabir ibn Hayyan") around 700 AD. [Marco Polo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Polo "Marco Polo") brought some glazes back to Italy in the 13th century. [Georgius Agricola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgius_Agricola "Georgius Agricola"), in around 1600, reported the use of borax as a flux in [metallurgy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallurgy "Metallurgy"). In 1777, [boric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boric_acid "Boric acid") was recognized in the hot springs ([soffioni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soffioni "Soffioni")) near [Florence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence "Florence"), Italy, at which point it became known as _sal sedativum_, with ostensible medical benefits. The mineral was named [sassolite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sassolite "Sassolite") after [Sasso Pisano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sasso_Pisano "Sasso Pisano") in Italy. Sasso was the main source of [European](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe") borax from 1827 to 1872, when [American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") sources replaced it.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-borates-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-boron-19) Boron compounds were rarely used until the late 1800s when [Francis Marion Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Marion_Smith "Francis Marion Smith")'s [Pacific Coast Borax Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Coast_Borax_Company "Pacific Coast Borax Company") first popularized and produced them in volume at low cost.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-20)

Boron was not recognized as an element until it was isolated by Sir [Humphry Davy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humphry_Davy "Humphry Davy")[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-Davy-12) and by [Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Louis_Gay-Lussac "Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac") and [Louis Jacques Thénard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Jacques_Th%C3%A9nard "Louis Jacques Thénard").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-Lussac-11) In 1808, Davy observed that electric current sent through a solution of borates produced a brown precipitate on one of the electrodes. In his subsequent experiments, he used potassium to [reduce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reducing_agent "Reducing agent") boric acid instead of [electrolysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrolysis "Electrolysis"). He produced enough boron to confirm a new element and named it _boracium_.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-Davy-12) Gay-Lussac and Thénard used iron to reduce boric acid at high temperatures. By oxidizing boron with air, they showed that boric acid is its oxidation product.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-Lussac-11)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-weeks-21)[Jöns Jacob Berzelius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%B6ns_Jacob_Berzelius "Jöns Jacob Berzelius") identified it as an element in 1824.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-22) Pure boron was arguably first produced by the American chemist Ezekiel Weintraub in 1909.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-Laubengayer-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-25)

## Characteristics of the element

### Isotopes

Main article: [Isotopes of boron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotopes_of_boron "Isotopes of boron")

Boron has two naturally occurring and stable [isotopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotope "Isotope"), 11 B (80.1%) and 10 B (19.9%). The mass difference results in a wide range of δ 11 B values, which are defined as a fractional difference between the 11 B and 10 B and traditionally expressed in parts per thousand, in natural waters ranging from −16 to +59. There are 13 known isotopes of boron; the shortest-lived isotope is 7 B which decays through [proton emission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proton_emission "Proton emission") and [alpha decay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_decay "Alpha decay") with a [half-life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half-life "Half-life") of 3.5×10−22 s. Isotopic fractionation of boron is controlled by the exchange reactions of the boron species B(OH)3 and [[B(OH)4]−](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrahydroxyborate "Tetrahydroxyborate"). Boron isotopes are also fractionated during mineral crystallization, during H 2 O phase changes in [hydrothermal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrothermal "Hydrothermal") systems, and during [hydrothermal alteration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrothermal_alteration "Hydrothermal alteration") of [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_(geology) "Rock (geology)"). The latter effect results in preferential removal of the [10 B(OH)4]−[ion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ion "Ion") onto clays. It results in solutions enriched in 11 B(OH)3 and therefore may be responsible for the large 11 B enrichment in seawater relative to both [oceanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ocean "Ocean") crust and [continental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continent "Continent") crust; this difference may act as an [isotopic signature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotopic_signature "Isotopic signature").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-26)

The exotic 17 B exhibits a [nuclear halo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_halo "Nuclear halo"), i.e. its radius is appreciably larger than that predicted by the [liquid drop model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-empirical_mass_formula "Semi-empirical mass formula").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-27)

#### NMR spectroscopy

Both 10 B and 11 B possess [nuclear spin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_spin "Nuclear spin"). The nuclear spin of 10 B is 3 and that of 11 B is ⁠3/2⁠. These isotopes are therefore of use in [nuclear magnetic resonance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_magnetic_resonance "Nuclear magnetic resonance") spectroscopy, and spectrometers specially adapted to detecting the boron-11 nuclei are available commercially. The 10 B and 11 B nuclei also cause splitting in the [resonances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resonances "Resonances") of attached nuclei.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-28)

### Allotropes

Main article: [Allotropes of boron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allotropes_of_boron "Allotropes of boron")

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/34/Bor_1.jpg/250px-Bor_1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bor_1.jpg)

Boron chunks

Boron forms four major [allotropes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allotrope "Allotrope"): α-rhombohedral[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-29) and β-rhombohedral[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-30) (α-R and β-R), γ-orthorhombic[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-31) (γ), and β-tetragonal[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-32) (β-T). All four phases are stable at [ambient conditions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_temperature_and_pressure "Standard temperature and pressure"). β-rhombohedral is the most stable and the most common. An α-tetragonal phase also exists (α-T) but is difficult to produce without significant contamination. Most of the phases are based on B 12 icosahedra, but the γ phase can be described as a [rocksalt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_chloride "Sodium chloride")-type arrangement of the icosahedra and B 2 atomic pairs.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-oganov-33) It can be produced by compressing other boron phases to 12–20 GPa and heating to 1500–1800°C; it remains stable after releasing the temperature and pressure. The β-T phase is produced at similar pressures, but higher temperatures of 1800–2200°C. The α-T and β-T phases might coexist at ambient conditions, with the β-T phase being the more stable.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-oganov-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-widom-35) Compressing boron above 160 GPa produces a boron phase with an as yet unknown structure, and this phase is a [superconductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superconductor "Superconductor") at temperatures below 6–12 K.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-prl-37)
