### Atomic structure

Atomic boron is the lightest element having an [electron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron "Electron") in a [p-orbital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_orbital "Atomic orbital") in its ground state. Its first three [ionization energies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionization_energies "Ionization energies") are higher than those for heavier group III elements, reflecting its electropositive character.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-Greenwood&Earnshaw2nd-17):144

## Chemistry of the element

Main article: [Boron compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron_compounds "Boron compounds")

### Preparation

Elemental boron is rare and poorly studied because the pure material is extremely difficult to prepare. Most studies of "boron" involve samples that contain small amounts of carbon. Highly pure boron is produced with difficulty because of contamination by carbon or other elements that resist removal.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-45)

Some early routes to elemental boron involved the reduction of [boric oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boric_oxide "Boric oxide") with metals such as [magnesium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnesium "Magnesium") or [aluminium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium "Aluminium"). However, the product was often contaminated with [borides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boride "Boride") of those metals.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-46) Pure boron can be prepared by reducing volatile boron halides with [hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen "Hydrogen") at high temperatures. Ultrapure boron for use in the semiconductor industry is produced by the decomposition of [diborane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diborane "Diborane") at high temperatures and then further purified by the [zone melting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zone_melting "Zone melting") or [Czochralski processes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czochralski_process "Czochralski process").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-berger-47)

### Reactions of the element

[Crystalline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystalline "Crystalline") boron is a hard, black material with a melting point of above 2000°C. Crystalline boron is chemically inert and resistant to attack by boiling [hydrofluoric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrofluoric_acid "Hydrofluoric acid") or [hydrochloric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrochloric_acid "Hydrochloric acid"). When finely divided, it is attacked slowly by hot concentrated [hydrogen peroxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_peroxide "Hydrogen peroxide"), hot concentrated [nitric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitric_acid "Nitric acid"), hot [sulfuric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfuric_acid "Sulfuric acid"), or hot mixture of sulfuric and [chromic acids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromic_acid "Chromic acid").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-Laubengayer-24)

Since elemental boron is rare, its chemical reactions are of little significance. The elemental form is not typically used as a precursor to compounds. Instead, boron compounds are produced from borates.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-Brotherton-48)

When exposed to air, under normal conditions, a [protective oxide or hydroxide layer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passivation_(chemistry) "Passivation (chemistry)") forms on the surface of boron, which prevents further corrosion.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-49) The rate of oxidation of boron depends on the crystallinity, particle size, purity and temperature. At higher temperatures boron burns to form [boron trioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron_trioxide "Boron trioxide"):[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-HollemanAF-50)

4 B + 3 O 2 → 2 B 2 O 3[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/26/Tetraborate-xtal-3D-balls.png/250px-Tetraborate-xtal-3D-balls.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tetraborate-xtal-3D-balls.png)

Ball-and-stick model of tetraborate anion, [B 4 O 5(OH)4]2−, as it occurs in crystalline borax, Na 2[B 4 O 5(OH)4]·8H 2 O. Boron atoms are pink, with bridging oxygens in red, and four hydroxyl hydrogens in white. Note two borons are trigonally bonded sp 2 with no formal charge, while the other two borons are tetrahedrally bonded sp 3, each carrying a formal charge of −1. The oxidation state of all borons is III. This mixture of boron coordination numbers and formal charges is characteristic of natural boron minerals.

## Chemical compounds

Main article: [Boron compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron_compounds "Boron compounds")

### General trends

In some ways, boron is comparable to [carbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon "Carbon") in its capability to form stable [covalently bonded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covalent_bond "Covalent bond") molecular networks (even nominally disordered ([amorphous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amorphous_solid "Amorphous solid")) boron contains boron [icosahedra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icosahedra "Icosahedra"), which are bonded randomly to each other without [long-range order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-range_order "Long-range order").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-52)). In terms of chemical behavior, boron compounds resemble [silicon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon "Silicon") due to their [diagonal relationship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diagonal_relationship "Diagonal relationship"). [Aluminium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium "Aluminium"), the heavier congener of boron, does not behave analogously to boron: it is far more electropositive, it is larger, and it tends not to form homoatomic Al-Al bonds. In the most familiar compounds, boron has the formal oxidation state III. These include the common oxides, sulfides, nitrides, and halides, as well as organic derivatives.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-HollemanAF-50)

Boron compounds often violate the [octet rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octet_rule "Octet rule").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-Key-53)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-Greenwood&Earnshaw2nd-17):139

### Halides

Boron forms the complete series of trihalides, i.e. BX 3 (X = F, Cl, Br, I). The trifluoride is produced by treating borate salts with [hydrogen fluoride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_fluoride "Hydrogen fluoride"), while the trichloride is produced by [carbothermic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbothermic_reaction "Carbothermic reaction") reduction of boron oxides in the presence of chlorine gas:[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-Brotherton-48)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-HollemanAF-50)

B 2 O 3 + 3 C + 6 Cl 2 → 2 BCl 3 + 3 CO[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Boron-trifluoride-pi-bonding-2D.png/250px-Boron-trifluoride-pi-bonding-2D.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Boron-trifluoride-pi-bonding-2D.png)

[Boron (III) trifluoride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron_trifluoride "Boron trifluoride") structure, showing "empty" boron p orbital in pi-type [coordinate covalent bonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinate_covalent_bond "Coordinate covalent bond")

The trihalides adopt a planar trigonal structures, in contrast to the behavior of aluminium trihalides. All charge-neutral boron halides violate the octet rule; hence, they are typically [Lewis acidic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_acid "Lewis acid"). For example, [boron trifluoride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron_trifluoride "Boron trifluoride") (BF 3) combines eagerly with fluoride sources to give the [tetrafluoroborate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrafluoroborate "Tetrafluoroborate") anion, BF 4−. Boron trifluoride is used in the petrochemical industry as a catalyst. The halides react with water to form [boric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boric_acid "Boric acid").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-HollemanAF-50) Other boron halides include those with B-B bonding, such as [B 2 F 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diboron_tetrafluoride "Diboron tetrafluoride") and B 4 Cl 4.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-Greenwood&Earnshaw2nd-17) Larger polyhedral boron(I) halides also exist, e.g. B 7 Br 7, B 8 Cl 8 and B 9 I 9.

### Oxide derivatives

Boron-containing minerals exclusively exist as oxides of B(III), often associated with other elements. More than one hundred [borate minerals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borate_mineral "Borate mineral") are known. These minerals resemble silicates in some respect, although it is often found not only in a tetrahedral coordination with oxygen, but also in a trigonal planar configuration. The borates can be subdivided into two classes, anhydrous and the far more common hydrates. The hydrates contain B-OH groups and sometimes water of crystallization. A typical motif is exemplified by the tetraborate anions of the common mineral [borax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borax "Borax"). The formal negative charge of the tetrahedral borate center is balanced by sodium (Na+).[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-HollemanAF-50) Some of the complexity of the borates is exemplified by the inventory of zinc borates, which are common [wood preservatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wood_preservative "Wood preservative") and [fire retardants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire_retardant "Fire retardant"):[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-UllBO-54) 4ZnO·B 2 O 3·H 2 O, ZnO·B 2 O 3·1.12H 2 O, ZnO·B 2 O 3·2H 2 O, 6ZnO·5B 2 O 3·3H 2 O, 2ZnO·3B 2 O 3·7H 2 O, 2ZnO·3B 2 O 3·3H 2 O, 3ZnO·5B 2 O 3·14H 2 O, and ZnO·5B 2 O 3·4.5H 2 O.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-Schubert-55)

As illustrated by the preceding examples, borate anions tend to condense by formation of B-O-B bonds. Borosilicates, with B-O-Si, and borophosphates, with B-O-P linkages, are also well represented in both minerals and synthetic compounds.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-56)

Related to the oxides are the [alkoxides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkoxide "Alkoxide") and [boronic acids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boronic_acid "Boronic acid") with the formula B(OR)3 and R 2 BOH, respectively. Boron forms a wide variety of such metal-organic compounds, some of which are used in the synthesis of pharmaceuticals. These developments, especially the [Suzuki reaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suzuki_reaction "Suzuki reaction"), was recognized with the 2010 [Nobel Prize in Chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Chemistry "Nobel Prize in Chemistry") to [Akira Suzuki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akira_Suzuki "Akira Suzuki").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-57)

### Hydrides

Main article: [Boranes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boranes "Boranes")

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ed/Deltahedral-borane-cluster-array-numbered-3D-bs-17.png/250px-Deltahedral-borane-cluster-array-numbered-3D-bs-17.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Deltahedral-borane-cluster-array-numbered-3D-bs-17.png)

[Ball-and-stick models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ball-and-stick_model "Ball-and-stick model") showing the structures of the boron skeletons of [borane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boranes "Boranes")[clusters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atom_cluster "Atom cluster"). The structures can be rationalised by [polyhedral skeletal electron pair theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyhedral_skeletal_electron_pair_theory "Polyhedral skeletal electron pair theory").[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-58)

Boranes and [borohydrides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borohydride "Borohydride") are compounds of boron and hydrogen that are neutral and anionic, respectively. [Sodium borohydride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_borohydride "Sodium borohydride") is the progenitor of the boranes. Sodium borohydride is obtained by [hydrogenation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogenation "Hydrogenation") of [trimethylborate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trimethylborate "Trimethylborate"):[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-Brotherton-48)

B(OCH 3)3 + 4 Na + 2H 2 → NaBH 4 + 3 NaOCH 3
Sodium borohydride is a white, fairly air-stable salt, and it converts to diborane by treatment with [boron trifluoride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron_trifluoride "Boron trifluoride"):[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-Brotherton-48)

3 NaBH 4 + 4 BF 3 → 2 (BH 3)2 + 3 NaBF 4
[Diborane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diborane "Diborane") is the dimer of the parent called [borane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borane "Borane"), BH 3. Having a formula akin to ethane's (C 2 H 6), diborane adopts a markedly different structure, featuring a pair of bridging H atoms. This unusual structure, which was deduced only in the 1940s, was an early indication of the complexity of boron chemistry.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-Brotherton-48)

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/Diborane-2D-dimensions.svg/250px-Diborane-2D-dimensions.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Diborane-2D-dimensions.svg)

Structure of diborane

Pyrolysis of diborane gives [boron hydride clusters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron_hydride_cluster "Boron hydride cluster") such as [pentaborane(9)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentaborane(9) "Pentaborane(9)")B 5 H 9 and [decaborane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decaborane "Decaborane")B 10 H 14.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-Greenwood&Earnshaw2nd-17):164,170,173 A large number of anionic boron hydrides are also known, e.g. [[B 3 H 8]−](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octahydrotriborate "Octahydrotriborate") and [[B 12 H 12]2−](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dodecaborate "Dodecaborate"). In these [cluster compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cluster_compound "Cluster compound"), boron has a [coordination number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordination_number "Coordination number") greater than four.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-HollemanAF-50) When at least one boron atom is replaced by another elements, [heteroboranes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heteroboranes "Heteroboranes") are formed. They have similar structures of their parent boranes. The analysis of the bonding in these polyhedra clusters earned [William N. Lipscomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_N._Lipscomb "William N. Lipscomb") the 1976 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for "studies on the structure of boranes illuminating problems of chemical bonding". Not only are their structures unusual, many of the boranes are extremely reactive. For example, a widely used procedure for [pentaborane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentaborane "Pentaborane") states that it will "spontaneously inflame or explode in air".[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-59)

### Organoboron compounds

Main article: [Organoboron chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organoboron_chemistry "Organoboron chemistry")

A large number of organoboron compounds, species with B-C bonds, are known. Many organoboron compounds are produced from [hydroboration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydroboration%E2%80%93oxidation_reaction "Hydroboration–oxidation reaction"), the addition of [B-H bonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boranes "Boranes") to C=C and C≡C bonds.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-60)[Diborane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diborane "Diborane") is traditionally used for such reactions, as illustrated by the preparation of trioctylborane:[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-61)

B 2 H 6 + 6 H 2 C=CH(CH 2)5 CH 3 → 2 B((CH 2)7 CH 3)3
This [regiochemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regiochemistry "Regiochemistry"), i.e. the tendency of B to attach to the terminal carbon - is explained by the polarization of the bonds in boranes, which is indicated as B δ+-H δ-.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-Greenwood&Earnshaw2nd-17):144,166

Hydroboration opened the doors for many subsequent reactions, several of which are useful in [the synthesis of complex organic compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organic_synthesis "Organic synthesis").[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-HCB-62) The significance of these methods was recognized by the award of [Nobel Prize in Chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Chemistry "Nobel Prize in Chemistry") to [H. C. Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._C._Brown "H. C. Brown") in 1979. Even complicated boron hydrides, such as [decaborane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decaborane "Decaborane"), undergo hydroboration.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-Greenwood&Earnshaw2nd-17):181 Like the volatile boranes, the alkyl boranes ignite spontaneously in air.

In the 1950s, several studies examined the use of [boranes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boranes "Boranes") as energy-increasing "[Zip fuel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zip_fuel "Zip fuel")" additives for jet fuel.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-63)

Triorganoboron(III) compounds are trigonal planar and exhibit weak [Lewis acidity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_acid "Lewis acid"). The resulting adducts are tetrahedral. This behavior contrasts with that of [triorganoaluminium compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organoaluminium_compound "Organoaluminium compound") (see [trimethylaluminium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trimethylaluminium "Trimethylaluminium")), which are tetrahedral with bridging alkyl groups.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-65)

A compound with the B≡C triple bond was synthesized for the first time in 2025.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-66)

### Nitrides

Main article: [Boron nitride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron_nitride "Boron nitride")

The boron-nitrides follow the pattern of avoiding B-B and N-N bonds; only B-N bonding is observed generally. The [boron nitrides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron_nitride "Boron nitride") exhibit structures analogous to various [allotropes of carbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allotropes_of_carbon "Allotropes of carbon"), including graphite, diamond, and nanotubes. This similarity reflects the fact that B and N have eight valence electrons as does a pair of carbon atoms. In cubic boron nitride (tradename [Borazon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borazon "Borazon")), boron and nitrogen atoms are tetrahedral, just like carbon in [diamond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diamond "Diamond"). Cubic boron nitride, among other applications, is used as an abrasive, as its [hardness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardness "Hardness") is comparable with that of diamond. Hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) is the BN analogue of graphite, consisting of sheets of alternating B and N atoms. These sheets stack with boron and nitrogen in registry between the sheets. Graphite and h-BN have markedly different properties, although both are lubricants, as these planes slip past each other easily. However, h-BN is a relatively poor electrical and thermal conductor in the planar directions.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-dkg-67)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-b1-68) Molecular analogues of boron nitrides are represented by [borazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borazine "Borazine"), (BH)3(NH)3.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-Greenwood&Earnshaw2nd-17):167

### Carbides

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/14/Borfig11a.png/250px-Borfig11a.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Borfig11a.png)

Unit cell of B 4 C. The green sphere and [icosahedra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icosahedron "Icosahedron") consist of boron atoms, and black spheres are carbon atoms.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-zhangyb28.5c4-69)

[Boron carbide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron_carbide "Boron carbide") is a ceramic material. It is obtained by [carbothermal reduction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbothermal_reduction "Carbothermal reduction") of B 2 O 3 in an electric furnace:[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-70)

2 B 2 O 3 + 7 C → B 4 C + 6 CO
Boron carbide's structure is only approximately reflected in its formula of B 4 C, and it shows a clear depletion of carbon from this suggested stoichiometric ratio. This is due to its complex structure. The substance can be seen with [empirical formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empirical_formula "Empirical formula") B 12 C 3 (i.e., with B 12 dodecahedra being a motif), but with less carbon, as the suggested C 3 units are replaced with C-B-C chains, and some smaller (B 6) octahedra are present as well (see the boron carbide article for structural analysis). The repeating polymer plus semi-crystalline structure of boron carbide gives it great structural strength per weight.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-71)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-72)

### Borides

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/Magnesium-diboride-3D-balls.png/250px-Magnesium-diboride-3D-balls.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Magnesium-diboride-3D-balls.png)

Ball-and-stick model of superconductor magnesium diboride. Boron atoms lie in hexagonal aromatic graphite-like layers, with a charge of −1 on each boron atom. Magnesium(II) ions lie between layers

Binary metal-boron compounds, the metal borides, contain only boron and a metal. They are metallic, exceptionally hard, with high [melting points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melting_point "Melting point"). [TiB 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titanium_diboride "Titanium diboride"), [ZrB 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zirconium_diboride "Zirconium diboride"), and [HfB 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hafnium_diboride "Hafnium diboride") have melting points above 3000°C.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-b1-68) The borides can be classified loosely as boron rich or metal rich, for example the compound [YB 66](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yttrium_boride "Yttrium boride") at one extreme through to Nd 2 Fe 14 B at the other. The generally accepted definition is that if the ratio of boron atoms to metal atoms is 4:1 or more, the compound is boron rich; if it is less, then it is metal rich. Some metal borides find specialized applications as hard materials for cutting tools.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-73)

## Occurrence

Main article: [Borate minerals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borate_minerals "Borate minerals")

See also: [Category:Borate minerals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Borate_minerals "Category:Borate minerals")

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/Borax_crystals.jpg/250px-Borax_crystals.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Borax_crystals.jpg)

Borax crystals

Boron is rare in the universe and Solar System. The amount of boron formed in the [Big Bang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Bang "Big Bang") was negligible. Boron is not generated in the normal course of stellar nucleosynthesis, and is destroyed in stellar interiors.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-74)

In the high oxygen environment of the Earth's surface, boron is always found fully oxidized to borate. Boron does not appear on Earth in elemental form. Extremely small traces of elemental boron were detected in Lunar regolith.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-76)

Although boron is a relatively rare element in the Earth's crust, representing only 0.001% of the crust mass, it can be highly concentrated by the action of water, in which many borates are soluble. It is found naturally combined in compounds such as [borax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borax "Borax") and [boric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boric_acid "Boric acid") (sometimes found in [volcanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcano "Volcano") spring waters). Over a hundred [borate minerals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borate_minerals "Borate minerals") are known.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-77)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-78)

## Production

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/Ulexita_br.jpg/250px-Ulexita_br.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ulexita_br.jpg)

A fragment of ulexite

Economically important sources of boron are the minerals [colemanite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colemanite "Colemanite"), rasorite ([kernite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kernite "Kernite")), [ulexite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulexite "Ulexite"), and [tincal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tincal "Tincal"). Together, these constitute 90% of mined boron-containing ore. The largest global borax deposits known, many still untapped, are in Central and Western [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey"), including the provinces of [Eskişehir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eski%C5%9Fehir "Eskişehir"), [Kütahya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%BCtahya "Kütahya") and [Balıkesir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bal%C4%B1kesir "Balıkesir").[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-79)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-80)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-81) Global proven boron mineral mining reserves exceed one billion metric tonnes, against a yearly production of about four million tonnes.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-82)

[Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey") and the United States are the largest producers of boron products. Turkey produces about half of the global yearly demand through [Eti Mine Works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eti_Mine_Works "Eti Mine Works") ([Turkish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_language "Turkish language"): _Eti Maden İşletmeleri_), a [Turkish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey")[state-owned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State-owned_company "State-owned company")[mining](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mining_industry "Mining industry") and [chemicals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_industry "Chemical industry") company focusing on boron products. It holds a [government monopoly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_monopoly "Government monopoly") on the mining of [borate minerals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borate_minerals "Borate minerals") in Turkey, which possesses 72% of the world's known deposits.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-83) In 2012, it held a 47% [share](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_share "Market share") of production of global borate minerals, ahead of its main competitor, [Rio Tinto Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_Tinto_Group "Rio Tinto Group").[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-84)

Almost a quarter (23%) of global boron production comes from the [Rio Tinto Borax Mine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_Tinto_Borax_Mine "Rio Tinto Borax Mine") (also known as the U.S. Borax Boron Mine) [35°2′34.447″N 117°40′45.412″W / 35.04290194°N 117.67928111°W / 35.04290194; -117.67928111 (Rio Tinto Borax Mine)](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Boron&params=35_2_34.447_N_117_40_45.412_W_type:landmark_globe:earth_region:US-CA&title=Rio+Tinto+Borax+Mine) near [Boron, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron,_California "Boron, California").[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-85)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-86)

### Market trend

The average cost of crystalline elemental boron was US$5/g in 2008.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-87) Elemental boron is chiefly used in making boron fibers, where it is deposited by [chemical vapor deposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_vapor_deposition "Chemical vapor deposition") on a [tungsten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tungsten "Tungsten") core (see below). Boron fibers are used in lightweight composite applications, such as high strength tapes.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-88) This use is a small fraction of total boron use. Boron is introduced into semiconductors as boron compounds by ion implantation.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-89)

Estimated global consumption of boron (almost entirely as boron compounds) was about 4 million tonnes of B 2 O 3 in 2012. The cost of boron compounds such as borax and kernite was cumulatively US$377/tonne in 2019.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-90)

Increasing demand for boric acid has led a number of producers to invest in additional capacity. Turkey's state-owned [Eti Mine Works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eti_Mine_Works "Eti Mine Works") opened a new boric acid plant with the production capacity of 100,000 tonnes per year at [Emet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emet "Emet") in 2003. [Rio Tinto Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_Tinto_Group "Rio Tinto Group") increased the capacity of its boron plant from 260,000 tonnes per year in 2003 to 310,000 tonnes per year by May 2005, with plans to grow this to 366,000 tonnes per year in 2006.

The rise in global demand has been driven by high growth rates in [glass fiber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass_fiber "Glass fiber"), [fiberglass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiberglass "Fiberglass"), and [borosilicate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borosilicate "Borosilicate") glassware production. A rapid increase in the manufacture of reinforcement-grade boron-containing fiberglass in Asia has offset the development of boron-free reinforcement-grade fiberglass in Europe and the US. The recent rises in energy prices may lead to greater use of insulation-grade fiberglass, with consequent growth in the boron consumption. Roskill Consulting Group forecasts that world demand for boron will grow by 3.4% per year to reach 21 million tonnes by 2010. The highest growth in demand is expected to be in Asia where demand could rise by an average 5.7% per year.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-roskill-91)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-92)

## Applications

Nearly all boron ore extracted from the Earth is refined as [boric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boric_acid "Boric acid") and [sodium tetraborate pentahydrate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_tetraborate "Sodium tetraborate"). In the United States, 70% of the boron is used for the production of glass and ceramics.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-93)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-CRC-94) The major global industrial-scale use of boron compounds (about 46% of end-use) is in production of [glass fiber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass_fiber "Glass fiber") for boron-containing insulating and structural [fiberglasses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiberglass "Fiberglass"), especially in Asia. Boron is added to the glass as borax pentahydrate or boron oxide to influence the strength or fluxing qualities of the glass fibers.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-95) Another 10% of global boron production is for [borosilicate glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borosilicate_glass "Borosilicate glass") as used in high strength glassware. About 15% of global boron is used in boron ceramics, including super-hard materials discussed below. Agriculture consumes 11% of global boron production. Bleaches and detergents consume about 6%.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-96)

### Boronated fiberglass

Main article: [Fiberglass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiberglass "Fiberglass")

Fiberglasses, a [fiber reinforced polymer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiber_reinforced_plastic "Fiber reinforced plastic"), sometimes contains borosilicate, borax, or boron oxide that is added to increase the strength of the glass. The highly boronated glasses, E-glass (named for "Electrical" use), are alumino-borosilicate glass. Another common high-boron glass, C-glass, also has a high boron oxide content and is used for glass staple fibers and insulation. D-glass is a [borosilicate glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borosilicate_glass "Borosilicate glass") named for its low dielectric constant.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-ullmann1-97)

Because of the ubiquitous use of fiberglass in construction and insulation, boron-containing fiberglasses consume over half the global production of boron and are the single largest commercial boron market.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-98)

### Borosilicate glass

Main article: [Borosilicate glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borosilicate_glass "Borosilicate glass")

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/Schott_Duran_glassware.jpg/250px-Schott_Duran_glassware.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Schott_Duran_glassware.jpg)

Borosilicate glassware. Displayed are two beakers and a test tube.

[Borosilicate glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borosilicate_glass "Borosilicate glass"), which is typically 12–15% B 2 O 3, 80% SiO 2, and 2% Al 2 O 3, has a low [coefficient of thermal expansion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coefficient_of_thermal_expansion "Coefficient of thermal expansion"), giving it a good resistance to [thermal shock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermal_shock "Thermal shock"). [Schott AG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schott_AG "Schott AG")'s "Duran" and [Owens-Corning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owens-Corning "Owens-Corning")'s trademarked [Pyrex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrex "Pyrex") are two major brand names for this glass, used both in [laboratory glassware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laboratory_glassware "Laboratory glassware") and in consumer [cookware and bakeware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cookware_and_bakeware "Cookware and bakeware"), chiefly for this reason.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-99)

### Elemental boron fiber

[Boron fibers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron_fiber "Boron fiber") (boron filaments) are high-strength, lightweight materials that are used chiefly for advanced [aerospace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerospace "Aerospace") structures as a component of [composite materials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composite_material "Composite material"), as well as limited production consumer and sporting goods such as [golf clubs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golf_club_(equipment) "Golf club (equipment)") and [fishing rods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fishing_rod "Fishing rod").[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-100)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-101) The fibers can be produced by [chemical vapor deposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_vapor_deposition "Chemical vapor deposition") of boron on a [tungsten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tungsten "Tungsten") filament.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-USGS-YB-B-2008-102)[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-103)

Boron fibers and sub-millimeter sized crystalline boron springs are produced by [laser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laser "Laser")-assisted [chemical vapor deposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laser_chemical_vapor_deposition "Laser chemical vapor deposition"). Translation of the focused laser beam allows production of complex helical structures. Such structures show good mechanical properties ([elastic modulus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elastic_modulus "Elastic modulus") 450 GPa, fracture strain 3.7%, fracture stress 17 GPa) and can be applied as reinforcement of ceramics or in [micromechanical systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microelectromechanical_systems "Microelectromechanical systems").[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-104)

### Boron carbide ceramic

Main article: [Boron carbide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron_carbide "Boron carbide")

Boron carbide's ability to absorb neutrons without forming long-lived [radionuclides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radionuclide "Radionuclide") (especially when doped with extra boron-10) makes the material attractive as an [absorbent for neutron radiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_poison "Neutron poison") arising in nuclear power plants.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-105) Nuclear applications of boron carbide include shielding, control rods, and shut-down pellets. Within control rods, boron carbide is often powdered to increase its surface area.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-106)

Boron carbide and cubic boron nitride powders are widely used as abrasives. [Boron nitride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron_nitride "Boron nitride") is a material isoelectronic to [carbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon "Carbon"). Similar to carbon, it has both hexagonal (soft graphite-like h-BN) and cubic (hard, diamond-like c-BN) forms. h-BN is used as a high temperature component and lubricant. c-BN, also known under commercial name [borazon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borazon "Borazon"), is a superior abrasive. Its hardness is only slightly less than that of diamond, while its chemical stability is greater.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-109)[Heterodiamond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heterodiamond "Heterodiamond") (also called BCN) is another diamond-like boron compound.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-110)

### Metallurgy

Main articles: [Boron steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron_steel "Boron steel") and [Boriding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boriding "Boriding")

Boron is added to [boron steels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron_steel "Boron steel") at the level of a few parts per million to increase [hardenability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardenability "Hardenability"). Higher percentages are added to steels used in the [nuclear industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_industry "Nuclear industry") due to boron's neutron absorption ability.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-111)

Boron can also increase the surface hardness of steels and alloys through [boriding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boriding "Boriding"). Additionally metal [borides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boride "Boride") are used for coating tools through [chemical vapor deposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_vapor_deposition "Chemical vapor deposition") or [physical vapor deposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_vapor_deposition "Physical vapor deposition"). Implantation of boron ions into metals and alloys, through [ion implantation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ion_implantation "Ion implantation") or [ion beam deposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ion_beam_deposition "Ion beam deposition"), results in a spectacular increase in surface resistance and microhardness. Laser alloying has also been used successfully for the same purpose. These borides are an alternative to diamond coated tools, and their surfaces have similar properties to those of the bulk boride.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-112)

For example, [rhenium diboride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhenium_diboride "Rhenium diboride") can be produced at ambient pressures but is rather expensive because of the cost of rhenium. The hardness of ReB 2 exhibits considerable [anisotropy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anisotropy "Anisotropy") because of its hexagonal layered structure. Its value is comparable to that of [tungsten carbide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tungsten_carbide "Tungsten carbide"), [silicon carbide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_carbide "Silicon carbide"), [titanium diboride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titanium_diboride "Titanium diboride"), or [zirconium diboride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zirconium_diboride "Zirconium diboride").[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-qin-108) Similarly, AlMgB 14 + TiB 2 composites possess high hardness and wear resistance and are used in either bulk form or as coatings for components exposed to high temperatures and wear loads.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-tib1-113)

### Detergent formulations and bleaching agents

[Borax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borax "Borax") is used in various household laundry and cleaning products.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-114) It is also present in some [tooth bleaching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tooth_bleaching "Tooth bleaching") formulas.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-CRC-94)

[Sodium perborate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_perborate "Sodium perborate") is a source of [active oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Active_oxygen "Active oxygen") in many [detergents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detergent "Detergent"), [laundry detergents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laundry_detergent "Laundry detergent"), [cleaning products](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleaning_product "Cleaning product"), and laundry [bleaches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bleach_(chemical) "Bleach (chemical)"). However, despite its name, "Borateem" laundry bleach no longer contains any boron compounds, using [sodium percarbonate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_percarbonate "Sodium percarbonate") instead as a bleaching agent.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-115)

### Insecticides and antifungals

Zinc borates and boric acid, popularized as [fire retardants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire_retardant "Fire retardant"), are widely used as wood preservatives and insecticides. Boric acid is also used as a domestic insecticide.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-116)[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-117)[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-118)

### Semiconductors

Boron is a useful [dopant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dopant "Dopant") for such semiconductors as [silicon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon "Silicon"), [germanium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germanium "Germanium"), and [silicon carbide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_carbide "Silicon carbide"). Having one fewer valence electron than the host atom, it donates a [hole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron_hole "Electron hole"), resulting in [p-type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-type_semiconductor "P-type semiconductor") conductivity. The traditional method of doping semiconductors with boron is via [atomic diffusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_diffusion "Atomic diffusion") at high temperatures. This process uses either solid (B 2 O 3), liquid (BBr 3), or gaseous boron sources (B 2 H 6 or BF 3). However, after the 1970s, it was mostly replaced by [ion implantation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ion_implantation "Ion implantation"), which relies mostly on BF 3 as a boron source.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-119) Boron trichloride gas is also an important chemical in the semiconductor industry for the [plasma etching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plasma_etching "Plasma etching") of metals and their oxides.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-120)[Triethylborane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triethylborane "Triethylborane") is also injected into [vapor deposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_vapor_deposition "Chemical vapor deposition") reactors as a boron source.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-121) Examples are the plasma deposition of boron-containing hard carbon films, silicon nitride–boron nitride films, and the [doping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doping_(semiconductor) "Doping (semiconductor)") of [diamond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diamond "Diamond") film with boron.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-122)

### Magnets

Boron is a component of [neodymium magnets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neodymium_magnet "Neodymium magnet") (Nd 2 Fe 14 B), which are among the strongest type of permanent magnet. These magnets are found in a variety of electromechanical and electronic devices such as in [magnetic resonance imaging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_resonance_imaging "Magnetic resonance imaging") (MRI) medical imaging systems and in compact and relatively small motors and [actuators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Actuator "Actuator"). As examples, computer [hard disk drive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_disk_drive "Hard disk drive"), [CD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_disc "Compact disc"), and [DVD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DVD "DVD") players rely on neodymium magnet motors to deliver intense rotary power in a compact package. In mobile phones, "Neo" magnets provide the magnetic field which allows tiny speakers to deliver appreciable audio power.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-123)

### Shielding and neutron absorber in nuclear reactors

Boron shielding is used as a control for [nuclear reactors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_reactor "Nuclear reactor"), taking advantage of its high [cross-section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_cross_section "Neutron cross section") for neutron capture.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-124)

In [pressurized water reactors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pressurized_water_reactor "Pressurized water reactor"), a variable concentration of boronic acid in the cooling water is used as a [neutron poison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_poison#Soluble_poison "Neutron poison") to compensate the variable reactivity of the fuel. When new rods are inserted, the concentration of boronic acid is maximal. It then is reduced during its lifetime.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-PastinaIsabey1999-125)

### Pharmaceutical and biological applications

See also: [Boron deficiency (plant disorder)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron_deficiency_(plant_disorder) "Boron deficiency (plant disorder)") and [Boron deficiency (medicine)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron_deficiency_(medicine) "Boron deficiency (medicine)")

Boron plays a role in pharmaceutical and biological applications as it is found in various antibiotics produced by bacteria, such as [boromycins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boromycin "Boromycin"), [aplasmomycins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aplasmomycin "Aplasmomycin"), [borophycins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borophycin?action=edit&redlink=1 "Borophycin (page does not exist)"), and [tartrolons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tartrolon "Tartrolon"). These antibiotics have shown inhibitory effects on the growth of certain bacteria, fungi, and protozoa. Boron is also being studied for its potential medicinal applications, including its incorporation into biologically active molecules for therapies like boron neutron capture therapy for brain tumors. Some boron-containing biomolecules may act as signaling molecules interacting with cell surfaces, suggesting a role in cellular communication.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-pmid17991498-137)

[Boric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boric_acid "Boric acid") and its salts, known as [borates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borate "Borate"), are widely used in cleaners and fertilizers. Boric acid is a major component of some skin treatments; however, dermal exposure to high concentrations of boron can lead to severe adverse health effects including death, particularly when the skin is damaged. Consumption of boric acid can also lead to abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea. The chemical is absorbed by the gastrointestinal system.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-138) Mild solutions of boric acid have been used as eye antiseptics.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-139)

Boron appears as an active element in the organic pharmaceutical [bortezomib](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bortezomib "Bortezomib"), a class of drug called the proteasome inhibitor, for treating myeloma and one form of lymphoma. The boron atom in bortezomib binds the catalytic site of the [26S proteasome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proteasome "Proteasome").[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-pmid17268529-140)

*   A number of potential boronated pharmaceuticals using [boron-10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron-10 "Boron-10") have been prepared for use in [boron neutron capture therapy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron_neutron_capture_therapy "Boron neutron capture therapy") (BNCT).[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-PharmInfo_BNCT-141)
*   Some boron compounds show promise in treating [arthritis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthritis "Arthritis"), though none have as yet been generally approved for the purpose.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-142)

[Tavaborole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tavaborole "Tavaborole") is an [aminoacyl tRNA synthetase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aminoacyl_tRNA_synthetase "Aminoacyl tRNA synthetase") inhibitor which is used to treat toenail fungus. It gained FDA approval in July 2014.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-Thompson-143)

Dioxaborolane chemistry enables radioactive [fluoride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluoride "Fluoride") ([18 F](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluorine-18 "Fluorine-18")) labeling of [antibodies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antibody "Antibody") or [red blood cells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_blood_cell "Red blood cell"), which allows for [positron emission tomography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Positron_emission_tomography "Positron emission tomography") (PET) imaging of [cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cancer "Cancer")[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-144) and [hemorrhages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hemorrhages "Hemorrhages"),[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-145) respectively. A Human-Derived, Genetic, Positron-emitting and Fluorescent (HD-GPF) reporter system uses a human protein, [PSMA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glutamate_carboxypeptidase_II "Glutamate carboxypeptidase II") and non-immunogenic, and a small molecule that is positron-emitting (boron bound [18](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluorine-18 "Fluorine-18")[F](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluorine-18 "Fluorine-18")) and fluorescence for dual modality PET and fluorescent imaging of genome modified cells, e.g. [cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cancer "Cancer"), [CRISPR/Cas9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CRISPR/Cas9-mediated_genome_editing "CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing"), or [CAR T](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CAR-T_cell "CAR-T cell")-cells, in an entire mouse.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-146) The dual-modality small molecule targeting [PSMA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glutamate_carboxypeptidase_II "Glutamate carboxypeptidase II") was tested in humans and found the location of primary and [metastatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metastasis "Metastasis")[prostate cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prostate_cancer "Prostate cancer"), aided the fluorescence-guided removal of cancer, and detected single cancer cells in tissue margins.[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-147)

## Research

### MgB 2

[Magnesium diboride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnesium_diboride "Magnesium diboride") (MgB 2) is a [superconductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superconductor "Superconductor") with a transition temperature of 39 K.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-148)[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-Canfield2003-149) MgB 2 wires are produced with the [powder-in-tube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Powder-in-tube "Powder-in-tube") process and applied in superconducting magnets.[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-Canfield2003-149)[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-150) A project at [CERN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CERN "CERN") to make MgB 2 cables has resulted in superconducting test cables able to carry 20,000 amperes for extremely high current distribution applications, such as the contemplated high luminosity version of the [Large Hadron Collider](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_Hadron_Collider "Large Hadron Collider").[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-151)

### Commercial isotope enrichment

Because of its high neutron cross-section, boron-10 is often used to control fission in nuclear reactors as a neutron-capturing substance.[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-152) Several industrial-scale enrichment processes have been developed; however, only the fractionated vacuum distillation of the [dimethyl ether](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimethyl_ether "Dimethyl ether") adduct of [boron trifluoride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron_trifluoride "Boron trifluoride") (DME-BF 3) and column chromatography of borates are being used.[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-153)[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-154)

### Radiation-hardened semiconductors

[Cosmic radiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_radiation "Cosmic radiation") produces secondary neutrons when it hits spacecraft structures. Those neutrons are captured in 10 B if it is present in the spacecraft's [semiconductors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor "Semiconductor"), producing a [gamma ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_ray "Gamma ray"), an [alpha particle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_particle "Alpha particle"), and a [lithium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithium "Lithium") ion. Those resultant decay products may then irradiate nearby semiconductor "chip" structures, causing data loss (bit flipping, or [single event upset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_event_upset "Single event upset")). In [radiation-hardened](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiation-hardened "Radiation-hardened") semiconductor designs, one countermeasure is to use _depleted boron_, which is greatly enriched in 11 B and contains almost no 10 B. This is useful because 11 B is largely immune to radiation damage. Depleted boron is a byproduct of the [nuclear industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_power "Nuclear power") (see above).[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-reactor-155)

### Proton–boron fusion

Main article: [Proton–boron fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proton%E2%80%93boron_fusion "Proton–boron fusion")

11 B is also a candidate as a fuel for [aneutronic fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aneutronic_fusion "Aneutronic fusion"). When struck by a proton with energy of about 500 k[eV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronvolt "Electronvolt"), it produces three alpha particles and 8.7 MeV of energy. Most other fusion reactions involving hydrogen and helium produce penetrating neutron radiation, which weakens reactor structures and induces long-term radioactivity, thereby endangering operating personnel. The [alpha particles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_particles "Alpha particles") from 11 B fusion can be turned directly into electric power, and all radiation stops as soon as the reactor is turned off.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-156)

### Enriched boron (boron-10)

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5c/Neutroncrosssectionboron.png/500px-Neutroncrosssectionboron.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Neutroncrosssectionboron.png)

Neutron cross section of boron (top curve is for 10 B and bottom curve for 11 B)

The 10 B isotope is useful for capturing [thermal neutrons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermal_neutron "Thermal neutron") (see [neutron cross section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_cross_section#Typical_cross_sections "Neutron cross section")). The [nuclear industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_power "Nuclear power") enriches natural boron to nearly pure 10 B. The less valuable by-product, depleted boron, is nearly pure 11 B.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-Hawthorne-1993-157)

Enriched boron or 10 B is both used in radiation shielding and is the primary nuclide used in [neutron capture therapy of cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_capture_therapy_of_cancer "Neutron capture therapy of cancer"). In the latter ("boron neutron capture therapy" or BNCT), a compound containing 10 B is incorporated into a pharmaceutical which is selectively taken up by a malignant tumor and tissues near it. The patient is then treated with a beam of low energy neutrons at a relatively low neutron radiation dose. The neutrons trigger energetic and short-range secondary [alpha particle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_particle "Alpha particle") and lithium-7 heavy ion radiation that are products of the boron-neutron [nuclear reaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_reaction "Nuclear reaction"), and this ion radiation additionally bombards the tumor, especially from inside the tumor cells.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-158)[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-159)[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-160)[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-PharmInfo_BNCT-141)

In nuclear reactors, 10 B is used for reactivity control and in [emergency shutdown systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scram "Scram"). It can serve either function in the form of [borosilicate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borosilicate "Borosilicate")[control rods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Control_rods "Control rods") or as [boric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boric_acid "Boric acid"). In [pressurized water reactors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pressurized_water_reactor "Pressurized water reactor"), 10 B [boric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boric_acid "Boric acid") is added to the reactor coolant after the plant is shut down for refueling. When the plant is started up again, the boric acid is slowly filtered out over many months as [fissile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fissile "Fissile") material is used up and the fuel becomes less reactive.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-reactor-155)

### Nuclear fusion

Boron has been investigated for possible applications in [nuclear fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fusion "Nuclear fusion") research. It is commonly used for conditioning the walls in [fusion reactors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fusion_reactors "Fusion reactors") by depositing boron coatings on plasma-facing components and walls to reduce the release of hydrogen and impurities from the surfaces.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-161) It is also being used for the dissipation of energy in the fusion plasma boundary to suppress excessive energy bursts and heat fluxes to the walls.[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-162)[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-163)

### Neutron capture therapy

In [neutron capture therapy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_capture_therapy_of_cancer "Neutron capture therapy of cancer") (NCT) for malignant brain tumors, boron is researched to be used for selectively targeting and destroying tumor cells. The goal is to deliver higher concentrations of the non-radioactive boron isotope (10 B) to the tumor cells than to the surrounding normal tissues. When these 10 B-containing cells are irradiated with low-energy thermal neutrons, they undergo nuclear capture reactions, releasing high linear energy transfer (LET) particles such as alpha particles and lithium-7 nuclei within a limited path length. These high-LET particles can destroy the adjacent tumor cells without causing significant harm to nearby normal cells. Boron acts as a selective agent due to its ability to absorb thermal neutrons and produce short-range physical effects primarily affecting the targeted tissue region. This binary approach allows for precise tumor cell killing while sparing healthy tissues. The effective delivery of boron involves administering boron compounds or carriers capable of accumulating selectively in tumor cells compared to surrounding tissue. BSH and BPA have been used clinically, but research continues to identify more optimal carriers. Accelerator-based neutron sources have also been developed recently as an alternative to reactor-based sources, leading to improved efficiency and enhanced clinical outcomes in NCT. By employing the properties of boron isotopes and targeted irradiation techniques, NCT offers a potential approach to treating malignant brain tumors by selectively killing cancer cells while minimizing the damage caused by traditional radiation therapies.[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-pmid32676954-164)

BNCT has shown promising results in clinical trials for various other malignancies, including [glioblastoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glioblastoma "Glioblastoma"), [head and neck cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_and_neck_cancer "Head and neck cancer"), [cutaneous melanoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melanoma "Melanoma"), [hepatocellular carcinoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hepatocellular_carcinoma "Hepatocellular carcinoma"), [lung cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lung_cancer "Lung cancer"), and [extramammary Paget's disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extramammary_Paget's_disease "Extramammary Paget's disease"). The treatment involves a nuclear reaction between nonradioactive boron-10 isotope and low-energy thermal or high-energy epithermal neutrons to generate α particles and lithium nuclei that selectively destroy DNA in tumor cells. The primary challenge lies in developing efficient boron agents with higher content and specific targeting properties tailored for NCT. Integration of tumor-targeting strategies with NCT could potentially establish it as a practical personalized treatment option for different types of cancers. Ongoing research explores new boron compounds, optimization strategies, [theranostic agents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theranostic "Theranostic"), and radiobiological advances to overcome limitations and cost-effectively improve patient outcomes.[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-pmid37728998-165)[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-pmid37102375-166)[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-pmid35240726-167)

## Biological role

See also: [Boron deficiency (plant disorder)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron_deficiency_(plant_disorder) "Boron deficiency (plant disorder)")

Boron is an essential plant [nutrient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nutrient "Nutrient"), required primarily for maintaining the integrity of cell walls. However, high soil concentrations of greater than 1.0[ppm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parts_per_million "Parts per million") lead to marginal and tip necrosis in leaves as well as poor overall growth performance. Levels as low as 0.8 ppm produce these same symptoms in plants that are particularly sensitive to boron in the soil. Nearly all plants, even those somewhat tolerant of soil boron, will show at least some symptoms of boron toxicity when soil boron content is greater than 1.8 ppm. When this content exceeds 2.0 ppm, few plants will perform well and some may not survive.[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-168)[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-169)[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-170)

Some boron-containing [antibiotics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antibiotic "Antibiotic") exist in nature.[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-171) The first one found was [boromycin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boromycin "Boromycin"), isolated from [streptomyces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streptomyces "Streptomyces") in the 1960s.[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-172)[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-173) Others are [tartrolons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tartrolon "Tartrolon"), a group of antibiotics discovered in the 1990s from culture broth of the [myxobacterium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myxobacteria "Myxobacteria")-group _[Sorangium cellulosum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sorangium\_cellulosum "Sorangium cellulosum")_.[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-wiley199419940310-174)

In 2013, chemist and synthetic biologist [Steve Benner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_A._Benner "Steven A. Benner") suggested that the conditions on [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars") three billion years ago were much more favorable to the stability of [RNA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RNA "RNA") and formation of oxygen-containing[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-177) boron and [molybdenum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molybdenum#Biological_role "Molybdenum") catalysts found in life. According to Benner's theory, primitive life, which is widely believed to have [originated from RNA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RNA_world "RNA world"),[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-Neveu_et_al-178)[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-179) first formed on Mars before [migrating to Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panspermia "Panspermia").[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-mars-180)

### In human health

Boron may have several essential roles in animals, including humans, but its exact physiological role is poorly understood.[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-181)[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-utrace-182)[Boron deficiency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron_deficiency_(medicine) "Boron deficiency (medicine)") has only been clearly established in [livestock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Livestock "Livestock").[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-183)[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-184) In humans, boron deficiency may affect [bone mineral density](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bone_mineral_density "Bone mineral density"), though it has been noted that additional research on the effects of bone health is necessary.[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-bhp-185)

Boron is not classified as an essential human nutrient because research has not established a clear biological function for it.[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-pmid31639188-186)[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-bhp-185) The U.S. [Food and Nutrition Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_and_Nutrition_Board "Food and Nutrition Board") (FNB) found the existing data insufficient to derive a [Recommended Dietary Allowance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recommended_Dietary_Allowance "Recommended Dietary Allowance") (RDA), [Adequate Intake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adequate_Intake "Adequate Intake") (AI), or [Estimated Average Requirement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estimated_Average_Requirement "Estimated Average Requirement") (EAR) for boron and the U.S. [Food and Drug Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_and_Drug_Administration "Food and Drug Administration") (FDA) has not established a daily value for boron for food and dietary supplement labeling purposes.[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-pmid31639188-186)[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-bhp-185) While low boron levels can be detrimental to health, with studies suggesting that they increase the risks of [osteoporosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osteoporosis "Osteoporosis"), poor immune function, and cognitive decline, high boron levels are associated with cell damage and toxicity.[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-pmid29546541-187)

Still, studies suggest that boron may exert beneficial effects on reproduction and development, [calcium metabolism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calcium_metabolism "Calcium metabolism"), [bone formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ossification "Ossification"), brain function, [insulin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insulin "Insulin") and energy substrate metabolism, immunity, and [steroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steroid "Steroid")[hormone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hormone "Hormone") (including [estrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estrogen "Estrogen")), and [vitamin D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitamin_D "Vitamin D") function, among other functions.[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-pmid26770156-188)[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-bhp-185) In a small human trial published in 1987 reported on postmenopausal women first made boron deficient and then repleted with 3 mg/day, boron supplementation markedly reduced urinary calcium excretion and elevated the serum concentrations of [17 β-estradiol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estradiol "Estradiol") and [testosterone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Testosterone "Testosterone").[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-189) Environmental boron appears to be [inversely correlated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inversely_correlated "Inversely correlated") with [arthritis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthritis "Arthritis").[[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-190)

The exact mechanism by which boron exerts its physiological effects is not fully understood but may involve interactions with [adenosine monophosphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adenosine_monophosphate "Adenosine monophosphate") (ADP) and [_S_-adenosyl methionine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S-Adenosyl_methionine "S-Adenosyl methionine") (SAM-e), two compounds involved in important cellular functions. Furthermore, boron appears to inhibit cyclic [ADP-ribose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adenosine_diphosphate_ribose "Adenosine diphosphate ribose"), thereby affecting the release of calcium ions from the [endoplasmic reticulum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endoplasmic_reticulum "Endoplasmic reticulum") and affecting various biological processes.[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-pmid29546541-187) Some studies suggest that boron may reduce levels of [inflammatory biomarkers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inflammatory_biomarker "Inflammatory biomarker").[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-pmid26770156-188)[Congenital endothelial dystrophy type 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congenital_endothelial_dystrophy_type_2 "Congenital endothelial dystrophy type 2"), a rare form of [corneal dystrophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corneal_dystrophy_(human) "Corneal dystrophy (human)"), is linked to mutations in [SLC4A11](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SLC4A11 "SLC4A11") gene that encodes a transporter reportedly regulating the intracellular concentration of boron.[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-191)

In humans, boron is usually consumed with food that contains boron, such as [fruits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fruit "Fruit"), [leafy vegetables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leaf_vegetable "Leaf vegetable"), and [nuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nut_(fruit) "Nut (fruit)").[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-pmid31639188-186) Foods that are particularly rich in boron include [avocados](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avocado "Avocado"), dried fruits such as [raisins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raisin "Raisin"), [peanuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peanut "Peanut"), [pecans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pecan "Pecan"), [prune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prune "Prune") juice, [grape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grape "Grape") juice, [wine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wine "Wine") and [chocolate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chocolate "Chocolate") powder.[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-pmid26770156-188)[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-pmid31639188-186) According to 2-day food records from the respondents to the [Third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Health_and_Nutrition_Examination_Survey "National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey") (NHANES III), adult dietary intake was recorded at 0.9 to 1.4 mg/day.[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-nationalacademies-192)

Chemical compound

Elemental boron, [boron oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron_trioxide "Boron trioxide"), [boric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boric_acid "Boric acid"), [borate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borate "Borate"), and many [organoboron compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organoboron_chemistry "Organoboron chemistry") are relatively nontoxic to humans and animals (with toxicity similar to that of table salt). The [LD 50](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Median_lethal_dose "Median lethal dose") (dose at which there is 50% mortality) for animals is about 6 g per kg of body weight. Substances with an LD 50 above 2 g/kg are considered nontoxic. An intake of 4 g/day of boric acid was reported without incident, but more than this is considered toxic in more than a few doses. Intakes of more than 0.5 grams per day for 50 days cause minor digestive and other problems suggestive of toxicity.[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-195)

[Boric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boric_acid "Boric acid") is more toxic to insects than to mammals, and is routinely used as an insecticide.[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-Klotz_1994_1534%E2%80%931536-196) However, it has been used in [neutron capture therapy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_capture_therapy_of_cancer "Neutron capture therapy of cancer") alongside other boron compounds such as [sodium borocaptate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_borocaptate?action=edit&redlink=1 "Sodium borocaptate (page does not exist)") and [boronophenylalanine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boronophenylalanine "Boronophenylalanine") with reported low toxicity levels.[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-197)

The [boranes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boranes "Boranes") (boron hydrogen compounds) and similar gaseous compounds are quite poisonous. As usual, boron is not an element that is intrinsically poisonous, but the toxicity of these compounds depends on structure (for another example of this phenomenon, see [phosphine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphine "Phosphine")).[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-borates-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-boron-19) The boranes are also highly flammable and require special care when handling. Some combinations of boranes and other compounds are highly explosive. Sodium borohydride presents a fire hazard owing to its reducing nature and the liberation of hydrogen on contact with acid. Boron halides are corrosive.[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-198)

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b7/Boron_toxicity_%282313046082%29.jpg/250px-Boron_toxicity_%282313046082%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Boron_toxicity_(2313046082).jpg)

Boron toxicity in rose leaves

Boron is necessary for plant growth, but an excess of boron is toxic to plants, and occurs particularly in acidic soil.[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-Boron_(B)_and_Chlorine_(Cl)_for_Citrus_Trees-199)[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-PeverillSparrow1999-200) It presents as a yellowing from the tip inwards of the oldest leaves and black spots in barley leaves, but it can be confused with other stresses such as magnesium deficiency in other plants.[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron#cite_note-Reynolds2001-201)
