### Organic nitrogen compounds

Nitrogen is one of the most important elements in [organic chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organic_chemistry "Organic chemistry"). Many organic [functional groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_group "Functional group") involve a [carbon–nitrogen bond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon%E2%80%93nitrogen_bond "Carbon–nitrogen bond"), such as [amides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amide "Amide") (RCONR 2), [amines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amine "Amine") (R 3 N), [imines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imine "Imine") (RC(=NR)R), [imides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imide "Imide") (RCO)2 NR, [azides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azide "Azide") (RN 3), [azo compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azo_compound "Azo compound") (RN 2 R), [cyanates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyanate_ester "Cyanate ester") (ROCN), [isocyanates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isocyanate "Isocyanate") (RNCO), [nitrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrate "Nitrate") (RONO 2), [nitriles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrile "Nitrile") (RCN), [isonitriles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isonitrile "Isonitrile") (RNC), [nitrites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrite#Organic_nitrites "Nitrite") (RONO), [nitro compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitro_compound "Nitro compound") (RNO 2), [nitroso compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitroso_compound "Nitroso compound") (RNO), [oximes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxime "Oxime") (RC(=NOH)R), and [pyridine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyridine "Pyridine") derivatives. C–N bonds are strongly polarised towards nitrogen. In these compounds, nitrogen is usually trivalent (though it can be tetravalent in [quaternary ammonium salts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaternary_ammonium_salt "Quaternary ammonium salt"), R 4 N+), with a lone pair that can confer basicity on the compound by being coordinated to a proton. This may be offset by other factors: for example, amides are not basic because the lone pair is delocalised into a double bond (though they may act as bases at very low pH, being protonated at the oxygen), and [pyrrole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrrole "Pyrrole") is not basic because the lone pair is delocalised as part of an [aromatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aromaticity "Aromaticity") ring.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-Jerry-71) The amount of nitrogen in a [chemical substance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_substance "Chemical substance") can be determined by the [Kjeldahl method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kjeldahl_method "Kjeldahl method").[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-72) In particular, nitrogen is an essential component of [nucleic acids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nucleic_acids "Nucleic acids"), [amino acids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amino_acid "Amino acid") and thus [proteins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protein "Protein"), and the energy-carrying molecule [adenosine triphosphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adenosine_triphosphate "Adenosine triphosphate") and is thus vital to all life on Earth.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-Jerry-71)

## Occurrence

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Nitrogen_Cycle.svg/500px-Nitrogen_Cycle.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nitrogen_Cycle.svg)

Schematic representation of the [flow of nitrogen compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen_cycle "Nitrogen cycle") through a land environment

See also: [Nitrogen cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen_cycle "Nitrogen cycle")

Nitrogen is the most common pure element in the earth, making up 78.1% of the volume of the [atmosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmosphere_of_Earth "Atmosphere of Earth")[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-Greenwood406-10) (75.5% by mass), around 3.89 million [gigatonnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gigatonnes "Gigatonnes") (3.89×10 18 kg). Despite this, it is [not very abundant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abundance_of_elements_in_Earth's_crust "Abundance of elements in Earth's crust") in Earth's crust, making up somewhere around 19[parts per million](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parts_per_million "Parts per million") of this, on par with [niobium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niobium "Niobium"), [gallium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium "Gallium"), and [lithium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithium "Lithium"). (This represents 300,000 to a million gigatonnes of nitrogen, depending on the mass of the crust.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-73)) The only important nitrogen minerals are [nitre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitre "Nitre") ([potassium nitrate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potassium_nitrate "Potassium nitrate"), saltpetre) and [soda nitre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodanitre "Sodanitre") ([sodium nitrate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_nitrate "Sodium nitrate"), Chilean saltpetre). However, these have not been an important source of nitrates since the 1920s, when the industrial synthesis of ammonia and nitric acid became common.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-Greenwood407-74)

Nitrogen compounds constantly interchange between the atmosphere and living organisms. Nitrogen must first be processed, or "[fixed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen_fixation "Nitrogen fixation")", into a plant-usable form, usually ammonia. Some nitrogen fixation is done by lightning strikes producing the nitrogen oxides, but most is done by [diazotrophic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diazotroph "Diazotroph") bacteria through enzymes known as [nitrogenases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogenase "Nitrogenase") (although today industrial nitrogen fixation to ammonia is also significant). When the ammonia is taken up by plants, it is used to synthesise proteins. These plants are then digested by animals who use the nitrogen compounds to synthesise their proteins and excrete nitrogen-bearing waste. Finally, these organisms die and decompose, undergoing bacterial and environmental oxidation and [denitrification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denitrification "Denitrification"), returning free dinitrogen to the atmosphere. Industrial nitrogen fixation by the [Haber process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haber_process "Haber process") is mostly used as fertiliser, although excess nitrogen–bearing waste, when leached, leads to [eutrophication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eutrophication "Eutrophication") of freshwater and the creation of marine [dead zones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_zone_(ecology) "Dead zone (ecology)"), as nitrogen-driven bacterial growth depletes water oxygen to the point that all higher organisms die. Furthermore, nitrous oxide, which is produced during denitrification, attacks the atmospheric [ozone layer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozone_layer "Ozone layer").[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-Greenwood407-74)

Many saltwater fish manufacture large amounts of [trimethylamine oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trimethylamine_oxide "Trimethylamine oxide") to protect them from the high [osmotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osmosis "Osmosis") effects of their environment; conversion of this compound to [dimethylamine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimethylamine "Dimethylamine") is responsible for the early odour in unfresh saltwater fish.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-75) In animals, [free radical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_radical "Free radical")[nitric oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitric_oxide "Nitric oxide") (derived from an [amino acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amino_acid "Amino acid")), serves as an important regulatory molecule for circulation.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-ocean-76)

Nitric oxide's rapid reaction with water in animals results in the production of its metabolite [nitrite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrite "Nitrite"). Animal [metabolism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metabolism "Metabolism") of nitrogen in proteins, in general, results in the [excretion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excretion "Excretion") of [urea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urea "Urea"), while animal metabolism of [nucleic acids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nucleic_acids "Nucleic acids") results in the excretion of [urea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urea "Urea") and [uric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uric_acid "Uric acid"). The characteristic odour of animal flesh decay is caused by the creation of long-chain, nitrogen-containing [amines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amine "Amine"), such as [putrescine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Putrescine "Putrescine") and [cadaverine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadaverine "Cadaverine"), which are breakdown products of the amino acids [ornithine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornithine "Ornithine") and [lysine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lysine "Lysine"), respectively, in decaying proteins.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-77)

## Production

Nitrogen gas is an [industrial gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_gas "Industrial gas") produced by the [fractional distillation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractional_distillation "Fractional distillation") of [liquid air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_air "Liquid air"), or by mechanical means using gaseous air (pressurised reverse [osmosis membrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osmotic_pressure "Osmotic pressure") or [pressure swing adsorption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pressure_swing_adsorption "Pressure swing adsorption")). Nitrogen gas generators using membranes or pressure swing adsorption (PSA) are typically more cost and energy efficient than bulk-delivered nitrogen.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-78) Commercial nitrogen is often a byproduct of air-processing for industrial concentration of [oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen "Oxygen") for steelmaking and other purposes. When supplied compressed in cylinders it is often called OFN (oxygen-free nitrogen).[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-79) Commercial-grade nitrogen already contains at most 20 ppm oxygen, and specially purified grades containing at most 2 ppm oxygen and 10 ppm [argon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argon "Argon") are also available.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-Greenwood409-80)

In a chemical laboratory, it is prepared by treating an aqueous solution of [ammonium chloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammonium_chloride "Ammonium chloride") with [sodium nitrite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_nitrite "Sodium nitrite").[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-labProduction-81)

NH 4 Cl + NaNO 2 → N 2 + NaCl + 2 H 2 O
Small amounts of the impurities NO and HNO 3 are also formed in this reaction. The impurities can be removed by passing the gas through aqueous sulfuric acid containing [potassium dichromate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potassium_dichromate "Potassium dichromate").[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-labProduction-81)

It can also be obtained by the thermal decomposition of [ammonium dichromate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammonium_dichromate "Ammonium dichromate").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-82)

3(NH 4)2 Cr 2 O 7 → 2N 2 + 9H 2 O + 3Cr 2 O 3 + 2NH 3 + 3⁄2 O 2
Very pure nitrogen can be prepared by the thermal decomposition of [barium azide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barium_azide "Barium azide") or [sodium azide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_azide "Sodium azide").[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-83)

2 NaN 3 → 2 Na + 3 N 2

## Applications

The applications of nitrogen compounds are naturally extremely widely varied due to the huge size of this class: hence, only applications of pure nitrogen itself will be considered here. Two-thirds (2/3) of nitrogen produced by industry is sold as gas and the remaining one-third (1/3) as a liquid.

### Gas

The gas is mostly used as a low reactivity safe atmosphere wherever the oxygen in the air would pose a fire, explosion, or oxidising hazard. Some examples include:[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-Greenwood409-80)

*   As a [modified atmosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modified_atmosphere "Modified atmosphere"), pure or mixed with [carbon dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_dioxide "Carbon dioxide"), to nitrogenate and preserve the freshness of packaged or bulk foods (by delaying [rancidity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rancidification "Rancidification") and other forms of [oxidative damage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redox "Redox")). Pure nitrogen as food additive is labelled in the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") with the [E number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E_number "E number") E941.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-84)
*   In [incandescent light bulbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incandescent_light_bulb "Incandescent light bulb") as an inexpensive alternative to [argon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argon "Argon").[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-85)
*   In [fire suppression systems for Information technology (IT) equipment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaseous_fire_suppression "Gaseous fire suppression").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-Greenwood409-80)
*   In the manufacture of [stainless steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stainless_steel "Stainless steel").[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-86)
*   In the [case-hardening](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Case-hardening "Case-hardening") of steel by [nitriding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitriding "Nitriding").[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-Duplex-87)
*   In some aircraft fuel systems to reduce fire hazard (see [inerting system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inerting_system "Inerting system")).
*   To inflate race car and aircraft [tires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tire "Tire"),[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-88) reducing the problems of inconsistent expansion and contraction caused by moisture and [oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redox "Redox") in natural air.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-Greenwood409-80)

Nitrogen is commonly used during sample preparation in [chemical analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_analysis "Chemical analysis"). It is used to concentrate and reduce the volume of liquid samples. Directing a pressurised stream of nitrogen gas perpendicular to the surface of the liquid causes the solvent to evaporate while leaving the solute(s) and un-evaporated solvent behind.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-89)

Nitrogen can be used as a replacement, or in combination with, [carbon dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_dioxide "Carbon dioxide") to pressurise kegs of some [beers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beer "Beer"), particularly [stouts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stout "Stout") and British [ales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ale "Ale"), due to the smaller [bubbles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_bubble "Liquid bubble") it produces, which makes the dispensed beer smoother and [headier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beer_head "Beer head").[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-90) A pressure-sensitive nitrogen capsule known commonly as a "[widget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Widget_(beer) "Widget (beer)")" allows nitrogen-charged beers to be packaged in [cans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverage_can "Beverage can") and [bottles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bottle "Bottle").[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-91)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-92) Nitrogen tanks are also replacing carbon dioxide as the main power source for [paintball guns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paintball_gun "Paintball gun"). Nitrogen must be kept at a higher pressure than CO 2, making N 2 tanks heavier and more expensive.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-93)

#### Equipment

Some construction equipment uses pressurised nitrogen gas to help [hydraulic system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydraulics "Hydraulics") to provide extra power to devices such as [hydraulic hammer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breaker_(hydraulic) "Breaker (hydraulic)"). Nitrogen gas, formed from the decomposition of [sodium azide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_azide "Sodium azide"), is used for the inflation of [airbags](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airbag "Airbag").[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-94)

#### Execution

Further information: [Inert gas asphyxiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inert_gas_asphyxiation "Inert gas asphyxiation")

As nitrogen is an asphyxiant gas in itself, some jurisdictions have considered asphyxiation by inhalation of pure nitrogen as a means of [capital punishment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_punishment "Capital punishment") (as a substitute for [lethal injection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lethal_injection "Lethal injection")).[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-Time-apr2015-95)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-96)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-97) In January 2024, [Kenneth Eugene Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Execution_of_Kenneth_Eugene_Smith "Execution of Kenneth Eugene Smith") became the first person executed by nitrogen asphyxiation.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-98)

### Liquid

Main article: [Liquid nitrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_nitrogen "Liquid nitrogen")

[Video 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f4/Nitrogen.ogv?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original)

Air balloon submerged in liquid nitrogen

Liquid nitrogen is a [cryogenic liquid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryogen "Cryogen") which looks like [water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water "Water"). When insulated in proper containers such as [dewar flasks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewar_flask "Dewar flask"), it can be transported and stored with a low rate of [evaporative loss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evaporation "Evaporation").[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-99)

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/48/A_cylinder_container%2C_containing_liquid_nitrogen.jpg/250px-A_cylinder_container%2C_containing_liquid_nitrogen.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:A_cylinder_container,_containing_liquid_nitrogen.jpg)

A container vehicle carrying liquid nitrogen

Like [dry ice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dry_ice "Dry ice"), the main use of liquid nitrogen is for cooling to low temperatures. It is used in the [cryopreservation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryopreservation "Cryopreservation") of biological materials such as blood and reproductive cells ([sperm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sperm "Sperm") and [eggs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ovum "Ovum")). It is used in [cryotherapy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryotherapy "Cryotherapy") to remove cysts and warts on the skin by freezing them.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-100) It is used in laboratory [cold traps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_trap "Cold trap"), and in [cryopumps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryopump "Cryopump") to obtain lower pressures in [vacuum pumped](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vacuum_pump "Vacuum pump") systems. It is used to cool heat-sensitive electronics such as [infrared detectors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrared_detector "Infrared detector") and [X-ray detectors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-ray_detector "X-ray detector"). Other uses include freeze-grinding and machining materials that are soft or rubbery at room temperature, shrink-fitting and assembling engineering components, and more generally to attain very low temperatures where necessary. Because of its low cost, liquid nitrogen is often used for cooling even when such low temperatures are not strictly necessary, such as refrigeration of food, [freeze-branding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freeze-branding "Freeze-branding") livestock, freezing pipes to halt flow when valves are not present, and consolidating unstable soil by freezing whenever excavation is going on underneath.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-Greenwood409-80)

## Safety

### Gas

Although nitrogen is non-toxic, when released into an enclosed space it can displace oxygen, and therefore presents an [asphyxiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen_asphyxiation "Nitrogen asphyxiation") hazard. This may happen with few warning symptoms, since the human [carotid body](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carotid_body "Carotid body") is a relatively poor and slow low-oxygen (hypoxia) sensing system.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-101) An example occurred shortly before the launch of the [first Space Shuttle mission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-1 "STS-1") on March 19, 1981, when two technicians died from asphyxiation after they walked into a space located in the [Space Shuttle's mobile launcher platform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_launcher_platform#Saturn_V_and_Space_Shuttle "Mobile launcher platform") that was pressurised with pure nitrogen as a precaution against fire.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-102)

When inhaled at high [partial pressures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_pressure "Partial pressure") (more than about 4 bar, encountered at depths below about 30 m in [scuba diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuba_diving "Scuba diving")), nitrogen is an anaesthetic agent, causing [nitrogen narcosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen_narcosis "Nitrogen narcosis"), a temporary state of mental impairment similar to [nitrous oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrous_oxide "Nitrous oxide") intoxication.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-103)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-104)

Nitrogen dissolves in the [blood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood "Blood") and body fats. Rapid decompression (as when divers ascend too quickly or astronauts decompress too quickly from cabin pressure to spacesuit pressure) can lead to a potentially fatal condition called [decompression sickness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_sickness "Decompression sickness") (formerly known as caisson sickness or _the bends_), when nitrogen bubbles form in the bloodstream, nerves, joints, and other sensitive or vital areas.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-DCShx-105)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-Kindwall-106) Bubbles from other "inert" gases (gases other than carbon dioxide and oxygen) cause the same effects, so replacement of nitrogen in [breathing gases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breathing_gas "Breathing gas") may prevent nitrogen narcosis, but does not prevent decompression sickness.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-usn1-107)

### Liquid

As a [cryogenic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryogenic "Cryogenic") liquid, liquid nitrogen can be dangerous by causing [cold burns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_burn "Cold burn") on contact, although the [Leidenfrost effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leidenfrost_effect "Leidenfrost effect") provides protection for very short exposure (about one second).[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-108) Ingestion of liquid nitrogen can cause severe internal damage. For example, in 2012, a young woman in England had to have her stomach removed after ingesting a cocktail made with liquid nitrogen.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-109)

Because the liquid-to-gas [expansion ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expansion_ratio "Expansion ratio") of nitrogen is 1:694 at 20°C, a tremendous amount of force can be generated if liquid nitrogen is rapidly vaporised in an enclosed space. In an incident on January 12, 2006, at [Texas A&M University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_A&M_University "Texas A&M University"), the pressure-relief devices of a tank of liquid nitrogen were malfunctioning and later sealed. As a result of the subsequent pressure buildup, the tank failed catastrophically. The force of the explosion was sufficient to propel the tank through the ceiling immediately above it, shatter a reinforced concrete beam immediately below it, and blow the walls of the laboratory 0.1–0.2 m off their foundations.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-110)

Liquid nitrogen readily evaporates to form gaseous nitrogen, and hence the precautions associated with gaseous nitrogen also apply to liquid nitrogen.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-BCGACOPCP30-111)[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-112)[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-113) For example, [oxygen sensors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_sensor "Oxygen sensor") are sometimes used as a safety precaution when working with liquid nitrogen to alert workers of gas spills into a confined space.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-usn-114)

Vessels containing liquid nitrogen can [condense oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_oxygen "Liquid oxygen") from air. The liquid in such a vessel becomes increasingly enriched in oxygen (boiling point −183°C, higher than that of nitrogen) as the nitrogen evaporates, and can cause violent oxidation of organic material.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-115)

### Oxygen deficiency monitors

[Oxygen sensors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_sensor "Oxygen sensor") are used to measure oxygen levels in confined spaces and any place where nitrogen gas or liquid are stored or used. In the event of a nitrogen leak, and a decrease in oxygen to a pre-set alarm level, an oxygen deficiency monitor can be programmed to set off audible and visual alarms. Most commonly, the oxygen range to alert personnel is when oxygen levels drop below 19.5%. In the U.S., [OSHA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occupational_Safety_and_Health_Administration "Occupational Safety and Health Administration") specifies that a hazardous atmosphere may include one where the oxygen concentration is below 19.5% or above 23.5%.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen#cite_note-116)

**Beryllium** is a [chemical element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_element "Chemical element"); it has [symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symbol_(chemistry) "Symbol (chemistry)")**Be** and [atomic number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_number "Atomic number") 4. It is a steel-gray, hard, strong, lightweight and brittle [alkaline earth metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkaline_earth_metal "Alkaline earth metal"). It is a [divalent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divalent "Divalent") element that occurs naturally only in combination with other elements to form minerals. [Gemstones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gemstone "Gemstone") high in beryllium include [beryl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryl "Beryl") ([aquamarine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquamarine_(gemstone) "Aquamarine (gemstone)"), [emerald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerald "Emerald"), [red beryl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_beryl "Red beryl")) and [chrysoberyl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrysoberyl "Chrysoberyl"). It is a [relatively rare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abundance_of_the_chemical_elements#Universe "Abundance of the chemical elements") element in the [universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universe "Universe"), usually occurring as a product of the [spallation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spallation "Spallation") of larger atomic nuclei that have collided with [cosmic rays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_ray "Cosmic ray"). Within the cores of stars, beryllium is depleted as it is fused into heavier elements. Beryllium constitutes about 0.0004 percent by mass of Earth's crust. The world's annual beryllium production of 220 tons is usually manufactured by extraction from the mineral beryl, a difficult process because beryllium bonds strongly to [oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen "Oxygen").

In structural applications, the combination of high [flexural rigidity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flexural_rigidity "Flexural rigidity"), [thermal stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermostability "Thermostability"), [thermal conductivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermal_conductivity "Thermal conductivity") and low [density](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Density "Density") (1.85 times that of water) make beryllium a desirable [aerospace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerospace "Aerospace") material for aircraft components, [missiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missile "Missile"), [spacecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacecraft "Spacecraft"), and [satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite "Satellite").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-deGruyter-15) Because of its low density and [atomic mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_mass "Atomic mass"), beryllium is relatively transparent to [X-rays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-ray "X-ray") and other forms of [ionizing radiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionizing_radiation "Ionizing radiation"); therefore, it is the most common window material for X-ray equipment and components of [particle detectors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particle_detector "Particle detector").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-deGruyter-15) When added as an [alloying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alloy "Alloy") element to [aluminium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium "Aluminium"), [copper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copper "Copper") (notably the alloy [beryllium copper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_copper "Beryllium copper")), [iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron "Iron"), or [nickel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nickel "Nickel"), beryllium improves many physical properties.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-deGruyter-15) For example, tools and components made of beryllium copper alloys are [strong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strength_of_materials "Strength of materials") and [hard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardness "Hardness") and do not create sparks when they strike a steel surface. In air, the surface of beryllium oxidizes readily at room temperature to form a [passivation layer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passivation_(chemistry) "Passivation (chemistry)") 1–10 nm thick that protects it from further oxidation and corrosion.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-16) The metal oxidizes in bulk (beyond the passivation layer) when heated above 500°C (932°F),[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-Tomastik2005-17) and burns brilliantly when heated to about 2,500°C (4,530°F).[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-Ma%C4%8Dek-1969-18)

The commercial use of beryllium requires the use of appropriate dust control equipment and industrial controls at all times, because inhaled beryllium-containing dusts is toxic, and can cause [berylliosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berylliosis "Berylliosis"), a chronic life-threatening allergic disease, in some people.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-19) Berylliosis is typically manifested by chronic [pulmonary fibrosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulmonary_fibrosis "Pulmonary fibrosis") and, in severe cases, [right-sided heart failure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_failure#Right-sided_failure "Heart failure") and death.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-20)

## Characteristics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beryllium&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Characteristics")]

### Physical properties

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beryllium&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Physical properties")]

Beryllium is a [steel gray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steel_gray "Steel gray") and hard [metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metal "Metal") that is brittle at room temperature and has a [close-packed hexagonal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Close_packed_hexagonal "Close packed hexagonal")[crystal structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal_structure "Crystal structure").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-deGruyter-15) It has exceptional [stiffness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stiffness "Stiffness") ([Young's modulus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young's_modulus "Young's modulus") 287 GPa) and a [melting point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melting_point "Melting point") of 1287°C. The [modulus of elasticity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulus_of_elasticity "Modulus of elasticity") of beryllium is approximately 35% greater than that of steel. The combination of this modulus and a relatively low density results in an unusually high [sound conduction speed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_of_sound "Speed of sound") in beryllium – about 12.9 km/s at [ambient conditions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_temperature_and_pressure "Standard temperature and pressure"). Among all metals, beryllium dissipates the most heat per unit weight, with both high specific heat (1925 J·kg−1·K−1) and thermal conductivity (216 W·m−1·K−1). Beryllium's conductivity and relatively low coefficient of linear [thermal expansion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermal_expansion "Thermal expansion") (11.4×10−6 K−1) make it uniquely stable under extreme temperature differences.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-Behrens-2003-21):11.1

### Nuclear properties

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beryllium&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Nuclear properties")]

Naturally occurring beryllium, save for slight contamination by the [radioisotopes created by cosmic rays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmogenic_nuclide "Cosmogenic nuclide"), is isotopically pure beryllium-9,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-CIAAWberyllium-1) which has a [nuclear spin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin_(physics) "Spin (physics)") of ⁠3/2⁠−.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-NUBASE2020-13) The inelastic scattering [cross section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_section_(physics) "Cross section (physics)") of beryllium increases with relation to neutron energy,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-22) allowing for significant slowing of higher-energy neutrons.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-23) Therefore, it works as a [neutron reflector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_reflector "Neutron reflector") and [neutron moderator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_moderator "Neutron moderator"); the exact strength of neutron slowing depends on the purity and size of the crystallites in the material.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-24)

The isotope 9 Be can undergo a (n, 2n) neutron reaction with fast neutrons, to produce [8 Be](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium-8 "Beryllium-8"), which almost immediately breaks into two alpha particles. Thus, for high-energy neutrons, beryllium is a neutron multiplier, releasing more neutrons than it absorbs. This nuclear reaction is:[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-BeMelurgy-25)

9

4 Be + n → 2 4

2 He + 2 n
The isotope can liberate the neutron when struck by an alpha particle.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-Behrens-2003-21) The nuclear reaction

9

2 He → 12

6 C + n
is strongly exothermic, liberating a fast neutron.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-BeMelurgy-25)

The isotope can also release the neutron when absorbing a gamma ray of sufficient energy ([photodisintegration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photodisintegration "Photodisintegration"))[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-Byrne-2011-26) at a useful cross-section:

9

4 Be + gamma → 2 4

2 He + n
Thus, natural beryllium bombarded by alpha or gamma radiation from a suitable radioisotope is the most common radioisotope-powered [neutron source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_source "Neutron source") for laboratory use.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-NRC-2010-27)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-28)

Finally, small amounts of [tritium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tritium "Tritium") are also liberated by the high-energy neutrons in the three-step nuclear reaction

Tritium is a radioisotope of concern in nuclear reactor waste streams.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-29)

### Optical properties

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beryllium&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Optical properties")]

As a metal, beryllium is [transparent or translucent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transparency_and_translucency "Transparency and translucency") to most wavelengths of [X-rays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-ray "X-ray") and [gamma rays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_ray "Gamma ray"), making it useful for the output windows of [X-ray tubes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-ray_tube "X-ray tube") and other such apparatus.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-30)

### Isotopes and nucleosynthesis

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beryllium&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Isotopes and nucleosynthesis")]

Main article: [Isotopes of beryllium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotopes_of_beryllium "Isotopes of beryllium")

Natural beryllium is made up of solely the stable isotope beryllium-9. Beryllium is the only [monoisotopic element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monoisotopic_element "Monoisotopic element") with an even atomic number.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-CIAAWberyllium-1)

Beryllium-7 and beryllium-8 are key intermediates in stellar nucleosynthesis, but do not last long. It is believed that the beryllium in the universe was created in the interstellar medium when [cosmic rays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_ray "Cosmic ray") induced fission in heavier elements found in interstellar gas and dust, a process called [cosmic ray spallation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_ray_spallation "Cosmic ray spallation").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-31)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-32)

About one billionth (10−9) of the primordial atoms created in the [Big Bang nucleosynthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Bang_nucleosynthesis "Big Bang nucleosynthesis") were 7 Be. This is a consequence of the low density of matter when the temperature of the universe cooled enough for small nuclei to be stable. Creating such nuclei requires nuclear collisions that are rare at low density.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-Peacock-1998-33):297 Although 7 Be is unstable and decays by [electron capture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron_capture "Electron capture") into 7 Li, with a half-life of 53.22 days under standard conditions, in the early universe the atoms were fully ionized and electron capture not significant. The conversion of 7 Be to Li was only complete near the time of [recombination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recombination_(cosmology) "Recombination (cosmology)").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-34)

The isotope 7 Be is also a [cosmogenic nuclide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmogenic_nuclide "Cosmogenic nuclide") and shows an atmospheric abundance inversely proportional to solar activity.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-35) It decays exclusively by [electron capture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron_capture "Electron capture"), and the 2s electrons of beryllium are the valence electrons responsible for chemical bonding. Therefore, when 7 Be decays by L-electron capture, it does so by taking electrons from its [atomic orbitals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_orbital "Atomic orbital") that may be participating in bonding. This makes its decay rate dependent to a measurable degree upon its chemical surroundings – a rare occurrence in nuclear decay.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-36)

7 Be is also produced in cooling water of high-energy accelerators; it can be extracted from the water at high purity and sold for scientific experiments.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-37)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/60/Solar_Activity_Proxies.png/500px-Solar_Activity_Proxies.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Solar_Activity_Proxies.png)

Plot showing variations in solar activity, including variation in sunspot number (red) and 10 Be concentration (blue). Note that the beryllium scale is inverted, so increases on this scale indicate lower 10 Be levels

The isotope 10 Be is similarly cosmogenic, and is produced in the same way – by [cosmic ray spallation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_ray_spallation "Cosmic ray spallation") of nitrogen and oxygen.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-38) Its behavior differs only because of its much longer half-life of 1.387 million years. It entirely accumulates at the [soil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soil "Soil") surface and has a long [residence time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Residence_time_(fluid_dynamics) "Residence time (fluid dynamics)") before decaying to [boron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boron "Boron")-10. Thus, 10 Be and its daughter product are used to examine natural [soil erosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soil_erosion "Soil erosion"), [soil formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soil_formation "Soil formation") and the development of [lateritic soils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laterite "Laterite"), and as a [proxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proxy_(climate) "Proxy (climate)") for measurement of the variations in [solar activity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_variation "Solar variation") and the age of [ice cores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_core "Ice core").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-39) As with 7 Be, production of 10 Be is inversely related to solar activity, because increased [solar wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_wind "Solar wind") during periods of high solar activity decreases the flux of galactic cosmic rays that reach the Earth.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEmsley200156-40) Nuclear explosions also form 10 Be by the reaction of fast neutrons with 13 C in the carbon dioxide in air. This is one of the indicators of past activity at [nuclear weapon test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapon_test "Nuclear weapon test") sites.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-41)

8 Be is unstable but has a ground state [resonance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resonance_(particle_physics) "Resonance (particle physics)") with an important role in the [triple-alpha process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple-alpha_process "Triple-alpha process") in stellar [helium burning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helium_burning "Helium burning"). As first proposed by British [astronomer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomer "Astronomer") Sir [Fred Hoyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Hoyle "Fred Hoyle") based solely on astrophysical analysis, the energy levels of 8 Be and 12 C allow carbon nucleosynthesis by increasing the effective cross-section between the three alpha particles in the carbon production process. The main carbon-producing reaction in the universe is {\displaystyle ^{4}{\textrm {He}}\ +\ ^{8}{\textrm {Be}}\rightarrow \ ^{12}{\textrm {C}}+\gamma }![Image 10: {\displaystyle ^{4}{\textrm {He}}\ +\ ^{8}{\textrm {Be}}\rightarrow \ ^{12}{\textrm {C}}+\gamma }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/205d78cf5a8df11297130eaa4847f795100bbd7e) where 4 He is an alpha particle.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-42)

The exotic isotopes 11 Be and 14 Be are known to exhibit a [nuclear halo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halo_nucleus "Halo nucleus"). That is, their nuclei have, respectively, 1 and 4 neutrons orbiting substantially outside the expected nuclear radius[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-43) and in each case the core the neutrons float around is one of 10 Be.

[Emerald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerald "Emerald") is a naturally occurring [compound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_compound "Chemical compound") of beryllium.

Beryllium is found in over 100 minerals,[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-44) but most are uncommon to rare. The more common beryllium-containing minerals include: [bertrandite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertrandite "Bertrandite") (Be 4 Si 2 O 7(OH)2), [beryl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryl "Beryl") (Al 2 Be 3 Si 6 O 18), [chrysoberyl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrysoberyl "Chrysoberyl") (Al 2 BeO 4) and [phenakite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phenakite "Phenakite") (Be 2 SiO 4). Precious forms of beryl are [aquamarine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquamarine_(gemstone) "Aquamarine (gemstone)"), [red beryl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_beryl "Red beryl") and [emerald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerald "Emerald").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-Behrens-2003-21)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-45)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-46) The green color in gem-quality forms of beryl comes from varying amounts of chromium (about 2% for emerald).[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEmsley200158-47)

The two main ores of beryllium, beryl and bertrandite, are found in Argentina, Brazil, India, Madagascar, Russia and the United States.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEmsley200158-47) Total world reserves of beryllium ore are greater than 400,000 tonnes.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEmsley200158-47)

### Abundance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beryllium&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Abundance")]

The Sun has a concentration of 0.1 [parts per billion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parts_per_billion "Parts per billion") (ppb) of beryllium.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-48) Beryllium has a concentration of 2 to 6 [parts per million](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parts_per_million "Parts per million") (ppm) in the Earth's crust and is the 47th-most abundant element.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-Merck-49)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEmsley200159-50) It is most concentrated (6 ppm) in the soils.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEmsley200159-50) Trace amounts of 9 Be are found in the Earth's atmosphere.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEmsley200159-50) The concentration of beryllium in sea water is 0.2–0.6 [parts per trillion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parts_per_trillion "Parts per trillion").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEmsley200159-50)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-51) In stream water, however, beryllium is more abundant, with a concentration of 0.1 ppb.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-52)

## Extraction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beryllium&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Extraction")]

The extraction of beryllium from its compounds is a difficult process due to its high affinity for oxygen at elevated temperatures, and its ability to reduce water when its oxide film is removed. Currently the United States, China and Kazakhstan are the only three countries involved in the industrial-scale extraction of beryllium.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-53) Kazakhstan produces beryllium from a concentrate stockpiled before the [breakup of the Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Soviet_Union "Dissolution of the Soviet Union") around 1991. This resource had become nearly depleted by the mid-2010s.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-54)

Production of beryllium in Russia was halted in 1997, and is planned to be resumed in the 2020s.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-55)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-56)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e2/Beryllium_%28Be%29.jpg/250px-Beryllium_%28Be%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Beryllium_(Be).jpg)

A bead of beryllium from a melt

Beryllium is most commonly extracted from the mineral [beryl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryl "Beryl"), which is either [sintered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sintering "Sintering") using an extraction agent or melted into a soluble mixture. The sintering process involves mixing beryl with [sodium fluorosilicate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_fluorosilicate "Sodium fluorosilicate") and soda at 770°C (1,420°F) to form [sodium fluoroberyllate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrafluoroberyllate "Tetrafluoroberyllate"), [aluminium oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium_oxide "Aluminium oxide") and [silicon dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_dioxide "Silicon dioxide").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-deGruyter-15)[Beryllium hydroxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_hydroxide "Beryllium hydroxide") is precipitated from a solution of sodium fluoroberyllate and [sodium hydroxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_hydroxide "Sodium hydroxide") in water. The extraction of beryllium using the melt method involves grinding beryl into a powder and heating it to 1,650°C (3,000°F). The melt is quickly cooled with water and then reheated 250 to 300°C (482 to 572°F) in concentrated [sulfuric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfuric_acid "Sulfuric acid"), mostly yielding [beryllium sulfate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_sulfate "Beryllium sulfate") and [aluminium sulfate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium_sulfate "Aluminium sulfate"). Aqueous [ammonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammonia "Ammonia") is then used to remove the aluminium and sulfur, leaving beryllium hydroxide.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-deGruyter-15)

Beryllium hydroxide created using either the sinter or melt method is then converted into [beryllium fluoride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_fluoride "Beryllium fluoride") or [beryllium chloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_chloride "Beryllium chloride"). To form the fluoride, aqueous [ammonium hydrogen fluoride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammonium_hydrogen_fluoride "Ammonium hydrogen fluoride") is added to beryllium hydroxide to yield a precipitate of ammonium [tetrafluoroberyllate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrafluoroberyllate "Tetrafluoroberyllate"), which is heated to 1,000°C (1,830°F) to form beryllium fluoride.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-deGruyter-15) Heating the fluoride to 900°C (1,650°F) with [magnesium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnesium "Magnesium") forms finely divided beryllium, and additional heating to 1,300°C (2,370°F) creates the compact metal.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-deGruyter-15) Heating beryllium hydroxide forms [beryllium oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_oxide "Beryllium oxide"), which becomes beryllium chloride when combined with carbon and chlorine. [Electrolysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrolysis "Electrolysis") of molten beryllium chloride is then used to obtain the metal.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-deGruyter-15)

## Chemical properties

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beryllium&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Chemical properties")]

See also: [Category:Beryllium compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Beryllium_compounds "Category:Beryllium compounds")

A beryllium atom has the electronic configuration [He] 2s 2. The predominant [oxidation state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxidation_state "Oxidation state") of beryllium is +2; the beryllium atom losing both of its [valence electrons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valence_electron "Valence electron"). Beryllium's chemical behavior is largely a result of its small [atomic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_radius "Atomic radius") and [ionic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionic_radius "Ionic radius") radii. It thus has very high [ionization potentials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionization_potential "Ionization potential") and does not form divalent cations. Instead it forms two covalent bonds with a tendency to [polymerize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polymerize "Polymerize"), as in solid BeCl 2.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-deGruyter-15):37 Its chemistry has similarities to that of aluminium, an example of a [diagonal relationship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diagonal_relationship "Diagonal relationship").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-Greenwood-57):107 In the other direction, beryllium is attracted to electron density, generating intermolecular forces similar to [hydrogen bonding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_bonding "Hydrogen bonding").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-58)

At room temperature, the surface of beryllium forms a 1−10 nm-thick oxide [passivation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passivation_(chemistry) "Passivation (chemistry)") layer that prevents further reactions with air, except for gradual thickening of the oxide up to about 25 nm. When heated above about 500°C, oxidation into the bulk metal progresses along grain boundaries.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-Tomastik2005-17) Once the metal is ignited in air by heating above the oxide melting point around 2500°C, beryllium burns brilliantly,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-Ma%C4%8Dek-1969-18) forming a mixture of [beryllium oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_oxide "Beryllium oxide") and [beryllium nitride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_nitride "Beryllium nitride"). Beryllium dissolves readily in non-[oxidizing acids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxidizing_acid "Oxidizing acid"), such as HCl and diluted H 2 SO 4, but not in [nitric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitric_acid "Nitric acid") or water as this forms the oxide. This behavior is similar to that of aluminium. Beryllium also dissolves and reacts with alkali solutions.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-deGruyter-15)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-Greenwood-57):112

Binary compounds of beryllium(II) are polymeric in the solid state. [BeF 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_fluoride "Beryllium fluoride") has a [silica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silica "Silica")-like structure with corner-shared BeF 4 tetrahedra. [BeCl 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_chloride "Beryllium chloride") and [BeBr 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_bromide "Beryllium bromide") have chain structures with edge-shared tetrahedra. [Beryllium oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_oxide "Beryllium oxide"), BeO, is a white [refractory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refractory "Refractory") solid which has a [wurtzite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zinc_sulfide "Zinc sulfide") crystal structure and a thermal conductivity as high as some metals. BeO is [amphoteric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amphoteric "Amphoteric"). [Beryllium sulfide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_sulfide "Beryllium sulfide"), [selenide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_selenide?action=edit&redlink=1 "Beryllium selenide (page does not exist)") and [telluride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_telluride "Beryllium telluride") are known, all having the [zincblende structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubic_crystal_system#Zincblende_structure "Cubic crystal system").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-Wiberg&Holleman-59)[Beryllium nitride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_nitride "Beryllium nitride"), Be 3 N 2, is a high-melting-point compound which is readily hydrolyzed. [Beryllium azide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_azide "Beryllium azide"), BeN 6 is known and [beryllium phosphide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_phosphide?action=edit&redlink=1 "Beryllium phosphide (page does not exist)"), Be 3 P 2 has a similar structure to Be 3 N 2. A number of beryllium [borides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boride "Boride") are known, such as Be 5 B, Be 4 B, Be 2 B, BeB 2, BeB 6 and BeB 12. [Beryllium carbide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_carbide "Beryllium carbide"), Be 2 C, is a refractory brick-red compound that reacts with water to give [methane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methane "Methane").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-Wiberg&Holleman-59) Beryllium [silicides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicide "Silicide") have been identified in the form of variously sized [nanoclusters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanocluster "Nanocluster"),[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-60) formed through a spontaneous reaction between pure beryllium and silicon.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-61) The halides BeX 2 (X = F, Cl, Br, and I) have a linear monomeric molecular structure in the gas phase.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-Greenwood-57):117

Lower oxidation states complexes of beryllium are exceedingly rare. For example, a stable complex with a Be-Be bond, which formally features beryllium in the +1 oxidation state, has been described.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-BCWABe(I)-8) Beryllium in the 0 oxidation state is also known in a complex with a Mg-Be bond.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-Be(0)-6)

### Aqueous solutions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beryllium&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Aqueous solutions")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8f/Beacetate.png/250px-Beacetate.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Beacetate.png)

Schematic structure of [basic beryllium acetate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_beryllium_acetate "Basic beryllium acetate")

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1f/BeHydrolysis.png/250px-BeHydrolysis.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BeHydrolysis.png)
