[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/Be3OHW6.svg/250px-Be3OHW6.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Be3OHW6.svg)

Structure of the trimeric hydrolysis product of beryllium(II)

Solutions of beryllium salts, such as [beryllium sulfate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_sulfate "Beryllium sulfate") and [beryllium nitrate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_nitrate "Beryllium nitrate"), are acidic because of hydrolysis of the [Be(H 2 O)4]2+ ion. The concentration of the first hydrolysis product, [Be(H 2 O)3(OH)]+, is less than 1% of the beryllium concentration. The most stable hydrolysis product is the [trimeric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trimer_(chemistry) "Trimer (chemistry)") ion [Be 3(OH)3(H 2 O)6]3+. [Beryllium hydroxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_hydroxide "Beryllium hydroxide"), Be(OH)2, is insoluble in water at pH 5 or more. Consequently, beryllium compounds are generally insoluble at biological pH. Because of this, inhalation of beryllium metal dust leads to the development of the fatal condition of [berylliosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berylliosis "Berylliosis"). Be(OH)2 dissolves in strongly [alkaline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkalinity "Alkalinity") solutions.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-Lucia-62)

Beryllium(II) forms few complexes with monodentate ligands because the water molecules in the aquo-ion, [Be(H 2 O)4]2+ are bound very strongly to the beryllium ion. Notable exceptions are the series of water-soluble complexes with the [fluoride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluoride "Fluoride") ion:[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-63)

[Be(H 2 O)4]2+ + _n_ F− ⇌ Be[(H 2 O)2−_n_ F _n_]2− + _n_ H 2 O
Beryllium(II) forms many complexes with bidentate ligands containing oxygen-donor atoms.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-Lucia-62) The species [Be 3 O(H 2 PO 4)6]2− is notable for having a 3-coordinate oxide ion at its center. [Basic beryllium acetate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_beryllium_acetate "Basic beryllium acetate"), Be 4 O(OAc)6, has an oxide ion surrounded by a tetrahedron of beryllium atoms.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-64)

With organic ligands, such as the [malonate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malonate "Malonate") ion, the acid deprotonates when forming the complex. The donor atoms are two oxygens.

H 2 A + [Be(H 2 O)4]2+ ⇌ [BeA(H 2 O)2] + 2 H+ + 2 H 2 O H 2 A + [BeA(H 2 O)2] ⇌ [BeA 2]2− + 2 H+ + 2 H 2 O
The formation of a complex is in competition with the metal ion-hydrolysis reaction and mixed complexes with both the anion and the hydroxide ion are also formed. For example, derivatives of the cyclic trimer are known, with a bidentate ligand replacing one or more pairs of water molecules.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-KSMisleadingTitle-65)

Aliphatic [hydroxycarboxylic acids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydroxycarboxylic_acid "Hydroxycarboxylic acid") such as [glycolic acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glycolic_acid "Glycolic acid") form rather weak monodentate complexes in solution, in which the hydroxyl group remains intact. In the solid state, the hydroxyl group may deprotonate: a hexamer, Na 4[Be 6(OCH 2(O)O)6], was isolated long ago.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-KSMisleadingTitle-65)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-66) Aromatic hydroxy ligands (i.e. [phenols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phenol "Phenol")) form relatively strong complexes. For example, log K 1 and log K 2 values of 12.2 and 9.3 have been reported for complexes with [tiron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiron_(chemical) "Tiron (chemical)").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-KSMisleadingTitle-65)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-67)

Beryllium has generally a rather poor affinity for [ammine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammine "Ammine") ligands.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-KSMisleadingTitle-65)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-MDCBMVChelate-68) There are many early reports of complexes with amino acids, but unfortunately they are not reliable as the concomitant hydrolysis reactions were not understood at the time of publication. Values for log β of ca. 6 to 7 have been reported. The degree of formation is small because of competition with hydrolysis reactions.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-KSMisleadingTitle-65)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-MDCBMVChelate-68)

### Organic chemistry

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beryllium&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Organic chemistry")]

Main article: [Organoberyllium chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organoberyllium_chemistry "Organoberyllium chemistry")

Organometallic beryllium compounds are known to be highly reactive.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-naglav-69) Examples of known organoberyllium compounds are dineopentylberyllium,[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-70)[beryllocene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllocene "Beryllocene") (Cp 2 Be),[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-71)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-72)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-73)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-74) diallylberyllium (by exchange reaction of diethyl beryllium with triallyl boron),[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-75) bis(1,3-trimethylsilylallyl)beryllium,[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-76) Be([mes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesitylene "Mesitylene"))2,[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-naglav-69) and (beryllium(I) complex) diberyllocene.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-BCWABe(I)-8) Ligands can also be aryls[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-77) and alkynyls.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-78)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beryllium&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: History")]

The mineral [beryl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryl "Beryl"), which contains beryllium, has been used at least since the [Ptolemaic dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ptolemaic_dynasty "Ptolemaic dynasty") of Egypt.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeeks1968535-79) The [Papyrus Graecus Holmiensis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papyrus_Graecus_Holmiensis "Papyrus Graecus Holmiensis"), written in the third or fourth century CE, contains notes on how to prepare artificial emerald and beryl.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeeks1968536-80)

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/25/Louis_Nicolas_Vauquelin.jpg/250px-Louis_Nicolas_Vauquelin.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Louis_Nicolas_Vauquelin.jpg)

[Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis-Nicolas_Vauquelin "Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin") discovered beryllium

Early analyses of emeralds and beryls by [Martin Heinrich Klaproth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Heinrich_Klaproth "Martin Heinrich Klaproth"), [Torbern Olof Bergman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torbern_Olof_Bergman "Torbern Olof Bergman"), [Franz Karl Achard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franz_Karl_Achard "Franz Karl Achard"), and [Johann Jakob Bindheim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Jakob_Bindheim?action=edit&redlink=1 "Johann Jakob Bindheim (page does not exist)")[[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann%20Jakob%20Bindheim "de:Johann Jakob Bindheim")] always yielded similar elements, leading to the mistaken conclusion that both substances are [aluminium silicates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium_silicate "Aluminium silicate").[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeeks1968537-81) Mineralogist [René Just Haüy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Just_Ha%C3%BCy "René Just Haüy") discovered that both crystals are geometrically identical, and he asked chemist [Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis-Nicolas_Vauquelin "Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin") for a chemical analysis.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeeks1968535-79)

In a 1798 paper read before the [Institut de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institut_de_France "Institut de France"), Vauquelin reported that he found a new "earth" by dissolving [aluminium hydroxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium_hydroxide "Aluminium hydroxide") from emerald and beryl in an additional [alkali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkali "Alkali").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-82) The editors of the journal _[Annales de chimie et de physique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annales\_de\_chimie\_et\_de\_physique "Annales de chimie et de physique")_ named the new earth "glucine" for the sweet taste of some of its compounds.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-83)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeeks1968538-84) The name _beryllium_ was first used by [Friedrich Wöhler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_W%C3%B6hler "Friedrich Wöhler") in 1828.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-NameGame-2023-85)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-W%C3%B6hler-86) Both beryllium and glucinum were used concurrently until 1949, when the [IUPAC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUPAC "IUPAC") adopted beryllium as the standard name of the element.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-87)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-88)

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/Friedrich_W%C3%B6hler_Stich.jpg/250px-Friedrich_W%C3%B6hler_Stich.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Friedrich_W%C3%B6hler_Stich.jpg)

[Friedrich Wöhler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_W%C3%B6hler "Friedrich Wöhler") was one of the men who independently isolated beryllium

[Friedrich Wöhler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_W%C3%B6hler "Friedrich Wöhler")[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-W%C3%B6hler-86) and [Antoine Bussy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoine_Bussy "Antoine Bussy")[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-89) independently isolated beryllium in 1828 by the [chemical reaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_reaction "Chemical reaction") of metallic [potassium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potassium "Potassium") with [beryllium chloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_chloride "Beryllium chloride"), as follows:

BeCl 2 + 2 K → 2 KCl + Be
Using an alcohol lamp, Wöhler heated alternating layers of beryllium chloride and potassium in a wired-shut platinum crucible. The above reaction immediately took place and caused the crucible to become white hot. Upon cooling and washing the resulting gray-black powder, he saw that it was made of fine particles with a dark metallic luster.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeeks1968539-90) The highly reactive potassium had been produced by the [electrolysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrolysis "Electrolysis") of its compounds.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-Enghag2004-91) He did not succeed in melting the beryllium particles.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeeks1968539-90)

The process of producing beryllium was prohibitively expensive at the start of the 20th century. This changed once a cost effective process for extracting beryllium from beryl ore. In 1920, the price of producing a pound of beryllium was $5,000, but by 1931, it was $50.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-Brewer-1942-92)

The direct electrolysis of a molten mixture of [beryllium fluoride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_fluoride "Beryllium fluoride") and [sodium fluoride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_fluoride "Sodium fluoride") by [Paul Lebeau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Lebeau "Paul Lebeau") in 1898 resulted in the first pure (99.5 to 99.8%) samples of beryllium.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeeks1968539-90) However, industrial production started only after the First World War. The original industrial involvement included subsidiaries and scientists related to the [Union Carbide and Carbon Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Carbide "Union Carbide") in Cleveland, Ohio, and [Siemens & Halske](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siemens_&_Halske "Siemens & Halske") AG in Berlin. In the US, the process was ruled by Hugh S. Cooper, director of The Kemet Laboratories Company. In Germany, the first commercially successful process for producing beryllium was developed in 1921 by [Alfred Stock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Stock "Alfred Stock") and [Hans Goldschmidt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Goldschmidt "Hans Goldschmidt").[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-93)

A sample of beryllium was bombarded with [alpha rays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_ray "Alpha ray") from the decay of [radium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radium "Radium") in a 1932 experiment by [James Chadwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Chadwick "James Chadwick") that uncovered the existence of the [neutron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron "Neutron").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEmsley200158-47) This same method is used in one class of radioisotope-based laboratory [neutron sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_source "Neutron source") that produce 30 neutrons for every million α particles.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-Merck-49)

Beryllium production saw a rapid increase during World War II due to the rising demand for hard beryllium-copper alloys and [phosphors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphor "Phosphor") for [fluorescent lights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluorescent_light "Fluorescent light"). Most early fluorescent lamps used [zinc orthosilicate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zinc_orthosilicate "Zinc orthosilicate") with varying content of beryllium to emit greenish light. Small additions of magnesium [tungstate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tungstate "Tungstate") improved the blue part of the spectrum to yield an acceptable white light. Halophosphate-based phosphors replaced beryllium-based phosphors after beryllium was found to be toxic.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-94)

Electrolysis of a mixture of [beryllium fluoride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_fluoride "Beryllium fluoride") and [sodium fluoride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_fluoride "Sodium fluoride") was used to isolate beryllium during the 19th century. The metal's high melting point makes this process more energy-consuming than corresponding processes used for the [alkali metals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkali_metal "Alkali metal"). Early in the 20th century, the production of beryllium by the thermal decomposition of [beryllium iodide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_iodide "Beryllium iodide") was investigated following the success of a similar process for the production of [zirconium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zirconium "Zirconium"), but this process proved to be uneconomical for volume production.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-95)

Pure beryllium metal did not become readily available until 1957, even though it had been used as an alloying metal to harden and toughen copper much earlier.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEmsley200158-47) Beryllium could be produced by reducing beryllium compounds such as [beryllium chloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_chloride "Beryllium chloride") with metallic potassium or sodium. Currently, most beryllium is produced by reducing beryllium fluoride with [magnesium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnesium "Magnesium").[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-crc84hammond-96) The price on the American market for [vacuum-cast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casting_(metalworking) "Casting (metalworking)") beryllium ingots was about $338 per pound ($745 per kilogram) in 2001.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-USGS-97)

Between 1998 and 2008, the world's production of beryllium had decreased from 343 to about 200 [tonnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonne "Tonne"). It then increased to 230 metric tons by 2018, of which 170 tonnes came from the United States.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-USGSMCS2000-98)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-USGSMCS2010-99)

### Etymology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beryllium&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Etymology")]

Beryllium was named for the semiprecious mineral [beryl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryl "Beryl"), from which it was first isolated.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-100)[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-101)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-102) Martin Klaproth, having independently determined that beryl and emerald share an element, preferred the name "beryllina" due to the fact that [yttria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yttria "Yttria") also formed sweet salts.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-103)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-NameGame-2023-85)

Although [Humphry Davy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humphry_Davy "Humphry Davy") failed to isolate it, he proposed the name _glucium_ for the new metal, derived from the name _glucina_ for the earth it was found in; altered forms of this name, _glucinium_ or _glucinum_ (symbol Gl) continued to be used into the 20th century.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-104)

## Applications

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beryllium&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Applications")]

### Radiation windows

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beryllium&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Radiation windows")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/Beryllium_target.jpg/250px-Beryllium_target.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Beryllium_target.jpg)

Beryllium target which converts a proton beam into a neutron beam[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-105)

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/Be_foil_square.jpg/250px-Be_foil_square.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Be_foil_square.jpg)

A square beryllium foil mounted in a steel case to be used as a window between a vacuum chamber and an [X-ray microscope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-ray_microscope "X-ray microscope"). Beryllium is highly transparent to X-rays owing to its low [atomic number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_number "Atomic number").

Because of its low atomic number and very low absorption for X-rays, the oldest and still one of the most important applications of beryllium is in radiation windows for [X-ray tubes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-ray_tube "X-ray tube").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEmsley200158-47) Extreme demands are placed on purity and cleanliness of beryllium to avoid artifacts in the X-ray images. Beryllium is used in X-ray windows because it is transparent to X-rays, allowing for clearer and more efficient imaging.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-106) Thin beryllium foils are used as radiation windows for X-ray detectors, and their extremely low absorption minimizes the heating effects caused by high-intensity, low energy X-rays typical of [synchrotron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synchrotron "Synchrotron") radiation. Vacuum-tight windows and beam-tubes for radiation experiments on synchrotrons are manufactured exclusively from beryllium. In scientific setups for various X-ray emission studies (e.g., [energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy-dispersive_X-ray_spectroscopy "Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy")) the sample holder is usually made of beryllium because its emitted X-rays have much lower energies (≈100 eV) than X-rays from most studied materials.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-Behrens-2003-21)

Low [atomic number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_number "Atomic number") also makes beryllium relatively transparent to energetic [particles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elementary_particle "Elementary particle"). Therefore, it is used to build the [beam pipe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beamline "Beamline") around the collision region in [particle physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particle_physics "Particle physics") setups, such as all four main detector experiments at the [Large Hadron Collider](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_Hadron_Collider "Large Hadron Collider") ([ALICE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Large_Ion_Collider_Experiment "A Large Ion Collider Experiment"), [ATLAS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ATLAS_experiment "ATLAS experiment"), [CMS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_Muon_Solenoid "Compact Muon Solenoid"), [LHCb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LHCb "LHCb")),[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-107) the [Tevatron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tevatron "Tevatron") and at [SLAC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SLAC "SLAC"). The low density of beryllium allows collision products to reach the surrounding detectors without significant interaction, its stiffness allows a powerful vacuum to be produced within the pipe to minimize interaction with gases, its thermal stability allows it to function correctly at temperatures of only a few degrees above [absolute zero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_zero "Absolute zero"), and its [diamagnetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diamagnetic "Diamagnetic") nature keeps it from interfering with the complex multipole magnet systems used to steer and [focus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_focusing "Strong focusing") the [particle beams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particle_beam "Particle beam").[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-108)

### Mechanical applications

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beryllium&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Mechanical applications")]

Because of its stiffness, light weight and dimensional stability over a wide temperature range, beryllium metal is used for lightweight structural components in the defense and [aerospace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerospace "Aerospace") industries in high-speed [aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft "Aircraft"), [guided missiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guided_missile "Guided missile"), [spacecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacecraft "Spacecraft"), and [satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite "Satellite"), including the [James Webb Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Webb_Space_Telescope "James Webb Space Telescope"). Several [liquid-fuel rockets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid-fuel_rocket "Liquid-fuel rocket") have used [rocket nozzles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocket_engine_nozzle "Rocket engine nozzle") made of pure beryllium.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-109)[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-110) The high elastic stiffness of beryllium has led to its extensive use in precision instrumentation, e.g. in [inertial guidance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inertial_guidance "Inertial guidance") systems and in the support mechanisms for optical systems.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-Behrens-2003-21) Beryllium powder was itself studied as a [rocket fuel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocket_fuel "Rocket fuel"), but this use has never materialized.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEmsley200158-47) A small number of extreme high-end [bicycle frames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_frame "Bicycle frame") have been built with beryllium.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-museum-111) From 1998 to 2000, the [McLaren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McLaren "McLaren")[Formula One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formula_One "Formula One") team used [Mercedes-Benz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercedes-Benz "Mercedes-Benz") engines with [beryllium–aluminium alloy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium-aluminium_alloy "Beryllium-aluminium alloy") pistons.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-112) The use of beryllium engine components was banned following a protest by [Scuderia Ferrari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuderia_Ferrari "Scuderia Ferrari").[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-113) An earlier major application of beryllium was in [brakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brake "Brake") for military [airplanes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airplane "Airplane") because of its hardness, high melting point, and exceptional ability to [dissipate heat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_dissipation "Heat dissipation"). Environmental considerations have led to substitution by other materials.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-Behrens-2003-21)

#### Alloys

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beryllium&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Alloys")]

Mixing about 2.0% beryllium into [copper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copper "Copper") forms an [alloy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alloy "Alloy") called [beryllium copper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_copper "Beryllium copper") that is six times stronger than copper alone.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-McGraw-Hill2004-114) Beryllium alloys are used in many applications because of their combination of elasticity, high [electrical conductivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_conductivity "Electrical conductivity") and [thermal conductivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermal_conductivity "Thermal conductivity"), high strength and [hardness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardness_(materials_science) "Hardness (materials science)"), nonmagnetic properties, as well as good [corrosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corrosion "Corrosion") and [fatigue resistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatigue_(material) "Fatigue (material)").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEmsley200158-47)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-deGruyter-15) These applications include non-sparking tools that are used near flammable gases ([beryllium nickel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_nickel?action=edit&redlink=1 "Beryllium nickel (page does not exist)")), [springs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spring_(device) "Spring (device)"), membranes (beryllium nickel and [beryllium iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_iron?action=edit&redlink=1 "Beryllium iron (page does not exist)")) used in surgical instruments, and high temperature devices.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEmsley200158-47)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-deGruyter-15) As little as 50 parts per million of beryllium alloyed with liquid [magnesium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnesium "Magnesium") leads to a significant increase in oxidation resistance and decrease in flammability.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-deGruyter-15)

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/Beryllium_Copper_Adjustable_Wrench.jpg/250px-Beryllium_Copper_Adjustable_Wrench.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Beryllium_Copper_Adjustable_Wrench.jpg)

Beryllium copper adjustable wrench

Beryllium-copper alloys were also applied as a hardening agent in "[Jason pistols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Needlegun_scaler "Needlegun scaler")", which were used to strip the paint from the hulls of ships.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-115)

Beryllium–copper alloys are also widely used in modern aerospace and defense applications, particularly in high-performance electrical connectors, battery safety fuses, and microswitches that require a balance of conductivity, corrosion resistance, and fatigue strength.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-116)

A metal matrix composite material combining beryllium with [aluminium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium "Aluminium") developed under the trade name [AlBeMet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AlBeMet "AlBeMet") for the high performance aerospace industry has low weight but four times the stiffness of aluminum alone.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-117)

### Mirrors

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beryllium&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Mirrors")]

Large-area beryllium [mirrors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirror "Mirror"), frequently with a [honeycomb support structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honeycomb_mirror "Honeycomb mirror"), are used, for example, in [meteorological satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meteorological_satellite "Meteorological satellite") where low weight and long-term dimensional stability are critical. Smaller beryllium mirrors are used in [optical guidance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optical_guidance "Optical guidance") systems and in [fire-control systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire-control_system "Fire-control system"), e.g. in the German-made [Leopard 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leopard_1 "Leopard 1") and [Leopard 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leopard_2 "Leopard 2")[main battle tanks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_battle_tank "Main battle tank"). In these systems, very rapid movement of the mirror is required, which again dictates low mass and high rigidity. Usually the beryllium mirror is coated with hard [electroless nickel plating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electroless_nickel_plating "Electroless nickel plating") which can be more easily polished to a finer optical finish than beryllium. In some applications, the beryllium blank is polished without any coating. This is particularly applicable to [cryogenic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryogenic "Cryogenic") operation where thermal expansion mismatch can cause the coating to buckle.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-Behrens-2003-21)

The [James Webb Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Webb_Space_Telescope "James Webb Space Telescope") has 18 hexagonal beryllium sections for its mirrors, each plated with a thin layer of gold.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-118) Because JWST will face a temperature of 33 K, the mirror is made of gold-plated beryllium, which is capable of handling extreme cold better than glass. Beryllium contracts and deforms less than glass and remains more uniform in such temperatures.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-119) For the same reason, the optics of the [Spitzer Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spitzer_Space_Telescope "Spitzer Space Telescope") are entirely built of beryllium metal.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-120)

### Magnetic applications

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beryllium&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Magnetic applications")]

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/02/BERYLLIUM_-_KUGEL_1.JPG/250px-BERYLLIUM_-_KUGEL_1.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BERYLLIUM_-_KUGEL_1.JPG)

A hollow beryllium sphere used in a [gyrocompass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyrocompass "Gyrocompass") of the [Boeing B-52 Stratofortress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_B-52_Stratofortress "Boeing B-52 Stratofortress") aircraft[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-121)

Beryllium is non-magnetic. Therefore, tools fabricated out of beryllium-based materials are used by naval or military [explosive ordnance disposal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explosive_ordnance_disposal "Explosive ordnance disposal") teams for work on or near [naval mines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_mine "Naval mine"), since these mines commonly have [magnetic fuzes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuze "Fuze").[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-122) They are also found in maintenance and construction materials near [magnetic resonance imaging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_resonance_imaging "Magnetic resonance imaging") (MRI) machines because of the high magnetic fields generated.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-123)

### Nuclear applications

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beryllium&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Nuclear applications")]

High purity beryllium can be used in nuclear reactors as a moderator,[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-124) reflector, or as cladding on fuel elements.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-125)[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-126) Thin plates or foils of beryllium are sometimes used in [nuclear weapon designs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapon_design "Nuclear weapon design") as the very outer layer of the [plutonium pits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plutonium_pit "Plutonium pit") in the primary stages of [thermonuclear bombs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermonuclear_bomb "Thermonuclear bomb"), placed to surround the [fissile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fissile "Fissile") material. These layers of beryllium are good "pushers" for the [implosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Implosion_(mechanical_process) "Implosion (mechanical process)") of the [plutonium-239](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plutonium-239 "Plutonium-239"), and they are good [neutron reflectors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_reflector "Neutron reflector"), just as in beryllium-moderated [nuclear reactors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_reactor "Nuclear reactor").[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-weapons-127)

Beryllium is commonly used in some [neutron sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_source "Neutron source") in laboratory devices in which relatively few neutrons are needed (rather than having to use a nuclear reactor or a [particle accelerator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particle_accelerator "Particle accelerator")-powered [neutron generator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_generator "Neutron generator")). For this purpose, beryllium-9 is mixed with a source of alpha particles such as [polonium-210](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polonium-210 "Polonium-210"), [radium-226](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radium-226 "Radium-226"), [plutonium-238](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plutonium-238 "Plutonium-238"), or [americium-241](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americium-241 "Americium-241").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-NRC-2010-27) In the nuclear reaction that occurs, a beryllium nucleus is [transmuted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_transmutation "Nuclear transmutation") into carbon-12, and one free neutron is emitted, traveling in about the same direction as the alpha particle was heading. Such [alpha decay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_decay "Alpha decay")-driven beryllium neutron sources, named ["urchin"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulated_neutron_initiator "Modulated neutron initiator") neutron initiators, were used in some early [atomic bombs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_bomb "Atomic bomb").[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-weapons-127) Neutron sources in which beryllium is bombarded with [gamma rays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_ray "Gamma ray") from a [gamma decay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_decay "Gamma decay") radioisotope are also used to produce laboratory neutrons.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-Byrne-2011-26)

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/57/CANDU_fuel_bundles.jpg/500px-CANDU_fuel_bundles.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CANDU_fuel_bundles.jpg)

Two CANDU fuel bundles: Each about 50 cm in length and 10 cm in diameter. Notice the small appendages on the fuel clad surfaces

Beryllium is used in fuel fabrication for [CANDU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CANDU "CANDU") reactors. The fuel elements have small appendages that are resistance brazed to the fuel cladding using an induction brazing process with Be as the braze filler material. Bearing pads are brazed in place to prevent contact between the fuel bundle and the pressure tube containing it, and inter-element spacer pads are brazed on to prevent element to element contact.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-128)

Beryllium is used at the [Joint European Torus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_European_Torus "Joint European Torus")[nuclear-fusion research laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fusion "Nuclear fusion"), and it will be used in the more advanced [ITER](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITER "ITER") to condition the components which face the plasma.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-129) Beryllium has been proposed as a [cladding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cladding_(nuclear_fuel) "Cladding (nuclear fuel)") material for [nuclear fuel rods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fuel_rod "Nuclear fuel rod"), because of its good combination of mechanical, chemical, and nuclear properties.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-Behrens-2003-21)[Beryllium fluoride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_fluoride "Beryllium fluoride") is one of the constituent salts of the eutectic salt mixture [FLiBe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FLiBe "FLiBe"), which is used as a solvent, moderator and coolant in many hypothetical [molten salt reactor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molten_salt_reactor "Molten salt reactor") designs, including the [liquid fluoride thorium reactor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_fluoride_thorium_reactor "Liquid fluoride thorium reactor") (LFTR).[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-130)

### Acoustics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beryllium&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Acoustics")]

The low weight and high rigidity of beryllium make it useful as a material for high-frequency [speaker drivers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaker_driver "Speaker driver"). Because beryllium is expensive (many times more than [titanium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titanium "Titanium")), hard to shape due to its brittleness, and toxic if mishandled, beryllium [tweeters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tweeter "Tweeter") are limited to high-end home,[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-131)[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-132)[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-133)[pro audio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro_audio "Pro audio"), and [public address](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_address "Public address") applications.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-134)[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-135) Some high-fidelity products have been fraudulently claimed to be made of the material.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-136)

Beryllium was used for [cantilevers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantilever "Cantilever") in high-performance [phonograph cartridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_cartridge "Magnetic cartridge") styli, where its extreme stiffness and low density allowed for tracking weights to be reduced to 1 gram while still tracking high frequency passages with minimal distortion.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-137)

In sound amplification systems, the speed at which sound travels directly affects the resonant frequency of the [amplifier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amplifier "Amplifier"), thereby influencing the range of audible high-frequency sounds. Beryllium stands out due to its exceptionally high speed of sound propagation compared to other metals.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-138) This unique property allows beryllium to achieve higher resonant frequencies, making it an ideal material for use as a [diaphragm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diaphragm_(acoustics) "Diaphragm (acoustics)") in high-quality loudspeakers.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-139)

### Electronics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beryllium&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Electronics")]

Beryllium is a [p-type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-type_semiconductor "P-type semiconductor")[dopant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dopant "Dopant") in [III-V compound semiconductors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_semiconductor_materials "List of semiconductor materials"). It is widely used in materials such as [GaAs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium_arsenide "Gallium arsenide"), [AlGaAs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AlGaAs "AlGaAs"), [InGaAs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/InGaAs "InGaAs") and [InAlAs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/InAlAs "InAlAs") grown by [molecular-beam epitaxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molecular-beam_epitaxy "Molecular-beam epitaxy") (MBE).[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-140) Cross-rolled beryllium sheet is an excellent structural support for [printed circuit boards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printed_circuit_board "Printed circuit board") in [surface-mount technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-mount_technology "Surface-mount technology"). In critical electronic applications, beryllium is both a structural support and [heat sink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_sink "Heat sink"). The application also requires a coefficient of [thermal expansion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermal_expansion "Thermal expansion") that is well matched to the alumina and [polyimide-glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass-reinforced_plastic "Glass-reinforced plastic")[substrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Substrate_(materials_science) "Substrate (materials science)"). The beryllium-beryllium oxide [composite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metal_matrix_composite "Metal matrix composite") "[E-Materials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E-Material "E-Material")" have been specially designed for these electronic applications and have the additional advantage that the thermal expansion coefficient can be tailored to match diverse substrate materials.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-Behrens-2003-21)

[Beryllium oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium_oxide "Beryllium oxide") is useful for many applications that require the combined properties of an [electrical insulator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_insulator "Electrical insulator") and an excellent heat conductor, with high strength and hardness and a very high melting point. Beryllium oxide is frequently used as an insulator base plate in [high-power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_semiconductor_device "Power semiconductor device")[transistors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transistor "Transistor") in [radio frequency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_frequency "Radio frequency")[transmitters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transmitter "Transmitter") for telecommunications. Beryllium oxide is being studied for use in increasing the [thermal conductivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermal_conductivity "Thermal conductivity") of [uranium dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uranium_dioxide "Uranium dioxide")[nuclear fuel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fuel "Nuclear fuel") pellets.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-141) Beryllium compounds were used in [fluorescent lighting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluorescent_light "Fluorescent light") tubes, but this use was discontinued because of the disease [berylliosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berylliosis "Berylliosis") which developed in the workers who were making the tubes.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-142)

### Medical applications

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beryllium&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Medical applications")]

Beryllium is a component of several [dental alloys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dental_material "Dental material").[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-143)[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-ElshahawyWatanabe2014-144) In addition to standard X-ray equipment mentioned in [Beryllium §Radiation windows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#Radiation_windows), in medical imaging equipment, such as CT scanners and mammography machines, beryllium's strength and light weight enhance durability and performance.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-145) Beryllium is used in analytical equipment for blood, HIV, and other diseases.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-146) Beryllium alloys are used in surgical instruments, optical mirrors, and laser systems for medical treatments.[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-147)[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-148)

### Biological effects

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beryllium&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Biological effects")]

Approximately 35 micrograms of beryllium is found in the average human body, an amount not considered harmful.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEmsley200157-150) Beryllium is chemically similar to [magnesium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnesium "Magnesium") and therefore can displace it from [enzymes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enzyme "Enzyme"), which causes them to malfunction.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEmsley200157-150) Because Be 2+ is a highly charged and small ion, it can easily get into many tissues and cells, where it specifically targets cell nuclei, inhibiting many enzymes, including those used for synthesizing DNA. Its toxicity is exacerbated by the fact that the body has no means to control beryllium levels, and once inside the body, beryllium cannot be removed.[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-Venugopal-151)

### Inhalation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beryllium&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Inhalation")]

Chronic beryllium disease (CBD), or [berylliosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berylliosis "Berylliosis"), is a [pulmonary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulmonary "Pulmonary") and [systemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systemic_circulation "Systemic circulation")[granulomatous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granuloma "Granuloma") disease caused by inhalation of dust or fumes contaminated with beryllium; either large amounts over a short time or small amounts over a long time can lead to this ailment. Symptoms of the disease can take up to five years to develop; about a third of patients with it die and the survivors are left disabled.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEmsley200157-150) The [International Agency for Research on Cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Agency_for_Research_on_Cancer "International Agency for Research on Cancer") (IARC) lists beryllium and beryllium compounds as [Category 1 carcinogens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_IARC_Group_1_carcinogens "List of IARC Group 1 carcinogens").[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-152)

### Occupational exposure

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beryllium&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Occupational exposure")]

In the US, the [Occupational Safety and Health Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occupational_Safety_and_Health_Administration "Occupational Safety and Health Administration") (OSHA) has designated a [permissible exposure limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permissible_exposure_limit "Permissible exposure limit") (PEL) for beryllium and beryllium compounds of 0.2 μg/m 3 as an 8-hour time-weighted average (TWA) and 2.0 μg/m 3 as a [short-term exposure limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short-term_exposure_limit "Short-term exposure limit") over a sampling period of 15 minutes. The [National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institute_for_Occupational_Safety_and_Health "National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health") (NIOSH) has set a [recommended exposure limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recommended_exposure_limit "Recommended exposure limit") (REL) upper-bound threshold of 0.5 μg/m 3. The [IDLH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IDLH "IDLH") (immediately dangerous to life and health) value is 4 mg/m 3.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-153) The toxicity of beryllium is on par with other toxic metalloids/metals, such as [arsenic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsenic "Arsenic") and [mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(element) "Mercury (element)").[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-154)[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-155)

Exposure to beryllium in the workplace can lead to a sensitized immune response, and over time development of [berylliosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berylliosis "Berylliosis").[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-cdc.gov-156) NIOSH in the United States researches these effects in collaboration with a major manufacturer of beryllium products. NIOSH also conducts genetic research on sensitization and CBD, independently of this collaboration.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-cdc.gov-156)

Acute beryllium disease in the form of [chemical pneumonitis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_pneumonitis "Chemical pneumonitis") was first reported in Europe in 1933 and in the United States in 1943. A survey found that about 5% of workers in plants manufacturing [fluorescent lamps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluorescent_lamp "Fluorescent lamp") in 1949 in the United States had beryllium-related lung diseases.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEmsley20015-157) Chronic berylliosis resembles [sarcoidosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarcoidosis "Sarcoidosis") in many respects, and the [differential diagnosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_diagnosis "Differential diagnosis") is often difficult. It killed some early workers in nuclear weapons design, such as [Herbert L. Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_L._Anderson "Herbert L. Anderson").[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-158)

Beryllium may be found in coal slag. When the slag is formulated into an abrasive agent for blasting paint and rust from hard surfaces, the beryllium can become airborne and become a source of exposure.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-shapiro-159)

Although the use of beryllium compounds in fluorescent lighting tubes was discontinued in 1949, potential for exposure to beryllium exists in the nuclear and aerospace industries, in the refining of beryllium metal and the melting of beryllium-containing alloys, in the manufacturing of electronic devices, and in the handling of other beryllium-containing material.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-160)

### Detection

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beryllium&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: Detection")]

Early researchers undertook the highly hazardous practice of identifying beryllium and its various compounds from its sweet taste. A modern test for beryllium in air and on surfaces has been developed and published as an international voluntary consensus standard, ASTM D7202. The procedure uses dilute [ammonium bifluoride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammonium_bifluoride "Ammonium bifluoride") for dissolution and fluorescence detection with beryllium bound to sulfonated hydroxybenzoquinoline, allowing up to 100 times more sensitive detection than the recommended limit for beryllium concentration in the workplace. Fluorescence increases with increasing beryllium concentration. The new procedure has been successfully tested on a variety of surfaces and is effective for the dissolution and detection of refractory beryllium oxide and siliceous beryllium in minute concentrations (ASTM D7458).[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-161)[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-162) The NIOSH Manual of Analytical Methods contains methods for measuring occupational exposures to beryllium.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_note-163)

101.   [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium#cite_ref-103)Klaproth, Martin Heinrich, _Beitrage zur Chemischen Kenntniss der Mineralkörper_ (Contribution to the chemical knowledge of mineral substances), vol. 3, (Berlin, (Germany): Heinrich August Rottmann, 1802), [pages 78–79](https://books.google.com/books?id=8A8KAAAAIAAJ&pg=PA78)[Archived](https://web.archive.org/web/20160426233710/https://books.google.com/books?id=8A8KAAAAIAAJ&pg=PA78) 26 April 2016 at the [Wayback Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayback_Machine "Wayback Machine"): "Als Vauquelin der von ihm im Beryll und Smaragd entdeckten neuen Erde, wegen ihrer Eigenschaft, süsse Mittelsalze zu bilden, den Namen _Glykine_, _Süsserde_, beilegte, erwartete er wohl nicht, dass sich bald nachher eine anderweitige Erde finden würde, welche mit völlig gleichem Rechte Anspruch an diesen Namen machen können. Um daher keine Verwechselung derselben mit der Yttererde zu veranlassen, würde es vielleicht gerathen seyn, jenen Namen _Glykine_ aufzugeben, und durch Beryllerde (_Beryllina_) zu ersetzen; welche Namensveränderung auch bereits vom Hrn. Prof. Link, und zwar aus dem Grunde empfohlen worden, weil schon ein Pflanzengeschlecht _Glycine_ vorhanden ist." (When Vauquelin conferred – on account of its property of forming sweet salts – the name _glycine_, _sweet-earth_, on the new earth that had been found by him in beryl and smaragd, he certainly didn't expect that soon thereafter another earth would be found which with fully equal right could claim this name. Therefore, in order to avoid confusion of it with yttria-earth, it would perhaps be advisable to abandon this name _glycine_ and replace it with beryl-earth (_beryllina_); which name change was also recommended by Prof. Link, and for the reason that a genus of plants, _Glycine_, already exists.)

Fluorine is a chemical element; it has the symbol F and atomic number 9. It is the lightest halogen and exists at standard conditions as pale yellow diatomic gas. Fluorine is extremely reactive as it reacts with all other elements except for the light noble gases. Fluorine in its elemental form is highly toxic.

Among the elements, fluorine ranks 24th in cosmic abundance and 13th in crustal abundance. Fluorite, the primary mineral source of fluorine, which gave the element its name, was first described in 1529; as it was added to metal ores to lower their melting points for smelting, the Latin verb fluo meaning 'to flow' gave the mineral its name. Proposed as an element in 1810, fluorine proved difficult and dangerous to separate from its compounds, and several early experimenters died or sustained injuries from their attempts. Only in 1886 did French chemist Henri Moissan isolate elemental fluorine using low-temperature electrolysis, a process still employed for modern production. Industrial production of fluorine gas for uranium enrichment, its largest application, began during the Manhattan Project in World War II.

Owing to the expense of refining pure fluorine, most commercial applications use fluorine compounds, with about half of mined fluorite used in steelmaking. The rest of the fluorite is converted into hydrogen fluoride en route to various organic fluorides, or into cryolite, which plays a key role in aluminium refining. The carbon–fluorine bond is usually very stable. Organofluorine compounds are widely used as refrigerants, electrical insulation, and PTFE (Teflon). Pharmaceuticals such as atorvastatin and fluoxetine contain C−F bonds. The fluoride ion from dissolved fluoride salts inhibits dental cavities and so finds use in toothpaste and water fluoridation. Global fluorochemical sales amount to more than US$15 billion a year.

Fluorocarbon gases are generally greenhouse gases with global-warming potentials 100 to 23,500 times that of carbon dioxide, and SF6 has the highest global warming potential of any known substance. Organofluorine compounds often persist in the environment due to the strength of the carbon–fluorine bond. Fluorine has no known metabolic role in mammals, but a few plants and marine sponges synthesize organofluorine poisons (most often monofluoroacetates) that help deter predation.[16]

Characteristicsedit
Electron configurationedit

Fluorine atoms have nine electrons, one fewer than neon, and electron configuration 1s22s22p5: two electrons in a filled inner shell and seven in an outer shell requiring one more to be filled. The outer electrons are ineffective at nuclear shielding, and experience a high effective nuclear charge of 9 − 2 = 7; this affects the atom's physical properties.[3]

Fluorine's first ionization energy is third-highest among all elements, behind helium and neon,[17] which complicates the removal of electrons from neutral fluorine atoms. It also has a high electron affinity, second only to chlorine,[18] and tends to capture an electron to become isoelectronic with the noble gas neon;[3] it has the highest electronegativity of any reactive element.[19] Fluorine atoms have a small covalent radius of around 60 picometers, similar to those of its period neighbors oxygen and neon.[20][21][note 1]

Reactivityedit
External videos
 Bright flames during fluorine reactions
 Fluorine reacting with caesium

The bond energy of difluorine is much lower than that of either Cl2 or Br2 and similar to the easily cleaved peroxide bond; this, along with high electronegativity, accounts for fluorine's easy dissociation, high reactivity, and strong bonds to non-fluorine atoms.[22][23] Conversely, bonds to other atoms are very strong because of fluorine's high electronegativity. Unreactive substances like powdered steel, glass fragments, and asbestos fibers react quickly with cold fluorine gas; wood and water spontaneously combust under a fluorine jet.[5][24]

Reactions of elemental fluorine with metals require varying conditions. Alkali metals cause explosions and alkaline earth metals display vigorous activity in bulk; to prevent passivation from the formation of metal fluoride layers, most other metals such as aluminium and iron must be powdered,[22] and noble metals require pure fluorine gas at 300–450 °C (572–842 °F).[25] Some solid nonmetals (sulfur, phosphorus) react vigorously in liquid fluorine.[26] Hydrogen sulfide[26] and sulfur dioxide[27] combine readily with fluorine, the latter sometimes explosively; sulfuric acid exhibits much less activity, requiring elevated temperatures.[28]

Hydrogen, like some of the alkali metals, reacts explosively with fluorine.[29] Carbon, as lamp black, reacts at room temperature to yield tetrafluoromethane. Graphite combines with fluorine above 400 °C (752 °F) to produce non-stoichiometric carbon monofluoride; higher temperatures generate gaseous fluorocarbons, sometimes with explosions.[30] Carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide react at or just above room temperature,[31] whereas paraffins and other organic chemicals generate strong reactions:[32] even completely substituted haloalkanes such as carbon tetrachloride, normally incombustible, may explode.[33] Although nitrogen trifluoride is stable, nitrogen requires an electric discharge at elevated temperatures for reaction with fluorine to occur, due to the very strong triple bond in elemental nitrogen;[34] ammonia may react explosively.[35][36] Oxygen does not combine with fluorine under ambient conditions, but can be made to react using electric discharge at low temperatures and pressures; the products tend to disintegrate into their constituent elements when heated.[37][38][39] Heavier halogens[40] react readily with fluorine as does the noble gas radon;[41] of the other noble gases, only xenon and krypton react, and only under special conditions.[42] Argon does not react with fluorine gas; however, it does form a compound with fluorine, argon fluorohydride.

Phasesedit
Main article: Phases of fluorine
Animation showing the crystal structure of β-fluorine. F2 molecules on the faces of the unit cell have rotations constrained to a plane, while those in the corners can rotate freely.

At room temperature, fluorine is a gas of diatomic molecules,[5] pale yellow when pure (sometimes described as yellow-green).[43] It has a characteristic halogen-like pungent and biting odor detectable at 20 ppb.[44] Fluorine condenses into a bright yellow liquid at −188 °C (−306.4 °F; 85.1 K), a transition temperature similar to those of oxygen and nitrogen.[45]

Fluorine has two solid forms, α- and β-fluorine. The latter crystallizes at −220 °C (−364.0 °F; 53.1 K) and is transparent and soft, with the same disordered cubic structure of freshly crystallized solid oxygen,[45][note 2] unlike the orthorhombic systems of other solid halogens.[47][48] Further cooling to −228 °C (−378.4 °F; 45.1 K) induces a phase transition into opaque and hard α-fluorine, which has a monoclinic structure with dense, angled layers of molecules. The transition from β- to α-fluorine is more exothermic than the condensation of fluorine, and can be violent.[47][48]

Isotopesedit
Main article: Isotopes of fluorine

Natural fluorine consists entirely of the stable isotope 19F. It has a high magnetogyric ratio[50] and exceptional sensitivity to magnetic fields; because it is also the only isotope, it is highly suited for NMR and use in magnetic resonance imaging.[51] Eighteen radioisotopes with mass numbers 13–31 have been synthesized, of which 18F is the most stable with a half-life of 109.734 minutes.[15][52] 18F is a natural trace radioisotope produced by cosmic ray spallation of atmospheric argon as well as by reaction of protons with natural oxygen: 18O + p → 18F + n.[53] Other radioisotopes have half-lives less than 70 seconds; most decay in less than half a second. The isotopes 17F and 18F undergo β+ decay and electron capture, lighter isotopes decay by proton emission, and those heavier than 19F undergo β− decay (the heaviest ones with delayed neutron emission). Two metastable isomers of fluorine are known, 18mF, with a half-life of 162(7) nanoseconds, and 26mF, with a half-life of 2.2(1) milliseconds.[54]

Among the lighter elements, fluorine's abundance value of 400 ppb (parts per billion) – 24th among elements in the universe – is exceptionally low: other elements from carbon to magnesium are twenty or more times as common.[56] This is because stellar nucleosynthesis processes bypass fluorine, and any fluorine atoms otherwise created have high nuclear cross sections, allowing collisions with hydrogen or helium to generate oxygen or neon respectively.[56][57]

Beyond this transient existence, three explanations have been proposed for the presence of fluorine:[56][58]

during type II supernovae, bombardment of neon atoms by neutrinos could transmute them to fluorine;
the solar wind of Wolf–Rayet stars could blow fluorine away from any hydrogen or helium atoms; or
fluorine is borne out on convection currents arising from fusion in asymptotic giant branch stars.
Earthedit
See also: List of countries by fluorite production

Fluorine is the 13th most abundant element in Earth's crust at 600–700 ppm (parts per million) by mass.[59] Though believed not to occur naturally, elemental fluorine has been shown to be present as an occlusion in antozonite, a variant of fluorite.[60] Most fluorine exists as fluoride-containing minerals. Fluorite, fluorapatite and cryolite are the most industrially significant.[59][61] Fluorite (CaF2), also known as fluorspar, abundant worldwide, is the main source of fluoride, and hence fluorine. China and Mexico are the major suppliers.[61][62][63][64][65] Fluorapatite (Ca5(PO4)3F), which contains most of the world's fluoride, is an inadvertent source of fluoride as a byproduct of fertilizer production.[61] Cryolite (Na3AlF6), used in the production of aluminium, is the most fluorine-rich mineral. Economically viable natural sources of cryolite have been exhausted, and most is now synthesized commercially.[61]

Fluorite: Pink globular mass with crystal facets
 
Fluorapatite: Long, prismatic crystal, dull in lustre, protruding, at an angle, from matrix of aggregate-like rock
 
Cryolite: A parallelogram-shaped outline with diatomic molecules arranged in two layers

Other minerals such as topaz contain fluorine. Fluorides, unlike other halides, are insoluble and do not occur in commercially favorable concentrations in saline waters.[61] Trace quantities of organofluorines of uncertain origin have been detected in volcanic eruptions and geothermal springs.[66] The existence of gaseous fluorine in crystals, suggested by the smell of crushed antozonite, is contentious;[67][60] a 2012 study reported the presence of 0.04% F2 by weight in antozonite, attributing these inclusions to radiation from the presence of tiny amounts of uranium.[60]

Historyedit
Main article: History of fluorine
Early discoveriesedit
Steelmaking illustration from De re metallica

In 1529, Georgius Agricola described fluorite as an additive used to lower the melting point of metals during smelting.[68][69][note 3] He penned the Latin word fluorēs (fluor, flow) for fluorite rocks. The name later evolved into fluorspar (still commonly used) and then fluorite.[62][73][74] The composition of fluorite was later determined to be calcium difluoride.[75]

Hydrofluoric acid was used in glass etching from 1720 onward.[note 4] Andreas Sigismund Marggraf first characterized it in 1764 when he heated fluorite with sulfuric acid, and the resulting solution corroded its glass container.[77][78] Swedish chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele repeated the experiment in 1771, and named the acidic product fluss-spats-syran (fluorspar acid).[78][79] In 1810, the French physicist André-Marie Ampère suggested that hydrogen and an element analogous to chlorine constituted hydrofluoric acid.[80] He also proposed in a letter to Sir Humphry Davy dated August 26, 1812 that this then-unknown substance may be named fluorine from fluoric compounds and the -ine suffix of other halogens.[81][82] This word, often with modifications, is used in most European languages; however, Greek, Russian, and some others, following Ampère's later suggestion, use the name ftor or derivatives, from the Greek φθόριος (phthorios, destructive).[83] The New Latin name fluorum gave the element its current symbol F; Fl was used in early papers.[84][note 5]

Isolationedit
1887 drawing of Moissan's apparatus

Initial studies on fluorine were so dangerous that several 19th-century experimenters were deemed "fluorine martyrs" after misfortunes with hydrofluoric acid.[note 6] Isolation of elemental fluorine was hindered by the extreme corrosiveness of both elemental fluorine itself and hydrogen fluoride, as well as the lack of a simple and suitable electrolyte.[75][85] Edmond Frémy postulated that electrolysis of pure hydrogen fluoride to generate fluorine was feasible and devised a method to produce anhydrous samples from acidified potassium bifluoride; instead, he discovered that the resulting (dry) hydrogen fluoride did not conduct electricity.[75][85][86] Frémy's former student Henri Moissan persevered, and after much trial and error found that a mixture of potassium bifluoride and dry hydrogen fluoride was a conductor, enabling electrolysis. To prevent rapid corrosion of the platinum in his electrochemical cells, he cooled the reaction to extremely low temperatures in a special bath and forged cells from a more resistant mixture of platinum and iridium, and used fluorite stoppers.[85][87] In 1886, after 74 years of effort by many chemists, Moissan isolated elemental fluorine.[86][88]

In 1906, two months before his death, Moissan received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry,[89] with the following citation:[85]

[I]n recognition of the great services rendered by him in his investigation and isolation of the element fluorine ... The whole world has admired the great experimental skill with which you have studied that savage beast among the elements.[note 7]

Later usesedit
An ampoule of uranium hexafluoride

The Frigidaire division of General Motors (GM) experimented with chlorofluorocarbon refrigerants in the late 1920s, and Kinetic Chemicals was formed as a joint venture between GM and DuPont in 1930 hoping to market Freon-12 (CCl2F2) as one such refrigerant. It replaced earlier and more toxic compounds, increased demand for kitchen refrigerators, and became profitable; by 1949 DuPont had bought out Kinetic and marketed several other Freon compounds.[78][90][91][92] Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE, Teflon) was serendipitously discovered in 1938 by Roy J. Plunkett while working on refrigerants at Kinetic, and its superlative chemical and thermal resistance lent it to accelerated commercialization and mass production by 1941.[78][90][91]

Large-scale production of elemental fluorine began during World War II. Germany used high-temperature electrolysis to make tons of the planned incendiary chlorine trifluoride[93] and the Manhattan Project used huge quantities to produce uranium hexafluoride for uranium enrichment. Since UF6 is as corrosive as fluorine, gaseous diffusion plants required special materials: nickel for membranes, fluoropolymers for seals, and liquid fluorocarbons as coolants and lubricants. This burgeoning nuclear industry later drove post-war fluorochemical development.[94]

Compoundsedit
Main article: Fluorine compounds

Fluorine has a rich chemistry, encompassing organic and inorganic domains. It combines with metals, nonmetals, metalloids, and most noble gases.[95] Fluorine's high electron affinity results in a preference for ionic bonding; when it forms covalent bonds, these are polar, and almost always single.[96][97][note 8]

Oxidation statesedit

In compounds, fluorine almost exclusively assumes an oxidation state of −1. Fluorine in F2 is defined to have oxidation state 0. The unstable species F2− and F3−, which decompose at around 40 K (−233.2 °C; −387.7 °F), have intermediate oxidation states;[98] F4+ and a few related species are predicted to be stable.[99]

Metalsedit
See also: Fluoride volatility

Alkali metals form ionic and highly soluble monofluorides; these have the cubic arrangement of sodium chloride and analogous chlorides.[100][101] Alkaline earth difluorides possess strong ionic bonds but are insoluble in water,[84] with the exception of beryllium difluoride, which also exhibits some covalent character and has a quartz-like structure.[102] Rare earth elements and many other metals form mostly ionic trifluorides.[103][104][105]

Covalent bonding first comes to prominence in the tetrafluorides: those of zirconium, hafnium[106][107] and several actinides[108] are ionic with high melting points,[109][note 9] while those of titanium,[112] vanadium,[113] and niobium are polymeric,[114] melting or decomposing at no more than 350 °C (662 °F).[115] Pentafluorides continue this trend with their linear polymers and oligomeric complexes.[116][117][118] Thirteen metal hexafluorides are known,[note 10] all octahedral, and are mostly volatile solids but for liquid MoF6 and ReF6, and gaseous WF6.[119][120][121] Rhenium heptafluoride, the only characterized metal heptafluoride, is a low-melting molecular solid with pentagonal bipyramidal molecular geometry.[122] Gold heptafluoride is a low-temperature complex of molecular F2 with NPA calculations indicating that the fluorine in the F2 ligand is nearly neutral while those in the AuF5 portion of the molecule have strong negative partial charges. This is consistent with the F2 ligand representing fluorine in the zero oxidation state.[123] Metal fluorides with more fluorine atoms are particularly reactive.[124]
